exp.5:18:
Gideon goes into his house and prepares a young goat and unleavened cakes made with an ephah of flour (about twenty liters, though the exact measure is debated). He puts the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot, and takes it out to the visitor, who is waiting for him under an oak, a sturdy kind of tree.

Gideon is a young Israelite whom the angel of the Lord has just called to deliver Israel from the Midianites. He hesitates and asks for a sign so that he can be sure God is speaking to him. That is why he prepares this offering, which was an act of hospitality and worship. Then the fire from the rock consumes the food, and this confirms to him that the message comes from God.

For today: when God calls you to something great and you have doubts, do not stay frozen. Bring Him honestly what you have, even if it seems little, and let Him confirm and guide the next step.
exp.4:14:
The explanation says that the princes of Issachar went with Deborah to the war. Barak also went down on foot into the valley to fight, without horses or chariots. On the other hand, among the divisions of Reuben there were great thoughts of heart, that is, many doubts and deliberations, but apparently they did not go out to fight.

This is part of the song of Deborah and Barak, after they defeated the army of Sisera. They praise God and remember who helped and who stayed behind. Reuben appears as a tribe that stayed thinking for a long time, but without acting. Some scholars understand the text this way; others see it as a milder rebuke.

For today: thinking and praying before deciding is good, but we should not remain in mere doubts when God calls us to serve. Let us ask for courage to take the concrete step.
exp.12:15:
Here the angel of the LORD refuses the food that Manoah offers him. He tells him that, even if Manoah insists on holding him back, he will not eat his bread. But if Manoah wishes to offer a burnt offering, a whole offering burned completely, he must offer it to the LORD. The text makes clear that Manoah still did not understand that this visitor was an angel of the LORD.

Manoah and his wife had no children. The angel announced to them that they would have a son, Samson, set apart for God from his birth. Manoah, out of his custom of hospitality, wanted to honor the visitor, without knowing who he was. The angel directs attention toward God, not toward himself.

For today: when God acts in our lives, let us give Him gratitude and worship. And let us be attentive, because sometimes God works in the midst of everyday life, and we are slow to recognize Him.
exp.19:43:
This verse says that in that battle eighteen thousand men of the tribe of Benjamin died, and all of them were trained fighters, men of valour. The word "pursue" means chasing someone without giving them any rest, and "trample" means stamping down.

The book of Judges is a narrative, and here it is not God speaking but the narrator. It tells of the war between the tribes of Israel and Benjamin, whose people protected the guilty men responsible for a terrible crime in Gibeah instead of handing them over to justice. The text does not celebrate the slaughter. Rather, it shows a people broken, who "did what was right in their own eyes." When the fear of God is lost, uncorrected sin drags everyone into tragedy.

For today: do not excuse or hide wrongdoing in order to protect your own. Correcting it in time, with humility and truth, keeps a small fault from ending in much greater harm.
exp.12:17:
Here the angel answers with another question: "Why askest thou thus after my name, seeing it is secret?" He says that his name is "secret." In other versions it is rendered "wonderful" or "marvelous." That is, it is a name that lies beyond what Manoah can understand.

Manoah and his wife received the promise of a son, Samson. Manoah, not knowing that he was speaking with an angel, wanted to know his name so that he could honor him when the promise was fulfilled. The angel redirects the attention toward the Lord, to whom the sacrifice was to be offered. Then he ascends in the flame of the altar, and only then does Manoah understand who he was.

Today, God does not always answer all our questions or reveal all his plans. We can trust that he is wonderful and faithful, and direct our gratitude and honor to God, not to the messengers or to the blessings.
exp.15:13:
Here, the account tells how Delilah once again got the secret of Samson's strength out of him, and once again he deceived her. She fastened the pin (a peg that held the loom in place) with Samson's hair woven into the cloth, and cried out that the Philistines were upon him. He awoke and pulled away the pin and the whole web.

The narrator recounts this third attempt by Delilah. The Philistine lords had asked her to discover the source of Samson's strength, and their spies waited in hiding. Samson was playing with her, but he was already very close to revealing the truth, since he had mentioned his hair.

For today: playing near danger usually ends badly. Samson believed he could control the situation, but each step brought him closer to his fall. It is wise to move away quickly from what tempts us, rather than testing how far we can go.
exp.19:17:
The Israelites got up and went to the house of God, which was probably Bethel, and asked him: "Which of us shall go up first to the battle against Benjamin?" Asking God here means inquiring of him. He answered: "Judah shall go up first."

The Israelites are speaking, gathered to punish a terrible crime committed in Gibeah, a city of Benjamin. The Benjamites refused to hand over the guilty men. Before fighting, Israel asks God. He only tells them who goes to the front; he does not promise victory. In fact, in the verses that follow, Israel suffers defeats first.

For today: before making hard decisions, seek God's guidance in prayer. But do not confuse his direction with a guarantee that everything will be easy; sometimes he leads us by a path that requires patience and humility.
exp.17:22:
Here, Micah and his neighbors cry out to the men of Dan, who are walking away with his belongings. The Danites turn around and ask him with irony: "What is the matter with you, that you have gathered together a crowd?" The reference to "crying out" means shouting, and the old-fashioned spelling of "to" is simply the older form of the word.

The men of Dan had just stolen Micah's idols and taken his priest with them. Micah, together with his neighbors, pursues them. The Danites pretend not to understand, even though they know very well what they did. Shortly afterward they threaten him, and he is left with nothing. The book shows a time of disorder, when everyone did whatever seemed right to them.

For today: when our faith depends on things we can lose, such as possessions or people, it becomes fragile. Let us ask God to be our security, and to give us the honesty not to justify what we know is wrong.
exp.19:19:
The explanation says the Israelites went out to fight against the tribe of Benjamin and lined up for battle in front of Gibeah. "They drew up the battle line" means they took their places in ranks, ready to fight. "Men" are the men, the soldiers.

This is part of the account in the book of Judges, when Israel had no king and disorder reigned. A terrible injustice had happened in Gibeah, and the Benjamites protected the guilty instead of handing them over. So the tribes came together to punish the evil. They had consulted God, and He told them that Judah should go first. Even so, the next verse shows that they lost that day. This reminds us that being right in a cause does not guarantee an easy path.

For today: when you seek to do what is right and things go wrong, do not give up or doubt everything at once. Keep seeking God with humility, examine your heart, and move forward with patience.
exp.3:21:
What the passage says: Barak was pursuing Sisera, the commander of the enemy army. Jael came out to meet him and told him she would take him to the man he was looking for. Barak went into the tent and found Sisera dead, with the nail driven into his temple. The "nail" is a large peg used to secure the tent, and "lay" means that he was lying stretched out.

Context: The narrator tells the end of the battle between Israel and King Jabin of Canaan. The prophetess Deborah had announced that the honor of defeating Sisera would go to a woman (Judges 4:9). The verses that follow say that it was God who brought down Jabin. The text reports the event without approving or condemning Jael's methods, and some readers debate that point.

For today: God can keep his promises in ways we do not expect, and through people whom almost no one takes into account. Trust that he is at work, and ask him for courage and wisdom to act justly and faithfully wherever you are.
exp.8:6:
This verse tells how Jotham, on hearing that the people of Shechem had made Abimelech king, went up to the top of Mount Gerizim. From there he lifted up his voice and cried out, asking them to hear him. He said, "that God may hearken unto you," meaning: just as you listen to me, may God listen to you. The phrase "Hearken unto me" is a request to listen to me, and "ye men of Shechem" refers to the men, the leaders of the city.

Jotham speaks. He is Gideon's youngest son (also called Jerubbaal), the only one who survived when Abimelech killed his seventy brothers. From a high place, where his voice could carry far, he wants to denounce the injustice of crowning a murderer. He will do it through a fable about the trees.

For today: when we see someone in power acting wrongly, and others applaud, we can speak with courage and truth, without violence, trusting that God hears and judges with justice.
exp.5:20:
He says the angel of the Lord stretched out the staff he carried in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened bread with its tip. Then fire came up out of the rock and consumed everything. After that the angel left, and Gideon no longer saw him.

Gideon was a fearful Israelite, and his people were suffering under the oppression of Midian. The angel had told him that God would use him to deliver Israel. Gideon asked for a sign and prepared an offering. The fire confirmed that the message truly came from God. Some believe this angel represents God himself, since the text also calls him Jehovah; others see him as a special messenger.

For today: when God calls you to something that frightens you, you can bring your doubts to him honestly. He knows how to confirm his word and to give you the peace to obey.
exp.8:46:
This verse says that someone told Abimelech that all the people of the tower of Shechem had come together in one place. "Was told" means "they informed him." "Were gathered together" means that they had assembled, as we saw earlier, in the stronghold of the temple of Baal-berith.

Here no particular character speaks; only a fact is reported. Abimelech, who had come to power by violence, had already destroyed the city. Now he is told where his enemies have taken refuge. That information allows him to attack them all at once. The account shows the consequences of ambition and violence, and it fulfills the curse that Jotham had announced earlier.

For today: taking refuge in places or things that cannot save us, such as a false temple, is useless. Let us seek our security in God, not in power or in religion without true faith.
exp.10:13:
This verse says that Jephthah sent messengers once more to the king of the Ammonites. The phrase "sent messengers again" is the verse's own wording, and it means he sent them a second time. "Messengers" are people who speak on behalf of someone else. The verse is short, but it opens Jephthah's second response.

The Ammonite king had just claimed that Israel took his land when they came up out of Egypt. Jephthah, who was a judge of Israel, did not rush to fight. First he sent messengers to talk and clarify the facts. In the verses that follow he explains Israel's journey through the wilderness. In this way he tries to avoid a war, although in the end peace is not achieved.

For today: before responding in anger in a conflict, try to speak calmly and truthfully. Dialogue does not always resolve everything, but it shows wisdom and respect.
exp.15:8:
There were Philistine men hiding in a room of Delilah's house, waiting for their moment. She cried out, "Samson, the Philistines are upon you!" and he snapped the ropes with ease. Rods of green willow are flexible, and the tow is a very weak fiber that breaks as soon as it nears the fire. So the Philistines did not discover the secret of his strength.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Philistine lords had asked Delilah to find out why Samson was so strong. Samson gave her a false answer, and she tested it. Even so, he kept playing with her and with danger.

For today: do not play with whatever can pull you away from God. Samson escaped this time, but staying close to temptation was wearing him down. Get away quickly from what tempts you, and guard the relationships that lead you into dishonesty.
exp.5:3:
They camped against them and ruined the crops across the land, all the way to the city of Gaza in the southwest. They left nothing to eat, neither animals nor food. The phrase "camp" here means to set up camp, and the animals meant are donkeys.

It is the narrator of the book of Judges, who tells the story of Israel. Every time Israel planted, the invaders came and took everything. The text has already said that the people were suffering this oppression because they had done what was evil before God. That is why they lived hidden in caves. This suffering prepares the way for the people's cry to the LORD, and then for Gideon's call.

For today: when you feel that everything is running out and you have no way out, do not hide your need. Like Israel, you can cry out to God sincerely. He listens, even when the difficulties seem enormous.
exp.4:9:
This verse is an invitation to speak. It is addressed to three groups: those who ride on white asses (people of good standing, since the white or light-colored donkey was a distinguished mount), those who sit in judgment, and those who simply walk along the way. To all of them it says: speak, that is, tell what God has done.

The one singing is Deborah, together with Barak, after Israel's victory over the army of Sisera. Before this there was fear and injustice, and the roads were unsafe. Now, with the deliverance, everyone must proclaim the works of the LORD. Some details of the Hebrew text allow different interpretations.

For today: do not keep silent about what God has done in your life. Whatever your place, at work, at home, or on the road, tell with humility and gratitude how God has helped you.
exp.15:19:
Dalila wakes Samson with a cry: the Philistines are coming for him. He gets up confident, thinking he will escape as on other occasions. But he did not know something very serious: the Lord had already departed from him. The phrase in the source, "Se había de él apartado," means that God had already withdrawn.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. Samson was a Nazirite, set apart for God from his birth. He had revealed the secret of his hair to Delilah, and she betrayed him for money. The text does not say that his strength was in his hair as a kind of magic; the hair was the sign of his consecration, and that vow was already broken.

For today: let us not confuse past blessings with the presence of God. If we have played with what God has entrusted to us, we can become so used to sin that we fail to notice the danger. It is wise to guard our relationship with Him every day, and to remember that God still receives those who return to Him with humility.
exp.10:30:
Before going into battle, Jephthah makes a promise to God: whatever comes out of the door of his house to meet him when he returns victorious will belong to the Lord, and he will offer it up as a burnt offering, meaning an offering burned up completely.

Jephthah, a judge of Israel, speaks here as a warrior called to defend his people against the Ammonites. The text says that the Spirit of the Lord was already upon him, yet he still made this vow. It is not made clear whether he had in mind an animal or a person; scholars interpret this in different ways. What follows in the story is painful.

For today: before promising something to God, let us think calmly. God was already with Jephthah without any need for that vow; we should not bargain with Him or speak in haste.
exp.19:38:
The explanation says that the men of Israel pretended to retreat in the battle. The men of Benjamin pursued them, struck down about thirty men of Israel, and became filled with confidence. They thought: "Surely they are smitten down before us, as in the first battle." The phrase "smite and kill" means to strike down and leave some of them dead or lying on the ground. "Turned their backs" means that they turned around to flee.

Context: the one narrating is the author of the book of Judges. Israel was fighting against the tribe of Benjamin for having protected the guilty parties of a terrible crime in Gibeah. Earlier, Benjamin had won twice. Now Israel used a trap: an ambush and a signal of smoke. Benjamin trusted in their past victory and did not see the danger behind them.

For today: yesterday's success does not guarantee today's. If we defend what is wrong, sooner or later it collapses. Let us seek humility, and examine whether we stand on the side of justice.
exp.17:12:
These six hundred men of the tribe of Dan continued on their way from Kiriath-jearim. They passed through the hill country of Ephraim and arrived at the house of Micah, a man who had a shrine of his own.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The Danites were looking for a territory where they could settle. Five scouts had already passed by that house before and had seen the ephod (a garment used in worship), the household idols, and the carved image. Now the group draws near, and the account prepares what follows: they will take those objects. Judges shows a time of spiritual disorder.

For today: let us not trust a religion made to suit ourselves. Before we move forward with our plans, let us ask God to examine whether what we follow comes from Him or only from our own convenience.
exp.4:0:
That same day, Deborah and Barak, the son of Abinoam, sang a song together. "That day" refers to the day of Israel's great victory over its enemies. What follows is the song itself, which praises the LORD.

Deborah was a prophetess and judge in Israel, and Barak was the military leader who led the battle against the army of Sisera, captain of Jabin, the Canaanite king (Judges 4). After God gave them the victory, they both sang to give thanks. Many scholars regard this poem as one of the oldest texts in the Bible, though not all agree on its exact date.

When God helps us, it is good to pause and thank Him clearly and publicly, not only in silence. Telling what He has done encourages others to trust Him. Today you can write down, or share with someone, a recent answer to prayer.
exp.19:12:
The explanation says that the tribes of Israel asked Benjamin to hand over the wicked men of Gibeah, whom it calls "the children of Belial," an old expression meaning perverse people, without moral worth. They wanted to punish them with death to remove the evil from among the people. But the people of Benjamin refused to listen to their brothers.

Here the tribes of Israel speak together after the terrible crime committed in Gibeah against the concubine of a Levite. First they asked what had happened, and now they demand justice. Benjamin, instead of correcting the guilty, defended them, and that led to a war between brothers.

For today: when someone in our group, family, or church does something wrong, defending them out of loyalty only makes the harm worse. Truly loving someone includes acknowledging the wrong, seeking justice, and accepting correction with humility.
exp.10:23:
The verse says: "Wilt not thou possess that which Chemosh thy god giveth thee to possess? So whomsoever the Lord our God shall drive out from before us, them will we possess." The word "drive out" means "cast out" or "make to leave." "Possess" here means "to keep as one's own."

Jephthah, judge of Israel, is the one speaking. He sends a message to the king of the Ammonites, who claimed lands east of the Jordan. Jephthah argues that Israel received that land legitimately and occupied it for a long time without dispute. His argument uses the logic of the Ammonites themselves: each people honors what it believes its god has given it. Scholars note that Chemosh was the god of Moab; the Bible itself does not make clear why it attributes him to Ammon.

For today: before claiming something, it is wise to recognize what God has already given us and to give thanks for it, rather than living always fighting over what belongs to others.
exp.9:11:
This verse continues God's question to Israel. He reminds them that the Zidonians, the Amalekites, and the Maonites also oppressed them, and that when they cried out to God, He delivered them from their hand.

God speaks here, answering Israel's cry. The people said they were sorry, but they had served the Baals. God reminds them of his faithfulness in the past to show that their abandonment of him was unjust and ungrateful. His words that follow are harsh, but they aim to make their repentance sincere.

For today: let us not remember God only when there are problems. Let us recall the times he helped us and respond to him with gratitude and faithfulness, not only with words, but with a life that truly follows him.
exp.4:22:
It says that the angel of the Lord commands that Meroz and its people be cursed with a strong curse. The reason is that they did not help the Lord, that is, his people, in the battle against the mighty enemies. "Curse ye" means calling for punishment to fall; "inhabitants" are the people who lived there.

This comes from the Song of Deborah and Barak, after the victory over the army of Sisera. They speak of how the river Kishon helped bring about the victory. Meroz is a place whose location is not known for certain, and the Bible does not explain in detail what they failed to do. Their fault was staying out and not taking part when Israel was in danger. Then the song contrasts this with Jael, whom it blesses.

For today: do not confuse neutrality with prudence when God gives you a clear opportunity to help. Ask him today where you can serve, and take one concrete step, even a small one.
exp.18:10:
It says the group was already near Jebus, and that the day was almost over. The servant suggests to his master that they enter that city of the Jebusites to spend the night there. The phrase "declined" means the sun was already going down, and the word for the servant is the attendant who traveled with them.

The servant speaks for a Levite who was returning home with his concubine. They had lingered in Bethlehem, at the father-in-law's house, and left late. The servant thinks practically: find shelter before the darkness. Jebus is the old name of Jerusalem. His master rejects the idea because the city belonged to foreigners, and he prefers to reach Gibeah, where Israelites lived. That leads to a very painful story.

For today: when a decision seems sensible, stop to pray and seek counsel. Choosing out of pride, prejudice, or haste, without seeking God, can bring serious consequences.
exp.11:6:
This verse closes the story of Jephthah in a few words. It says he judged Israel for six years, that he died, and that he was buried in one of the cities of Gilead, his homeland. The phrase "the Gileadite" means he came from the region of Gilead, and "judged" here means that he governed and led the people, not only that he handed down verdicts.

The narrator tells this right after the conflict between Jephthah and the men of Ephraim, which ended in great tragedy. It is a sober summary, without praise. The Bible shows Jephthah with both light and shadow: a brave leader, but also rash, as seen in his earlier vow.

For today: our life will be brief, and in the end what matters is how we have treated others. Let us ask God for wisdom to resolve conflicts with peace and not with pride or violence.
exp.9:12:
It says that God reminds the Israelites that they abandoned him and worshiped other gods. That is why he declares to them: "I will deliver you no more."

God himself speaks here, answering the cry of Israel, which was suffering oppression from the Ammonites and the Philistines. He reminds them of the many times he rescued them, and yet they returned to idolatry. His words sound harsh, but they aim to shake them so that they recognize their sin. Then they confess and repent, and the account shows that God, moved by compassion, does not leave them entirely (v. 16).

For today: do not use God's kindness as an excuse for living far from him. If you have given your heart to other things, return to him sincerely, confess, and ask for his help.
exp.13:12:
Samson goes on with his wager at the wedding feast. He says that if the thirty young men cannot solve his riddle, they must give him thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothes for festive wear. They agree and ask him to put forth his riddle, that they may hear it.

Samson, a judge of Israel, speaks during the seven-day wedding banquet of his marriage to a Philistine woman. The thirty companions were Philistine guests. Samson uses the riddle as a game, but the account shows that the wager soon brings pressure, deception, and violence. The text does not justify every action of Samson; it only tells what happened.

For today: think before making wagers or promises lightly, even in jokes or celebrations. What seems like a game can hurt relationships and bring consequences you did not expect.
exp.18:6:
This verse tells how the Levite got up to leave, but his father-in-law urged him strongly to stay one more night. The word "urged" in the verse means he pressed him or pushed him with force. "Lodged there again" means that he spent the night in that house once more.

The Levite had gone to Bethlehem in Judah to bring back his concubine, who had left his side. Her father received him with great hospitality and, day after day, kept encouraging him to stay. Here the father-in-law speaks, and he seems to want to enjoy more time with his son-in-law and his daughter. The text does not say whether he had other reasons. What is clear is that these delays would end up making the journey start late.

For today: kindness is good, but it is wise to know when to say "it is time for me to go." Let us plan with wisdom and not let the pressure of others make us postpone what is important.
exp.19:28:
This verse says that the people of Israel set ambushes around Gibeah. An ambush is a group of soldiers hidden in wait, ready to attack by surprise. Gibeah was the city of the tribe of Benjamin where a terrible crime had taken place.

At this point, the writer of the book tells how Israel prepared its third attack against Benjamin. They had already lost two battles. This time they asked God, and He promised them victory. After receiving that answer, Israel made a plan with strategy, not only with strength.

For today: trusting God does not mean ceasing to think or to plan. We can ask Him for direction and then act with wisdom, effort and patience, knowing that the outcome is in His hands.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that the people of Israel did what displeases God, that is, they did evil in the sight of the Lord. The Lord is the name of God. To serve the Baals means to worship Baal, a Canaanite god, in his various local forms. The plural form is used because he was worshiped in many places.

The one who tells the story is the author of the book of Judges, who is not known with certainty. He explains that, after Joshua and his contemporaries died, a generation arose that did not know God or what He had done. Thus begins a sad cycle: Israel turns away, suffers the consequences, and then cries out to God.

For today: our faith needs to be nurtured and passed on. Tell at home and at church what God has done, and maintain a personal relationship with Him every day.
exp.13:6:
The verse says that Samson went down to Timnah and talked with the Philistine woman who had pleased him. "She pleased Samson well" means that he liked her very much and was drawn to her. It is a simple step, but he had already made up his mind to marry her.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges. He tells how Samson pressed on with his desire, even though his parents did not agree that he should marry a woman from a people who were enemies of Israel. Earlier, the Spirit of the LORD had helped him against the lion. The text says that God was seeking an occasion against the Philistines, but that does not mean everything Samson did was an example to follow.

For today: before following a desire of the heart, stop to pray and ask for wise counsel. Feeling drawn to something does not prove that it is the best choice or what God wants.
exp.14:17:
Samson is very thirsty and speaks to God with honesty. He reminds God that he has just given him a great victory, which he calls "deliverance," meaning rescue or liberation. Then he asks whether he is now going to die of thirst and fall into the hands of the "uncircumcised," a way of naming the Philistines, who did not belong to the covenant people.

He is speaking as Samson, judge of Israel, right after defeating a thousand Philistines with a donkey's jawbone. He went from celebration to exhaustion. He acknowledges that the victory came from God, though it was carried out through his own hand. God answers by bringing water out of the ground, and Samson is revived.

For today: after a great achievement, we still depend on God. When you are tired or in need, speak to him honestly, without pretending to strength. He cares for us not only in our battles but also in our daily needs.
exp.7:11:
Zebah and Zalmunna, the two kings of Midian, fled, but Gideon pursued them and captured them. "Discomfited" here means that he threw the whole enemy army into panic and disorder. "Taken" means that they were seized as prisoners.

It is part of the account in the book of Judges. The narrator tells how Gideon, with his three hundred men, followed the Midianites to Karkor, where the army was confident and unguarded. Gideon surprised them and captured their kings. No one speaks directly; the author only relates the events. Then Gideon returns and deals with the men of Succoth, who had not helped him.

For today: Gideon did not stop halfway, even though he was tired. When God gives us a task, it is good to finish it with perseverance and to trust that He sustains our strength.
exp.13:5:
This verse tells how Samson, when a young lion attacked him, received a special strength from God. The phrase "the Spirit of the Lord came mightily upon him" means that God empowered him in a powerful way. With nothing in his hand, he tore the lion apart as one would tear apart a young goat. Afterward, he told neither his father nor his mother what he had done.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Israel was under the rule of the Philistines, and the text says that God was looking for an opportunity against them. Samson was on his way to Timnah, where the woman who had pleased him lived. His parents did not know that God was at work in all of this.

For today: true strength comes from God, not from ourselves. And when He helps us overcome something, we can acknowledge it with humility, without boasting about it.
exp.5:19:
What it says: God's angel tells Gideon to place the meat and the unleavened bread on a rock, and to pour out the broth over them. A "rock" here is a large stone, and the "broth" is the liquid from the cooked meat. Gideon obeys without arguing.

Context: Gideon was an Israelite who felt small and afraid, and he asked for a sign to confirm that God was speaking to him. He had prepared a young goat and bread as an offering of hospitality. The angel changes the purpose of that meal: he turns it into an offering on the rock, and then a fire rises up and consumes it. Some believe this angel is a special appearance of God himself, and others see him as a messenger; the text calls him "the angel of the LORD."

For today: When God asks you to do something, even if you don't fully understand it, you can take a simple step of obedience. He often affirms the faith of those who trust and obey.
exp.19:1:
This verse says that the leaders of all the tribes of Israel came to the assembly of God's people. With them were four hundred thousand foot soldiers, that is, men who went on foot and knew how to use the sword. The phrase "were present" in this explanation means that they gathered there together.

The book of Judges tells this without an identified narrator. Israel comes together at Mizpah because of a terrible crime committed in Gibeah, in the territory of Benjamin, against the concubine of a Levite. The tribes gather to learn what happened and to decide how to respond. The figure of four hundred thousand can be understood literally, though some scholars debate how numbers were used in these accounts.

For today: when there is a serious injustice, it is wise to come together, hear the facts, and seek God before acting. Unity is valuable, but it needs truth, calm, and justice, not just anger.
exp.9:16:
This verse describes two armies preparing for war. The Ammonites gathered together and camped in Gilead, and the Israelites also came together and camped in Mizpeh. The phrase "encamped" in the verse means set up a military camp.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Israel had just acknowledged its sin, had removed its foreign gods, and had returned to serving the LORD. Now it faces the threat of Ammon, but it still has no leader. The next verse shows that the leaders of Gilead were looking for someone to lead the battle. The text does not say here how everything would end.

For today: true repentance includes giving up whatever pulls us away from God. But problems do not disappear right away. When you face a difficulty, keep trusting God even when you do not yet see the solution.
exp.10:17:
This verse tells that Israel, after being refused, did not fight against Edom or Moab, but went around through the wilderness. It passed along the east side of Moab and camped on the other side of the Arnon River, which was the border of Moab. So Israel did not enter their land. The verse's wording "came not within the border of Moab" is rendered here as "did not enter their land," and "the other side of Arnon" refers to the far bank of the river.

Jephthah, judge of Israel, speaks here and sends a message to the king of the Ammonites. This king was claiming lands, and Jephthah reminds him of the history: Israel respected the boundaries of Edom and Moab and did not take what was not theirs.

For today: when someone shuts a door in our face, we do not always have to force it open. Sometimes wisdom means respecting limits, taking the longer road, and waiting with patience, trusting that God is still guiding.
exp.10:22:
Here Jephthah tells the king of the Ammonites that the Lord, the God of Israel, is the one who drove the Amorites out of that land to give it to his people. Then he asks them firmly: "And shouldest thou possess it?" The word "dispossessed" means that he drove them out, and "possess" means to take as one's own property.

Jephthah speaks as the leader of Israel, and he sends this message to the king of the Ammonites, who was claiming those lands. Jephthah argues that Israel received the territory from the Amorites, not from Ammon, and that Israel has lived there for a long time. He tries to settle the conflict with words before going to war. Some scholars point out that Jephthah mentions Chemosh, the god of Moab, alongside the god of Ammon, and the Bible does not fully clarify that detail.

For today: before fighting for something, it is wise to think with clarity and calm. Recognizing what God has given us gives us firmness and humility to engage in dialogue.
exp.16:5:
The explanation says that in those days Israel had no king to rule, and that each person acted according to his own judgment. "Each did what was right in his own eyes" means acting on one's own view, without asking what God thought.

The narrator of the book is the one speaking, and no one knows for certain who he was. He wants to explain why the people were so disordered after the judges. Micah makes an image, an ephod (a priestly garment) and household idols, and he appoints his son as priest. All of this went against God's law, yet he did it as if it were a good thing.

Today we can ask ourselves: do I follow only what I feel or what suits me? It is wise to measure our decisions by God's Word and to seek counsel from other mature believers, rather than trusting only our own opinion.
exp.4:18:
The explanation says that several Canaanite kings joined together to fight against Israel at Taanach, near the waters of Megiddo. The phrase "they took no gain of money" refers to the plunder or payment they hoped to carry off after winning. But they left with nothing: they lost the battle and gained no riches.

This verse is part of the song of Deborah and Barak, which celebrates the victory over Sisera and the army of Jabin. Deborah praises the tribes that answered the call and rebukes those that did not. The kings came with confidence and ambition, but God intervened. The following verse shows that the victory came from on high, and the torrent of Kishon swept the enemy away.

For today: plans based only on ambition or power can fail, even when they seem strong. We can trust that God cares for his people, and we are called to obey him with courage, without depending on money or human strength.
exp.8:50:
The verse tells that Abimelech took the city of Thebez, and all the people took refuge in a strong tower in the center. Men, women and leaders went inside, shut the doors and climbed to the upper floor, the roof or the top part of the tower. They were looking to be safe from an attack.

It is part of the story of Abimelech, who made himself king by killing his brothers. Here it is not a character speaking, but the narrator. Shortly before, Abimelech had burned the tower of Shechem. Now he repeats the same method in Thebez, but the next verse shows that this time something turns out differently: a woman strikes him with a millstone.

For today: violence and pride may seem to succeed for a while, but they do not have the last word. God sees injustice. Trust that he acts in his own time, and seek refuge in him, not only in human towers.
exp.8:29:
This verse says that Zebul, the ruler or governor of the city of Shechem, became very angry when he heard what Gaal, the son of Ebed, said. "Assistant" means that Zebul was an official placed there to administer the city. The phrase "his anger was kindled" means that his anger flared up strongly.

Gaal had just spoken badly of Abimelech and of Zebul, and he encouraged the people of Shechem to rebel. Zebul served Abimelech, so he felt that he and his lord were under attack. The Bible does not explain all his motives, but his anger led him to send a secret message to Abimelech so that he would prepare an ambush.

For today: anger can push us to act with cunning and violence. Before responding to an offense, it is wise to stop, pray, and seek a fair and calm answer, as James 1:19-20 teaches.
exp.8:47:
Abimelech goes up with his men to Mount Zalmon. There he takes an axe, cuts a branch, and puts it on his shoulder. Then he orders everyone to do the same, and to do it "prestamente," that is, quickly and without hesitation.

Abimelech was the son of Gideon, and he had made himself king of Shechem by killing his brothers. Now the leaders of the tower of Shechem had rebelled against him and taken refuge in the stronghold of the temple of Baal-berith. Abimelech, as the military leader, sets the example so that his men will follow him. With those branches they will set the place on fire, and about a thousand people will die.

A leader draws others along by his example, for good or for evil. Before following someone, let us ask where he is leading us. And if we guide others, let us make sure our example brings them closer to God, not to violence.
exp.8:21:
This verse says that Abimelech ruled over Israel for three years. The word "reigned" means that he gave orders and held power, and it sounds more like forcing one's way to control than like serving. It is a short phrase that sets up what comes next.

The one speaking here is the narrator of the book of Judges. Abimelech had come to power by killing his brothers, and Jotham, the only one who escaped, had warned that this fire of violence would turn back on him and on Shechem. These three years seem to be a time of calm before that warning comes true. The verses that follow say that God sent an evil spirit between them, and the Bible does not explain in detail how that happened.

For today: power gained through injustice may seem firm for a time, but it does not go unanswered. Let us seek to act with justice and trust that God sees everything.
exp.8:8:
Here the olive tree refuses the offer to become king over the trees. It says it will not leave its rich, abundant oil, which serves to honor God and people. For the olive tree, giving up that work to rule over the others is not worth it.

Jotham, the son of Gideon, speaks from Mount Gerizim to the men of Shechem. He tells them this fable because they made Abimelech king, and Abimelech had killed Jotham's brothers. The olive tree stands for those who serve well and do not seek power. Many understand that oil was used in offerings and to honor people, which is why it is said to honor God and men.

For today: value the good gift God has given you to do, and do not trade it for a position or fame. Faithful service is worth more than rising at any cost.
exp.18:20:
This verse tells that the old man brought the travelers to his house. First he gave food to the donkeys, and then the visitors washed their feet, ate, and drank. Donkeys are the animals meant here, and the verse's wording refers to them as the animals that were fed. Washing the feet was a common gesture of courtesy, because people walked along dusty roads.

A Levite was traveling with his concubine and his servant, and no one in Gibeah took them in at the square. An old man who was coming in from the fields offered them his house and took charge of everything they needed. The narrator shows his kindness just before telling of the terrible wickedness of the men of the city. In this way the contrast is visible between the hospitality of one man and the violence of many.

Today we can practice a simple and genuine hospitality: opening the door, sharing the table, and caring for someone who is far from home or has nowhere to stay. Like the old man, one can do what is good even when everything around is wrong.
exp.14:8:
The Philistines, enemies of Israel, went up into the territory of Judah and set up their camp. They spread out across an area called Lehi. The phrase "set up their camp" means they settled in with their army, and "spread out" means they deployed across the region.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. The Philistines were dominating Israel, and Samson had struck them hard in revenge for what they had done to his wife and her father. Now they respond with force, but they do not attack Samson directly. Instead they pressure the whole tribe of Judah to hand him over. This shows how violence breeds more violence.

For today: when someone wounds us, revenge seems just, but it almost always brings consequences that reach other people. Before responding in anger, it is wise to think about who else will be affected and to seek, calmly, the path of forgiveness.
exp.20:24:
It says that in those days Israel had no king to rule over the whole people. So each person decided what was right according to their own opinion. "Right" here means correct or just, and the phrase "in his own eyes" means "as it seemed to each one."

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges, and he closes the book with this sentence. He has just recounted episodes of violence and disorder among the tribes, and his final chapters show a people who had turned away from God. Many understand the sentence as pointing to the need for good leadership, and others understand the missing foundation as obedience to God. Both readings can be defended.

For today: before deciding something important, don't ask only "what seems good to me?" but "what does God say in his Word?" Ask him for wisdom and allow yourself to be corrected.
exp.8:23:
God allowed the conflict between Abimelech and the men of Shechem so that the wickedness committed against the seventy sons of Jerubbaal (Gideon) would receive its answer. The injustice done to them would be repaid. The men of Shechem who backed him were guilty too.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Judges. Abimelech had killed his brothers to become king, and the men of Shechem supported him. Three years later the relationship breaks down. The text says that God sent an evil spirit between them, and that expression is understood in several ways. What is clear is that the account shows the crime did not go without consequences, both for the one who committed it and for those who helped him.

For today: it is not enough to avoid doing evil; we are also responsible if we back it or make it possible. Let us ask God for the courage to refuse to support injustice, even when it would be convenient for us.
exp.3:22:
This verse says that it was God who humbled or defeated Jabin, king of Canaan, that day, in the sight of the people of Israel. The word for "subdued" means to bring down, lower, or overcome.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges. He summarizes what happened: Israel had been oppressed by Jabin, and his military commander, Sisera, died at the hands of Jael. Although Deborah, Barak, and Jael all acted, the account credits the victory to God. The following verse shows that Jabin's downfall was a process, since Israel kept growing stronger until it destroyed him.

For today: when you accomplish something difficult, recognize that God works even through people and unexpected circumstances. Give thanks, stay humble, and trust that He continues to act in long processes.
exp.10:19:
It says that King Sihon did not trust Israel and for that reason did not let them pass through his land. Instead, he gathered all his army, camped at Jahaz, and attacked Israel.

The speaker is Jephthah, judge of Israel. He is answering the king of the Ammonites and explaining how Israel came to possess that land. According to his account, Israel asked for passage in peace, respected the borders of Edom and Moab, and fought only when Sihon attacked them first. Jephthah wants to show that Israel did not take the land out of greed.

For today: distrust can lead us to shut doors and start conflicts that could have been avoided. Let us seek peace and speak with clarity. And if others attack us without cause, we can place our cause in God's hands.
exp.12:11:
Manoah answers the man and says, "Now let your words come to pass." That is, he believes and accepts what he was told. Then he asks how the child should be raised and what he will need to do. Here "order" refers to the way of life or the instructions for his upbringing.

Manoah is the husband of the barren woman to whom it was announced that she would have a son. She ran to tell him about the visit of the man, who later appears as the angel of the LORD. Manoah does not doubt the announcement, but he wants to know how to carry out the task well. The child would be Samson, set apart for God from his birth.

When God entrusts us with something important, believing is not enough: it is also wise to ask humbly how to do it well. We can seek his guidance in prayer and in his Word before we act.
exp.12:9:
Here the wife of Manoah, whom the Bible does not name, runs out in a hurry to tell her husband that the man who visited her before has appeared to her again. "Quickly" means fast, and "told him" means she reported it to him. "Man" is simply the word for the man.

Manoah had prayed that the man of God would come back to teach them how to raise the promised child. God heard, and the angel returned, but he found the woman alone in the field. She speaks because she wants her husband to meet the messenger as soon as possible. The child would be Samson, though here he has not yet been born.

When God answers a prayer, sometimes we are the ones who must move. This woman did not stay still or keep the news to herself. If God has given you an answer or guidance, share it with those you love and move forward promptly and humbly.
exp.3:12:
Sisera, commander of the Canaanite army, gathered all his military strength: nine hundred chariots fitted with iron, and all the people who were with him. He led them from Harosheth of the Gentiles, his base, to the brook of Kishon.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Sisera had learned that Barak had gone up to Mount Tabor, and he responded by preparing for battle. Israel had been oppressed for twenty years, and the chariots were a symbol of human strength. The text does not say that God was taken by surprise; Deborah soon announces that the LORD had already given Sisera into Barak's hands.

For today: sometimes our problems look enormous, with "chariots of iron" standing before us. This passage invites us not to measure everything by visible strength, but to trust that God works even when human resources seem superior.
exp.1:7:
It says that Joshua, son of Nun, died at the age of 110. He is called "the servant of the Lord," a title of honor that Moses also received. It is a way of saying that his whole life was devoted to obeying and serving God. The name "the Lord" stands in this translation for God's personal name.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges. He is summarizing how the time of Joshua came to an end. As long as he and the elders lived, the people served the Lord, because they had seen his works. But the text immediately tells us that another generation came along that did not know the Lord. This sets up the cycle of disobedience that dominates the book.

For today: faith is not passed on by itself. We can tell our children and others what God has done in our lives, and live with steadiness, so that the next generation also comes to know him.
exp.18:15:
This verse presents an elderly man who returns at evening from working in the field. He was from the hill country of Ephraim, but he was living as a stranger in Gibeah, a town inhabited by people of the tribe of Benjamin. Here, "stranger" means someone who lives in a place that is not his own. "At evening" means as the day was coming to an end.

The narrator tells this while a Levite and his group wait in the square, and no one receives them. Among so many neighbors, the only one who notices them is a foreigner like them. The text does not explain his motives, but the contrast is clear: the hospitality came from someone from outside, not from the people of the place.

For today: let us think about who is alone or without a place around us, such as someone new in the church, at work, or in the neighborhood, and let us offer a simple welcome, even when no one else does.
exp.4:6:
It says that in Israel the villages ceased to exist, meaning that life in the open towns faded and declined. This lasted until Deborah arose as a mother in Israel, someone who cares for, guides, and protects her people. Some understand the word for "villages" as referring to the farmers or the people living in areas without walls; the Hebrew here carries some uncertainty.

Deborah speaks in her song of victory, together with Barak, after defeating the army of Sisera. She describes the earlier time: there was fear, the roads were unsafe, and people hid. She recognizes that God used her to rouse the people and restore peace.

For today: when everything around you seems dim or filled with fear, do not wait for someone else to take the step. God can use your courage and your care to encourage your family, your church, or your community.
exp.5:7:
It says that God sent a prophet, a "varón profeta," that is, a man who spoke on God's behalf, to speak to the people of Israel. The message begins by reminding them of something very basic: God brought them out of Egypt and freed them from the house of bondage, an old expression for the place where they had been slaves.

The people were greatly impoverished by the Midianites, who oppressed them, and they cried out to God asking for help. Before sending a deliverer, God speaks to them through this prophet, whose name is not mentioned. He reminds them of what he had already done for them and, in the verses that follow, points out that they had not obeyed him.

For today: when you are in trouble, before asking for help, remember how God has cared for you before. That strengthens trust, and it also invites us to examine whether we are obeying him.
exp.18:13:
This verse tells how the Levite, his concubine, and his servant kept walking until the sun went down near Gibeah, a town in the tribe of Benjamin. The phrase "the sun went down upon them" means that evening overtook them.

The one speaking is the narrator, who follows this Levite on his journey home. He had decided not to stay in a foreign city, because he thought he would be safer among his own people. So they passed by and came to Gibeah. The book of Judges shows a time of great moral disorder in Israel, and this story will end in a very painful way.

For today: an appearance of safety can be deceiving. Belonging to a group, a church, or a town does not guarantee that justice will be done. Let us ask God for wisdom, and seek to live and practice hospitality.
exp.2:6:
This verse says that the people of Israel did what displeased God. They forgot the Lord, their God, and served the Baals, which were false gods of the Canaanites, and the images in the groves. Some translations say "Asherah" or "Asherahs," which were probably religious symbols of a Canaanite goddess, although experts debate the details.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges. He explains why trouble came: Israel mixed with the neighboring peoples, married them, and ended up adopting their gods. Then would come the punishment, the cry of the people, and deliverance through Othniel.

For today: forgetting God almost never happens all at once, but little by little. Guard your influences and keep your relationship with God alive. If you have drifted away, remember that he listens when you cry out.
exp.13:7:
What it says: Samson returns some days later to take the Philistine woman as his wife. He turns aside from the road to look at the carcass of the lion he had killed. There he finds a swarm of bees and honey in the carcass of the lion. The word "turned aside" means that he left the path, and "honeycomb" is the wax structure where bees store honey.

Context: It is the narrator of the book of Judges who tells this. Samson was going to marry a Philistine woman, and God used that situation to act against the Philistines, who dominated Israel. The text does not explain every detail, but the honey from a dead animal becomes the basis of the riddle Samson will propose later. In addition, touching a corpse made a Nazirite unclean, and this shows that Samson was not a perfect example.

For today: God can bring something good from unexpected places, but that does not justify neglecting what He asks. Let us seek to obey Him sincerely and give thanks for His blessings.
exp.5:15:
God answers Gideon with a promise: "Surely I will be with thee." Because of that presence, Gideon would defeat the Midianites "as one man," that is, in a single blow and without any remaining resistance. The word "smite" means to strike down or defeat.

The Lord, who had appeared to Gideon, speaks. Israel was oppressed by Midian, and Gideon felt small: his family was poor, and he was the youngest in his house. God does not correct his weakness with praise, but with a promise. Afterward Gideon asks for a sign, and God patiently waits.

When God calls you to something that seems bigger than you, do not look first at your limits, but at his company. Take the step you can, trusting that his presence sustains you, and speak with him honestly about your fears.
exp.5:10:
The explanation tells how the angel of the Lord came to a town called Ophrah and sat down under a large tree, which some translate as oak or terebinth. That tree belonged to Joash. His son Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress, which was normally a pit for treading grapes, in order to hide the grain from the Midianites.

Israel was oppressed by Midian, which took away their harvests. Before this verse, God reminded them through a prophet that He had brought them out of Egypt, but they had not obeyed Him. Even so, God does not abandon them: He sends His angel to seek out Gideon.

For today: God can call us in the middle of fear and of our daily tasks. Gideon was working in hiding, but God saw him. If you feel small or afraid today, remember that God sees you and can use you where you are.
exp.7:16:
This verse tells that Gideon, after punishing the leaders of Succoth, tore down the tower of Penuel and killed the men of that city. The tower was probably a strong place for defense.

Gideon was pursuing the Midianite kings, Zebah and Zalmunna, while his men were exhausted. The people of Succoth and Penuel refused to give him bread and mocked him, as if the victory were not certain. He had promised to return and answer them. The text narrates what he did, but it does not say that God commanded him to do it, so many read it as a personal revenge.

For today: when someone refuses us help or mocks us, revenge can lead us too far. It is better to help the one who is tired and leave justice in God's hands.
exp.16:7:
This man, a young Levite, left Bethlehem in Judah to look for a place to live. On his way he reached the hill country of Ephraim and stopped at the house of Micah. He was only passing through, heading toward some other place. The phrase "to sojourn where he could find a place" means he had no fixed destination.

It is the narrator of Judges who tells us this. The Levites were to serve in worship and live in the towns God had assigned them, but this young man wanders without direction. The book says there was no king and that everyone did what seemed right to them, and it shows how the lack of direction affected even those who served God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are seeking only comfort or whether we are seeking God's guidance when we make decisions. Praying and asking for wise counsel helps us not to drift aimlessly.
exp.19:27:
This verse tells how Israel again asked God whether they should fight against Benjamin. Phinehas, the grandson of Aaron, was serving before the ark. The question "Shall I yet again go out?" is asked directly, and the words "shall I cease?" ask whether they should hold back. God answers that they should go up, because the next day he would give them the victory.

The Israelites had suffered two heavy defeats at the hands of Benjamin, their own brother tribe, who was protecting the men guilty of a terrible crime in Gibeah. Now they weep, fast, offer sacrifices, and seek God through the priest. The Israelites speak, and the Lord answers. Earlier they had gone to battle without waiting for so long.

For today: before making hard decisions, it is wise to stop, pray with humility, and seek God's guidance, not simply trust in our own strength or in our anger.
exp.0:27:
It says that when the Israelites grew stronger, they forced the Canaanites to work for them and to pay them tribute, but they did not drive them out of the land. "Yet" is the word used here, meaning "but," and "subject to tribute" means that they had to pay or serve through labor.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges, who summarizes how the tribes gradually took over Canaan, is speaking. God had commanded them to drive those peoples out of the land. But the tribes, such as Manasseh, Ephraim, and Zebulun, were content to profit from them. The text shows a beginning of disobedience that would later bring trouble.

For today: sometimes we tolerate a sin or bad habit because it benefits us, or because we think we have it under control to some degree. Ask God for strength to remove it at the root, not just to manage it.
exp.0:13:
This verse tells that Achsah, Caleb's daughter, was on her way to her new home with her husband Othniel. He encouraged her to ask her father for a field. Then she got down from the donkey, and Caleb asked her what she wanted. The wording "moved him to ask" means she urged him to ask, and "lighted from off her ass" means she got down from the donkey.

Caleb is Judah's great warrior. He had offered his daughter as the prize to whoever conquered Kiriath-sepher, and Othniel succeeded. Now she, already married, approaches her father with respect to ask for something. Some believe it was Othniel who encouraged her; the text suggests this, but gives no further details.

For today: draw near with confidence to your heavenly Father and ask him simply for what you need. He listens and cares for you, just as Caleb listened to his daughter.
exp.5:27:
It says that when the people of the town got up in the morning, they found the altar of Baal torn down. The wooden pole beside it had also been cut down; here it refers to a post or tree used in pagan worship (some versions call it Asherah). Also, the second bull had been offered as a burnt offering, that is, burned completely, on a new altar.

God had commanded Gideon to do this. Israel was oppressed by Midian and had fallen into idolatry. Gideon obeyed, but he did it at night because he was afraid of his family and the people. His fear did not keep him from obeying.

For today: sometimes obeying God frightens us. God does not ask us to feel no fear, but to take the step of faith in spite of it. Do today what you know God is asking of you, even if it is a little at a time.
exp.8:56:
This verse says that God brought upon the men of Shechem the evil they had themselves done. The word "returned" means "gave back," and "upon their heads" means that they received the consequences of their actions. The curse that Jotham had spoken against them also came true.

This is the narrator's comment closing the story of Abimelech. He killed his seventy brothers, and the men of Shechem supported him and made him king. Jotham, the only brother who escaped, had warned that this agreement would bring destruction (Judges 9:20). Abimelech died in battle, and the city of Shechem was also destroyed. The text presents this as the justice of God.

For today: we cannot support injustice and expect nothing to happen. God sees what we do and calls us to act with honesty. If we have taken part in something wrong, we can repent and ask for forgiveness.
exp.0:12:
Here it is told that Othniel, son of Kenaz, captured the city of Debir. The word "took" in the verse means that he took it. As Caleb had promised, he gave his daughter Achsah to him as a wife.

The narrator of the book tells this at the beginning of Judges, when Israel was taking possession of the promised land. Caleb had offered his daughter to whoever conquered the city. The phrase "Caleb's younger brother" can be understood in two ways: as a younger brother or as a younger relative. The Hebrew text allows both readings. Later on, Othniel will become the first judge of Israel.

For today: Othniel acted with courage and carried out his task. Let us ask God for the courage to do what is ours to do, and trust that He keeps His promises in His own time.
exp.15:26:
This verse describes the place where Samson was: a temple full of people, with all the Philistine leaders present. On the upper level there were about three thousand men and women watching while they mocked him. "Mocked" means publicly ridiculed and humiliated. "Leaders" are the rulers or chiefs.

Here it is not a character speaking but the narrator. The Philistines were holding a feast to their god Dagon, because they believed they had defeated Samson. He was blind and a prisoner, and they used him as an entertainment. The text prepares for his prayer to God and his final act.

For today: even in moments of humiliation, when everything seems lost, we can turn back to God with humility and sincerity. Samson failed greatly, but in the end he called out to God. He still listens to those who come to Him.
exp.6:3:
God tells Gideon that there are still too many people in his army, even after twenty-two thousand have gone home. He orders him to bring them down to the water, and there God will test them so as to choose. God will say who goes and who does not. The words "yet" and "try" read today as "still" and "test."

Speaking is the LORD to Gideon, judge of Israel, before the battle against Midian. God wants Israel not to boast, saying, "I saved myself by my own strength." That is why he reduces the army, so that the victory is seen as his work.

For today: God does not depend on our strength, our numbers, or our resources. When you feel small or have little, trust that God can act precisely there. And when something turns out well, give him the glory.
exp.8:55:
This verse says that God paid Abimelech back for the evil he had done. He killed his seventy brothers in order to keep power for himself, and in the end he died in a shameful way.

The narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. After describing Abimelech's death, when a woman dropped a millstone on him and his armor-bearer finished him off, the author explains what happened: it was not simple chance, but God's justice. This fulfilled the curse that Jotham, the only brother who survived, had spoken earlier.

For today: do not lose heart when evil seems to go unpunished. God sees everything and is just. So instead of taking revenge, trust in Him, and make sure you do not gain anything through violence or deceit.
exp.0:10:
The explanation says that the tribe of Judah, after taking Hebron, continued its campaign and went against the inhabitants of Debir. This city was formerly called Kirjath-sepher, a name that is understood to mean "city of the book" or "city of letters," though the exact meaning is uncertain. The phrase "went against" in the verse corresponds to the verb "went" in the earlier part of the verse, and "the inhabitants" are its Canaanite residents.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. He tells how Judah, after the death of Joshua, continued the conquest of the promised land. It is an account similar to the one in Joshua 15:15-17. This advance shows a tribe acting together and taking the initiative, and Caleb encouraging others to join the task.

For today: God often gives us victories step by step. After an achievement, do not stop; take the next step in faith, without waiting to feel completely ready, and walk alongside others who can help you.
exp.9:0:
This verse tells us that, after Abimelech, God raised up Tola to defend Israel. He was the son of Puah and grandson of Dodo, from the tribe of Issachar. He lived in Shamir, in the hill country of Ephraim.

The book of Judges covers the period before the kings, when Israel repeatedly fell into disobedience. The narrator, whose identity is not known with certainty, introduces Tola right after the violent rule of Abimelech. The text does not tell us how he saved Israel, since it gives very few details. The verses that follow say that he judged Israel for twenty-three years.

For today: God also uses ordinary, little-known people to bring stability and good to others. You do not need fame to be useful; steady faithfulness in your own place and time counts before God.
exp.4:15:
This verse asks the tribe of Reuben a question: "Why did you stay among the sheepfolds?" Sheepfolds are the pens or enclosures where sheep are kept. The bleatings are the sounds that the flocks make. The "searchings of heart" are long deliberations or inner doubts: Reuben thought hard about it, but did not act.

Here Deborah sings, together with Barak, after the victory over the army of Sisera. In her song she praises the tribes that came to the battle and rebukes those that did not. Reuben had much debate, but stayed with its sheep. Some think the question is a serious criticism; others think it expresses sorrow.

Today, it is easy to stay with our comfort and talk about what we should do. God invites us to move from good intentions to concrete obedience. Ask yourself: what small step can I take today to help someone?
exp.2:19:
Ehud approaches King Eglon, who was alone in the cool room of his palace, which is described as a "summer room." Ehud tells him that he brings a "word from God" for him. Eglon, out of respect or curiosity, rises from his seat. The word that was rendered "came unto him" means simply "drew near to him."

Israel was under the control of Moab, and Eglon was its oppressive king. Ehud, a deliverer whom God raised up, had already delivered the tribute and managed to be alone with the king under the pretense of a secret message. The phrase "a message from God" can be understood in several ways: as a deception to gain access to the king, or as a proclamation of God's judgment that would really come. The text does not make this clear.

For today: this passage reminds us that God works in the middle of situations of oppression and uses ordinary people. It also invites us to be careful with the name of God: to use it honestly, without manipulating others with it.
exp.1:18:
When the judge whom God had raised up died, the people turned back. They behaved worse than their ancestors: they followed false gods, served them, and bowed down before them. The source's word "turned" is simply what it means here, and "other gods" refers to the gods of other nations. They did not give up their bad habits or their stubborn ways, meaning their obstinacy.

The book's narrator describes a cycle that kept repeating in Israel: the people drifted away from God, suffered oppression, cried out, God sent a judge who delivered them, and when that judge died they went right back to the same thing. That is why God grows angry in the next verse: they had broken his covenant.

For today: it is not enough to depend on a good leader or on a strong spiritual moment. Our faith needs its own roots in God. Today you can set aside a fixed time to pray and read the Bible, so that your obedience does not depend on other people or on circumstances.
exp.3:2:
The explanation says that the Israelites asked God for help with cries and pleas, because King Jabin, through his army, had been oppressing them harshly for twenty years. The verse speaks of nine hundred chariots of iron, which were war chariots reinforced with iron, a military force greatly feared. The verse says he mightily oppressed them, meaning he treated them cruelly and mistreated them.

It is the narrator of the book of Judges who speaks. He shows a cycle that repeats: the people turn away from God, suffer the consequences, and then cry out. The text does not say that their cry was a perfect return to God, but it does say that they turned to Him. Later Deborah will come, used by God to guide them.

For today: when you feel crushed by a problem that seems bigger than you, do not wait until you have strength or answers. Cry out to God sincerely, and if you have drifted away from Him, return. He listens.
exp.10:4:
This verse tells us that the Ammonites attacked Israel, and so the leaders of Gilead went to bring Jephthah, who lived in the land of Tob. The phrase "went to fetch Jephthah" means they went to bring him back. The "elders" were the older men who led the community.

This is part of the story of Jephthah. His brothers had driven him out of the family home, and he went to live in Tob, where men with no fixed trade gathered around him. Now the elders who had earlier rejected him need him, because he was a brave warrior. The narrator only reports the events; the reasons behind each person's actions become clearer in what follows.

Today, this text invites us not to close our hearts because of past pain. If someone who hurt us comes back, we can ask God for wisdom to speak with truth, set healthy boundaries, and remain open to reconciliation.
exp.12:14:
Manoah asks the angel of the Lord to stay a little longer. His request is polite and courteous, something like asking him to let them hold him there for a while. Manoah wants to prepare a young goat, which is a kid, and offer it to him as a meal.

Manoah is the husband of the woman who would become the mother of Samson. The angel had already announced to them the birth of a son. Manoah did not yet know that he was an angel; he took him for a man of God and wanted to honor him with hospitality, as was the custom. The angel redirects that gesture toward the Lord through a burnt offering.

For today: generosity is good, but we should ask to whom the honor is directed. Serve and be hospitable, but let every gesture end up pointing to God, not to people.
exp.17:27:
This verse tells us that no one came to help the people of Laish when they were attacked. They lived far from Zidon, the nearest Phoenician city, and they had no dealings with other peoples. They were in a valley near Beth-rehob. After the Danites destroyed the city, they rebuilt it and settled there to live.

The narrator of the book of Judges describes how the tribe of Dan, without having taken the land assigned to it, went looking for another place. They attacked a peaceful and unsuspecting people. The account shows the disorder of that time, when each person did whatever seemed right to them, and even stole the religious objects of Micah.

For today: security without connections is fragile. We should not live isolated lives; let us seek community and care for others. Moreover, it is not enough to succeed if we have taken the wrong path.
exp.4:1:
This verse opens a song of praise. Deborah and Barak invite everyone to bless the Lord for two reasons: God brought justice for Israel's wrongs and sufferings, and the people offered themselves freely, presenting themselves willingly and by their own choice. The first phrase in the Hebrew can be translated in several ways, and some versions say that the leaders took command.

Deborah, a prophetess and judge, and Barak, the military leader, are the ones speaking. They sing after the victory over Sisera's army, following years of oppression by the Canaanites. They recognize that the triumph came from God, and they also honor those who willingly offered to fight.

For today: serve God and others with joy, not out of obligation. And when you see his help, do not keep it silent; thank him and tell others about it.
exp.17:28:
The verse tells how the tribe of Dan renamed the city they had just taken. Before, it was called Laish, but now they called it Dan, in honor of their ancestor, one of the sons of Jacob, whom God also named Israel. The phrase "after the name of" is the same as "according to the name of."

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. It is a disorderly time, when each person did whatever seemed right to them. The Danites had not managed to take the land that belonged to them, and they attacked a peaceful people who had no one to defend them. They also carried off Micah's idols and his priest. The account does not approve of what they did; rather, it shows how far they were from God.

For today: a good name or an achievement does not make a decision good. Before we celebrate what we have accomplished, let us ask whether we achieved it in a way that pleases God.
exp.4:26:
It says that Sisera, the commander of the enemy army, fell bowed over and lay stretched out at Jael's feet. The repetition of "fell" and "bowed" makes the reader see the scene slowly, almost blow by blow. "Bowed over" means bent or fallen forward. The "temples" are the sides of the head.

The one speaking is Deborah, together with Barak, in a song of victory after the battle against the Canaanite army. They celebrate that God delivered Israel through an unexpected woman. The poem uses repetition to stress that the powerful oppressor was completely defeated. Interpreters discuss how to judge Jael's method, since the text narrates it and celebrates it, but does not present it as an example to imitate.

For today: God can work through people no one expected. We can trust that no human power is greater than He is, and be willing to serve with courage wherever we are placed.
exp.19:25:
After the second defeat, all the people of Israel went up to the house of God. They wept, sat there before the Lord, and fasted until evening. They offered burnt offerings (offerings burned up completely) and peace offerings (offerings of fellowship with God).

The narrator of Judges tells this in a time of great moral disorder. Israel was fighting against the tribe of Benjamin because of a terrible crime committed in Gibeah. They had already lost many men in two battles. Now, in sorrow, they seek God. The "house of God" was probably Bethel, although the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when you face a failure, do not rely only on your own plans. Come to God with sincerity, humility, and sorrow, and ask Him for direction before you move forward.
exp.2:27:
Ehud tells the Israelites to follow him, because God has already given them victory over Moab. They go down after him and take the fords of the Jordan, that is, the shallow places where the river could be crossed on foot. In this way they block Moab's escape, and not one man gets through.

The one speaking is Ehud, the judge whom God raised up to deliver Israel. Moab had ruled over them for eighteen years. Ehud had just killed King Eglon and fled. Then he blew the trumpet to gather the people. His confidence was not in his own plan, but in the fact that the Lord had already acted.

For today: when God gives you a sign that he is at work, do not just stand and look. Take the step of faith and do your part with courage and order. Trusting God does not remove action; it drives it forward. Today you can ask yourself: what concrete step is mine to take?
exp.8:43:
This verse describes a military strategy. Abimelech and his company rushed forward and stood at the entrance of the city gate, to keep the people from getting back in. Meanwhile, the other two companies attacked everyone who was out in the fields and killed them.

It is part of the account in Judges, where the narrator describes the war between Abimelech and the people of Shechem. Abimelech had made himself king through violence and murder, and Shechem had supported him. Now that alliance breaks apart, and both suffer the consequences, just as Jotham had foretold earlier (Judges 9:20).

For today: this passage does not present Abimelech as an example to follow, but as a warning. What is built through violence and deceit ends up destroying those who built it. Let us seek relationships and achievements grounded in truth and justice.
exp.8:25:
It says that a man named Gaal, son of Ebed, arrived at Shechem together with his relatives (or kinsmen), and settled there. The people of the city began to put their trust in him. "Shechem" is the city of Shechem, and the phrase about "went over" means that they moved or crossed over there.
