The narrator is describing how God allowed the sin of Abimelech and the men of Shechem, who killed the seventy sons of Jerubbaal (Gideon), to come back upon them as a consequence. The men of Shechem were already dissatisfied with Abimelech, and Gaal appears as a new leader. The Bible does not explain where he came from or who he exactly was; we only see that he took advantage of the tension.

For today: before trusting someone who promises solutions, let us observe their character and their motives. Someone who trusts whatever is convenient at the moment may end up in new troubles. Let us seek God's guidance and wise counsel.
exp.8:24:
This verse tells that the men of Shechem set ambushes on the tops of the mountains. Those men attacked everyone who passed along the road. People who lie hidden and wait to attack are described here as ambushers, and the verse says they robbed travelers. In the end, someone told Abimelech what was happening.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. Abimelech had killed his seventy brothers in order to rule, and the people of Shechem had supported him. The text says that God sent an evil spirit that set the two sides against each other. It is usually understood as a mistrust and hostility allowed by God, as a judgment for so much blood that had been shed. The people of Shechem now rebel against him.

For today: evil built on violence and betrayal does not bring lasting peace. Let us ask God to keep us from seeking power or advantage by doing harm, and let us trust that he is just.
exp.8:1:
Abimelech asks the leaders of Shechem to listen to him, and he poses a question: which is better, to be ruled by seventy men, all sons of Jerubbaal (another name for Gideon), or by just one man? Then he reminds them: "I am your bone and your flesh," meaning that they are family.

Abimelech speaks to the family of his mother, who was from Shechem. Gideon had died, and Abimelech wanted to be king. His question is a trap, because no one had said that the seventy brothers wanted to rule. He uses the family tie to gain support for his ambition.

Today, let us be wary of anyone who uses closeness or blood ties to gain power. Before backing someone, let us look at his character and his motives, not just at how close he seems to us.
exp.9:17:
It says that the leaders and the people of Gilead asked one another who would be willing to start the fight against the Ammonites. They promised that whoever did it would be "cabeza," that is, leader or ruler, over all the inhabitants of Gilead.

The Israelites of Gilead were camped in Mizpah, and the Ammonites had gathered to attack them. Earlier, the people had put away their false gods and had returned to serve the LORD. But they still did not have a military leader. This verse sets the scene for Jephthah to appear (Judges 11), although his name is not mentioned here.

For today: God asks us to return to Him with sincerity, but also to act responsibly in the face of problems. If there is a need around you, do not wait for someone else to take the first step. Pray and ask yourself what you can do with humility and courage.
exp.18:2:
The verse tells that the Levite got up and went after his concubine, who had gone to her father's house. He wanted to speak to her kindly, to win her back with gentle words, and to bring her home again. He took with him a servant and a pair of donkeys. She brought him into her father's house.

The narrator of the book tells this in a dark time, when there was no king in Israel and everyone did what seemed right to them. This story opens one of the saddest accounts in Judges. Scholars debate why she left and how the word "adulterated" should be understood, but the text shows the man seeking reconciliation.

For today: when a relationship breaks, reaching out to the other person with soft and humble words, instead of pride or silence, is a first step toward healing.
exp.3:9:
This verse tells that Barak gathered the tribes of Zebulun and Naphtali at Kedesh. From there he went out with ten thousand men following him, and Deborah went with him. The verse's word "went up" means they set out and marched forward, and "ten thousand men at his feet" means they followed behind him, going where he led.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel was oppressed by King Jabin of Canaan and his military commander, Sisera. God had called Barak through the prophetess Deborah. Barak hesitated and asked that she go with him, and she agreed. Now he obeys and sets out with the people.

For today: obedience to God does not require that everything be perfect or that we have no fear. Barak moved forward with his doubts, and God worked. Take the step God shows you, and seek the support of people of faith who encourage you to keep going.
exp.20:23:
This verse tells that the Israelites, after settling the matter of the wives for the men of Benjamin, took their leave and returned home. Each one went back to his tribe, to his family, and to his inheritance, which is the land that fell to him as his share.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. He closes a very painful story: a civil war among the tribes and a plan to keep Benjamin from disappearing. The verse that follows gives the background: there was no king, and each man did what seemed right to him. So the end of the scene sounds calm, but it leaves a sense of a people wounded and without direction.

For today: it is not enough that a conflict ends and each person goes back home. It is worth asking ourselves whether what we did was in line with God's will, and not merely with our own judgment.
exp.15:16:
Samson tells Delilah his secret. He opened his whole heart to her, and the words describe a complete disclosure. The razor is the blade used to shave the head. A Nazirite was someone set apart for God by a special vow, which included never cutting the hair. Samson says that if his head is shaved, he will lose his strength and become like any other man.

Samson, judge of Israel, had been dedicated to God since before he was born. Delilah pressed him every day, and he, worn out, gave in. The Philistine lords had offered her money to discover his secret. His strength did not lie in the hair itself, but in his relationship with God, which the hair represented.

For today: let us guard what God has entrusted to us and not hand it over out of weariness or pressure. Let us set healthy limits with anyone who insists on pushing us to give in, and ask God for the firmness to say "no" in time.
exp.10:33:
Jephthah returns victorious to his home in Mizpah, and his daughter comes out to greet him with tambourines and dancing, as was done to celebrate a victory. The text emphasizes that she was his only child, and that he had no other son or daughter. The word "timbrels" refers to the tambourines, and "his only child" means that she was everything he had.

Jephthah, a judge of Israel, had made a vow to God before the battle: he would offer whatever came out of his house to meet him first (Judges 11:30-31). Perhaps he did not think about the consequences. Interpreters debate what happened to her afterward: some believe she was sacrificed, others that she was dedicated to serving God her whole life, without marrying. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: before we promise something to God or to others, let us think calmly and sincerely about what we are really promising. Words spoken lightly can bring deep sorrow, and God values wisdom and obedience more than hasty promises.
exp.0:33:
The Amorites, a people who lived in that region, pressed the tribe of Dan hard and forced them to stay in the hill country. They did not allow them to come down to the plain, that is, the lowland, which was more fertile and better for planting and living. The word "forced" here means that they cornered them or dominated them.

The book of Judges tells how the tribes of Israel did not fully take the promised land. We do not know for certain who wrote the book, but the account shows that Dan was not able to occupy what had been assigned to it. The nearby verses speak of other tribes who also lived alongside the Canaanites instead of driving them out. Later on, Dan moves north (Judges 18).

When we leave a task half-finished or put up with what we should have confronted, those problems can grow and limit us. Today we can ask God for courage and perseverance to deal in time with what hinders us, trusting that He gives us strength.
exp.1:20:
It says that God will no longer keep driving out of the land the nations that Joshua left unconquered when he died.

The speaker is the LORD, the Lord. He speaks to Israel through his angel, after the people had repeatedly broken their covenant and worshiped other gods. Because they broke the agreement, God decides not to remove those remaining nations. The verses that follow explain that these nations would be a test to see whether Israel would return to following the way of the Lord.

For today: God sometimes allows trials or struggles to remain in our lives, and does not always remove them right away. We can ask ourselves whether there is something God is asking us to leave behind or correct, and answer him with sincere obedience, trusting that he remains close and is patient with us.
exp.0:28:
This verse says that the tribe of Ephraim did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in the city of Gezer. Instead of removing them, they let them live alongside them. Here "drive out" means to expel or remove from the land, and "Canaanites" refers to the ancient inhabitants of that region.

Context: the one telling this is the narrator of the book of Judges, not a character in the story. He records it as part of a list of tribes that did not complete the conquest of the promised land. Before this passage, Manasseh had done something similar. Afterward, Zebulun and Asher also fail. The book thus shows a pattern of partial obedience, which later brings trouble to the people.

For today: sometimes we allow habits or attitudes to remain among us that we know do not please God, thinking they do no harm. Today you can ask God for strength to face one concrete thing honestly and not leave it half done.
exp.7:21:
The men of Israel ask Gideon to be their ruler, and that after him his son and his grandson should rule as well. They want a dynasty, meaning that the leadership would pass from father to son. Here the idea of ruling means being king or a leader with authority.

The people of Israel speak, grateful that God saved them from Midian through Gideon. They have just seen a great victory and want to secure their protection with a human leader. Gideon answers in the following verse that only the LORD should rule. However, the Bible does not say that their request was entirely wrong, and later Gideon does something that becomes a snare for the people.

For today: when God gives us a victory, let us give Him the glory and not put a person in the place that belongs only to God.
exp.3:4:
She lived under a palm tree, called the palm of Deborah, in a place between Ramah and Bethel, in the hill country of Ephraim. The people of Israel would go up to her to have their disputes settled.

The phrase about going up to her is explained as follows: they went to her to have their disputes resolved and to be told what was right. The hill country of Ephraim refers to the area of hills belonging to the tribe of Ephraim.

The narrator then describes Deborah just after saying that Israel had been oppressed for twenty years by an enemy with many chariots of iron. She was a prophetess and she ruled over Israel. Her open and simple place shows that the people could come near to her. Later she will call Barak to give him the word of God.

For today: God uses people who are approachable and trustworthy. We can be someone others turn to for wise counsel, and we can seek out people who will guide us according to the Word of God.
exp.8:34:
This verse tells how Gaal, the son of Ebed, went out and stood at the entrance of the gate of the city of Shechem. At that moment, Abimelech and all his people rose up from where they had been hidden.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Zebul, the ruler of the city and loyal to Abimelech, had advised the attack. Gaal had rebelled against Abimelech and boasted before the people. Now he goes out without noticing the danger, and Abimelech's plan begins to take effect.

For today: big words and self-confidence can blind us. It is wise to be humble, to watch carefully, and to seek God's wisdom before facing any situation.
exp.2:3:
This verse says that God left those nations in the land as a test for Israel. He wanted to see whether his people would obey the commandments that the Lord gave their ancestors through Moses. The sentence that explains "prove" and "prescribed" is removed, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks, explaining why neighboring peoples remained in Canaan. Israel had not finished obeying God in the conquest. The verses that follow show that they failed: they mixed with those peoples, married them, and worshiped their gods.

For today: difficulties can show how much we trust God and how much we obey him. Rather than blaming our circumstances, we can ask him for help to follow his word, especially when it is easier to go along with what everyone else is doing.
exp.1:3:
It says that when the angel of the Lord finished speaking to all of Israel, the people wept loudly, aloud. The weeping shows that the words reached their hearts.

Context: the angel of the Lord speaks on God's behalf and reminds Israel that they did not obey. God had told them not to make alliances with the peoples of Canaan and to tear down their altars, but they did not do it. Because of this, those peoples would remain a threat to them. The place was called Bochim, which means "those who weep." The explanation does not say here whether their repentance was deep or temporary; the book later shows that they failed again.

For today: weeping over sin is a good beginning, but God also seeks a real change. If He shows you something you must leave behind, respond with humility and with concrete steps of obedience.
exp.3:11:
This verse says that news reached Sisera that Barak, son of Abinoam, had gone up to Mount Tabor. The word "news" here means the reports. Sisera was the commander of the Canaanite army that oppressed Israel. When he heard, he knew that Israel was preparing to fight.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Barak had gathered ten thousand men from Zebulun and Naphtali, encouraged by the prophetess Deborah. Tabor was a high mountain, a safe place to gather. The account shows that Sisera reacted quickly, for he gathered his nine hundred chariots of iron. Humanly speaking, Israel was at a disadvantage.

For today: God sometimes asks us to take a step of faith even when the enemy's resources seem greater. Barak went up the mountain without yet seeing the victory, and he trusted in God's word. Obey what God places on your heart, even when you feel small.
exp.0:4:
This verse tells how the tribes of Judah and Simeon found Adoni-bezek in a place called Bezek. There they fought against him and defeated the Canaanites and the Perizzites, who were peoples living in that land. The word "found" here means they came upon him, and "slew" means they struck them down in battle.

It is part of the account in the book of Judges, which does not name its narrator. After the death of Joshua, Judah asked his brother Simeon for help to conquer the territory that had fallen to them. The text says it was the LORD who delivered these peoples into their hands. Adoni-bezek seems to have been a local king, and his story continues in the verses that follow.

For today: Judah did not want to fight alone, but asked his brother for help. In the same way, we do not have to face difficult tasks by ourselves. Let us seek the support of brothers and sisters in the faith, and trust that God works through our united effort.
exp.12:0:
It says that the people of Israel again did what God regarded as evil. As a result, God allowed the Philistines to rule over them for forty years. The verse uses the word "again," and "delivered them into the hand of" means that he left them under the power of others.

This verse opens a new stage in the book of Judges. The one who narrates is the author of the book, who is not named. It repeats a pattern: Israel turns away from God, suffers oppression, and then cries out for help. This time it is notable that the text does not mention the people asking for help. Even so, God begins to prepare a deliverer, Samson, as seen in what follows.

For today: when you notice that you have turned away from God and feel the consequences, do not wait until you are desperate. Return to him soon and with humility, trusting that his grace continues to work even when we have not asked for it.
exp.4:21:
The verse says the horses' hooves were broken by the pounding, the pounding of their mighty ones. It means that the hooves were worn down or broken from running so hard. "Pounding" refers to violent charges, and "gallops" refers to the leaping gallop of the horses. "Their mighty ones" refers to Sisera's warriors, who were fleeing in great haste.

This verse is part of the Song of Deborah and Barak, a victory song. Israel defeated the army of Sisera, which had chariots and horses. Earlier the text says the river Kishon swept the enemies away. Some understand that a storm flooded the plain; the text gives no further detail. Here the desperate flight of the army is described.

For today: human strength, however great it may seem, cannot stand against what God decides. When you face something that intimidates you, trust God and obey Him, without depending only on your own resources.
exp.0:20:
The explanation says that the tribe of Benjamin failed to drive out the Jebusites, a people who lived in Jerusalem. For this reason, they lived together in the city. The verse's phrase about the Jebusites remaining "unto this day" means that this situation was still ongoing when the book was written.

The book of Judges begins by telling how each tribe tried to conquer the promised land. The narrator, whose name we do not know for certain, shows successes, such as that of Judah, but also failures. Here Benjamin does not complete the task that God had entrusted to it. A pattern can be seen: partial obedience that, little by little, brings problems later on.

For today: sometimes we leave something unfinished that we know we must resolve, like a bad habit or a damaged relationship. What we tolerate today can grow tomorrow. Ask God for strength to finish what He asks of you, step by step.
exp.8:38:
This verse tells how Gaal, pushed on by Zebul's words, goes out at the head of the men of Shechem to fight against Abimelech. "Went out before" means that he was leading them toward the battle. "Shechem" is the city of Shechem.

Here the narrator is the author of the book of Judges. Gaal had spoken proudly against Abimelech, but Zebul, the governor of the city and loyal to Abimelech, threw his words back at him. He challenged Gaal to prove his courage. The Bible does not say that Gaal wanted to fight at that moment; what it shows is that his boasting left him with no way out. The result, as the story goes on, was his defeat.

For today: let us be careful about what we say in pride or anger, because afterward we will have to answer for it. It is better to speak with humility and seek peace than to promise what we cannot fulfill.
exp.1:2:
This verse says that God, because of Israel's disobedience, would no longer drive out the peoples who lived in Canaan. Those peoples would be a constant irritation to them, like a pain in the side. And their gods would be a trap, a snare in which Israel would fall when tempted to worship them.

The speaker is the angel of the LORD, a messenger who speaks on God's behalf. He comes to Bochim and confronts the people because they did not tear down the altars or avoid alliances with the inhabitants of the land, as God had commanded them. The consequences of that disobedience become real.

For today: what we tolerate and do not remove from our lives, even when it seems small, can end up binding us. Yet the people's weeping shows that God still receives a repentant heart. Today we can obey Him from the start and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.18:8:
This verse tells us that the Levite had already risen to leave with his concubine and his servant. But the young woman's father urges him to stay one more night. He tells him that the day is already drawing to a close, that is, the sun is about to set, and he begs him to rest and let his heart be merry. The phrase "your house" means his home, and the young woman is the daughter.

The one speaking is the father-in-law, who had already kept the Levite for several days with food and hospitality. He seems to want to enjoy his daughter's company a while longer and to take good care of his son-in-law. But the Levite refuses and leaves late, which leads him to look for lodging at night and into a very painful story. The Bible does not say that the father-in-law had bad intentions; his insistence seemed to be affection and courtesy.

For today: it invites us to think carefully about when to decide and when to set out. Hospitality is good, but it is also wise to make decisions with prudence, without rushing into situations that expose us to unnecessary risks.
exp.2:18:
Ehud, after delivering the tribute, turned back from the quarries near Gilgal and told King Eglon that he had a secret message for him. The king answered by telling everyone to be quiet, and he ordered all his attendants to leave. So Ehud was left alone with the king.

Ehud was a deliverer whom God raised up for Israel, since the people had been under the rule of Moab for years because of their sin. Using the excuse of carrying the tribute, Ehud looked for a way to get close to the king without arousing suspicion. Scholars do not fully agree on what those stone quarries near Gilgal were; some believe they were stones or carved images.

For today: Ehud was patient and knew how to wait for the right moment. Often God works through people who act with prudence rather than haste. We can ask Him for wisdom to know when to speak and when to wait.
exp.10:18:
This verse tells how Israel sent messengers to Sihon, king of the Amorites, who ruled from Heshbon. They asked for permission to pass through his land on the way to the place where they were going to settle. "Messengers" are men sent to speak on behalf of a people. Their request was made with respect, asking politely.

The one speaking is Jephthah, judge of Israel. He reminds the Ammonites how Israel came to that land after leaving Egypt. He wants to show that Israel did not seek a fight: first they asked for passage peacefully, as they had done with Edom and Moab. Sihon distrusted them and attacked, and the account says that God gave Israel the victory.

For today: before entering a conflict, try to speak with respect and seek peace. Asking humbly does not guarantee that the other person will agree, but it leaves the conscience at rest.
exp.19:32:
At the agreed moment, the whole army of Israel left the place where it had pretended to flee and lined up for battle at Baal-tamar. At the same time, the men hidden in ambush (groups that wait in concealment to attack by surprise) came out of their hiding place, out of the open field of Gibeah.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Israel was fighting against the tribe of Benjamin, which had protected the guilty men responsible for a terrible crime in Gibeah. Twice Israel had been defeated, so now it used a strategy: pretending to retreat in order to draw Benjamin away from its city. Some scholars note that the text summarizes the plan in a way that is somewhat hard to follow.

For today: even when we are right, fighting leaves pain behind. Before we act against others, it is wise to seek God with humility and to prepare ourselves with wisdom and patience.
exp.15:15:
It says that Delilah pressed Samson every day with her words and would not leave him alone. She insisted so much that Samson felt a distress so strong he could barely bear it. The phrase about her pressing him explains that she was badgering him with persistent insistence. Here "his soul was vexed unto death" means that his spirit was worn down, exhausted to the point of death.

The narrator is the author of the book of Judges. Delilah, paid by the Philistine lords, wanted to learn the secret of Samson's strength. She had already tried three times, and now she uses emotional pressure: "How can you say you love me?" Samson gives in shortly afterward and reveals his Nazirite vow.

For today: constant pressure can wear us down and make us give in on what we know is sacred. It is wise to surround ourselves with people who respect us, to set limits in time, and not to hand our heart over to someone who uses it to harm us.
exp.16:10:
The explanation says that the Levite agreed to stay and live with Micah, and that Micah treated him like a son. "Agreed" means he was in agreement, and "dwell" means to live.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Micah had in his house a shrine with idols, and he was looking for a Levite to be his priest. The young Levite was wandering without direction, looking for a place to live, and he accepted pay, clothing, and food. Judges repeats that in those days there was no king and everyone did what seemed right to them. So this scene shows a disorderly religion, shaped to suit each person.

For today: comfort and good company do not prove that something is right before God. Before accepting an opportunity, ask yourself whether it brings you closer to the Word of God or only meets your needs of the moment.
exp.1:21:
God says he left some nations in the land to test Israel. He wanted to see whether his people would follow the way of the Lord, that is, their manner of living and obeying, as their fathers had done, or whether they would not. The explanation of the word "prove" is simply to test, and the word "keep" here means to follow and practice.

God himself speaks, according to the account in the book of Judges. Israel had broken the covenant and disobeyed, so God decided not to drive out the nations that remained after the death of Joshua. The text presents these nations as a test to see the faithfulness of the people.

Today we can remember that trials and difficulties reveal what is in our hearts. Instead of blaming circumstances, we can ask God for help to follow him faithfully each day, even when it is not easy.
exp.4:3:
It says that when God went out of Seir, that is, out of the region of Edom south of Canaan, all of creation responded: the earth trembled and the sky let fall rain. The sentence about the word "dropped" is removed because it explains a word the reader does not see, and the verse's own wording covers the idea.

Here Deborah, together with Barak, speaks in a song of victory after defeating the army of Sisera. She begins by recalling how God acted in the past, near Sinai, to remind the people that the present victory comes from the same powerful God. Some think the rain also points to the storm that helped in the battle, but the text does not say this clearly.

For today: when you face something that seems too big, remember what God has done before. His faithfulness in the past encourages you to trust Him now and to give Him thanks.
exp.5:26:
This verse tells how Gideon gathered ten of his servants and did what the Lord had commanded him. But he was afraid of how his family and the people of the town would react, so he did it at night and not in broad daylight. The wooden pole or tree used in false worship is what the verse is about here; the word translated as "grove" in the King James Version is the one that refers to it.

God had ordered him to tear down the altar to Baal that belonged to his father and to offer a bull to the Lord. Israel was oppressed by Midian and had turned away from God. Gideon was still unsure of himself, but God was preparing him to free his people.

Obeying God does not always feel easy, and fear can stay with us. Gideon did not wait until he was completely brave; he obeyed while afraid. Take the step God shows you, even if your knees are shaking.
exp.0:21:
These verses say that the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, called "the house of Joseph" because they descended from his two sons, went up to attack the city of Bethel. The word "went up" is used because the region was hilly. Most importantly, "the Lord was with them": God accompanied them.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. After the death of Joshua, each tribe was to conquer the portion of land allotted to it. Just before this, a failure of Benjamin is recounted, who did not drive out the Jebusites. This verse contrasts with that: the house of Joseph acts, and the Lord is with them. However, the account that follows shows that they also used spies and careful planning.

For today: when you face a difficult task, plan wisely and take concrete steps, but first seek the presence of God. His companionship gives you more security than your own strength.
exp.5:36:
Gideon tells God that he will put a fleece, that is, a piece of sheep's wool, on the threshing floor, which is the open-air place where wheat was beaten out. If in the morning only the fleece is wet with dew and all the ground is dry, he will understand that God will indeed save Israel through him, just as he promised.

Gideon is the one speaking. God had already called him and had promised to free Israel from its oppressors. Now the enemy armies are drawing near, and Gideon has gathered people from several tribes. Even so, he feels fear and asks for a sign to confirm the promise.

For today: God invites us to trust what he has already told us in his Word. Gideon asked for a sign because of his weakness, and God was patient with him. But we do not need to keep asking for signs over and over. We can pray with sincerity, admit our fears, and move forward in faith, relying on the promises God has already given us.
exp.15:0:
It says Samson went to Gaza, a city of the Philistines, and there he saw a harlot, that is, a prostitute, and he had relations with her. The phrase "went in unto her" is an old way of speaking about sexual relations. The word "went" appears in the verse as "went," shown here as in the King James wording.

The narrator of the book of Judges tells this without softening it. Samson was a judge of Israel and had been set apart for God from his birth, yet here he acts according to his desires. The verses that follow show that the people of Gaza surrounded him to kill him, and that God, even so, gave him strength to escape. The text does not approve of his conduct; it shows his weakness and God's patience.

For today: God can use imperfect people, but that does not justify sin. It is wise to watch our steps and not toy with temptation, because it always brings consequences.
exp.12:18:
Manoah takes a young goat with a grain offering and offers them to the Lord on a rock, which served as an altar. Then the angel does something wonderful, a miracle, before the eyes of Manoah and his wife.

Manoah and his wife were expecting a son, Samson, and the angel had given them instructions for raising him. Manoah wanted to know the visitor's name so he could honor him, but the angel answered that his name was secret. The text does not fully explain the wonder; the next verse tells how the angel rose up in the flame.

For today: when God shows us his goodness, let us respond with gratitude and worship, even when we do not understand everything about him. We can trust what he reveals, without demanding that we have all the answers.
exp.6:19:
The explanation says that Gideon's three hundred men, divided into three companies, blew the trumpets and broke the pitchers that covered the torches. In their left hands they held the lamps, and in their right hands the trumpets, with which they blew. Then they cried out: "The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon!"

Gideon had given these instructions to his men. God had reduced the army to three hundred so that Israel would know that the victory came from Him. It was night, and the camp of Midian was surrounded. The confusion that followed was the work of God, not of human strength.

For today: God can use our simple obedience, even when it seems small or illogical. We do not have to be the strongest or the most numerous. It is enough to do with faith what He asks of us and to leave the result to Him.
exp.2:1:
This verse says that God left some peoples in the land so that the new generations of Israel would learn to fight. The phrase "so that at least the descendants might know" means that the descendants, the children and grandchildren, would have that experience. The word "at least" in the verse, which means "even if only," refers to those who had not lived through the earlier wars in Canaan.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks, explaining why enemy nations remained in the land. The generation that conquered Canaan with Joshua had already died. The younger people did not have that experience. The text says this also served to test whether Israel would obey the commandments of the Lord.

For today: difficulties can be a school of faith. God does not always remove right away what He asks of us, but in those challenges we can learn to trust Him and obey Him with greater firmness.
exp.12:16:
Manoah asks the angel of the Lord what his name is. He wants to know it so that he can honor him when the promise he gave them comes true.

Manoah and his wife had no children. The angel told them they would have a son, Samson. Manoah still did not understand that he was speaking with a messenger of God. That is why he treats him as a visitor and wants to thank him. The angel answers that his name is secret, and he directs attention toward the Lord through the sacrifice.

For today: when God gives us something, it is natural to want to give thanks. But gratitude should reach God himself, not stop at the messenger or at the gift. We can take a moment to thank him directly.
exp.19:14:
It says that the men of Benjamin were counted for war. Twenty-six thousand came out of the cities, all able to fight with the sword, and in addition seven hundred chosen men who lived in Gibeah.

The verse speaks of men who were able to fight, that is, skilled in battle. Men who were wicked and without moral worth are the ones the text describes as worthless and corrupt.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel had asked the people of Benjamin to hand over the wicked men of Gibeah, who had committed a terrible crime, so that they could be punished. Benjamin refused to listen to their brothers and chose instead to prepare for war. So one tribe ended up set against the others.

For today: when someone points out a wrong that needs to be corrected, it is easy to defend our own group and trust in our own strength. But misplaced loyalty leads to ruin. It is better to listen, to admit the mistake, and to seek justice with humility.
exp.10:8:
Jephthah answers the elders of Gilead with a careful question: if he goes back with them, fights against the Ammonites, and the Lord gives them the victory, will he really become their head, that is, their leader and ruler? The phrase "bring me home again" means "make me return." "Deliver them before me" means "hand them over to me." "Head" means leader.

Jephthah had been rejected by his brothers and driven out of his father's house because he was the son of another woman. Now Gilead was in danger from Ammon, and the same elders who had cast him out were looking for him. He does not accept their offer without more ado; he wants a clear promise. Notice that he recognizes that the victory depends on the Lord, not only on himself.

Today, when someone who hurt us comes looking for us out of need, we can ask for clarity and honesty without bitterness. And in any task, let us remember that success comes from God.
exp.16:11:
It says that Micah "consecrated" the Levite, that is, he officially set him apart to be his priest. That young man stayed on living in Micah's house and served him in the family's religious matters.

The book of Judges describes a disorderly time, and the text sums it up by saying that everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes. Micah had his own shrine with idols, and now he hired a Levite out of convenience. According to the law of Moses, priests were to be descendants of Aaron, and God was not to be worshiped with images. Micah believes that this way God will bless him, but he does it his own way and not according to what God had commanded.

For today: having religious things is not enough to please God. It is worth asking ourselves whether we worship Him as He says in His Word or as is comfortable for us.
exp.2:14:
After eighteen years under King Eglon, the people of Israel cried out to God for help. God raised up a deliverer for them: Ehud, the son of Gera, from the tribe of Benjamin. He is described as a man lefthanded, which is usually understood to mean he was left-handed, though this is not known for certain. The people of Israel sent a gift with him, which was the tribute they were required to pay to Eglon.

The narrator of the book of Judges explains that Israel had done evil in the sight of God, and for that reason they were brought under the rule of Moab and its allies. Here we see the pattern that repeats through the book: sin, oppression, crying out, and rescue.

For today: when you feel trapped by your mistakes or by a difficult situation, cry out to God with sincerity. He can use unexpected people and means to help you.
exp.6:24:
This verse tells how the men of Ephraim captured Oreb and Zeeb, two leaders of Midian. Oreb was killed at a place called "the rock of Oreb," and Zeeb was killed at "the winepress of Zeeb," which was the place where grapes were trodden. Then they kept pursuing the Midianites and brought the heads of both men to Gideon, on the other side of the Jordan.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Judges. Gideon had won with only three hundred men, and now he asked Ephraim for help to cut off the enemy's escape at the fords of the Jordan. The places took the names of these leaders, according to the account.

For today: God uses many people in one work. Gideon began it, but Ephraim also did its part. Respond promptly when someone asks you for help, without waiting to be first.
exp.4:8:
Deborah says that her heart is with the governors of Israel, that is, with the leaders who offered themselves willingly for the battle. At the end, she calls on everyone to bless the Lord. Where the explanation comments on the wording, it says that "governors" here means leaders or rulers, and that "offered themselves willingly" means they presented themselves freely, without anyone forcing them. "Bless ye the Lord" means "praise the Lord."

Deborah, a prophetess and judge, speaks in the song of victory that follows the defeat of Sisera's army. Before that, she describes a time of fear and neglect, when Israel had turned away from God. Now she acknowledges those who stepped forward and directs the praise toward God, not toward people.

For today: God delights in service given with joy. Think of a place where you can offer yourself willingly, in your church or your community, and do it wholeheartedly. When things go well, give thanks to God.
exp.14:6:
Samson speaks to the Philistines after they burned his wife and her father. In the old wording, he asks them: "Though ye have done this..." — that is, "Is this what you did?" He announces that he will take revenge on them and that after that he will stop, meaning he will then hold back.

Samson had been in conflict with the Philistines since they took his wife and gave her to another man. He burned their fields, and they answered by killing the woman and her father. Now Samson responds with even more violence. The Bible shows here a cycle of revenge, not an example that we should imitate.

For today: when someone hurts us, revenge promises to end the pain, but it almost always prolongs it. Let us ask God for help to forgive, to seek justice in a healthy way, and not to let anger make our decisions for us.
exp.10:39:
This verse says that in Israel it became a custom that, each year, the young women would go to mourn and lament for the daughter of Jephthah the Gileadite, for four days. "Lament" means to sing or express sorrow for a person who has died or been lost. "Maidens" are young girls.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. Jephthah had made a rash vow to God, and his daughter, the first to come out to greet him, was the one caught up in it. The text does not clearly explain what happened to her: some believe she was sacrificed, others that she was dedicated to live alone in the service of God. Believers have debated this for centuries. What is certain is that Israel remembered her grief.

For today: let us think before we promise something, especially before God. And let us learn to remember with respect and compassion those who suffer because of other people's decisions, without forgetting them.
exp.2:23:
It says that when Ehud had gone out, the servants of King Eglon came and saw that the doors of the room were locked. So they thought the king was covering his feet, an old expression that means he was relieving himself in private. The "summer chamber" was a cool, private room in the palace.

The king's servants speak. Ehud had killed Eglon, king of Moab, who oppressed Israel, and he had locked the doors when he left. The servants suspected nothing and, out of respect, they waited. That time allowed Ehud to escape. Some understand this as part of the deliverance God gave his people through Ehud.

For today: we sometimes draw quick conclusions without having all the information, and we get it wrong. Before assuming the worst or the best about a situation, it is wise to stop, ask questions, and pray for wisdom.
exp.7:10:
Gideon went up by the way of those who lived in tents, that is, nomadic people who wandered through the desert, to the east of Nobah and Jogbehah. There he attacked the enemy camp by surprise, for the army was secure, that is, confident and not expecting any danger.

This is what the narrator of the book of Judges tells us. Gideon pursued the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna, who had fled with about fifteen thousand men. He had already warned the people of Penuel that he would return. The exact location of his route through the desert is hard to pin down, and scholars do not fully agree on the details.

For today: Gideon finished what he had started, even when he was tired and the pursuit was difficult. May God give us perseverance to faithfully carry out what He has entrusted to us, and may we not lower our guard by trusting ourselves too much.
exp.8:51:
It says that Abimelech came to the tower of Thebez and attacked it. He went up to the door to burn it, because the people of the city had taken refuge inside. "Attacking it" means assaulting it, and "setting fire to it" means setting it on fire.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. Abimelech was the son of Gideon, and he had made himself king of Shechem by killing his brothers. He had already destroyed Shechem in the same way, by burning its tower. Now he repeats his method at Thebez. The account shows how his violence leads him to an end he himself does not control, and the Bible presents it as a judgment from God (vv. 56-57).

For today: whoever trusts in force and pride to get their way may fall in the most unexpected manner. Let us seek to serve with humility and justice, and not with ambition.
exp.1:22:
God allowed some nations to remain in the land of Canaan. He did not drive them out quickly, and he did not hand them over to Joshua to be defeated. The word "hastily" means done quickly, without delay. The phrase "without driving them out" means not forcing them out completely.

This verse closes the narrator's comment in Judges 2. Earlier, God had said that he would no longer drive out those nations, because Israel had broken the covenant. God left them to test whether the people would keep to the path their fathers had walked. Some see discipline here and others see a test; both ideas appear in the text.

For today: the difficulties God allows can show us what is in our hearts. Instead of only asking why something remains, we can ask him for help to stay faithful to him in the middle of the trial.
exp.5:17:
Gideon asks the visitor not to leave yet. He wants to bring out a "present," that is, an offering or gift of hospitality, and set it before him. The visitor replies that he will wait until Gideon returns.

Gideon speaks with the angel of the LORD, who is calling him to deliver Israel from the Midianites. Gideon feels small and unsure, so he asked for a sign to be certain that it was God who was speaking. His present is a way of worshiping and of testing what he is seeing. Then the angel uses that offering as the sign.

When we doubt, we can speak with God honestly and respectfully, without hiding our questions. He is patient with those who seek him. Even so, it is good to respond with humility, preparing the heart to listen and obey.
exp.8:42:
Abimelech, it says, took his men and divided them into three groups. He set ambushes in the field, that is, he hid soldiers so they could attack by surprise. When he saw that the people of Shechem were coming out of the city, he rose up against them and struck them down. The verse says he took the people and divided them, and that he struck them; in the wording the reader sees, "divided" and "smote" are the words to notice.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Abimelech was the son of Gideon, and he had made himself king by violence, killing his brothers. Now Shechem had rebelled against him. The passage shows how the curse that Jotham had announced comes to pass: the violence and betrayal turned back on them.

For today: God sees the evil that is done through deceit and ambition. Whoever seeks power by trampling on others ends up reaping destruction. It is wise to seek what is just and to trust God, not force or cunning.
exp.4:23:
This verse says that Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, is highly blessed, more than all the women who live in tents. "Blessed" here means praised and favored by God. "Kenite" refers to a nomadic people who lived in tents.

The one speaking is Deborah, together with Barak, in a song of victory after Israel defeated Sisera's army. Deborah celebrates that Jael brought down the enemy commander, while others, such as those of Meroz, did not help. Some scholars point out that the way Jael acted, with deception and violence, is a difficult account, and the text does not say that God approves all of her methods, but that it praises her courage.

For today: God calls us not to stay silent or passive when what is right needs defending. Ask him for wisdom to act with courage, but with integrity and love.
exp.5:8:
God reminds the Israelites that he rescued them from slavery in Egypt and also from other peoples who mistreated them. Moreover, he drove those enemies out of the land and gave it to Israel. The phrase "drave them out" means that he expelled them so that Israel could enter.

A prophet, whose name is not mentioned, speaks on behalf of the LORD. Israel was suffering under the Midianites and cried out to God. Before sending a deliverer, God reminds them of his past faithfulness. He then points out that they had not obeyed him, since they were following the ways of the gods of the Amorites.

For today: when you go through a difficulty, remember how God helped you before. That strengthens your trust and encourages you to obey him, giving him the place that belongs to him in your life.
exp.7:27:
This verse says that the Midianites were defeated and left without strength before Israel. The word "subdued" means defeated and brought under control. "Lifted up their heads" means regaining power or daring to attack again. After that victory, the land had peace for forty years while Gideon lived.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is summing up the result of Gideon's victory. But the preceding context shows a sad contrast: Gideon made an ephod from the gold that was gathered, and the people turned aside after it. An ephod was a sacred garment; the Bible does not explain in detail its purpose here, but it calls it a snare.

For today: God can give us victories and peace, but afterward we must guard the heart. Let what we receive from God not become a stumbling block or take the place of God Himself.
exp.8:36:
Gaal speaks again and says that he sees people coming down through the middle of the land, and that a group of soldiers is coming by the way of the plain of Meonenim. "Again" simply means "once more." A "company" is an armed group, a band of soldiers. About "Meonenim," some think it refers to a place known for a tree, and others translate it as "the diviners' oak"; it is not known for certain.

Gaal speaks with Zebul, the ruler of the city of Shechem, who was secretly supporting Abimelech. Gaal had challenged Abimelech with bold words. Now, seeing that real danger was approaching, Zebul deceived him with his words, and Gaal could no longer deny what he saw: the army was coming toward him.

For today: be careful about speaking with great confidence and pride. When trials come, our words are exposed. It is better to live with humility and to choose well whom we trust.
exp.12:20:
This verse says that the angel of the Lord did not appear again to Manoah or to his wife.

The narrator goes on to describe what happened after the angel announced the birth of Samson. Manoah had offered a sacrifice, and the angel rose up in the flame of the altar. Until that moment, Manoah had not understood who he was. His wife, by contrast, seems to have trusted more from the beginning. Some scholars see in this angel a messenger sent by God; others think it is a special appearance of God himself. The Bible does not make this entirely clear here.

For today: sometimes we only understand late how God has been at work. It is fitting to respond with worship and humility, and to remember that he is faithful even when we did not recognize it right away.
exp.19:46:
This verse tells that, out of the whole tribe of Benjamin, only six hundred men managed to escape. They fled into the wilderness, to a rock called Rimmon, and stayed there for four months. The word "rock" in this verse means a high, rugged place that is hard to attack.

It is part of the civil war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, which had defended men guilty of a terrible crime in Gibeah. The narrator of the book recounts these events without fully approving of them; the book shows a time of great violence, when everyone did what seemed right in their own eyes. These six hundred are the survivors who will later allow the tribe to continue.

For today: when sin is not corrected in time, its consequences can be very painful for everyone. We should seek justice with humility, and not let pride or misplaced loyalty lead us to defend what is wrong.
exp.19:39:
This verse describes the key moment of the battle. When the flame began to rise up out of the city (Gibeah) with a pillar of smoke, the men of Benjamin looked back and saw that all the fire of the city was rising up to heaven.

It is part of the account of the war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, after the terrible crime committed in Gibeah. The author of the book is the one telling the story. The Israelites pretended to flee in order to draw Benjamin away from the city, while an ambush set it on fire. The smoke was the agreed signal. Benjamin believed it was winning, but it had fallen into the trap.

For today: confidence in oneself can blind us. Benjamin only looked at its apparent victory and did not see the danger behind it. It is good to stop, look with humility, and ask ourselves whether we have set aside justice and the guidance of God.
exp.0:16:
Judah went with his brother Simeon, and together they attacked the Canaanites who lived in Zephath. They completely destroyed the city and changed its name to Hormah, a name connected with the idea of being utterly destroyed or devoted to destruction.

This is part of the book of Judges, which tells how the tribes of Israel took possession of the promised land after the death of Joshua. Judah and Simeon had agreed to help each other in the conquest (Judges 1:3). The text does not say who is speaking; it is the narrator showing that, at the beginning, obedience and unity brought victories.

For today: we do not move forward alone. God gives us brothers and sisters in the faith to help us face our battles. Find someone with whom you can pray and walk together in what is hard for you today.
exp.0:18:
It says that God was with the tribe of Judah and helped them drive out the peoples who lived in the mountains. But they could not drive out those who lived in the plains, that is, in the flat lands, because they had chariots that were "reinforced," meaning war chariots reinforced with iron.

The narrator of the book of Judges tells how the tribes of Israel kept conquering Canaan after the death of Joshua. The text does not fully explain why Judah could not overcome the people of the plains. Some think it was a lack of faith, others that it was a military limitation. What it does show is that the conquest was left incomplete.

For today: God is with us, but we should not let the fear of the "chariots of iron" in life hold us back. When something seems too big for us, let us trust in God and keep moving forward in faith.
exp.17:16:
The explanation says that the five men of the tribe of Dan, who had earlier gone out to explore the land, came back and went into Micah's house. There they took the religious objects: a carved image, the ephod (a priest's garment used to seek God's guidance), the teraphim (household figures or idols), and a cast metal image (made of molten metal). Meanwhile, the priest was standing at the gate with the six hundred armed men.

Here the narrator speaks. It is a disordered time in Israel, when each person did whatever seemed right to them. The Danites were looking for territory and wanted to secure a religion of their own. They used force and distracted the Levite priest so they could take what was not theirs.

For today: let us not seek God by shortcuts, or by things we can control or take by force. Let us worship God as He has asked, and not use faith to justify what is unjust.
exp.12:12:
The angel of the Lord answered Manoah that his wife should be careful about everything he had already told her. The phrase "let her beware" means that she must avoid or stay away from certain things. "The Lord" is the name of God, and "the angel of the Lord" is a messenger sent by Him.

Manoah and his wife were expecting a child, who would be Samson. The angel had already given instructions to the woman, and Manoah, concerned about raising the boy well, asked that they be repeated to him. The angel adds nothing new: he points back to what had already been said, and then explains the details, such as not drinking wine or eating anything unclean.

For today: when God has already shown us the way, we do not always need more information, but obedience. We can ask ourselves what God's Word has already told us and begin to put it into practice faithfully.
exp.5:37:
He said that God did what Gideon asked. When Gideon got up early, he wrung the fleece and squeezed out enough dew to fill a bowl with water.

The fleece is the wool from a sheep, and the threshing floor is the place where grain was beaten out. "And it was so" means "it happened just like that."

Gideon was called to deliver Israel from their oppressors, the Midianites. Although God had already spoken to him, he still hesitated and asked for a sign with the fleece. The Bible tells this without presenting it as a model to follow. Some see it as a weakness of faith, others as humility. Even so, God answered with patience.

For today: when you have doubts, bring them honestly to God. But do not depend only on signs; also seek his Word, prayer, and the wise counsel of other believers.
exp.8:12:
The explanation says that the vine, when the trees ask her to be their queen, refuses. She values her new wine, that is, the juice of the grape, which brings joy to God and to people. She does not want to trade that useful task for a position of power over the other trees.

Jotam, the youngest son of Gideon, tells this fable to the people of Shechem. They had made Abimelech king, and he had killed his brothers to reign. Jotam uses the trees to show that good and fruitful people did not seek the throne, and that the one who did want it was someone who knew only how to harm.

For today: value the good gifts God has given you to serve, even if they bring you no fame or authority. Being useful and faithful is worth more than rising in position at any cost.
exp.10:29:
It says that Jephthah, before going into battle, made a solemn promise to God. A "vow" was a commitment someone made before the Lord, promising to give something if God granted what they asked. Here Jephthah asks that God deliver the Ammonites into his hands, that is, that God give him victory over them.

Jephthah, judge of Israel, had already tried to settle the conflict with words, but the king of Ammon would not listen. The Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and even so he added this vow. The text does not say that God asked for it. What Jephthah promised afterward has been much debated, and interpreters understand it in different ways.

For today: when we ask something of God, let us do it with confidence, but with humility, and think carefully before making promises in haste. God does not need us to bargain for his help; we can trust in his grace.
exp.2:15:
Ehud made himself a dagger with two edges, a cubit long (about 45 centimeters, though the exact Hebrew measure is debated). The phrase about Ehud fastening it at his waist, hidden under his clothing on the right side, is what the verse describes.

The one who tells the story is the narrator of the book of Judges. Israel had been oppressed for eighteen years by Eglon, king of Moab, and had cried out to God. God raised up Ehud as a deliverer. He was left-handed or had limited use of his right hand, and so a weapon on that side might not raise suspicion. The text describes what happened; it does not tell us we should imitate it.

For today: God can use someone who has limitations and does not fit what is expected. When you feel you are not enough, cry out to God, prepare yourself with wisdom, and trust that He can work through you.
exp.2:25:
The explanation describes how, while the servants of King Eglon waited outside, unwilling to open the door, Ehud used that time to escape. He passed beyond the place of the carved stones (some understand these to have been carved images or boundary stones near Gilgal; the Hebrew term is interpreted in several ways) and reached Seirath safely, a place whose exact location is not known, in the hill country of Ephraim.

The narrator tells how God used Ehud to deliver Israel from Moab, which had oppressed them for eighteen years. The servants assumed the king was in private, so the waiting gave Ehud an advantage. His escape opened the way for the call to arms that follows.

For today: trust that God works even in small details, such as a delay, and then act with decision, rather than freezing when he opens the way.
exp.19:37:
This verse says that the men of Israel and the men hidden in the ambush had agreed on a sign. The men in the ambush were to make a great fire, so that a large column of smoke would rise up from the city of Gibeah.

It is part of the account of the war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, after the terrible crime committed in Gibeah. The narrator explains Israel's plan: to make Benjamin believe it was winning, as it had the previous time, and then to surprise them. The smoke would signal that the city had already been taken.

For today: this passage reminds us how dangerous it is to trust in an apparent victory without looking at the whole situation. It also invites us to be humble and to ask God to show us what we cannot see.
exp.15:25:
Samson asks the young man who is leading him by the hand to bring him close to the pillars that hold up the building. He wants to feel them and lean against them.

Samson speaks as a blind prisoner of the Philistines. They had brought him out of prison to mock him at a feast in honor of their god. His request seems simple, but it sets up what follows: his prayer to God for strength one last time. The Bible does not say whether the young man understood what Samson intended to do.

For today: even when we have failed and feel weak or humbled, we can return to God. He can use our last resort, and the best thing is to lean on Him with humility.
exp.8:33:
He says that Abimelech rose up by night with all his people and set an ambush against the city of Shechem. He divided his men into four groups to surround the city. The word "ambush" means hiding in order to attack by surprise, and the word for "companies" means groups or squads of soldiers.

The plan came from Zebul, an officer of Shechem loyal to Abimelech, who sent him word in secret. Shechem had turned against Abimelech and was supporting Gaal. Zebul advised him to attack at dawn, when Gaal went out. The account shows violence and revenge in a time of disorder in Israel.

For today: this passage reminds us that ambition and violence bring more violence. We can ask God to help us resolve conflicts with humility, without deceit or revenge, seeking peace with others.
exp.6:4:
God brings the people down to the water to test them. He tells Gideon to set apart those who lap up the water with their tongue, the way a dog does, and also those who kneel down to drink. "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "proclaim" means to announce aloud. The text that follows makes clear that those who lapped did so by bringing water to their mouths with their hand.

God speaks to Gideon, who is about to fight against the Midianites. Twenty-two thousand men had already gone home out of fear, and ten thousand remained. God says that these are still too many, so that Israel will not boast that it won by its own strength. It is not known for certain why this test distinguishes the soldiers; it has been interpreted in several ways.

Today: when you face something that is bigger than you, remember that God does not need your abundance of resources. Do what you can faithfully, and trust that the victory comes from Him.
exp.5:33:
The Spirit of God came upon Gideon with power, as if he were putting on a garment. "Clothed" is an old way of saying that it covered him, and wrapped him around. Then Gideon sounded the horn, which was used to call people to war, and the family of Abiezer, his clan, came out and followed him.

The account is told by the narrator of the book of Judges. Midianites, Amalekites and peoples from the east had crossed the Jordan and camped in the valley of Jezreel to attack Israel. Gideon, who had already torn down the altar of Baal, now receives strength from God to lead the people. He goes from being a fearful man to being a leader.

For today: when God calls you to something difficult, it does not depend on your own strength, but on his Spirit. Take the step of obedience that lies before you, even if you feel small, and trust that God is with you and will give you what you need.
exp.9:7:
This verse tells that the Philistines and the Ammonites oppressed Israel severely for eighteen years. "Vexed and oppressed" means that they crushed and mistreated them without mercy. The suffering was hardest for the Israelites who lived east of the Jordan River, in the region of Gilead, a land where the Amorites had once lived.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks, not with a personal voice but by summarizing the story. He explains that this oppression came after Israel forsook the LORD and served many false gods. The book shows a cycle: the people turn away from God, suffer the consequences, and then cry out asking for help.

For today: when we give first place to things that are not God, they end up enslaving us. If you are tired of burdens you have brought on yourself, you can return to God with humility and sincerity, because He still listens to those who cry out.
exp.0:30:
This verse says that the tribe of Asher did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in several cities: Accho, Zidon, Ahlab, Achzib, Helbah, Aphik, and Rehob. The verse's wording refers to them as the inhabitants of those cities.

It is the narrator of the book of Judges who speaks (we do not know for certain who wrote it). He describes how, after the death of Joshua, the tribes did not finish the conquest. God had commanded them not to live alongside those peoples, and here we see only partial obedience. This prepares the account of the spiritual problems that come later in the book. Some of these cities lay on the northern coast, near Zidon.

For today: What we leave unresolved can grow and affect us. Let us ask God for the courage to face honestly whatever we know we must let go of, rather than getting used to living with it.
exp.17:6:
These five spies from the tribe of Dan came to Laish and found a people who were calm, carefree, and undefended. "Idle" here means without activity or alarm, and "secure" means they felt safe. They lived like the Sidonians, but they were far from them and had no dealings with anyone, so no one would come to their aid. No one held authority over them or troubled them.

The narrator describes how the Danites, who had not taken the land allotted to them, were looking for a place to settle. These five men had asked the priest of Micah for a word from God, and he gave them a reassuring answer. However, the book shows a time of great religious disorder, and it does not say that God approved of everything they did.

For today: let us not confuse an easy opportunity with the will of God. Before deciding, it is wise to pray, examine the Bible, and seek wise counsel.
exp.4:10:
Now that the danger has passed, at the watering places where people go for water, they will recount the righteous acts and victories of the Lord. The words for "archers" and "watering places" in the explanation describe, respectively, those who shoot arrows and places where animals are given water to drink. "Villages" refers to unwalled settlements. Then the people will return to the city gates, where judgment was given and agreements were made.

Deborah, together with Barak, sings this song of victory over the Canaanites. Before this, the fear of enemies and their arrows made the roads and the wells unsafe. Now there is peace to return to daily life. Some scholars translate the word for "archers" differently, because the Hebrew is difficult, but the central idea is the same.

Today we can make everyday conversations a place to remember what God has done. Tell someone this week, simply, how He helped you.
exp.7:6:
Gideon promises that, when God gives him victory over Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian, he will punish the leaders of Succoth. Here "tear" means to beat or tear apart, the way grain was threshed. The "thorns" are plants with hard, sharp spines. "Delivered into my hand" means that God would give him the win over them.

Gideon and his 300 men were exhausted, pursuing the enemy kings. He asked the people of Succoth for bread, but they refused with mockery, because they doubted he would win. Gideon answers with anger and a harsh threat. The text tells us what he said and then what he did, but it does not say that God ordered that revenge.

Today we can learn to help those who are tired from serving, without waiting to see results. We should also take care with our reactions: anger, even when justified, can lead us to excess.
exp.13:2:
Sansón's parents challenge him: is there no woman among your own people, that you have to go looking for a wife among the uncircumcised Philistines, that is, those who did not share the sign of God's covenant? Samson insists: "Get her for me, for she pleases me well." Put plainly, he liked her.

His parents speak out of concern for their son's faith and identity, since the law warned against marrying into neighboring peoples who worshiped other gods. The following verse says that God was using this to act against the Philistines, who were dominating Israel. That does not mean everything about Samson's conduct was good.

For today: before deciding something important, such as marriage, do not be guided only by what attracts you. Listen to the counsel of wise people, and ask God what He wants for your life.
exp.17:10:
Six hundred men of the tribe of Dan set out from Zorah and Eshtaol, two towns in their own territory. They went "armed with weapons of war", that is, ready to fight. This was the start of their journey to conquer a new place to live.

Earlier, five Danite scouts had looked over the region of Laish, in the north, and came back urging their brothers to take it. They said God had handed it into their hands. The account in the book of Judges shows a disordered time, and not everything they do here is presented as an example to follow. The Bible does not make clear that God commanded this advance.

We can learn not to act simply because others encourage us with confident words. Before taking a big step, it is wise to pray, to seek God's guidance in his Word, and to ask ourselves whether our decision is just.
exp.17:21:
Judges 18:22 says that when the men of the tribe of Dan were already a good distance from Micah's house, the men who lived in the houses near Micah's home gathered together and went out to chase after them. Here "went after them" is the sense of the phrase. The "houses near" were the homes of the neighbors in that place.

The one telling the story is the narrator of the book of Judges. The Danites, who were looking for a territory to settle, had just taken Micah's religious objects (the ephod, the household idols, and the carved image) and also his priest. The neighbors react to help Micah and recover what was his. The text does not approve the theft or the idolatry; it simply recounts a time of disorder.

For today: what we build with our own hands to feel secure can be taken from us in a moment. It is wise to place our trust in God, who cannot be stolen or made by human hands.
exp.19:4:
The Levite tells how the men of Gibeah rose against him and surrounded the house at night, intending to kill him. He says they abused his concubine (a secondary wife) with such violence that she died. Here "oppressed" describes brutal abuse.

The Levite is speaking before the tribes gathered at Mizpah. He wants Israel to judge the crime of Gibeah. But his account is partial: according to chapter 19, he himself handed the woman over to the mob, and here he leaves that out. His version seeks to win the people's support.

For today: before judging or acting on what someone tells us, let us hear the whole story and seek the truth honestly. Also, let us care for and defend the vulnerable, rather than protecting ourselves.
exp.3:14:
It was God himself who brought Sisera, his chariots and his whole army to defeat. "Discomfited" means that he scattered them and filled them with confusion. "With the edge of the sword" means that they were defeated in battle. Sisera got down from his chariot and fled away on foot.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Judges. Deborah, a prophetess of Israel, had just encouraged Barak to attack, assuring him that God was going before him. Israel was oppressed by Jabin, and Sisera was his military commander with nine hundred iron chariots. The text credits the victory to God, not to Israel's strength.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, move forward with obedience and trust. God can work in ways you do not expect, and the glory belongs to him.
exp.16:9:
Micah makes the Levite an offer: stay in his house and be like a father and priest to him. In return, he will pay him ten shekels of silver a year (a shekel was a unit of weight for silver), his usual clothing, and his food. The Levite agrees and stays.

This happens in the time of the judges, when, according to the book, "everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes." Micah already had his own shrine with idols. The Levites were meant to serve in the worship God had established, not in a private shrine. Here Micah hires the Levite to lend legitimacy to his religion, and the Levite lets himself be guided by convenience.

For today: let us be careful not to use God to back up what we already want to do. And if we serve God, let it not be only for comfort or gain, but out of obedience to his Word.
exp.16:1:
Here Micah confesses to his mother that he was the one who had taken the eleven hundred shekels of silver that had been stolen from her. Because the mother had cursed the thief out loud, he becomes afraid and gives the money back. Instead of rebuking him, she blesses him in the name of the LORD. The word "taken" means that the silver was stolen from her, and "shekels" were a unit of weight used for silver.

The book of Judges describes a time of spiritual disorder, when "everyone did what was right in his own eyes." Micah confesses perhaps out of fear of the curse, and it is not clear that there was any deep repentance. The mother's blessing sounds pious, but what follows is the making of an image, something God had forbidden.

For today: confessing a wrong is good, but our faith needs to obey the Word of God, not merely use religious words. Let us examine whether what we do "for God" truly pleases Him.
exp.19:6:
Here the speaker says to all the gathered Israelites: "Now you are all present; give your opinion and your advice." The phrase "give here your advice and counsel" means "give here your opinion and propose what to do." It is an invitation to decide together.

The one speaking is the Levite whose concubine was abused and killed in Gibeah, a city of Benjamin. He tells his version of what happened before the assembly of Israel. Notice that his account has its own emphases, and it does not mention that he himself handed the woman over to her attackers. The story takes place in a time of great violence and moral disorder.

For today: before reacting to an injustice, it is wise to seek advice and listen calmly. But we should also ask for wisdom to weigh all the facts, and not let ourselves be carried away by only one version or by anger.
exp.7:9:
This verse tells us where the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, were. They were in Karkor with about fifteen thousand soldiers, all that was left of the huge army of the peoples from the east. Earlier, one hundred and twenty thousand men who drew the sword, that is, armed warriors, had been killed.

The narrator is speaking. Gideon had been pursuing the Midianites with three hundred weary men, and two cities, Succoth and Penuel, had refused to give them bread. This detail shows how hard the task was: the enemy still far outnumbered them. Even so, God had already given great victories. The Bible does not explain the exact location of Karkor, and scholars do not fully agree on it.

For today: do not give up halfway through the road just because what remains looks large. If God has helped you this far, you can keep going with faith and patience, taking the next step with Him.
exp.8:45:
When the people of the tower of Shechem heard that Abimelech had destroyed the city, they ran to take refuge in the strongest part of the house of Berith. The word "hold" here means a fortified place, a safe refuge inside the temple.

The narrator tells this within the story of Abimelech, son of Gideon, who made himself king by killing his brothers. The leaders of Shechem had supported him, and then they rebelled against him. Now he attacks them. These people sought protection in the temple of Baal-berith (Judges 9:4), a false god. Scholars do not know exactly what that building looked like.

For today: when trouble comes, we tend to run to whatever is at hand, such as money, influence, or other things. But only God is a safe refuge. Let us learn to turn to Him first.
exp.2:10:
After the victory that God gave through Othniel, the land had peace for forty years. Then Othniel died. The phrase "the land had rest" means there was calm, without wars. "Forty years" may be an exact number or a way of saying a full generation; the Bible does not make this clear.

The narrator of the book tells the story of the judges. Israel had disobeyed, suffered oppression, cried out to God, and God sent Othniel as a deliverer. This verse closes that cycle. But the text that follows shows that, once Othniel was gone, the people went back to doing evil. The peace depended greatly on his leadership.

For today: thank God for times of peace and do not take them for granted. Let your faith not depend only on one person, but on your own relationship with God, so that it stays firm even when circumstances change.
exp.5:31:
That day Gideon was given a new name: Jerubbaal. The name is understood to mean "let Baal plead against him," that is, "let Baal defend himself" or "let Baal bring his case." The verb in that phrase is an older form, meaning "let him contend" or "let him dispute the matter."

The speaker is the biblical narrative, which repeats the words of Joash, Gideon's father. The people of the town wanted to kill Gideon because he pulled down the altar of Baal, a false god. Joash challenged them: if Baal is truly a god, let him defend himself. The new name recalls that challenge. Scholars agree on the basics, though some debate the exact meaning of the name.

For today: you do not need to defend God with violence or fear. You can stand firm in your faith with calm and confidence, and let the truth speak for itself, while you obey with courage and humility.
exp.8:49:
Judges 9:50 tells us that Abimelech, after destroying the tower of Shechem, went to a city called Thebez. There he surrounded it with his army, attacked it, and captured it. "Encamped against" means surrounding a city so that no one can go in or out, and so forcing it to surrender. "Took it" means he captured it.

This is the account from the book of Judges. Abimelech was the son of Gideon, and he had made himself king of Shechem by killing his brothers. He had already burned the stronghold of Shechem with a thousand people inside. Now, with the same violence, he attacks Thebez. The narrator does not approve of this; he shows how power gained through wickedness keeps bringing destruction. The exact details of why he attacked Thebez are not explained.

For today: unlimited ambition is never satisfied, and it ends up harming many people. Let us ask God for a humble heart that serves and does not seek to dominate.
exp.13:16:
She wept before Samson the whole seven days of the wedding feast. On the seventh day he gave in and explained the riddle to her, because she pressed him hard, she kept at him and would not let up. Then she told the answer to her own people.

Samson had set a riddle for the Philistine guests. They could not solve it, and they threatened his wife, who was from that people. She used her tears and her complaint that he did not love her to get the answer out of him, and so she betrayed his trust.
