Today, constant pressure can push us to give in on things we know we should not. Let us ask for wisdom to keep what has been entrusted to us, and take care not to manipulate others with guilt or tears to get what we want.
exp.8:17:
This verse accuses the men of Shechem of a grave wrong. It says they rose up against the household of Gideon (Jerubbaal), killed seventy of his sons on one stone, and made Abimelech, the son of Gideon's female servant, king over them, only because he was their relative.

The one speaking is Jotham, the only son of Gideon who escaped with his life. From Mount Gerizim he shouts this to the people of Shechem after telling them a parable. He wants them to see that their treatment of Gideon's family was betrayal, not gratitude or justice.

For today: loyalty and gratitude matter. If someone has done us good, we should not repay them with harm, nor support violence out of convenience or because of family ties. Let us ask God for the courage to act with truth and integrity.
exp.7:33:
This verse says that the people of Israel forgot the LORD their God. It is not only that the thought slipped their minds: they stopped keeping Him present in their lives. And they forgot Him even though He had rescued them from all the enemies that surrounded them. The word "delivered" in the verse means saved or rescued.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges. He explains what happened when Gideon died, the leader who had led the people to defeat their enemies. Without their leader, Israel returned to idolatry and took Baal-berith as their god. The text shows that ingratitude toward God also led to ingratitude toward Gideon's family.

For today: remembering often what God has done for us helps us remain faithful, especially in times of change. We can thank Him every day and tell others how He has helped us.
exp.2:22:
Ehud went out through the porch and shut the doors of the parlour behind him. Here "parlour" is the cool room where King Eglon was, and "porch" is a Hebrew word that some translate as vestibule or corridor; it is not known with certainty.

The narrator tells how Ehud, judge of Israel, had just killed Eglon, king of Moab, who oppressed the people. By shutting the doors, he kept them from discovering the deed right away and gained time to escape. The story shows how God delivered Israel through an unexpected man, left-handed and of little renown.

For today: God can use people who seem ordinary to face great problems. This account describes what happened; it does not command us to use violence. What we can learn is to act with courage, wisdom, and trust in God when we face injustice.
exp.8:14:
Here a thorny shrub, the bramble (a wild rose bush, also called a brier), answers the trees that want it as their king. It says: "If you really choose me, come and take shelter under my shadow." But it also warns: if not, fire will come out of the bramble and burn even the cedars of Lebanon, the largest and strongest trees. The phrase "take shelter" simply means to put yourselves in safety.

The one speaking is Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon (Jerubbaal). He tells this fable from Mount Gerizim to criticize the people of Shechem, who had made Abimelech king after he killed his brothers. The good trees, like the vine, refused to reign; the bramble, which hardly gives any shade, represents Abimelech, who threatens to destroy.

For today: let us be wary of anyone who promises protection but governs with threats. Let us seek leaders who are humble and of good character, and let us be that way ourselves.
exp.12:7:
Manoah speaks to God with respect and humility. He asks that the man of God who appeared earlier come again. He wants him to teach them how they should raise the child who is going to be born.

Manoah is the husband of a woman who could not have children. She told him that a messenger of God announced the birth of a son, who would be a Nazarite, that is, set apart for God. Manoah did not see the visitor, so he prays to receive direction. The text does not say that he doubted his wife, although some readers interpret it that way.

When we receive a great responsibility, such as raising children or serving in something important, it is wise to pray first and ask God for guidance. Recognizing that we need direction is not weakness, but wisdom and humility.
exp.14:15:
Samson composes a short song or verse about his victory. There is a play on words: in the original language, the words for "donkey" and "heaps" sound very similar, and for this reason some translate it as "with the jawbone of a donkey, I have piled them in heaps." The jawbone is the bone of the lower jaw. He says that with that bone he defeated a thousand men.

He speaks after the Philistines came to Lehi to capture him. His own countrymen from Judah had handed him over, bound. Then the Spirit of the LORD came upon him, the ropes fell off his arms, and he fought with whatever he found at hand. The following verse shows that he acknowledges the deliverance came from God.

For today: God can use the little and the common things we have. But let us not forget to give Him the credit and to depend on Him, because Samson soon admitted his thirst and cried out to the LORD.
exp.6:18:
This verse tells how Gideon and his hundred men came to the edge of the enemy camp, just as the middle watch of the night was beginning, when the guards had only just changed shifts. Then they blew the trumpets, and they broke the clay jars they were carrying in their hands. Inside those jars, according to the account, they had hidden the torches.

It is part of the story of Gideon, whom God called to rescue Israel from the Midianites. God reduced his army to only 300 men so that it would be clear the victory came from Him. Here Gideon sets the example, and his men follow it, carrying out the plan God had given him.

For today: God can work through small resources and plans that seem strange, when we follow them with obedience. Do today, in faith, what He asks of you, even when it seems like very little.
exp.8:40:
Abimelech stayed in Arumah, a place near Shechem. Meanwhile, Zebul, the ruler of the city, threw out Gaal and his brothers so that they would no longer live there. "Thrust out" means that he drove them out by force. The phrase "that they should not dwell" means that they should not live or stay there.

The narrator of the book of Judges describes how Gaal had just lost a battle against Abimelech. Zebul was loyal to Abimelech and had been in conflict with Gaal. Seeing him weakened, he took the chance to drive him out of the city. The story shows a time of violence and betrayal, where the ambition for power brings division and pain.

Today we can remember that whoever relies on force or pride ends up falling. Let us seek to serve with humility, without fighting for power, and trust that God is the one who truly sustains.
exp.13:15:
Here the wife of Samson weeps and accuses him of not loving her, because he does not explain the riddle to her. "You hate me" means "you have rejected me." "Declare" means to explain or reveal. Samson answers that he has not told it even to his father and mother, so he will not tell her either.

The speaker is the Philistine woman whom Samson was marrying, during the wedding feast. Her countrymen had threatened to burn her and her family if she did not find out the answer. She uses tears and guilt to pressure him. Samson resists, but afterward he gives in.

For today: true love is not proven by demanding everything or manipulating with tears or fear. We also must take care whom we trust with what matters to us. Let us ask God for wisdom to be sincere, but also firm, without giving in to pressure.
exp.14:11:
Here the men of Judah tell Samson that they have come down to tie him up and hand him over to the Philistines. Samson does not resist right away; instead, he asks them for a promise: that they themselves will not attack him.

The three thousand men of Judah speak, frightened because the Philistines were ruling over them. They prefer to hand Samson over rather than face a conflict with their oppressors. Samson, for his part, wants to make sure his own people will not harm him. Later it will be seen that God acts with power in him.

For today: sometimes fear leads us to give in to pressure and let go of the one God has used. Let us pray for the courage to act with justice and to trust God, instead of seeking comfort alone.
exp.0:35:
This verse says that the territory of the Amorites extended from the "ascent of Akrabbim," a mountain pass, and from "the rock," upward. "Border" means frontier or boundary. Some think "the rock" is a place called Sela, but it is not known for certain where it was.

The author of the book, who is not named, summarizes how the conquest of the promised land was going. Several tribes had not finished driving out the peoples who lived there. The Amorites even pressed the tribe of Dan so that it could not go down into the valleys. This verse marks how far Amorite control reached.

For today: what we leave unfinished can grow and limit us. If there is something God has asked you to face, such as a bad habit or a pending decision, do not postpone it. Ask Him for strength and take one concrete step today.
exp.16:3:
This verse tells how Micah returned the money to his mother. She took two hundred shekels of silver (a quantity of silver measured by weight) and gave them to the founder, the craftsman who melts metal. With them he made a carved image and a cast image (made of molten metal), and they were placed in Micah's house.

The narrator of the book of Judges describes a time of spiritual disorder. The mother says she dedicated the silver to the LORD, yet she uses it to make an image, something the law of Moses forbade. In addition, the account notes that only part of the silver was used, and that there was no king in Israel. Each person did what seemed right to him.

For today: good intentions or using God's name is not enough to please him. It is wise to measure our customs and decisions by what God actually says in his Word, not only by what seems right to us.
exp.13:11:
Here Samson proposes a riddle to the thirty companions at the wedding. If they can solve it during the seven days of the feast, he will give them thirty sheets (fine linen garments) and thirty changes of clothing (festive garments). It is a challenge with a prize.

He speaks during the celebration of his wedding to a Philistine woman. It was customary to hold a feast, and the Philistines had assigned him thirty companions. Scholars do not know the exact reason, but Samson takes the occasion to set the challenge. Later it will become clear that the game brings serious consequences.

For today: before making a bet or a promise, think about what it might lead to. A seemingly harmless game can produce conflict, pressure, and resentment. Let us ask God for wisdom to speak with prudence.
exp.3:23:
The explanation says that Israel's power grew and became firmer against Jabin, king of Canaan, until they wiped him out completely. The phrase "the hand of" is an old way of speaking about strength or power.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges, who closes the story of Deborah and Barak. Israel had been oppressed for about twenty years by Jabin, and his general Sisera had died at the hands of Jael. The verse before this one says it was God who brought down Jabin. So Israel's growth is not presented as its own achievement, but as the fruit of what God did.

For today: when God gives you a victory, do not expect everything to change overnight. Keep moving forward with steadiness and trust, and thank God for each step, because he is the one who gives the strength.
exp.8:27:
Gaal says with contempt: "Who is Abimelech, and who is Shechem, that we should serve him?" He reminds them that Abimelech is the son of Jerubbaal (another name for Gideon), and that Zebul is only his "officer," that is, his deputy or the one he has put in charge. He proposes to serve instead the descendants of Hamor, the ancient founder of Shechem. And he asks: why should we serve Abimelech?

Gaal is a newcomer who gains the trust of the people of Shechem. They were already angry with Abimelech, and after the feast the curses came. Gaal speaks in the middle of that atmosphere, and his speech aims to stir up a rebellion. Some think he appeals to the people's pride in their ancient roots; the text does not fully explain this.

Speaking with pride and sowing division may seem like courage, but it almost always leads to more violence. Before following someone who criticizes harshly, it is wise to ask what they really seek and to look for peace.
exp.12:21:
Manoah tells his wife that they are going to die, because they have seen God. The words that need explaining are "á" (a) and "moriremos" (we are going to die). Manoah understands that the visitor was the angel of the LORD, and he feels a very great fear.

Manoah and his wife were expecting a child, and the angel had announced that the boy would be Samson. When the angel went up in the flame of the altar, Manoah was terrified. At that time it was believed that seeing God meant death (Exodus 33:20). His wife, calmly, reasons that God would not have accepted their offering or given them this promise if he wanted to kill them.

When we feel fear before something of God that we do not understand, we can remember what he has already done for us. His past goodness helps us to trust, as this woman did.
exp.18:16:
This verse tells that an old man lifted up his eyes and saw a traveler sitting in the city square. Then he asked him: "Where are you going, and where have you come from?" The word "saw" is the one used in the verse above, and "said to him" is the same as the verse's "said." A "traveler" is a man walking through who is only passing by.

The speaker is an older man, from the region of Ephraim, who was living in Gibeah as a foreigner. He was returning from work in the fields as the evening came on. The traveler and his companions had arrived in the city, but no one offered them lodging. That the square was their only shelter shows the lack of hospitality in the place. The old man notices him and asks in order to learn his situation.

For today: do not walk past the one who is alone or without help. Sometimes a sincere question, asked with genuine interest, is the first step toward offering help, companionship, or a place to rest.
exp.7:29:
It says that Gideon had seventy sons. The phrase "came from his body" is an old way of saying they were his own sons by blood. It also explains that he had many wives, that is, he practiced polygamy.

The book of Judges tells this as a narrator, with no one speaking. It comes right after Gideon defeated Midian and after he refused to become king. Yet he later made an ephod that the people worshiped (v. 27). This verse shows his household growing with the customs of his time, and the text immediately mentions Abimelech, whose story will end in violence. The Bible does not approve of polygamy here; it only reports it, and its consequences appear later.

For today: a life of victories can have neglected areas. Examine your decisions at home and in your relationships with humility, because what seems normal today may bring pain to your children tomorrow.
exp.7:28:
This verse says that Jerubbaal, another name for Gideon, returned to his house and lived there. The verse uses the word "went" and "dwelt," which means he settled down and remained there. It seems like a quiet ending after the war.

The narrator of the book is the one speaking. Gideon had freed Israel from Midian and had refused to become king. However, the ephod he made from the gold of the spoils became a snare for the people, and the sons and later history of his household show that his withdrawal did not close the matter. Some see here a well-earned rest; others, a warning that something had been left crooked.

For today: stepping back from a season does not erase the effect of your decisions. Take care with what you leave to your family and to others, so that your example draws them near to God and not to things that take his place.
exp.5:39:
This verse tells us that God did that night what Gideon had asked of him. The fleece, which is a sheep's wool, was dry in the morning, while all the ground around it was wet with dew. It is the reverse of the first sign.

The narrator is the author of the book of Judges. Gideon, called by God to deliver Israel from the Midianites, felt fear and doubt. He had already asked for a sign with the wet fleece and the dry ground. Then he asked for a second one, begging God not to be angry for asking again. God answered him with patience. Some see here a weakness of faith, and others see God's kindness toward him.

For today: if you have doubts, bring them honestly and humbly to God. But do not keep asking for signs; seek to confirm his will in his Word, in prayer, and in the counsel of wise people, and then obey with confidence.
exp.8:54:
This verse says that when the Israelites saw that Abimelech was dead, each one went back to his own home. The sentence that explains an older form of the verb has been removed, since your reader's verse does not contain that word. With the death of the leader, the conflict ended, and the soldiers scattered.

The narrator of the book of Judges tells of the end of Abimelech, who had made himself king by killing his seventy brothers. His death, brought about by a woman and by his own armor-bearer, closes a story of violence and ambition. Without their leader, the men no longer had a reason to keep fighting. The following text makes clear that God brought justice for that wrong.

For today: power gained through violence and pride does not last. We can seek to lead and to live with humility and justice, trusting that God sees everything and that in the end he puts things in their place.
exp.20:1:
The explanation says that the whole people of Israel went to the house of God, which was in Bethel, and stayed there until evening. They were before God weeping loudly, with their voices raised. "Á" is the old form of "a", and "estuviéronse" means "they stayed".

The account speaks of the people of Israel. They had punished the tribe of Benjamin harshly for a terrible crime, and they had also sworn not to give them their daughters as wives. Now a tribe was about to disappear, and the people cry out to God in pain, asking why this happened. Some scholars see here genuine repentance; others note that they are weeping over the consequences of their own hasty decisions.

For today: when our hasty decisions cause pain, the best thing is to bring everything to God honestly, without excuses, and ask him for wisdom to repair what we can.
exp.8:28:
Gaal, speaking with pride, says that he wishes all the people were under his command. He then challenges Abimelech: to gather more soldiers and come out to fight.

Gaal, son of Ebed, speaks during a grape harvest festival in Shechem. The people were resentful toward Abimelech, who had ruled with violence. Gaal takes advantage of the people's anger by eating and drinking in the temple of their gods to gain power. His speech sparks a rebellion, and Zebul, the city's officer, warns Abimelech.

For today: beware of bold words spoken in the heat of the moment, especially when we are seeking power. True strength rests on God and on humility, not on pride or on the anger of the crowd.
exp.9:3:
This verse says that Jair had thirty sons, and that each one rode on a young donkey. They also had thirty towns, which were still called Havoth-jair when the book was written. They were in the region of Gilead. Here "towns" means small settlements, and "donkeys" means the animals that carry people and loads.

It is one detail within the list of judges, and the narrator does not say who wrote it. Riding donkeys was usually a sign of high social standing, so the sons seem to have had authority or wealth. No deed of Jair is recorded. After his death the people return to idolatry, which shows that a leader's prestige did not guarantee the faithfulness of the nation.

For today: a family's success, name, or possessions do not take the place of a life given to God. Let us ask him that our faith be sincere and not depend on what we have or on who our family is.
exp.4:7:
They chose new gods, the explanation says, meaning that when Israel left the LORD to follow idols, war came right up to the gates of their cities. And in that moment of danger, not a single shield or spear could be seen among forty thousand men. The gates were the place of a city's defense and its government. Some understand this to describe a people without weapons; others, a people without the courage to fight.

Deborah, a prophetess and judge, speaks in a song of victory together with Barak. She recalls how badly things stood for Israel before she rose up: unsafe roads, empty villages. She points out that the root of the problem was spiritual: abandoning God left the people weak and defenseless.

For today: when we put other things in the place of God, money, success or fear, we lose our inner strength. Let us return to Him every day, and He will sustain us.
exp.6:2:
Gideon is to announce to the people that whoever is afraid and trembling may return home. Twenty-two thousand went away and ten thousand remained.

The phrase "depart early" in the verse above describes leaving promptly, and the location named in the verse, "from mount Gilead," is a phrase whose exact sense is not entirely clear; some scholars take it as an expression or a place name that is hard to locate.

God speaks to Gideon before he faces the Midianites. The army was too large, and God wanted Israel not to boast that its own strength had won the victory. So he reduces the number, so that everyone would recognize that salvation comes from him.

God does not need our abundance of resources, talents, or support in order to act. Sometimes he makes us depend on him by taking away the things we trusted in. If today you feel you have little strength, remember that his power can shine in your weakness, and that the credit always belongs to him.
exp.18:21:
This verse tells how a group of men from the city surrounded the house where a traveler was staying. They pounded on the door and demanded that the owner bring out the guest so they could abuse him sexually. The men are called "sons of Belial," meaning wicked men with no regard for right or for anyone else. Pounding on the door is the forceful beating described here.

The narrator sets the scene in a dark time in Israel, when everyone did whatever seemed right to them. A Levite was traveling with his concubine, and an old man took them in so they would not have to sleep in the square. The violence of the city stands in sharp contrast with the old man's hospitality. The text reports what happened, but it does not approve of the response that follows, the offer of the women, which is unjust and terrible.

For today: when a society loses the fear of God, the most vulnerable suffer. We can defend and protect the weak, and practice hospitality with wisdom.
exp.10:26:
Jephthah tells the king of Ammon that Israel did him no harm, and that it is he who is acting wrongly by declaring war on them. Since they cannot agree, Jephthah asks that the LORD, the righteous judge, decide today between the two peoples. Asking for a decision means asking God to pass the verdict.

Jephthah is a leader of Israel in Gilead. Before fighting, he sends messengers to the Ammonite king and explains why the disputed lands belong to Israel, which had occupied them for three hundred years. In the end, the king does not listen to him, and then the Spirit of the LORD comes upon Jephthah.

For today: before entering a conflict, try to speak calmly and truthfully. Then place your cause in the hands of God, who is the righteous judge, and do not let yourself be carried away by pride or by revenge.
exp.15:22:
This verse tells that the lords of the Philistines gathered to hold a great feast. They offered a sacrifice to Dagon, who was their god, and rejoiced. They said that Dagon had delivered Samson, their enemy, into their hands.

The ones speaking are the Philistine rulers. Samson, a judge of Israel, had caused them great harm. Now he was blinded, a prisoner in Gaza, and forced to grind grain. They credited their victory to Dagon, not knowing that God allowed it. The text mentions that Samson's hair was growing back, and this prepares what happens next.

We can celebrate a triumph and believe everything is settled, but only God sees the end. It is better to be humble and not to boast. And if today you feel defeated, remember that God can still act.
exp.17:9:
The spies from the tribe of Dan tell what they saw in the north. They say that they will come to a people who feel secure, without fear, and to a large land (the word "large" here means wide, with plenty of room). They assure the others that God has given it into their hands and that nothing that the earth produces is lacking there.

The ones speaking are five men whom Dan sent to explore, and now they encourage their brothers in Zorah and Eshtaol to go and conquer. Dan had not yet taken the inheritance that had been assigned to it. Although they say "God has given it," the text does not show that God commanded this; it was their own interpretation, and the account soon shows violence against a peaceful people.

Today we can learn not to confuse a good opportunity with the will of God. Before acting, it is wise to pray, seek wise counsel, and ask ourselves whether what we desire is right and honors God.
exp.10:6:
Jephthah calls out to the elders of Gilead. He reminds them that they hated him and drove him out of his father's house. That is why he asks them why they have come to him now, just when they are in trouble, that is, in a time of anguish and need.

He is speaking as a man of Gilead. His half-brothers had driven him out because he was the son of another woman, and he went to live in the land of Tob. Now the Ammonites are making war against Israel, and the leaders who rejected him need a military commander. His question expresses pain and distrust, and it also serves him as a way to negotiate.

For today: when someone who wounded us comes looking for us only because they need us, it is healthy to be honest about the hurt without letting bitterness take charge. We can ask God for wisdom to decide whether to help, and how to do it, with clarity and with grace.
exp.4:19:
This verse says that the heavens themselves took part in the battle against Sisera, the commander of the Canaanite army. The "stars in their courses" are the stars moving along their paths across the sky. It is poetic language: the verse does not explain how they "fought." Some understand it as an image of God acting from on high; others take it to refer to forces of nature, such as the rain that filled the stream.

Here Deborah speaks in a song of victory, together with Barak. Israel had been oppressed by Jabin and Sisera. After the triumph, she praises those who risked their lives and acknowledges that the victory did not come by human strength alone. The next verse mentions the Kishon river, which swept the enemy away.

For today: when you face something greater than you, act with courage and do your part, but trust that God can work in ways you do not see. And when help arrives, give thanks for it.
exp.0:32:
This verse says that the tribe of Naphtali did not drive out the people of Beth-shemesh or of Beth-anath. Instead of driving them out, Naphtali lived among the Canaanites who were already in the land. Still, those towns paid tribute to them, that is, labor or taxes.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks, reviewing what happened after the death of Joshua. He lists the tribes that did not finish the conquest God had entrusted to them. He wants to show how Israel fell short in obeying, and that prepares the problems that will come later in the book.

For today: when we leave what God asks of us half done, and settle for what we should have changed, that small compromise can grow. Let us ask God for the courage to obey him fully, without settling for what is comfortable.
exp.19:30:
Judges 20:31 tells how the men of Benjamin went out to fight against Israel and were drawn away from their city, Gibeah. They began to strike down some of the Israelites, as they had done at other times, along two roads: one that goes up to Bethel, and another that goes to Gibeah across the open country. About thirty men of Israel died.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. It is the third day of fighting. Israel had lost twice, and now it pretended to retreat while preparing ambushes. The Benjamites believed they would win again, without seeing the trap. The text does not justify all the violence; it describes a time of great disorder in Israel.

For today: past success can make us overconfident and blind. Before we take anything for granted, it is wise to ask God for wisdom and to examine our situation humbly.
exp.14:0:
After a while, at the time of the wheat harvest, Samson went to visit his wife and brought her a young goat as a gift. He wanted to go into her room, but her father did not allow him to. The phrase about going into the room means being with her as her husband.

This is a story about Samson, a judge of Israel. Earlier, in Judges 14, he had left the wedding angry. As the story goes on, her father thought Samson had rejected her, and he gave her to another man. So Samson comes with good intentions, but he finds that the situation has already changed.

For today: when there are conflicts, let us not let time pass without speaking. Silence and misunderstandings can cause harm that is later hard to repair. Let us seek dialogue and reconciliation in good time.
exp.6:23:
Gideon sent messengers throughout the hill country of Ephraim. He asked them to come down to fight against the Midianites and to cut off their escape by taking the crossing points of the water, from Beth-barah as far as the Jordan River. Taking the waters means holding those passages so the enemy cannot get away. The men of Ephraim gathered together and did so.

Gideon, the judge of Israel, spoke after God had given the victory with only three hundred men. The Midianites were fleeing, and Gideon needed more people to close off their way out. The exact location of Beth-barah is not known with certainty.

For today: God can begin a work with a few, but He also wants others to take part. When He gives you an advance, invite others humbly to help and to finish what He has started.
exp.1:16:
This verse says that the people of Israel did not even listen to the judges God sent them. Instead of obeying, they went after other gods, that is, they were unfaithful to God and bowed down to idols, like someone who betrays a spouse. They turned away quickly from the path their ancestors had followed when they obeyed God.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks (tradition is not certain about who wrote it). He explains why Israel lived in cycles of sin, oppression, and rescue. The judges were leaders whom God raised up to deliver the people from their enemies, but the people's hearts did not truly change.

For today: it is not enough for help or relief to arrive; we need to obey God with steadiness. Ask yourself what things you have allowed to take the place of God, and ask Him to help you return to Him today.
exp.20:9:
The explanation says that the people of Israel sent twelve thousand of their bravest soldiers against Jabesh-gilead. They were ordered to strike down all its inhabitants, including the women and children. The phrase "with the edge of the sword" means killing with the sword. The assembly of all Israel is the gathering of the whole nation.

It is the assembly of the tribes that speaks. They had sworn at Mizpah that anyone who did not come would be put to death. Since no one from Jabesh-gilead came, they acted in this way. They wanted to get wives for the survivors of Benjamin, a tribe that had been nearly destroyed. The book ends by saying that at that time there was no king and each person did whatever seemed right to them. The text tells what happened, but it does not present it as an example to follow.

For today: before we promise something with force, let us ask God for wisdom. A hasty vow can lead us to commit injustice.
exp.15:6:
Samson tells Delilah that if they bind him with seven fresh bowstrings, that is, flexible branches freshly cut that have not yet dried out, he will lose his strength and become like any other man.

Samson, judge of Israel, speaks to Delilah. The Philistine lords had offered her money to discover the secret of his strength. Samson does not tell the truth; this is the first of several false answers. The verses that follow show that it was a trap, and that he frees himself easily. Even so, he plays with fire by continuing in that relationship.

For today: when we toy with temptation, believing we can control it, sooner or later it catches up with us. It is wise to step away in time from whatever puts our faith at risk and to guard what God has entrusted to us.
exp.0:29:
It says that the tribe of Zebulun did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Kitron and in Nahalol. Instead of driving them out, the Canaanites kept living among them, and Zebulun made them pay tribute. "Drive out" here means to expel, and "become tributaries" means they paid taxes or worked for them.

The narrator of the book of Judges, whose author is not known with certainty, reviews how each tribe settled in the promised land. God had commanded not to live alongside the peoples whose practices led to idolatry. Yet tribe after tribe settled for a convenient arrangement: profiting from the Canaanites instead of obeying fully. This account prepares the explanation of Israel's later stumbling.

For today: sometimes we tolerate a small sin because it seems useful or manageable. Let us ask God for courage not to bargain with what pulls us away from Him, even when it costs us.
exp.1:12:
This verse says that the people of Israel abandoned the Lord, their God, and began to worship Baal and Ashtaroth. "Forsook" means that they turned away from Him, and "served" means that they gave to other gods the honor that belonged to Him alone. Baal and Ashtaroth were gods of the neighboring peoples, commonly linked to rain and the fertility of the land.

The narrator of the book tells what happened after the death of Joshua. A new generation had not lived close to God's works, and they let themselves be drawn into the customs of their neighbors. Because of this, God allowed them to suffer at the hands of their enemies, just as He had warned.

For today: it is easy to trust in things that seem to give us security, such as money or success. Today we can ask ourselves what holds first place in our heart, and return to God with simplicity.
exp.7:20:
Zebah and Zalmunna, the two captured kings of Midian, ask Gideon to kill them himself, because a man is measured by his strength. Gideon does so and takes the ornaments that were on their camels' necks, which were crescent-shaped pieces hanging from the necks of the camels.

Gideon had pursued these kings because they had killed his brothers at Tabor. First he asked his son Jether to execute them, but the young man was afraid. That is why the kings ask Gideon himself to do it. It is a scene of justice and revenge in a time of war. Afterward, Gideon refuses to be king, saying that only God should rule.

Today, this passage invites us not to let pain dominate us, and to remember that God is the one who holds the highest place in our lives. Gideon knew how to reject the power that was offered to him. We can ask God for humility so that we do not seek our own honor.
exp.19:31:
The explanation says that the men of Benjamin thought they would win again, as in the two previous battles. But the Israelites pretended to flee. "Let us flee" is a strategy: they wanted the Benjamites to follow them, drawing them away from the city out onto the highways.

The narrator recounts a war between the tribes of Israel and Benjamin, after a terrible crime in Gibeah. Israel had already lost twice. Now it uses a trap: while some pretend to retreat, others wait hidden. The Benjamites trusted their past and did not see the danger close at hand.

For today: do not become overconfident just because things went well for you before. What worked yesterday does not guarantee tomorrow. Ask God for wisdom and humility to see what you are not seeing.
exp.18:26:
This verse tells that the Levite got up early, opened the door of the house where he had stayed, and got ready to continue his journey. Then he saw his concubine (a secondary wife) fallen before the door, with her hands on the threshold, which is the lower part of the entrance. She had spent the night suffering a terrible abuse.

It is part of the closing account of the book of Judges, which does not give a speech but a narrative. It shows how far the wickedness in Israel had gone. The book repeats that there was no king and that each person did whatever seemed right to them. The text does not approve of what happened; it presents it as a sign of a broken society.

For today: let us not be indifferent to the pain of the vulnerable. Let us listen to the one who suffers, protect the one who is in danger, and not look the other way.
exp.4:5:
According to the explanation, in the time of Shamgar and Jael, life in Israel came to a standstill because of fear. The main roads were left empty, and travelers abandoned the straight routes to take crooked, hidden paths. The phrase "the highways were unoccupied" means that it was no longer possible to travel safely.

The speaker is Deborah, in the song she sings together with Barak after the victory over Sisera's army. She remembers how difficult the situation had been before: the people were oppressed by the Canaanites and could not move about freely. Shamgar appears as a deliverer in Judges 3:31, but the oppression continued. Scholars debate some details of this period.

For today: when fear makes us go around and hide, let us remember that God still delivers. We can ask Him for courage to take the next straight step He shows us.
exp.7:22:
Gideon refuses to be ruler or governor over Israel, and he also refuses to let his son rule. He says that the true Lord of the people is the LORD, that is, God. The word "rule" means to govern or have authority over others.

The Israelites, grateful because Gideon had delivered them from Midian, ask him to be their ruler, and then to let his son and grandson rule after him. Gideon answers with humility, acknowledging that the victory came from God. However, the account goes on to show that Gideon later asks for gold and does something that becomes a snare for the people, so his life is a mixture of faith and failure.

For today: when you receive praise or success, give the glory back to God. Remember too that no one, neither you nor others, should take the place that belongs to Him alone in your life.
exp.10:7:
The elders of Gilead answer Jephthah that this is exactly why they have come back to look for him. They ask him to go with them, fight against the Ammonites, and be their head, that is, their leader and chief, over all who live in Gilead.

The leaders of Gilead, who had earlier driven Jephthah out of his family, are now speaking. Ammon is threatening them and they are in trouble. That is why they need Jephthah, a brave warrior. He points out their rejection of him, and they offer him more than a commander's role: they offer him rule. Even so, they seek his help out of necessity, and the verse does not say here that there was any deep repentance.

For today: if someone hurt you and later seeks you out for their own convenience, you can speak honestly about the pain and ask God for wisdom. And if you have failed someone, asking for their help is not enough; it is also wise to acknowledge the wrong and seek sincere reconciliation.
exp.17:18:
The men of the tribe of Dan tell the priest to keep quiet, to put his hand over his mouth, and to go with them. They want him to be their "father," that is, their spiritual guide and counselor, and their priest. They ask him whether it is not better for him to serve a whole tribe than the household of one man.

The five spies and the six hundred armed men of Dan speak. They are looking for a place to settle, and they take Micah's religious objects with them. The priest protests only weakly, and then he is pleased. Judges shows a time of disorder, when each person did what seemed right to him.

For today: let us make sure our decisions are not moved only by convenience or advancement. Let us first ask what pleases God, not only what benefits us.
exp.17:0:
In those days Israel had no king. The tribe of Dan was looking for a territory where it could settle, because it had not yet taken possession of the land that had fallen to it.

The narrator of the book of Judges is the one speaking. This phrase appears several times in the book and sums up a time of disorder, when everyone did whatever seemed right to them. Dan had not managed to conquer the territory assigned to it, and so it was looking for another place. Later it sends out scouts, and on that journey they will arrive at the house of Micah.

For today: when we do not put God in the place of guide, we tend to settle things our own way and end up far from what He has given us. Ask Him today to help you finish faithfully what He has already placed in your hands.
exp.8:22:
This verse says that God allowed a spirit of resentment and mistrust to arise between Abimelech and the people of Shechem. "Evil spirit" here means a mood of discord, and "rebelled" means that they turned against him. There are different ways to understand whether this was a spiritual being or an attitude of hostility; in either case, the text says that God allowed it or directed it.

The narrator of the book tells this after Abimelech had ruled for three years. He had killed his seventy brothers to become king, and Shechem had supported him. Now the story shows that this violence would bring consequences, as the following verses say.

For today: do not build your life on injustice or associate with those who practice it. Sooner or later, what is sown with wickedness produces division. Seek honest paths, even if they are slower.
exp.16:12:
Micah says that now he is sure the Lord will bless him, because he has a Levite as his priest. The phrase about the Lord doing him good means that God will give him prosperity and favor. The word about it being done or settled means that it has been put in place, or has come to be.

Micah had made an idol of silver and had a shrine in his house. It was a disordered time, when everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes. On finding a Levite, from the tribe set apart for the service of God, he believes that his home religion is now complete. But he himself appointed him, and his worship remained mixed with idols. Many understand this passage as a warning.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we trust that God blesses us because we meet certain religious requirements, or because we truly obey him according to his Word. Having religious things does not guarantee God's favor; he looks for a faithful and sincere heart.
exp.3:15:
Barak pursued the chariots and the enemy army as far as a place called Harosheth of the Gentiles. There all of Sisera's army died by the sword, and not a single man survived. Only Sisera, the commander, escaped on foot.

The narrator of Judges tells how God delivered Israel from twenty years of oppression under Jabin, the Canaanite king. Deborah, a prophetess and judge, encouraged Barak to fight, assuring him that the LORD was going out before him. The text credits the victory to God, not to Israel's own strength.

For today: when God calls you to obey, take the step even when the challenge seems enormous. Trust that He goes before you, and finish what you started without stopping halfway.
exp.18:23:
Here the elderly owner of the house wants to protect his guest, a Levite who was traveling. To do this, he offers to hand over his own virgin daughter and the Levite's concubine to the violent mob. "Humble them" means to abuse them, and "such a vile thing" refers to the sexual assault of the guest.

An elderly man from Gibeah, in the land of Benjamin, is speaking. The men of the city, called "sons of Belial" (wicked people), demand to abuse the visitor. The book presents this as part of the moral decline of Israel, when "every man did what was right in his own eyes." The Bible records this event but does not approve of it.

For today: protecting the vulnerable never justifies sacrificing another innocent person. Today we can courageously defend women and the weak, and reject any wickedness that tries to disguise itself as duty.
exp.8:44:
This verse tells that Abimelech fought against the city of Shechem for a whole day. In the end he captured it, killed the people who were inside, and tore the city down. Then he "sowed it with salt," that is, he scattered salt over it. Many understand this as a gesture to curse the city and leave it barren, although the Bible does not fully explain its meaning.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Abimelech, son of Gideon, had made himself king by killing his brothers with the help of the men of Shechem. Afterward they rebelled against him. His revenge was brutal, just as Jotham had warned in his parable.

For today: power used with violence and pride always ends up destroying, even the one who wields it. Let us ask God for humility to resolve conflicts with justice and mercy, not with revenge.
exp.17:2:
The five men from the tribe of Dan, who were traveling through the land to explore it, passed near the house of Micah. They recognized the voice of the young Levite who lived there and went over to him. They asked him three questions in a row: who brought him there, what he was doing, and what he had in that place. "They recognized his voice" may mean that they already knew him, or that they noticed his Levite accent; the text does not make this clear.

The speakers are the Danite scouts. Dan had not yet taken possession of its inheritance and was looking for a place to settle. It was a time of disorder, when there was no king in Israel. They are surprised to find a Levite, who was supposed to serve in the worship of the Lord, working as a private priest in a private home.

For today: when we find ourselves in a strange place, it is worth asking ourselves those same questions with sincerity: what am I doing here, and why? We should ask God for direction, instead of following only comfort or convenience.
exp.11:9:
He says that Ibzan died and was buried in Bethlehem. It is the brief close of his time as a judge of Israel, which lasted seven years. The explanation notes that the verse is a short summary, and that the word "buried" means laid to rest in the ground.

The book of Judges tells the story of Israel after Joshua, when the people were led by judges, leaders whom God raised up at different moments. Here the narrator records Ibzan very briefly. He does not recount any battles or feats of his. It is not certain whether this Bethlehem is the one in Judah or a town in Zebulun; scholars debate it.

Today it reminds us that every life ends and that God continues to work through different people and generations. Even when our work seems small or little known, God sees the faithfulness of each day. We can serve with humility, without needing applause.
exp.1:13:
This verse says that God became very angry with Israel. For that reason he allowed raiders to plunder them and their surrounding enemies to overpower them. The explanation of the quoted words is this: "hot anger" is a fierce burning anger; the "spoilers" are the plunderers; "sold them" means that he let them fall under the power of others; "stand before" means to resist or to face their enemies.

The narrator of the book tells what happened after the death of Joshua. The new generation abandoned the God who had brought them out of Egypt and worshiped Baal and Ashtaroth. God had warned that this would bring consequences, and here it comes true. But the following context shows that God did not abandon them completely: he raised up judges to rescue them.

For today: when we turn away from God, we lose the strength to face difficulties. Yet his discipline seeks to bring us back to himself, and his mercy remains open. Today you can return to him with sincerity.
exp.8:4:
Judges 9:5 tells how Abimelech went to his father's house at Ophrah and killed his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal (another name for Gideon). There were seventy of them, and he slew them on one stone. Only Jotham, the youngest son, survived, because he hid himself.

The narrator of the book of Judges describes how Abimelech, using money from Shechem and violent men he hired, sought to take power for himself. His relatives on his mother's side supported him in Shechem. To secure his rule, he eliminated those who could compete with him. Some scholars think that "seventy" is a rounded number, but the text presents it as a great family massacre.

For today: unlimited ambition destroys those closest to us. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that does not use people or money to climb, and that cares for family instead of harming it.
exp.19:15:
Among the men of Benjamin there were seven hundred chosen soldiers, very skilled with the sling. The word "ambidextrous" refers to their being able to use both hands well, although the Hebrew can also be understood to mean left-handed. Their aim was so precise that they could hurl a stone at a hair and not miss.

The narrator of the book tells how Benjamin prepared for war against the other tribes of Israel. Benjamin refused to hand over the men of Gibeah who had committed a terrible crime. Although they were few compared with Israel, they had very well-trained soldiers.

For today: talent or skill is a gift, but it does not make our cause just. Let us ask God for humility to use what we know how to do in the service of good and truth, and not to defend what is wrong.
exp.12:6:
Here the wife of Manoah tells her husband what the visitor said to her. She will have a son, and while she is expecting him she must not drink wine or strong drink (a fermented drink), nor eat anything unclean, that is, what the law considered impure. That child will be a Nazarite, someone set apart for God, from before birth until his death.

It is the wife of Manoah who speaks, repeating the angel's message. Israel was under the rule of the Philistines, and God prepares a deliverer, Samson. The Nazarite vow was normally temporary; here it is for life, which was uncommon.

For today: God calls us to live set apart for Him, and that can begin in everyday life, in what we eat, say, and decide. Ask Him today to show you one area where you can live more fully devoted to Him.
exp.19:26:
Here the text says that the Israelites, after a harsh defeat, sought direction from God. It mentions that the ark of the covenant was there, in Bethel, as a sign that God had committed himself to his people. The phrase about asking the Lord means that they consulted him about what to do.

The narrator of the book explains this detail in parentheses. Israel had lost two days of battle against the tribe of Benjamin, with thousands dead. Before this, they had fought trusting in themselves; now they weep, fast and offer sacrifices. Then Phinehas, the priest, ministers before the ark, and God gives them an answer.

For today: when everything goes wrong, it is not enough to keep trying with our own strength. We can stop, humble ourselves and seek God sincerely before deciding the next step. He knows how to guide us.
exp.20:15:
It says that Israel's leaders asked how they could get wives for the men of Benjamin who had survived. The word "destroyed" in the verse means wiped out or eliminated: almost all the women of that tribe had died.

The elders speak after the civil war against Benjamin. Israel had sworn not to give their daughters to that tribe, and now they grieved that a whole tribe might disappear. They had already been given women from Jabesh-gilead, but there were not enough. The elders look for a way out, and the book shows a nation in confusion, where each person did whatever seemed right to him.

For today: before making promises or taking hasty decisions, let us seek God's direction. Impulsive vows can bring painful consequences, and trying to fix them with human solutions often makes things more complicated.
exp.7:32:
As soon as Gideon died, the people of Israel turned away from God again. The word "fornicated" is an old biblical way of speaking about spiritual unfaithfulness: abandoning God to worship other gods. The Baals were Canaanite gods, and the name Baal-berith means "lord of the covenant." They set this god up as their own in place of the LORD.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Gideon had led Israel to a great victory and had encouraged them to follow God. But while he was alive, the faith of the people seemed to depend on their leader. When he was gone, they went back to their old habits. The verses that follow show that they forgot God and were not grateful to Gideon's family.

For today: do not let your faith depend only on one person or on a good season. Build your own relationship with God, remembering what he has done for you and thanking him every day.
exp.11:14:
This verse tells that Abdon, son of Hillel, died and was buried in Pirathon, his town, in the territory of the tribe of Ephraim. It says he was buried "in the mount of the Amalekites," a region that bears that name, though the Bible does not explain in detail why.

Here the speaker is not a character; it is the narrator of the book of Judges. Abdon was one of the judges, leaders whom God raised up to guide Israel. The preceding text says he judged for eight years and that his family was large and well off, since they rode on donkeys. No battle is recorded for him, only the close of his life.

For today: not everyone will serve in very visible things. God also values a faithful and simple life, lived with responsibility in the place where we find ourselves.
exp.5:24:
God tells Gideon that very night to take two bulls from his father's herd: one ordinary bull and another that is seven years old. With them he is to pull down his father's altar to Baal and cut down the sacred pole beside it. That pole was probably a wooden post or tree dedicated to a pagan goddess, called Asherah in Hebrew.

The Lord speaks just after Gideon saw him and received peace. Israel was oppressed by Midian and had fallen into idolatry. Before giving him the military victory, God first wants to cleanse Gideon's own household. The verses that follow show that he obeyed at night, out of fear, yet he did obey.

For today: before attempting great things for God, ask him what idols or bad habits are in your own home and heart. Obey even when you are afraid; God values the sincere step, even when it is small and trembling.
exp.16:2:
Here a mother says that she had dedicated the eleven hundred pieces of silver to the Lord, but she does so so that her son may have a carved image (carved from wood or stone) and a cast image (made of melted metal). Then she returns the money to Micah, whose name appears here as Micah. A shekel was a unit of weight used as money.

The mother is the one speaking. He had stolen the money, she had cursed it, and when he confessed, she blesses him. We are in a time when Israel had become disordered in spiritual matters. She mixes devotion to the Lord with making an image, something the law of Moses forbade (Exodus 20:4).

We may want to honor God with good intentions, but in our own way. A sincere promise does not make right what God has already said he does not want. It is worth asking ourselves whether we worship as God teaches in his Word or as it seems best to us.
exp.2:30:
After Ehud, Shamgar the son of Anath defeated six hundred Philistines using an ox goad. The ox goad was a long stick with a metal tip that farmers used to guide oxen while plowing. The verse also says that Shamgar delivered Israel as well.

This is a brief note from the narrator of the book of Judges, who does not say who wrote it. It appears between the story of Ehud and the story of Deborah. Shamgar is mentioned as another deliverer whom God used when Israel was threatened. Little is known about him; his origin and exact occupation are not clear, and it is debated whether he was an Israelite.

God can use what we have on hand, even when it seems common or unimpressive. Shamgar used a working tool. Ask yourself what skill, time, or simple resource you can offer today to help others.
exp.18:28:
He says that the Levite, on arriving at his house, took a knife and cut the body of his concubine into twelve pieces, bones included. Then he sent a part to each region of Israel. A "concubine" was a wife of secondary rank, and "regions" here means territories or areas.

This is the end of a very dark story. The woman was handed over to a mob in Gibeah, in the tribe of Benjamin, and died after being abused. The narrator is not approving of the Levite's act; he shows how far Israel had fallen. The book repeats that there was no king and everyone did what seemed right to them. The twelve pieces were meant to shake the tribes into reacting. How to judge the Levite's conduct is left by the text for the reader to decide.

For today: let us not become accustomed to injustice or to violence against the vulnerable. When a society sets God aside, the weakest people suffer first. Let us defend and care for those who cannot defend themselves.
exp.4:27:
This verse shows the mother of Sisera, commander of Israel's enemy army, looking out of a window. She peers through the lattice, which are wooden grilles that let her see without being seen. Anxiously she calls out, asking why her son is taking so long to return with his war chariots.

This is part of the song of Deborah and Barak, which celebrates Israel's victory. We already know that Sisera died at the hands of Jael. While his mother waits expecting a victory, the reader knows that her son will not return. Scholars see some irony here; others also notice a human touch of a mother's grief.

For today: it is easy to trust our own plans and take the outcome for granted, as she and her ladies did. Let us learn to place our plans in God's hands, and to treat with compassion even the grief of those on the other side.
exp.20:12:
This verse tells that all the people of Israel sent messengers to the men of the tribe of Benjamin, who had taken refuge in the rock of Rimmon, a high, rocky place. They offered them peace, that is, they invited them to return without fighting. The word "congregation" means the gathered community of Israel, and the phrase "called unto them" means they called out to them.

Israel and Benjamin had come out of a terrible civil war. Almost the whole tribe of Benjamin had been killed, and only about six hundred men remained. The other Israelites had sworn not to give them their daughters as wives. Now they grieved that a tribe would disappear, and they looked for a way out, though by very violent and questionable means, as the story shows.

For today: offering peace and reconciliation is good, but it must be done with justice and without causing new harm. Let us seek to heal broken relationships with humility and truth.
exp.10:12:
Here the king of the Ammonites answers Jephthah's messengers. He says that when Israel came up out of Egypt, they took away his land, the land that stretches from the Arnon to the Jabbok and the Jordan. For that reason he demands that the land be returned to him without a fight.

The king of Ammon speaks here because Jephthah had asked him why he had come to make war. Jephthah, newly chosen as leader of Gilead, first tries to settle the conflict with words. The king gives his reason, but in the next verse Jephthah will answer that this accusation is not true, and the history of Israel that he then recounts will show it.

For today: before fighting or responding in anger, it is worth asking questions, listening to the other side's reasons, and checking the facts honestly. Many conflicts calm down, or at least come to be better understood, when people seek peace through honest dialogue.
exp.10:25:
It says that Israel had been living in Heshbon, Aroer, and the cities along the Arnon River for about three hundred years. Jephthah asks the Ammonite king why, in all that time, he never tried to take back those lands. "Villages" are the small towns nearby, and "boundaries" means the borders or limits.

Jephthah, a judge of Israel, speaks in a message to the king of Ammon. The Ammonites claimed that Israel had taken that land from them. Jephthah tries to avoid war with a historical argument: no one made any claim for centuries. Some scholars debate how to calculate those three hundred years, but the point is that a long time had passed.

For today: before fighting over a conflict, it is wise to speak calmly and review the facts. Seeking the truth and dialogue can prevent harm, even when the other person does not want to listen, as happened here.
exp.20:20:
The explanation says that the men of Benjamin were to hide among the vineyards near Shiloh and wait. When the young women came out to dance in circles, they would rush out, each seize one of them by force as his wife, and return to their own land. The word "catch" in the verse means to take by force.

It is spoken by the elders of Israel. After a war that had nearly wiped out the tribe of Benjamin, the Israelites had sworn not to give them their daughters. To avoid breaking their oath, they devised this violent plan. The book of Judges places it within a chaotic period, when "every man did what was right in his own eyes." The text does not approve of the act; it presents it as a sign of moral decline.

For today: a badly made promise is not fixed by another injustice. When we go wrong, the way forward is to repent and seek God, not to justify wrongdoing with clever solutions that harm others.
exp.14:10:
They say that three thousand men of Judah went to the cave in the rock of Etam, where Samson was. They confronted him: "Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? Why have you done this to us?" Samson answered that he had only repaid them in the same way they had treated him.

The Philistines had invaded Judah to capture Samson, because he had caused them great harm. The men of Judah speak out of fear: they prefer peace with their oppressors to facing them. Samson defends himself by saying that he acted in revenge. We note that Israel, accustomed to oppression, did not expect God to deliver them.

For today: be careful about growing used to what oppresses us out of fear of conflict. And Samson's revenge reminds us that repaying evil with evil does not bring peace; it is better to trust God and seek what is good.
exp.8:32:
He tells Abimelek to wait until morning, just as the sun comes up, and then attack the city of Shechem. Gaal and his people will come out to fight against him. "To attack" means to strike at, and the phrase "as you find the opportunity" means: do to him whatever seems best as the situation presents itself.

The one speaking is Zebul, the governor of Shechem, who secretly sends messengers to Abimelek. Zebul pretends loyalty to Gaal, but in truth he serves Abimelek. He advises a night ambush. It is a story of intrigue and violence, and the account does not present it as an example to imitate. It shows how ambition and betrayal destroy one another.

For today: let us not resolve conflicts with deceit or harmful cunning. Let us seek truth, peace, and justice, trusting that God sees what is hidden.
exp.17:14:
The explanation says that the Danites came to the house of Micah and went to the young Levite, who lived there. They greeted him and asked how he was.

This story is from the time of the judges, when there was no king in Israel and each person did what seemed right to him. Six hundred men from the tribe of Dan were looking for a place to settle. Their five scouts already knew about Micah's religious objects. The friendly greeting seems polite, but it was the first step toward taking those objects from him and carrying off the Levite.

Today, a kind word does not always show good intentions. Let us be honest in how we treat others, and not use religion to get what we want, but instead seek God's guidance.
exp.2:21:
This verse describes with brutal frankness how Ehud drove the dagger into Eglon, king of Moab. The "haft" is the handle, and the "blade" is the sharp part. The king was so fat that the handle was swallowed up and Ehud could not pull the weapon out. The phrase about the dung means that the king's body emptied itself. Some translators understand this last phrase in other ways, since the Hebrew is unclear.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Israel had been oppressed by Moab for eighteen years, and God raised up Ehud as a deliverer. The book recounts the event without embellishment, to show how that oppression came to an end. It does not say that everything Ehud did is a model to imitate.

For today: God can work even in dark times and through imperfect people. When you feel oppressed, trust that He has not forgotten you, and seek His guidance before you act.
exp.20:22:
The explanation says that the men of Benjamin did what they were told: each one took a wife from among the women who were dancing at Shiloh, "snatching" them (that is, carrying them off by force). Then they returned to their territory, rebuilt their cities, and settled there.

The people of Israel had nearly wiped out the tribe of Benjamin in a civil war, and they had sworn not to give their daughters to them in marriage. So that a tribe would not disappear, the elders looked for this way out. The book does not approve of it: it ends by saying there was no king and everyone did what seemed right in their own eyes. Many read this as a criticism of that era.

For today: a rash promise can lead us into unjust arrangements. When we get things wrong, we should not cover one wrong with another, but seek God and act with justice and humility.
exp.19:20:
This verse tells that the men of the tribe of Benjamin came out of the city of Gibeah and defeated Israel on the first day of battle. Twenty-two thousand Israelites died. "Destroyed down to the ground" means that they were killed in combat.

The narrator of the book recounts a war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin. The Israelites wanted to punish a terrible crime committed in Gibeah, and Benjamin did not hand over the guilty men. Although Israel had the just cause and had gone to fight with a great number of men, it lost. Afterward they wept before the LORD and sought his counsel. The text does not fully explain why God allowed this defeat; some think Israel needed to humble itself and seek him with more seriousness.

For today: being in the right does not guarantee that everything will be easy. When something goes wrong, do not give up or rely only on your own strength; come to God with humility and sincerity, and ask him for direction.
exp.17:4:
The five men from the tribe of Dan ask the young Levite to seek God's counsel. They want to know whether the journey they are making will turn out well. "Prosperous" here means going well, succeeding. "Ask counsel, we pray thee, of God" is a request to seek divine guidance before going forward.

The Danites were looking for a territory where they could settle. When they arrived at the house of Micah, they recognized the voice of the Levite, who worked as Micah's priest. They asked him for a word from God, and he told them to go in peace. However, the whole atmosphere is one of religious disorder: there were idols in that house and a hired priest. For this reason, that answer does not guarantee that the plan truly came from God.

It is good to seek God's guidance before deciding. But we must consult him with sincerity, in the light of his Word, and not simply look for someone who will tell us what we want to hear.
exp.8:26:
They went out into the fields, gathered the grapes from their vineyards, trod them to make wine, and held a festival. Then they went into the house of their god, ate and drank, and cursed Abimelech. The word "cursed" here means that they insulted him and wished harm upon him. The "merry" celebrations were harvest festivals.

The narrator tells us that the people of Shechem had already turned against Abimelech, the one they had earlier supported as king, even after he had killed his brothers. With the arrival of Gaal, they gained confidence and dared to rebel. Their feast was religious, but it did not make them better; it only fed their anger.

For today: a celebration or outward religiosity does not change a heart full of resentment or injustice. Before complaining about others, it is wise to examine our own decisions and ask God to give us a humble heart.
exp.19:8:
This verse is part of a sentence that continues from the previous one. The Israelites say that they will not return to their homes until they do the following to Gibeah: cast lots to decide who will go up against it. Casting lots was a common way of making decisions fairly in those times, trusting that God guided the outcome.

The assembly of Israel is speaking, after a Levite has told them about the terrible crime committed against his concubine in Gibeah, a city of the tribe of Benjamin. The people unite as one man and organize the army: they choose by lot and gather supplies. Later the story shows that anger and hasty decisions led to much violence, so not everything they do is a model to imitate.

When faced with injustice, seeking unity and order is good, but it is wise to ask for God's guidance and to act with humility, without letting ourselves be carried away by anger.
exp.3:18:
Sisera, the commander of the enemy army, flees exhausted and asks Jael for a little water because he is thirsty. She does not give him water but milk, which was kept in a bottle, that is, a container made of animal skin. Then she covers him again.

Sisera speaks, having just lost the battle against Israel and now seeking shelter. Jael receives him with apparent kindness, and he trusts her because there was peace between her family and King Jabin. Many understand that the milk would help him fall asleep, although the text does not say so clearly.

For today: the story reminds us that not every kind gesture shows true intentions. Let us ask God for wisdom to discern, and let us strive for our own kindness to be sincere, without deceit.
exp.0:19:
It says that Hebron was given to Caleb, just as Moses had promised, and that Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, a people of very tall and feared men. The word "gave" in the verse means that Judah handed the city over to him, and the word "drove out" means that he removed them from his territory.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks, and he does not identify himself. He tells how the tribes began to conquer the promised land after the death of Joshua. The promise to Caleb appears in Numbers 14 and Joshua 14. The text shows that God gave victory, but also that other peoples were not completely driven out.

For today: God keeps his promises, even when many years pass. Caleb trusted God and faced giants without giving up. We can pray and act with faith in the face of our own challenges, knowing that God is faithful.
exp.9:14:
The Israelites say to God: "We have sinned." They make no excuses. They place themselves in his hands: "do thou unto us whatsoever seemeth good unto thee." Even so, they ask to be delivered "this day," that is, right now.

God had just reminded them that they had abandoned him for other gods, and he told them he would no longer deliver them. The Ammonites were oppressing them. So the people respond with confession. What follows shows they did not only speak: they removed the foreign gods and went back to serving the Lord. The text says that God was grieved over their suffering.

For today: when we fail, the best response is to confess honestly, without excuses, and to trust in God's mercy. True repentance also changes behavior, so we can ask ourselves what false god we should put away today.
exp.7:19:
Gideon orders Jether, his firstborn son, to get up and kill the two captured Midianite kings. But the young man did not draw his sword, because he was afraid. He was still just a youth.

Gideon is the one speaking. Zebah and Zalmunna had killed his brothers at Tabor, and he seeks justice for that family blood. In asking his son to do it, he may have meant to honor or prepare him, though the text does not explain this. Jether's fear is understandable given his age. Then Gideon himself kills them.

For today: not all of us are ready for every task. If something intimidates you, acknowledge your limits with humility and ask for help. As for young people, let us give them responsibilities little by little, without shaming them when they are not yet prepared.
exp.7:34:
This verse says that the people of Israel were not kind or grateful to the family of Gideon. The phrase "they showed mercy" means that they did not show kindness or loyalty. Gideon, also called Jerubbaal, had done much good for Israel, but after his death no one repaid his household for it.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is summing up the situation. Gideon had delivered Israel from the Midianites. But when he died, the people turned away from God and followed Baal, a false god. They forgot God, and they also forgot the good they had received through Gideon. The next chapter tells how his family was treated.

For today: let us cultivate gratitude. Remembering what God has done for us, and what others have done for our good, helps us to be loyal and to respond with kindness.
exp.19:29:
This verse tells how the Israelites attacked the tribe of Benjamin for the third time. They lined up for battle against Gibeah, just as they had done in the two earlier attempts. The phrase "put themselves in array" in the King James wording means they arranged their troops in order to fight.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel was at war with Benjamin because this tribe had protected the guilty men responsible for a terrible crime in Gibeah. Israel had already suffered two painful defeats. This time they sought God's guidance, and He told them to go up, promising them the victory. So they used an ambush, and the Benjamites, confident, fell into the trap.

For today: sometimes we fail more than once. Before trying again, let us seek God's direction with humility, and not simply repeat the same thing in our own strength.
exp.14:3:
Samson catches three hundred foxes. He ties the animals in pairs by their tails and puts a torch between each pair. Some scholars think the original word could also refer to jackals, but the text does not make this clear.

Samson has just learned that his father-in-law gave his wife to another man. He feels wronged and declares that he will now be blameless before the Philistines if he harms them. His plan aims to destroy their crops, which were their livelihood. The account shows that revenge produces more violence, since the Philistines later burn the woman and her father.

For today: when we are hurt, it is easy to respond with anger and revenge. This story warns us that getting even almost always harms others too. Ask God for wisdom and calm before you react.
exp.15:20:
The explanation says that the Philistines seized Samson, put out his eyes, and brought him down to Gaza. There they bound him with bronze chains and made him grind grain in the prison. Grinding was hard and humiliating work, normally done by slaves or animals. The phrase "took him" in the verse means that they seized him.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks, not a character. He recounts the consequences of Samson, having departed from his commitment to God, revealing his secret to Delilah. His strength left him, and he did not realize that God had departed from him. The Philistines took the opportunity to take revenge on their enemy.

For today: let us not toy with what God has entrusted to us. Small compromises can lead us to lose a great deal without our noticing. But the story goes on, and God can still restore whoever returns to him with humility.
exp.13:17:
The men of Timnah gave Samson the answer to his riddle just before the seventh day, the deadline of the agreement, came to an end. They answered him with a question of their own: "What is sweeter than honey? And what is stronger than a lion?" With these words they showed that they already knew the secret: the honey and the lion that Samson had seen before.

The speakers are the thirty guests at the wedding. They had pressured Samson's wife with threats to get the secret out of her. She wept for seven days until he gave in and told her. She then passed it on to her people, and so Samson was betrayed.

For today: constant pressure and tears can wear down our defenses. We should take care with whom we share what matters most, and look for relationships built on trust rather than manipulation.
exp.7:0:
The men of the tribe of Ephraim confront Gideon. They ask him why he treated them this way, since he did not call them when he went out to fight against Midian. "They rebuked him sharply" means that they scolded him harshly and argued with him in a very forceful way.

The Ephraimites speak here, an important tribe in Israel. Gideon came from the tribe of Manasseh, and he called them to fight only after the first battle, to pursue those who were fleeing. It seems they felt ignored and wounded in their pride. Gideon answers them with humility, as seen in what follows, and the tension is calmed.

When someone feels offended or ignored, sometimes they confront us with anger. We can imitate Gideon: listen without fighting, acknowledge the good the other person has done, and respond with gentle words. As Proverbs 15:1 says, a soft answer turns away wrath.
exp.13:14:
On the seventh day of the wedding feast, the Philistine guests pressured Samson's wife. They told her to coax her husband into revealing the answer to the riddle, and they threatened to burn her and her father's house with fire. Coax means to persuade or win over. To take what is ours here means to leave us without our belongings, that is, to strip us of them.

Speaking here are the thirty companions who accompanied Samson at the banquet. They had wagered thirty linen garments and thirty changes of clothing, and in three days they had not been able to solve the riddle. So they turned to fear and violence, and accused the woman of having invited them in order to leave them with nothing.

For today: pressure and threats can push us to betray someone's trust. Before giving in to fear, it is wise to seek help and act with honesty, caring for the relationships God has given us.
exp.0:8:
This verse tells that the tribe of Judah went out to fight the Canaanites who lived in three areas: the mountains, the south (the region that the Hebrew text calls the Negev, the dry region of the south), and the valley (the lowlands to the west). The word "Canaanites" refers to the peoples who inhabited that land before Israel.
