The one telling the story is the author of the book of Judges, who is not named. After the death of Joshua, Israel asks God who will go up first, and Judah goes at the front. It had already won at Jerusalem, and now it extends the conquest to other regions. Some scholars understand that Jerusalem later returned to enemy hands, and the text does not make this clear here.

For today: when God gives us a big task, it is wise to move forward step by step, with prayer and perseverance, not leaving halfway what He has entrusted to us.
exp.17:1:
This verse tells how the tribe of Dan sent five brave men from their own clans, from Zorah and Eshtaol, to spy out the land and search it for a place to settle. "Search" here means to examine or investigate the ground. On their way they came to the hill country of Ephraim, to the house of Micah, and they stayed there for the night.

The narrator of the book of Judges explains that in those days there was no king in Israel. Dan had not yet taken the inheritance that belonged to them, so they were looking for another territory. What follows shows spiritual disorder: a Levite serving in a private house as a priest, which was not the order God had established.

For today: before making an important decision, it is not enough to investigate carefully and to have courage. It is wise to ask God and to examine his Word, so that our plans do not follow only what seems good to us.
exp.18:9:
The explanation says that the Levite would not stay another night at his father-in-law's house. He got up and left with his concubine and his two donkeys with the load on them ("ready" means prepared for the journey). He came opposite Jebus, the old name for Jerusalem. A "concubine" was a woman joined to a man, with a lower standing than a wife.

It is part of a very dark story, from a time when everyone did what seemed right to him. The narrator tells how the father-in-law urged them to stay for several days, but the man decided to leave late, with the day already fading. That hasty decision left them travelling by night and led them into what happened next.

For today: decisions made in a hurry, without thinking about the risks, can bring painful consequences. Before you act, stop to pray, listen to counsel, and think things through calmly.
exp.5:2:
They did not wait for the harvest to grow; they arrived just in time to wipe it out.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. He explains that Israel had turned away from God, and that God allowed seven years of oppression. The people lived hidden in caves and strongholds, and they were left without food. Some understand this as God's discipline, meant to bring them back to him.

For today: when we feel that everything we sow is being lost, we can stop and pray honestly. God does not delight in our distress, but he can use it to draw us closer to him. Crying out to him is a good first step.
exp.3:16:
This verse tells how Sisera, commander of the Canaanite army, fled on foot after losing the battle and came to the tent of Jael, wife of Heber, a Kenite. Sisera sought refuge there. He chose that place because there was peace, that is, an alliance or good relations, between Jabin, king of Hazor, and Heber's family.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Israel had been oppressed by Jabin for years, and God had just given the victory through Barak and Deborah. Sisera believed he would be safe with allies, but his trust in that political friendship proved mistaken, as the rest of the story shows.

For today: human alliances and places that seem safe can fail. It is wise to place our trust in God, who truly sustains and protects us.
exp.20:10:
The explanation says that the people of Israel ordered the killing of all the men of Jabesh-gilead and of every woman who had already been with a man. The phrase about a woman who had known a man means she had had sexual relations. The virgins would be kept alive.

This happens at the end of Judges, a time of great disorder, when everyone did whatever seemed right to them. The tribes of Israel had nearly destroyed Benjamin and had sworn not to give them wives. Later they regretted it and looked for a way out, but they committed more violence. The Bible records the event; it does not approve of it as an example.

For today: when we try to fix one wrong with another, the harm grows. Let us seek God's guidance and not rely on our own ideas.
exp.8:0:
This verse tells that Abimelech, son of Jerubbaal (another name for Gideon), went to Shechem. There he met with his mother's brothers and with all the family of his mother's father. "He spoke with them" means that he began to persuade them of something. The word "went away" is an old way of saying "he went."

The one acting here is Abimelech, son of Gideon and of a concubine from Shechem (Judges 8:31). Gideon had died, and Abimelech was seeking power. He relied on his relatives in Shechem to gain influence. What follows shows that his plan was ambitious and violent. The Bible does not say that God sent him.

For today: be careful about using family ties to gain power or advantages. Before seeking a position or a goal, it is wise to ask ourselves whether our motive is to serve or simply to be above others. Let us ask God for humility and uprightness.
exp.18:24:
This verse describes a terrible crime. Some men of Gibeah wanted to abuse the guest, and they would not accept the offer of the host. So the Levite brought out his concubine, a secondary wife, and they abused her sexually all night long until morning. At dawn they let her go.

Context: the narrator of Judges describes a time of great wickedness in Israel, when everyone did whatever seemed right in their own eyes. No one in this scene acts justly: not the attackers, not the host who offered his own daughter and the concubine, and not the man who handed her over. The Bible recounts this as a denunciation of the people's moral collapse, not as an example to imitate.

For today: violence against women is never acceptable. As Christians, we must protect the vulnerable, listen to them, and speak up when someone is suffering abuse.
exp.18:12:
He says to his servant that they should go on a little further and reach Gibeah or Ramah to spend the night there. "Come" is an invitation, "let us draw near to one of these places" means "let us approach one of these towns," and "to lodge all night" means to spend the night there, to sleep there.

The Levite speaks while travelling back with his concubine and his servant. The day is already ending. The servant wanted to stay in Jebus, a city of foreigners, but the Levite preferred an Israelite city, believing he would be safer among his own people. What is sad is that in Gibeah no one receives them, and this sets up a very dark story.

For today: let us not assume that a place is safe just because it seems familiar or religious. It is wise to pray, to think carefully, and to practise hospitality, opening the door to someone who needs shelter.
exp.19:36:
It says that the Israelites hidden in the ambush suddenly came out and attacked Gibeah. They spread through the city and put everyone to death with the sword. The word "swiftly" in the verse means quickly, and "put to the sword" means killed with the edge of the blade.

This passage is part of the account in Judges 20, written as a narrative, not as a speech. The tribes of Israel were fighting against Benjamin because that tribe protected the guilty parties in a terrible crime in Gibeah. Israel pretended to retreat to draw Benjamin away from the city, while the ambush took Gibeah. The text shows a harsh war in a time of great moral and spiritual disorder in Israel.

For today: when wrongdoing is tolerated out of loyalty to "our own people," the consequences can grow until they destroy everything. We must seek justice with humility and not protect what is wrong.
exp.19:35:
This verse says that the men of Benjamin realized they were defeated. The Israelites had pulled back on purpose, making room for the Benjamites to advance. They did this because they trusted the ambush they had set up behind Gibeah. The ambushers are hidden groups who attack by surprise.

It is part of the account of the war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, after the terrible crime committed at Gibeah. The narrator describes the battle and says that the LORD struck Benjamin. Benjamin believed it would win, as in the previous days, but did not know that disaster was near.

Today we learn that confidence based only on appearances or past successes can deceive us. It is wise to examine our lives with humility and not to excuse the evil within us.
exp.0:0:
This verse opens the book of Judges. It says that after Joshua died, the people of Israel asked God who should be the first to go up and fight against the Canaanites. The phrase "asked the Lord" means they sought God's direction. The word "go up" is used because the land was hilly. The Canaanites were the peoples who lived in that land.

The speakers are the people, who no longer had their leader Joshua. They had received the promise of inheriting the land, but some territories still had to be taken. The text does not say exactly how they asked God; some think it was through the priest, but the passage does not make this clear. God answers that Judah will go first.

For today: when one stage ends or an important leader is missing, the first step is to ask God before acting. And as Judah did with Simeon, it is good to ask for help and to walk together with others.
exp.2:13:
The explanation says that the people of Israel were under the rule of Eglon, king of Moab, for eighteen years. The word "served" here means that they were subjected and forced to obey him and pay him tribute. "Eighteen" is simply eighteen.

It is the narrator of the book of Judges who speaks. He explains that Israel returned to doing evil, that is, to turning away from God, and that God allowed Eglon to grow strong against them. Eglon allied himself with the Ammonites and the Amalekites and took the city of palms, which many identify with Jericho, though this is not certain. Afterward, the people cried out to God, and he sent Ehud as their deliverer.

Turning away from God almost always brings consequences that weigh heavily for a long time. But the account also reminds us that God hears the sincere cry. If today you feel trapped by your mistakes, you can return to him in prayer, without waiting to be perfect.
exp.13:8:
Samson takes the honey in his hands and keeps eating as he walks. When he arrives at his father and mother, he gives them honey too. But he does not tell them that he took it out of the dead body of the lion.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. Samson had killed a lion and, on returning, found bees and honey inside the carcass. According to the law of Moses, touching a dead body made the one who did it unclean (Numbers 19:11), and Samson was a Nazirite. That is why his silence stands out. Some see it as carelessness and others as a way of hiding what he did. The text does not explain it.

Today, this passage invites us to consider whether we are sharing with others something that is neither clean nor honest. Let us ask God for help to be truthful and not to hide what we ought to acknowledge.
exp.10:24:
Here Jephthah asks the king of the Ammonites whether he considers himself better than Balak, a king of Moab. Jephthah reminds him that Balak never fought against Israel to claim those lands, and that he himself has no reason to do so now.

Jephthah, a judge of Israel, answers the king of Ammon by messengers. The king was demanding territory east of the Jordan. Jephthah argues from history: Israel received those lands after defeating the Amorites, and no one had claimed them for centuries. Some scholars debate the details of the dates and of who owned the territory, but Jephthah's point is clear.

For today: before entering a conflict, it is wise to look at the facts honestly and seek dialogue. And when someone makes a claim against us, we can respond with calm and truth, letting God be the final judge.
exp.2:7:
This verse says that God became very angry with Israel because of their unfaithfulness. The phrase "sold them into the hand of" means he handed them over, letting them fall under the power of another. So Israel was ruled over for eight years by Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia.

The book of Judges tells this moment in the voice of a narrator. Israel had mixed with the peoples of Canaan, married among them, and worshiped the Baals, false gods of that land. Because of this, God allowed this oppression. But the account goes on: when the people cried out, God sent Othniel to deliver them. About the king mentioned here we do not know much more than what the Bible says.

For today: our choices have consequences, and turning away from God leaves us enslaved to other things. But we can always cry out to Him, for He hears and rescues. Today you can return to God with sincerity.
exp.5:32:
The Midianites, the Amalekites, and the peoples of the east joined together as one army. They crossed the Jordan River and camped in the valley of Jezreel. The phrase quoted from the source, meaning "together, by common agreement," is simply the sense of their joining forces; the sense of camping is that they set up their camp.

The narrator is the author of the book of Judges. Israel had been oppressed by these peoples for years. Gideon had just torn down the altar of Baal, and his father Joash had defended him. Now the real threat arrives: a huge enemy army. This is the moment when God is about to call Gideon to act, as the next verse shows.

For today: sometimes, right after taking a step of faith, the greatest trials arrive. This does not mean that God has abandoned you. It is an opportunity to depend on Him, who strengthened Gideon with His Spirit.
exp.8:53:
Abimelech, struck on the head by a woman, calls to his armourbearer, the young man who carried his weapons. He orders him to kill him with the sword so that people will not say that a woman killed him. The young man runs him through, and Abimelech dies.

Abimelech is the one speaking. He had made himself king by killing his seventy brothers. He attacked the tower of Thebez, and a woman dropped a millstone on him. He cared more about his reputation than about his life. But the account says that his pride did not save him: God repaid him for the evil he had done. Moreover, the story is remembered just the same.

For today: caring about how we look can become more important than being honest with God. It is better to live with humility and justice than to seek to look good before others.
exp.12:2:
This verse says that the angel of the Lord appeared to Manoah's wife and told her that, though until then she had been unable to have children, she was now going to become pregnant and would have a son.

The people of Israel had long turned away from God, and for that reason they were under the rule of the Philistines for forty years. Even so, God takes the initiative and draws near to this woman, whom the Bible does not name here. The child who would be born would be a Nazirite, set apart for God, and he would begin to deliver Israel.

For today: God can act even where there seems to be no hope. When you feel there is no way out, remember that he sees your situation and can act in his own time and in his own way. Trust and keep seeking him.
exp.5:14:
Gideon tells God that he does not feel able to save Israel. He asks "wherewith shall I save Israel?", that is, with what strength or resources. He says that his family is the poorest in the tribe of Manasseh and that he is the least, meaning the youngest or the one of least importance in his father's house.

Israel was suffering under the oppression of the Midianites because of its disobedience. The angel of the Lord had already called Gideon and told him to go in the strength he had. Gideon answers with doubt and humility, looking at his own limits. God does not argue with his weakness, but instead promises him: "Surely I will be with thee."

Many times we feel small or poorly prepared for what God places before us. This story reminds us that what matters is not how much we have, but that God goes with us. We can take the step with humility, trusting in his company and not in our own strength.
exp.1:0:
This verse says that the angel of the Lord went up from Gilgal to Bochim and spoke to the people of Israel. He reminded them that God brought them out of Egypt, led them into the land he had promised to their forefathers, and assured them that he would never break his covenant with them. To break or cancel something is what it means to annul it, and a promise made under solemn oath is what the text calls a sworn promise.

The one speaking is the angel of the Lord, who here speaks in the first person as God's representative. Some scholars think he is a special messenger of God, and others see in him an appearance of the Lord himself. He speaks after the death of Joshua, when the people had not fully obeyed. The name Bochim means "those who weep." That is why he begins by recalling God's faithfulness.

For today: God is faithful even when we fail. His faithfulness is not an excuse for carelessness, but a reason to obey him with gratitude and not to make agreements with anything that draws us away from him.
exp.15:28:
Samson grabs the two central pillars that were holding up the building. The verse's older wording "took hold of" is the same as "grabbed," and the phrase about leaning on them means he pressed against them with all his strength, putting his full weight into each pillar, one with his right hand and the other with his left.

The account is told by the narrator of the book of Judges. Samson, captured and blinded, was in the Philistine temple, where he was being mocked during a festival. Shortly before this, he had prayed to God, asking for strength one last time. He was a man full of flaws, but in the end he returned to depending on God. His death is presented as part of his work of delivering Israel, although some readers debate how to judge his motives of revenge.

For today: even after failing, we can return to God with humility and sincerity. He can use our weakness, and an honest prayer is always a good place to begin again.
exp.17:20:
This verse says that the men of the tribe of Dan turned around and left. They put the children, the livestock and the things they carried at the front. "Baggage" means luggage or belongings. "Turned" means they came back around, that is, they changed direction.

The Danites were looking for a territory to settle, and they took with them the priest and the sacred objects of Micah. They placed the weakest and the most valuable at the front, away from Micah's house. Some think they did this to protect them from a possible attack from behind. The Bible does not explain this with certainty. It was a time of disorder, when each person did whatever seemed right to them.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are seeking God or merely using religious things for our own plans. Caring for the weak is good, but doing so while taking what belongs to others reminds us that good actions do not justify unjust means.
exp.9:6:
This verse says that God became angry with Israel and allowed their enemies to dominate them. The phrase that is usually rendered "was hot against" means that he was angry with a righteous indignation. The word "sold" means "handed over," like someone who places something into the hands of another. The Philistines and the Ammonites were neighboring peoples who became their oppressors.

The narrator of the book tells this after saying that Israel had abandoned the LORD and served the gods of the surrounding nations. This was not a whimsical anger. God had warned that idolatry would bring consequences. The text goes on to show that this oppression lasted eighteen years and was very painful.

For today: when we give first place to other things instead of God, sooner or later we feel the emptiness and the weight of that decision. But this account moves forward and shows that God listens when his people turn back and cry out to him. Today you can return to God with sincerity, without delay.
exp.20:14:
The explanation says that the people of Israel felt sorrow and grief over the tribe of Benjamin. They recognized that the Lord had made a breach in the tribes, that is, had left a gap or a wound: one of the twelve tribes was nearly gone.

This takes place at the end of the book of Judges, after a civil war between Israel and Benjamin. Almost the whole tribe died, and few men were left. The narrator describes how the people grieved, since they had made a vow that made it difficult to give wives to the survivors. They were looking for a solution, though the account shows a time of great disorder.

For today: when there is division and harm between brothers and sisters, grief can open the door to repentance and reconciliation. Before acting on impulse, it is wise to ask God for wisdom.
exp.15:3:
Samson falls in love with a woman named Delilah, who lived in the valley of Sorek, after what happened in Gaza. The text does not say that she was a Philistine or that she loved him; the explanation does not clarify this here.

The narrator of the book of Judges tells the story of Samson, a judge of Israel endowed with extraordinary strength. He has just shown his power by carrying off the gates of Gaza. Now the story changes direction: his physical strength stands in contrast to his weakness in relationships. Soon the Philistine rulers will seek out Delilah to discover the secret of his strength.

For today: love and emotions are powerful, but they need wisdom. Before we give our heart or our trust to someone, it is wise to pray, seek counsel, and notice whether that relationship draws us closer to God or pulls us away from Him.
exp.17:26:
The explanation says that the men of Dan took the idols that Micah had made and also carried off his priest. They came to Laish, a quiet and secure people, struck them with the edge of the sword, and burned the city with fire.

Here the narrator is telling the story, not speaking as a character. The tribe of Dan had not taken the land that had been assigned to it, so it went looking for another by force. The book of Judges shows a time of disorder, when everyone did what seemed right to them. The text describes what happened; it does not say that God approved of it.

For today: let us not confuse success with God's blessing. We can achieve what we want and still be far from his way. Let us ask him to teach us to seek what is right, not only what suits us.
exp.2:20:
Ehud, who was left-handed, drew with his left hand a dagger he had strapped to his right thigh, and thrust it into the king's belly. A "dagger" is a short blade. Normally a guard searches for weapons on the left side, which is where a right-handed man would carry one, and that is why no one suspected him.

We are in the time of the judges. Israel was oppressed by Eglon, king of Moab, because of their disobedience to God. Ehud, of the tribe of Benjamin, was raised up as a deliverer and carried the tribute to the king. Then he asked to be alone with him, saying that he had a message from God. The passage presents this as part of Israel's deliverance, though it is a raw and violent account.

For today: God can use people with traits that others overlook, as Ehud was used with his left hand. Do not look down on yourself, and trust that God works even in difficult times.
exp.19:13:
The explanation says that the people of Benjamin, instead of handing over the guilty men, gathered from their cities toward Gibeah to go out and fight against the rest of Israel. "On the contrary" is the meaning here. "Go out to battle" means to set out to war.

The narrator tells what happened after the terrible crime committed in Gibeah. The other tribes asked Benjamin to hand over those men, called "sons of Belial," that is, wicked people, so that justice could be done. Benjamin refused to listen to his brothers and chose to protect his own and fight. Thus a grave sin turned into a war between brothers.

For today: when someone from our own side does something wrong, defending them out of loyalty only makes the harm greater. Let us ask God for humility to recognize the wrong, correct it, and seek justice, even when it hurts.
exp.14:2:
Samson says that this time he will not be to blame before the Philistines if he harms them. By "without blame" he means that no one can accuse him of wrongdoing, because they had first done him an injury. The phrase "if I do them harm" means "if I cause them harm."

Samson speaks in anger and hurt. He went to visit his wife, and her father would not let him in, because he had given her to another man, believing that Samson had rejected her. Samson justifies himself before he acts, and right after this he sets fire to the Philistines' fields. The text tells what he did, but it does not say that God approved his anger or his revenge. Even so, the Bible shows that God was at work within this situation.

For today: when someone hurts us, it is easy to use the injustice we have received as an excuse for taking revenge. Before we react, it is wise to pray and ask God for self-control and wisdom.
exp.18:7:
It says that on the fifth day the Levite got up early to leave for home, but his father-in-law asked him, "Comfort your heart," that is, eat something and take heart. They ate together and stayed until the day was already fading. The young woman is his father-in-law's daughter, and the phrase "they stayed" means that they delayed.

The speaker is the young woman's father, who wants to keep his son-in-law with hospitality. The Levite had gone to bring back his concubine, and the father-in-law looks after him with food and rest. But each day he manages to prolong the departure, and that delay leads to a journey by night, with serious consequences that the story tells later.

For today: hospitality is good, but we also need wisdom to decide well about our timing. A kindness without prudence can lead us to postpone what matters. Let us ask God for discernment to know when to stay and when to leave.
exp.15:5:
Delilah asks Samson to tell her the secret of his great strength and how he could be tied up to be subdued. "Please" is the meaning of the earlier phrase. The word "tell" is what is being asked for here, meaning to explain it or reveal it. "Tormented" here refers to being subdued and humiliated.

It is Delilah who speaks, a woman with whom Samson had fallen in love. The Philistine rulers, enemies of Israel, offered her a great deal of money to discover that secret. She pretends affection, but her real purpose is to betray him. Samson responds with deceptions, yet he keeps toying with danger.

For today: let us guard our hearts and the relationships where we place our trust. If someone insists on knowing the most vulnerable parts of us and we notice signs of deceit, it is wise to set boundaries. Let us ask God for discernment so that we do not play with what can harm us.
exp.12:10:
Manoah got up and went after his wife. When he reached the man she had seen, he asked him whether he was the one who had spoken to her. The man answered, "I am." The word "man" here means simply a man, and the phrase about the news being passed along means that she had told him about it.

Manoah and his wife had no children. The angel of the Lord had told her that she would have a son, the future Samson. Manoah had prayed asking for more instructions, and God answered by sending the angel again. Manoah does not settle for hearing the news secondhand; he wants to confirm it for himself. Here he still sees the visitor as a man, even though the text calls him the angel of God.

For today: it is good to seek God with humility when we need direction, and also to listen to those whom He uses to speak to us, as Manoah did with his wife.
exp.0:34:
It says the Amorites were determined to keep living in the hill of Heres, in Aijalon and in Shaalbim. But when the tribe of Joseph (Ephraim and Manasseh) grew strong, it subdued them and made them pay tribute, that is, they had to pay taxes or work for them. Here "would" means they were stubborn and insisted on staying. "The hand prevailed" means that their power grew.

It is the narrator of the book of Judges, who summarizes how the tribes never fully drove out the peoples of Canaan. The Amorites had pressed on Dan, and now Joseph manages to dominate them in that area. Even so, the overall picture is of an incomplete conquest: they subdued some instead of driving them out, and that would bring problems later.

For today: partial victories can become a temptation to settle for less. It is worth asking ourselves what things we have kept under our own control instead of truly handing over to God, and asking him for strength to obey him completely.
exp.18:19:
The explanation says that the old man welcomed the traveler with a greeting of peace and took responsibility for everything he needed. His only condition was that he not spend the night in the square, that is, outdoors in the town square. The words "I will take care of it" is what the phrase means.

The one speaking is an old man from Gibeah who lived there, although he was from the region of Ephraim. The Levite was traveling with his concubine and his servant, and no one had invited them to spend the night. The old man sees the danger of sleeping in the street and takes them in. What follows shows that the danger was real: the town was full of wickedness.

Today, this scene encourages us to practice hospitality and to care for the one who is helpless. Perhaps we can offer concrete help to a traveler, a migrant, or a needy neighbor. But it also reminds us to be prudent, because good can face wickedness.
exp.10:35:
Here the daughter of Jephthah answers her father. She tells him that if he has made a solemn promise to God (to "open his mouth" means to make a vow), he must keep it, because God has already given him victory over the Ammonites. To "take vengeance" means that God gave them the win over their enemies.

Jephthah, a judge of Israel, had vowed to God that he would offer whatever came out of his house first if he won the battle. The one who came out was his only daughter. The text does not clearly explain what happened afterward: some understand that she was offered as a sacrifice, others that she was dedicated to live unmarried in the service of God. Interpreters debate this.

For today: let us think before we speak, especially when we make promises to God or to others. And let us value the humble faith of this young woman, who trusted God even in the midst of her grief.
exp.6:8:
God speaks to Gideon at night and commands him to get up and go down to the enemy camp. He assures him that he has already given the Midianites into his hand.

Here it is God himself who speaks. Gideon had already been left with only three hundred men, a very small group facing an enormous army. This made it clear that the victory would come from God and not from human strength. God knows that Gideon is afraid, and that is why, in the verses that follow, he offers that Gideon go down with his servant Purah to listen to the enemy and be encouraged.

For today: when you face something that frightens you, God is not angry at your fear. He encourages you to take the step you are able to take, and to trust his promise. Obey today in what is asked of you, even if you feel afraid.
exp.0:7:
It says that the men of Judah attacked Jerusalem and took it. "Put to the sword" means they killed its inhabitants with the sword, and "set on fire" means they burned the city.

The narrator of the book of Judges describes how the tribes of Israel, after the death of Joshua, tried to take the promised land. Judah goes first. This is a war account from that era, not an instruction for today. Later on, Jerusalem appears again in the hands of the Jebusites (Judges 1:21), so the victory may have been partial or temporary. Scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: this book shows that many victories are left half-finished. Ask God for perseverance to faithfully complete what He has entrusted to you, without settling for a good start that is left unfinished.
exp.4:17:
The explanation says that the people of the tribe of Zebulun risked their lives to the point of being willing to die, and that the tribe of Naphtali did the same in the heights of the field, that is, in the high places where the fighting took place. The phrase "jeoparded their lives unto the death" means that they did not look after their own safety, but threw themselves into danger.

It is part of the song of Deborah and Barak, after the victory over Sisera. Deborah praises the tribes that came to the battle and rebukes those that stayed behind: Reuben, Gilead, Dan and Asher. Zebulun and Naphtali appear as an example of commitment, since they were the tribes that Barak had gathered, according to Judges 4.

For today: God often uses those who respond with courage and commitment. Ask yourself what good task you have been waiting to do from the comfort of your position, and take one concrete step of service this week.
exp.14:18:
God split open a hollow place in the ground at a spot called Lehi, and water came gushing out of it. Samson drank, his strength returned, and his spirit revived. For this reason he named that place En-hakkore, which means something like "the spring of the one who called out." The word "hollow" here most likely refers to a hollow or cavity in the rock, though some understand it as a crack in the ground.

Samson had just defeated a thousand Philistines using the jawbone of a donkey. Exhausted and very thirsty, he recognized that God had given him the victory, and he feared dying at the hands of his enemies. So he called out to the LORD.

When you are worn out after a great battle, do not lean on your own strength. Speak to God honestly, as Samson did, and trust that he can give you what you need.
exp.16:6:
Here a young Levite is presented who was living as a foreigner in Bethlehem of Judah. "Sojourned" means that he was staying there for a time, without a home of his own. That he is called "out of Bethlehem-judah, of the family of Judah" may mean that he lived among the clan of Judah, since he was a Levite by birth. Some scholars explain it this way.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Judges. He has just told how Micah made his own shrine and set his son up as priest, at a time when everyone did what seemed right to them. The Levites were meant to serve God, and this young man wandered without direction. That emptiness prepares what comes next.

For today: it is not enough to feel good about what we do. Let us seek God's direction in his Word, and in his people, before we decide.
exp.20:13:
This verse tells how the men of Benjamin came back, and they were given as wives the four hundred young women of Jabesh-gilead who had been kept alive. "Virgins" here means unmarried young women. But those women were not enough for all the Benjamites who remained.

The narrator describes the end of a civil war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, which had nearly been wiped out. The Israelites had sworn not to give their daughters to Benjamin, and now they were looking for a way out. Their solution included the killing of the people of Jabesh-gilead. The book notes that in those days there was no king and everyone did what seemed right to them. For that reason, the story is not presented as a model to imitate.

For today: when we make mistakes, let us not fix them with other mistakes. Before deciding, let us seek God's guidance and his Word, and not only our own reasoning.
exp.15:23:
This verse tells that the Philistines saw Samson held captive and praised their god, Dagon. They said that their god had given them victory over the man who was ruining their land and had killed many of them. The words "praised" and "ruining" are rendered here as in the verse above.

The speakers are the Philistine people, gathered at a great religious feast. Samson was blind and imprisoned because he had revealed the secret of his strength. The Philistines credited their triumph to Dagon, but the account shows that Samson had fallen through his own disobedience. His hair was already beginning to grow back, which foreshadows that something would change.

For today: it is easy to celebrate too soon and to believe that everything is settled when someone falls. God continues to work even in moments of apparent defeat. It is wise to live with humility, without boasting of victories or giving up in our failures.
exp.7:24:
The people of Israel gladly accept Gideon's request. They spread a cloak or garment on the ground, and each soldier throws into it the earrings, that is, the gold earrings he had taken from the spoils.

Gideon had just defeated the Midianites. The Israelites wanted to make him king, but he said that only the LORD should rule. Then he asked for the gold. Afterward he made from it an ephod, a sacred garment, and the people ended up worshiping it. That is why the Bible calls it a snare. Gideon's motives are not explained with certainty.

A good decision can be twisted by one step taken without careful thought. Let us take care that what we do with good intentions does not take the place of God in our hearts.
exp.7:25:
The gold earrings that Gideon asked for weighed one thousand seven hundred shekels, about 19 kilos by common calculations. That did not include the ornaments, the pendants, the purple clothing of the kings of Midian, or the collars on their camels. "Earrings" are the rings worn in the ears, and the small hanging jewels are the ornaments that dangled from them.

Gideon speaks after defeating Midian. He asks his soldiers for part of the spoil, and they give willingly. The text shows how much wealth there was. Then Gideon makes an ephod from that gold, and the people worship it. Scholars debate exactly what that ephod was, but the text says it became a snare.

Today: a victory or a blessing can become a trap if we turn what God gave us into a symbol of pride. Give thanks to God, and do not place your trust in what you have achieved.
exp.8:19:
It says that, if the people of Shechem and Abimelech did not act with truth and integrity, God would let fire come out from Abimelech and burn up the men of Shechem and the house of Millo, and also let fire come out from them and burn up Abimelech. The house of Millo seems to be a house or stronghold of Shechem; its exact meaning is not entirely certain. The fire is a way of speaking about destruction and mutual conflict.

The speaker is Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon (Jerubbaal). He escaped when Abimelech killed his brothers. From Mount Gerizim he told a parable, and now he ends with this warning: if they did wrong in making Abimelech king, that wrong would turn back against all of them. Then he fled to Beer out of fear.

For today: alliances built on violence or injustice do not last, and in the end they harm everyone. Before we support a leader or a plan, let us ask whether it is based on truth and integrity.
exp.5:11:
This verse says that the angel of the Lord appeared to Gideon and told him that God was with him. He called him "mighty man of valour," which means a brave and strong man. The phrase "said unto him" simply means "told him."

The one speaking is the angel of the Lord, the messenger who brings God's word. Israel was suffering under the oppression of the Midianites because they had turned away from God. Gideon was threshing wheat in a winepress, hiding out of fear. Even so, God greets him as a valiant man, because He sees what God will do in him, not only his present fear. Gideon answered with doubts, and that shows he did not feel strong.

Today, God does not define us by our fears or failures. If you are discouraged, remember that His presence with you is what gives courage. You can take a step of obedience, even if you feel small.
exp.13:19:
The Spirit of the Lord came upon Samson with power. He went down to Ashkelon, killed thirty men from that city, and took their clothing. Those "changes of clothes" were sets of fine garments. He gave them to the men who had solved his riddle. Then, very angry, he returned to his father's house. In the meantime, his wife was given to the man who had been his companion, that is, the friend who had accompanied him at the wedding.

Samson had wagered thirty sets of clothing with the Philistines if they solved his riddle. They pressured his wife, she got the answer out of him and revealed it. Samson had to pay the wager. The text shows that God used this situation against the Philistines, but it does not approve of Samson's violence or his anger. The Bible here simply narrates what happened.

For today: anger handled badly destroys relationships and brings harm that cannot be undone. Before reacting, stop, pray, and seek to calm yourself.
exp.19:34:
It says that God defeated the tribe of Benjamin before the army of Israel. That day 25,100 Benjamites fell, all of them warriors who drew the sword, that is, men trained to fight. The word "smote" means that God struck them down or defeated them.

The narrator of the book tells this after a horrible crime in Gibeah. Benjamin did not hand over the guilty men and chose war against their own brothers. Israel had already lost two battles, and this time it used an ambush. The text credits the victory to God, though it also shows human strategy. It is a dark time, when everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes.

Today it reminds us that covering up evil and refusing to correct it brings painful consequences. If we know that something is wrong, it is good to acknowledge it with humility, ask for God's guidance, and not defend what is wrong merely out of loyalty to our own people.
exp.9:8:
The explanation says that the Ammonites, who were already oppressing the Israelites east of the Jordan, crossed the river to attack the tribes on the other side as well: Judah, Benjamin, and Ephraim. With this, Israel's suffering grew greatly. The phrase "so that Israel was sore distressed" means that they were deeply troubled and oppressed.

The narrator of the book of Judges explains that God allowed this oppression because the people had turned away from Him to serve the Baals, false gods of the neighboring peoples. They had already endured eighteen years of suffering. Now the trouble reached the heartland of the land, and this moved them to cry out to God, as seen in the next verse.

For today: sometimes we ignore small warnings, and the problem grows until we can no longer avoid it. When something in your life pulls you away from God, do not wait until you are desperate. Return to Him soon, with sincerity, and He will receive you.
exp.2:24:
They waited so long that the servants became confused, that is, ashamed and uneasy, because the door stayed shut. In the end they took the key, opened it, and found their lord fallen dead on the floor.

The upper room is the chamber on the upper floor, and "covered his feet" was a discreet way of saying that someone was relieving himself.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. Israel was under the rule of Moab, and God raised up Ehud as a deliverer. Ehud killed the king and left calmly, closing the doors behind him. The servants believed the king was resting or in the bathroom, and that delay gave Ehud time to escape and gather the people.

For today: God can use ordinary circumstances and people's patience to carry out his plans. Trust that he is at work even when everything seems still, and do not despair if answers take time.
exp.15:2:
According to the passage, Samson lay there until midnight, then got up. He tore up the doors of the city of Gaza, along with their two posts and their bar (the crossbar that held them shut), put them on his shoulders, and carried them to the top of the mountain that faces Hebron.

The narrator tells us that the people of Gaza had surrounded him, planning to kill him at dawn, while he was with a woman of loose morals. Samson, a judge of Israel, escapes the trap by the strength God had given him. Many see here a sign of his power, but also a contrast with his conduct, because the text does not present him as a moral example.

For today: God can sustain us and deliver us even when we get ourselves into dangerous situations, but we must not take advantage of his grace. If we have received his help, let us value that mercy and seek to live with more wisdom and purity.
exp.8:16:
This verse recalls what Gideon (also called Jerubbaal) did. He fought for the people, risked his life, and rescued them from the power of Midian. The phrase "adventured his life far" means that he put his life on the line without thinking of himself.

Jotham, the only son of Gideon who escaped the slaughter, is the one speaking. From Mount Gerizim he tells the people of Shechem a fable. He wants to show them their ingratitude: they owed their freedom to his father, yet they killed his seventy sons and crowned Abimelech. This verse is part of his complaint.

For today: remember those who sacrificed themselves for you, such as parents, teachers, or brothers and sisters in the faith, and repay them with gratitude and respect. May the favors you have received never be forgotten.
exp.5:12:
Gideon answers the angel honestly and with pain. If the Lord is with us, he asks, why has all this come upon us? He asks where the miracles are that our fathers told us about, such as the departure from Egypt. He feels that the Lord has forsaken them and handed them over into the hands of the Midianites. "Befallen" means that something has come down on them; "forsaken" means abandoned.

Gideon speaks in a time of oppression. The Midianites were raiding Israel's harvests, and for that reason he was threshing wheat in secret in a winepress. The angel greeted him by saying that the Lord was with him, and Gideon responds out of his hard experience. Some see here a lack of faith; others see an honest complaint. The text does not condemn him.

When pain makes you doubt God, do not hide it. Tell him honestly, as Gideon did. God hears your questions and can answer you, even when you do not yet understand what is happening.
exp.12:4:
She is told that a woman who could not have children will become pregnant and have a son. His hair will never be cut (the phrase about no razor coming on his head says this), because he will be a Nazirite, that is, someone set apart for God from before he is born. That son will begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines. The word "conceive" here simply means to become pregnant.

The angel of the Lord speaks to the wife of Manoah, at a time when Israel was oppressed by the Philistines. God chooses to act through a woman without children. The child is Samson. His Nazirite vow included not drinking wine and not cutting his hair. Notice that it says he will "begin" to save: his work would not be complete.

For today: God can start great things in situations that seem closed. Trust that your life has purpose, even if you see only the beginning.
exp.13:9:
This verse tells that Samson's father went down to the house of the Philistine woman whom Samson was going to marry, and that Samson held a wedding feast there. A "feast" is a meal with food and drink. The "young men" are the young men who attended. It says that this is what young men used to do at that time.

This is the account of the narrator of the book of Judges. Samson had already killed a lion and had eaten honey from its body without telling his parents. Now he celebrates his wedding in Philistine territory, following local customs. Scholars do not fully agree on whether this was an Israelite or a Philistine custom. The text only says it was usual. Later, this feast will lead to a riddle and to serious troubles.

For today: following a social custom does not always mean it is wise. Before we let ourselves be carried along by "what everyone does," it is good to ask God whether that path honors him and takes care of us.
exp.10:27:
This verse tells us that the king of the Ammonites would not listen to the message Jephthah sent him. "Would not listen" means that he paid no attention to it and did not consider what was said. The "reasons" were the arguments or explanations Jephthah gave him.

The narrator of the book explains what happened after Jephthah, a judge of Israel, sent messengers to the king of Ammon. The Ammonites wanted to fight against Israel over some lands. Jephthah defended Israel's claim with arguments, saying that Israel had lived in those lands for three hundred years, and he left the final judgment in God's hands. Even so, the king refused to hear him, and that opened the way to war.

For today: working for peace by speaking clearly and with respect is worth the effort, even when the other person will not listen. When we have done what we can, we can leave the outcome in God's hands, for he judges with justice.
exp.7:30:
This verse tells us that Gideon had another son with a woman who lived in Shechem, and he named him Abimelech. The word the verse uses for her is "concubine," a secondary wife who had fewer rights than a wife. The verse says she "bare" him a son, meaning she gave birth to him.

It is the narrator of the book of Judges who speaks here. After Gideon's great victory, the account shows us his family life: many wives and seventy sons. Abimelech is mentioned because his story will turn painful later on. The verses that follow say that Israel returned to idolatry after Gideon died. The Bible does not approve of this family life here; it simply reports it.

For today: a good start in faith does not guarantee a good finish. A person's decisions, especially within the home, affect those who come after them. Take care with your relationships and your example, and ask God for steady faithfulness.
exp.8:13:
The explanation says that after the other trees turned down the offer, all the trees go to the bramble and ask it to be their king. The bramble is a thorny shrub, of little value and without useful fruit.

It is a parable told by Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon (Jerubbaal). Abimelech had killed his brothers to make himself king of Shechem. Jotham uses the story to say that the good trees, like the vine, did not want to reign, and that only the thorny shrub accepted. Many understand that the bramble represents Abimelech, although the text gives no further details about the exact plant.

For today: before following a leader, do not look only at his ambition or his promises. Look at his character and at the fruit of his life. And if you are the one who must lead, do it with humility and service, not out of pride.
exp.20:16:
They say that the survivors of Benjamin, those who managed to escape, must keep the land that belonged to their tribe. In this way Benjamin would not disappear from Israel.

The elders of Israel are speaking after the war against Benjamin, which left that tribe almost destroyed. They were grieved by what had happened, but they were also trapped by an oath not to give their daughters to the Benjamites. They were looking for a way for the tribe to survive. The book shows a time of great disorder, and not all of its solutions are examples to follow.

For today: when a conflict leaves wounds, it is worth seeking restoration and not merely winning the fight. But before promising something lightly, let us think carefully, because hasty vows can bring difficult problems that are hard to resolve.
exp.19:44:
This verse tells of the end of the battle between the tribes of Israel and the tribe of Benjamin. The Benjaminites, defeated, fled toward the wilderness, to a rock called Rimmon. Along the way, the Israelites overtook five thousand of them, and they pursued them as far as Gidom, where they killed two thousand more.

It is part of an account in the book of Judges, written by a narrator who does not identify himself. It tells of the punishment of Benjamin for protecting the guilty in a terrible crime at Gibeah. The book describes a time without order, when everyone did what seemed right in their own eyes. It is an account of what happened, not a model to imitate.

For today: when injustice is tolerated, its consequences grow and wound many people. Today we can choose to act justly and humbly in time, before evil becomes larger.
exp.5:28:
Here we see that the people of the town wake up and find the altar of Baal destroyed. They ask one another who did it. After searching and questioning, they discover that it was Gideon, son of Joash. "Inquiring" means asking carefully, and the grove here probably refers to a pole or tree used in worship of a goddess called Asherah.

The men of Ophrah speak. Gideon had obeyed God, but he did it at night out of fear. Now his act comes to light, and the town, which worshiped Baal, becomes enraged and prepares to go against Gideon's family.

Obeying God can bring rejection, even from those close to us. Gideon was afraid and yet obeyed. God does not expect us to feel no fear, but to take the step of faith. Ask Him for courage to do what is right today.
exp.3:1:
And the Lord gave Israel into the hand of Jabin, a Canaanite king who ruled from Hazor. The verse says that God handed them over, leaving them under the power of another. Sisera, the commander of Jabin's army, lived in Harosheth of the Gentiles.

The narrator tells the story of Israel after the death of the judge Ehud. The people again turned away from God, and the text presents the oppression as the result of that disobedience. Soon after, Israel cries out to God, and He responds by raising up Deborah. In this way, the verse shows the problem before the help.

For today: the choices we make have consequences, and sometimes we must live with their effects. But we can always cry out to God sincerely. He hears, and in the middle of the trouble He can begin to prepare a way out.
exp.18:3:
This verse tells how the Levite's father-in-law, seeing him arrive at Bethlehem, went out happily to receive him. He persuaded him to stay, and the Levite spent three days there, eating, drinking and resting.

It is part of the story in Judges, which takes place in a time of moral disorder in Israel. A Levite goes to bring back his concubine, who had gone to her father's house. The narrator speaks here not of reproach but of a very warm welcome. Some interpreters see in the father a sincere desire to reconcile the couple; others note that the insistence on keeping him there prepares the delay that brings serious consequences later.

For today: hospitality and the joy of reconciliation are valuable, but we should take care that comfort does not lead us to postpone what we ought to do in time.
exp.5:1:
The verse tells how the people of Midian grew stronger than Israel and took control over them. Out of fear, the Israelites left their homes and hid in dens in the mountains, in caves, and in strong places.

The one who narrates is the author of the book of Judges. He explains that this happened because Israel did evil in the sight of God, and God allowed Midian to oppress them for seven years. The Midianites, together with other peoples, would come and destroy the harvests, and so the people lived hidden away and hungry.

For today: when we live in fear or in trouble, it is wise to ask ourselves humbly whether we have drifted away from God. Not all suffering comes from sin, but sometimes pain wakes us up to return to Him, who hears and rescues, as we will see later in this story.
exp.11:2:
Jephthah tells the men of Ephraim that when they did not come to help him, he risked his life and went out to fight against the Ammonites. The Lord gave them into his hand. Then he asks them why they have now come up to fight against him.

Jephthah, judge of Gilead, is speaking. The men of Ephraim, a proud tribe, were angry because they had not been invited to share in the victory, and they threatened to burn his house. Jephthah defends himself by saying that he did call them and they did not answer. This ended in a war between brothers, as the following text shows.

For today: when a conflict arises, do not let wounded pride lead you into fighting. Speak calmly, seek the truth, and work for peace before a small offense becomes a great harm.
exp.17:3:
Here the young Levite explains how he came to be Micah's priest. He says that Micah "has dealt with me thus and thus," that is, that Micah made an arrangement with him and hired him. The word "hired" means that Micah employed him and paid him a wage.

The Levite and the five scouts from Dan speak together. They recognize his voice, perhaps because of his accent or because they already knew him, and they ask what he is doing there. He explains his situation. He is a priest hired to serve in a house with idols, something foreign to what God had commanded. Afterward the Danites ask him for counsel, and he answers with confidence, though the text does not confirm that God spoke through him.

Today, before accepting a job or a position, it is wise to ask ourselves whether it draws us closer to God or leads us to keep the truth silent for convenience. A religious voice is not always the voice of God.
exp.5:25:
God tells Gideon to build an altar to the LORD on the top of this rock, in a suitable place. Then he is to take the second bull and offer it whole as a burnt offering, a sacrifice that was burned up completely. For the fire he would use the wood of the grove that he cuts down, which in other versions is rendered as the Asherah, a pole or sacred tree of pagan worship that Gideon was to cut down.

The LORD speaks the same night that Gideon is called. Israel was oppressed by Midian and had given itself over to idolatry. Before freeing the people, God wants to clean out Gideon's household: first to tear down the altar of Baal that his father had, and then to worship the true God.

For today: before asking God for great victories, it is wise to ask ourselves what things have taken his place in our hearts. Obeying in the small, nearby matters, even when it is frightening, as Gideon did, opens the way for God to work.
exp.15:10:
Samson tells Delilah that if they bind him tightly with new ropes that have never been used, he will lose his strength and be like any other man. The verse says the ropes must be new and never used. He is speaking to Delilah, who kept asking him to reveal the secret of his strength. She was working with the Philistines, who wanted to overpower him. He had already lied to her before with the fresh branches. This second answer is also false, and the Bible shows this when he easily breaks the ropes. Samson is playing with fire, and he comes closer and closer to revealing the truth.

For today: do not play with temptations or with those who seek your harm. Each small concession brings you closer to a greater fall, so set clear limits in time.
exp.11:7:
After Jephthah's death, this verse says, a man named Ibzan, from Bethlehem, became the next judge of Israel. To judge here means that he governed, guided, and settled matters for the people. Bethlehem is the town of Ibzan's origin. No deed of his is recorded here.

Context: the book of Judges describes a time when God raised up leaders to guide Israel. Here the narrator speaks, giving a brief bridge after the painful war between Gilead and Ephraim. The text does not explain why Ibzan is mentioned so briefly. Some think the Bethlehem named here is the one near Nazareth, and others think it is the one in Judah, but this is not certain.

For today: not all faithful service to God is famous or dramatic. You can be faithful in your family, your work, and your church, even when few notice. God does see it.
exp.18:18:
Here a Levite says he needs nothing from the old man. He already has straw and feed for his donkeys, and bread and wine for himself, for his concubine, and for his servant. The word for the dry feed given to animals is what the verse calls straw and provender. Only a place under a roof is still missing.

The one speaking is a Levite from the hill country of Ephraim, traveling with his companion and his servant. He arrived in Gibeah, but in the square no one took him in. An old man asks who he is, and he explains that he is not asking for food or money, but for hospitality. This shows how harsh the lack of welcome was in that town, as the book depicts in those dark days.

For today: sometimes the person nearby does not need gifts, but a safe place and a gesture of welcome. Think of someone in your church, workplace, or neighborhood who is alone or passing through, and open your door to them or invite them to eat.
exp.4:16:
This verse names three tribes that did not go to the battle. Gilead, the region east of the Jordan, stayed there. Dan stayed near the ships, and Asher stayed along the coast, in its harbors and landing places. The questions sound like a reproach.

Deborah, together with Barak, speaks in a song of victory over the Canaanites. She praises the tribes that risked their lives and points out those that did not help. Some think they stayed because of their work or comfort; the text gives no further reasons.

For today: when others need help, it is easy to retreat into our own occupations. Ask God for the courage to serve, even when it costs you.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that Joshua had already sent the people away, and that each family of Israel had gone to its own share, the land it was given to receive. There they were to live and take possession of it.

The book of Judges here looks back again, to the end of Joshua's life (see Joshua 24). After the weeping at Bochim, the narrator explains how the people came to that situation. First he recalls a time of faithfulness: while Joshua and the elders who had seen the works of God were alive, Israel served the LORD. In this way he prepares the story of what happened when that generation was gone.

For today: God gives us things that we are to hold on to with effort and faith. But the faith of others is not inherited automatically. Take care of your own relationship with God, and share with your children what He has done for you.
exp.20:11:
It says that the Israelites found among the inhabitants of Jabesh-gilead four hundred young virgins, that is, women who had never been intimate with a man. They brought them to the camp at Shiloh, in the land of Canaan. The narrator tells the ending of the book of Judges. The tribes of Israel had nearly destroyed Benjamin and had sworn not to give them their daughters as wives. Then they grieved over that tribe and looked for a way out. This solution is violent and tragic. The text does not approve it; it presents it as part of a chaotic time, when everyone did whatever seemed right to them (Judges 21:25).

For today: when we make hasty decisions or oaths without thinking, we sometimes try to fix one mistake with a bigger one. Before acting, let us seek God and his wisdom, and not let pride or anger guide us.
exp.3:3:
This verse presents Deborah as the person who led Israel at that time. She was a prophetess, that is, someone through whom God spoke to his people, and she was married to Lappidoth. Here, "led" means that she held leadership and judged, settling matters for the people.

The narrator of the book tells us that Israel had been oppressed for twenty years by Jabin, king of Canaan, and his commander Sisera, who had nine hundred iron chariots. The people had cried out to God. In that difficult moment, God had Deborah in a place of authority. The Israelites came to her to receive justice, and she would summon Barak to pass on the word of the Lord.

God can use whom He chooses, at the moment He chooses. When you face a difficult situation, seek His direction with humility and obey, no matter who brings it to you.
exp.19:3:
Here the Levite answers the question of Israel and begins to tell what happened. He says that he came to Gibeah, a town of the tribe of Benjamin, with his concubine (a wife of secondary rank), only to spend the night. The word "man" is the ordinary word for a person, and the phrase "to lodge" means to stay as a guest and sleep there.

The one speaking is the Levite, husband of the woman who died. The tribes gathered at Mizpah and asked for an account of that wickedness. He is the main witness, though his account is partial: later he tells the events in a way that makes him look better and leaves out details. This story takes place in a time of great moral chaos in Israel.

For today: before judging or acting in the face of injustice, it is wise to listen calmly and seek the whole truth. And as the Bible teaches, our response to wickedness should pursue justice without adding more violence.
exp.2:29:
That day Moab was defeated and brought under the power of Israel. The phrase "subdued" means brought under control, placed under authority. The phrase "the land had rest" means there was peace, without wars or oppression, for eighty years. Some understand that number as a long period of calm, and others as an exact count.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Earlier, Ehud, the judge whom God raised up, had killed King Eglon and called the people to follow him, trusting that the LORD was giving them the victory. Israel had suffered for years under Moab because they had turned away from God. Now the account shows that God delivers his people and gives them rest.

For today: when you face something that weighs you down, do not trust only in your own strength. Act with courage and obedience, but remember that true victory and peace come from God. Give him thanks when rest arrives.
exp.10:2:
This verse tells how Jephthah, rejected by his half-brothers, fled and went to live in the land of Tob. There men gathered around him and went out with him. The explanation says these were men without a steady job, probably adventurers or people with few resources, and the verse itself gives no further detail. They likely went out with him on armed expeditions, though the text does not say more.

It is the narrator who speaks. Jephthah was the son of a woman of poor reputation and was driven out of his father's house with no inheritance. Later, when the Ammonites attack Israel, the elders of Gilead will look for him precisely because he was a brave man. God had not forgotten him, even though his family had.

For today: if you have been rejected or looked down on, your past does not decide your future. Place your gifts in God's hands, be careful about who you associate with, and trust that He can use you in His time.
exp.17:11:
The explanation says that the 600 men of the tribe of Dan, while on their way, camped near Kirjath-jearim, in the territory of Judah. For this reason that place kept the name "camp of Dan" (in Hebrew, Mahaneh-dan), and it was still called that when the book was written. "Pitched camp" means they set up their camp.

It is the narrator of Judges who speaks. He explains where a place name that his readers already knew came from. The Danites did not yet have a secure land of their own, and they were looking for a place to settle. They travel armed toward Laish, and on the way they will pass by the house of Micah, where it is seen that their decisions do not consult God, but are guided by convenience.

For today: our decisions leave marks, sometimes for years. Before moving toward what seems safe and plentiful, it is wise to stop and ask God whether the path we are taking is also the one He approves.
exp.13:4:
This verse tells that Samson went down to Timnath together with his father and mother. When they came to the vineyards, a young lion came roaring toward him. The word "young lion" here refers to a young and strong lion, not a helpless cub. The roaring is the sound the lion made as it charged at him.

The one who narrates this is the writer of Judges. Samson was going to ask for a Philistine woman as his wife, something his parents did not approve of. Yet the text says that God was using that situation to act against the Philistines, who ruled over Israel. The lion appears suddenly, and afterward the Spirit of the LORD gives strength to Samson.

For today: God can work even in confusing or imperfect situations, but that does not justify our bad decisions. When we face unexpected trials, let us trust that God is the one who gives strength, not ourselves.
exp.4:20:
The explanation says that the river Kishon swept away Israel's enemies. It calls it the "ancient river," perhaps because it was a channel known for a long time, though some think the word carries a different nuance. The phrases "swept them away" and "thou hast trodden down strength" are rendered in the verse above, and the sentence that explains their meaning is set aside here, since the reader's wording already conveys it. Deborah addresses herself: with strength she trampled her adversaries.

This is the song of Deborah and Barak after defeating the army of Sisera. The text of Judges 4 and 5 suggests that a flooding of the river helped Israel, since the iron chariots were rendered useless. Deborah sees in this the hand of God, who fought for his people.

For today: God can use circumstances we do not control to help us. When you face something that seems greater than you, do your part with courage and trust that God is also at work where you cannot reach. Then, thank him.
exp.6:21:
The three hundred men of Gideon kept blowing their horns, which were rams' horns or trumpets. God made the enemy soldiers, confused in the darkness, turn and strike one another with their own swords. Then the whole army of Midian ran away toward places such as Beth-shittah, Zererath, and Abel-meholah, near Tabbath. "Companion" means the one who was at his side.

This is told by the narrator of the book of Judges. Israel was oppressed by Midian, and God had reduced Gideon's army to three hundred men so that it would be seen that the victory came from Him. The men did not fight with swords, but with pitchers, torches, and trumpets.

God can work with little when we obey Him with simplicity. We do not always have to be strong or many; it is enough to be faithful in what He asks of us, and to trust Him with the result.
exp.17:7:
Verse 8 tells us that the five men who had gone to scout the land returned to their people at Zorah and Eshtaol. There their brothers from the tribe of Dan asked them, "What say ye?", meaning, "How did it go, and what news do you bring?" And the scouts began to answer.

The background is that the tribe of Dan was looking for a place to settle. The five spies had seen Laish, a quiet city with no nearby allies. Earlier, a priest had told them to go in peace, and they took this as God's approval. Now they return with an enthusiastic report. Note: the Bible does not say that this priest spoke on God's behalf, and this account contains a great deal of disobedience.

For today: when we make an important decision, it is not enough that something sounds good or that someone tells us to go ahead. Let us ask God for wisdom, compare what we hear with his Word, and seek sound counsel.
exp.5:30:
Joash tells the angry men that it makes no sense to stand up for Baal. He asks whether they are going to take up Baal's cause, that is, plead for him, and whether they are going to save him. He warns that whoever pleads for him will be put to death early, in the morning. And he concludes: if Baal is a god, let him plead for himself against the one who pulled down his altar.

Joash, the father of Gideon, is speaking. The people of the town wanted to kill his son for tearing down the altar of Baal. It is striking that Joash, whose altar it was, now protects Gideon. We do not know everything that was going on in his heart, but his words show how weak that idol was. That is why Gideon received the name Jerubbaal.

For today: what is truly God does not need us to defend him with violence or with fear. Examine the things in which you trust too much, and rest in the living God.
exp.20:8:
The explanation says that the people of Israel were counted, that is, a tally was taken of those present at the assembly, and it was seen that not a single man from Jabesh-gilead was there. "Were counted" means they took attendance, and the word "inhabitants" in this verse means the people who lived there.

This happens after the nearly fatal war against the tribe of Benjamin. Israel had sworn not to give their daughters to the Benjamites, who were left without wives, and they were looking for a way out. They noticed that Jabesh-gilead had not come to the gathering at Mizpah. The account is told by the narrator, and what follows is violent. The Bible records it but does not approve of it; the book shows a time of moral chaos.

For today: be careful with hasty promises and with "fixes" that correct one wrong by committing a greater one. Before acting, let us ask God for wisdom and humility to correct things with justice and mercy.
exp.1:14:
This verse says that whenever the Israelites went out to fight or to undertake anything, God was against them and things turned out badly for them. This fulfilled what God had warned them of and had promised them with an oath. "Went out" refers to their military campaigns or ventures; "the hand of the Lord" speaks of his power at work; "distressed" means that he brought them great suffering.

The narrator of the book, whose author is not known with certainty, explains why Israel was defeated after the death of Joshua. The people had abandoned God to worship Baal and Ashtaroth. God had already warned them in the law (for example, Deuteronomy 28) that disobedience would bring consequences. Here we see his faithfulness to what he said.

For today: God is serious, but he is also patient. If you notice that you have drifted away from him, do not wait to suffer more; return to him soon and sincerely, for he remains ready to rescue.
exp.14:9:
The men of Judah ask the Philistines why they have come to attack them. The Philistines answer plainly: they have come to take Samson captive and to treat him just as he treated them. The word used for "taking" here means to seize or arrest him, and the phrase about going up reflects that they were heading toward the higher ground of Judah.

The Philistines were ruling over Israel at that time. Samson had struck them hard in revenge for earlier wrongs, and then he took refuge in a cave in Judah. The Philistines camped there and pressed on Judah. Then, as the next passage shows, three thousand men of Judah went to hand him over, instead of standing by him.

For today: revenge produces more revenge, and often innocent people end up paying the cost. Before responding in anger, it is wise to pause, ask God for wisdom, and look for ways of peace.
exp.20:18:
This verse says that every year there was a solemn feast in honor of the Lord in Shiloh. Its location is given in detail: on the north side of Beth-el, on the east side of the highway that goes from Beth-el to Shechem, and on the south of Lebonah. The words "north" and "south" are the directions shown in the verse itself.

The leaders of Israel are speaking, after a terrible war against the tribe of Benjamin. They had sworn not to give them their daughters as wives, but they did not want the tribe of Benjamin to disappear. They were looking for a way out of their problem, and they point to this place and this feast as the opportunity. What they propose afterward is a violent and very questionable plan; the Bible does not present it as an example to follow. The book describes it as a time when each person did whatever seemed right to him.

For today: before making hasty promises, let us think carefully. And if we get it wrong, let us look for solutions that honor God and do not add more harm.
exp.10:15:
It says that when Israel came out of Egypt, they traveled through the desert to the Red Sea, and after that they came to Kadesh, a place in the wilderness.

The speaker is Jephthah, a judge of Israel. The Ammonites were attacking and claiming that Israel had taken their land. Jephthah sends them a message and goes over the history of the people. He wants to show that Israel did not take territory from Moab or Ammon, but went around them with respect. Some scholars point out that Jephthah summarizes the events, and that the details can be read more fully in Numbers.

For today: when someone accuses you or misunderstands you, answer with the truth and with calm. Remembering honestly what happened, and how God guided you, helps you speak with firmness and without hatred.
exp.11:8:
This verse is about Ibzan, who was a judge of Israel. He had sixty children: thirty sons and thirty daughters. He gave his daughters in marriage to people from outside his own family or clan, and he brought in thirty wives from outside for his sons. He ruled for seven years. The word "judged" here means that he led and governed the people.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges, who gives a brief report between longer stories, such as that of Jephthah. It does not say why Ibzan arranged his children's marriages this way. Some think he was seeking alliances or showing his wealth and influence, but the text does not make this clear. It also does not say whether he did well or badly.

For today: our lives also leave a mark on our families and on others. Let us make our decisions with prayer and wisdom, thinking about how they help others know and follow God.
exp.5:38:
Gideon speaks to God carefully and asks him not to be angry with him for asking once more. He wants to make another test with the fleece, which is the wool of a sheep. Now he asks for the opposite of the first time: that only the fleece be dry, and that the dew, that is, the moisture of the night, fall upon all the ground.

Gideon is the one speaking, the man whom God called to deliver Israel from the oppression of Midian. He had already received promises from God, but he still felt fear and uncertainty. God, with patience, answered his request. Some see here a weakness of faith; others see an example of God's kindness toward someone fragile.

For today: when you have doubts, bring them to God with honesty and humility. But do not keep asking for signs; seek guidance in his Word, in prayer, and in the counsel of wise people.
exp.5:4:
This verse describes how the Midianites invaded Israel. They came with their livestock and their tents, and they were so numerous that they are compared to locusts, that is, to a plague of insects that devours the fields. Neither they nor their camels could be counted.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. He explains the hard situation of Israel, which suffered these attacks year after year just when the harvest was coming in. The book had already said that Israel did evil in the sight of God, and for that reason the people were left in the hands of Midian. But the people eventually cried out to the LORD, and that prepares the way for the calling of Gideon.

For today: when you feel overwhelmed by problems that seem like a plague too great to count, do not stay silent or alone. Cry out to God with sincerity. He hears, even when we have arrived at that situation through our own mistakes.
exp.19:21:
It says that, after losing the first day of battle, the people of Israel took heart again and lined up their ranks once more in the same place where they had fought before. The verse's "encouraged themselves" means to regain courage, and "set their battle again in array" means they organized and prepared for the fight once more.
