This is part of a passage from the book of Judges. The one speaking is not a character but the narrator. The tribes of Israel were fighting against Benjamin over a terrible crime committed in Gibeah. Israel had suffered a great defeat, with twenty-two thousand dead. Even so, they wept before the LORD and asked Him for guidance, and He told them to go up. The verses that follow show that this taking heart and returning to the place of defeat was joined to seeking God.

For today: when you fail or suffer a loss, do not stay paralyzed. Weep and pray sincerely, seek God's guidance, and with renewed courage take the next step.
exp.8:9:
It says that the trees, after the olive tree refused to be their king, ask the fig tree to reign over them. The phrase "Come thou" is like saying "come, you do it." "Reign" here means "rule as king."

It is part of a fable that Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon, tells from Mount Gerizim. The men of Shechem had just made Abimelech king, though he had killed his brothers. Jotham uses the trees to show that the best ones do not want to dominate, and that in the end the one who reigns is the one who serves not. The interpretation of each detail of the fable is debated, but its general message is clear.

Today we can notice that those who bear fruit and bless others tend to be humble. Before choosing leaders, it is wise to look at their character and not only at their ambition.
exp.19:47:
The explanation says that the men of Israel turned back against the people of Benjamin and struck them down with the edge of the sword. They did not only kill the people, but also the animals and every living thing they found in the city. In addition, they set fire to all the cities they came to. The word "turned" in the verse means "came back," and the phrase about striking them with the sword simply means they were killed by the sword.

The narrator of the book describes the end of a civil war between the tribes of Israel and Benjamin. It all began with a terrible crime in Gibeah, and Benjamin defended the guilty instead of handing them over. The book repeats that in those days there was no king in Israel and everyone did what seemed right in their own eyes. The text tells what happened, but it does not present it as an example to imitate.

For today: when we do not correct wrong in time and allow pride to grow, the consequences can be far more painful than we imagine. Let us seek justice with humility, and not with revenge.
exp.14:13:
The explanation says that when Samson came to Lehi, the Philistines came out to meet him shouting with joy, believing they already had him. Then the Spirit of the Lord came upon him with power, and the new ropes they had tied him with fell apart like burnt flax thread. The shouting of the crowd is described as a noisy celebration, and the phrase "became as" means that the ropes turned into, or were left like, burnt flax.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Men of Judah, out of fear of the Philistines, had bound Samson in order to hand him over. Samson allowed it, but the strength did not come from himself. The text stresses that it was the Spirit of God who acted, not Samson's own muscles.

For today: when you feel bound or without a way out, remember that your true strength comes from God. Ask Him humbly for His help, instead of trusting only in your own abilities.
exp.5:35:
Gideon speaks to God and begins a request: "If you are truly going to save Israel by my hand, as you have said...". The sentence is left open and is completed in the following verse. The word "á" is the old spelling of "a". "By my hand" means "through me" or "using my own effort".

Gideon had already received God's call and the promise of victory over Midian. Now the Spirit of the LORD clothes him, he blows the trumpet, and several tribes join him. With an army gathered and a great deal of responsibility, he asks for a sign with a fleece of wool. Some see in this a lack of faith; others see a desire to be sure. The Bible does not explain it, and God responds with patience.

For today: when you have doubts, bring them honestly before God, but do not stop trusting what he has already told you in his Word.
exp.18:1:
She was unfaithful to him and left him, the explanation says. She went back to her father's house in Bethlehem of Judah and stayed there four months.

The word translated here as "played the whore" is a Hebrew word that some understand to mean sexual unfaithfulness, and others understand to mean that she abandoned him or became angry with him; scholars do not agree. A secondary wife of lower rank is what the term for a secondary wife means.

Context: the narrator of Judges speaks, and begins a sad story from a time when there was no king in Israel. The book shows how the people went astray when each one did what seemed right to him. This account prepares the way for very painful events that come later.

For today: when a relationship breaks down, let us not allow time to pass in silence and pride. Let us seek God, ask for wisdom, and try to speak with humility and honesty, seeking reconciliation where it is possible and healthy.
exp.1:4:
This verse says the people gave that place the name Bochim, which means "the weepers." There they offered sacrifices to the Lord.

The angel of the Lord had just rebuked Israel for not obeying: they had made agreements with the peoples of the land and had not torn down their altars. As a result, those peoples would remain a pressure and a snare for them. Hearing this, the people wept. The sacrifices show that they wanted to draw near to God. The text does not say whether their repentance was deep, and the book later shows that it did not last.

For today: weeping over sin is a good beginning, but God also expects real change. If something pulls you away from Him, do not tolerate it; ask Him for help to leave it behind and to obey Him with steadiness.
exp.18:27:
He says to her, "Get up, let us go." But she does not answer. He puts her on his donkey and heads for his home. The text does not make clear whether she was already dead or died afterward. Many think she was already dead, but this is not stated with certainty.

The one speaking is the Levite, her husband. The night before, some men of Gibeah abused her while he was inside the house. His coldness in speaking to her shows that he did not care about her pain. The book presents a dark time, when everyone did whatever seemed right to them.

Today, let us not be indifferent to those who suffer. If we see mistreatment or injustice, let us not look away. Let us defend the vulnerable, listen to their pain, and act with compassion, as Jesus did with the wounded.
exp.0:14:
Axa answers her father Caleb with respect and asks him for a blessing, that is, a favorable gift. She reminds him that the land he gave her is dry ground, without water, and asks him also for springs of water. Caleb grants her the upper springs and the lower springs.

She speaks as Caleb's daughter, newly married to Othniel. Caleb had given her land in the Negev, a dry region where water was essential for living and for planting. She asks boldly and with good reason, and her father responds with generosity. The springs "above and below" show that she received abundance. The text does not detail exactly where they were.

For today: we can approach God with confidence and ask Him for what we truly need, without shame. If a gift is good but incomplete, like a land without water, He invites us to ask with simplicity and humility.
exp.17:25:
Micah saw that they were stronger than he was, so he turned around and went back home. "Stronger" refers to the fact that they were more numerous and armed.

This is part of the story in Judges 17 and 18. The Danites were looking for land to settle in. They passed by Micah's house, took his idols, and persuaded the priest to go with them. Micah followed them, demanding them back, but they threatened him. The narrator shows a time of disorder, when religion was used for convenience and force ruled.

For today: trusting in things we make ourselves, such as money, image, or control, leaves us empty when someone takes them away. Micah called "my gods" what he had made with his own hands, and he could not defend them. It is wise to place our security in God, who cannot be stolen or overcome.
exp.1:9:
It says that the whole generation that lived with Joshua died and was gathered to their fathers, that is, they died and were buried. Afterward another generation arose that did not know the Lord, nor the works he had done for Israel. The phrase about being gathered to their fathers is an old way of saying that they died. Here "know" means more than knowing facts; it means having a real relationship with God and remembering his works.

The one who narrates is the author of the book of Judges, whose identity is not known for certain. It explains why Israel fell into idolatry after Joshua. This new generation did not experience the departure from Egypt or the entry into the land, and the next verse shows the result: they served the Baals and forsook the Lord.

Today it reminds us that faith is not inherited on its own. Tell your children and others what God has done in your life, and live in a way that they too come to know him personally.
exp.11:12:
After him, the next one to lead Israel was Abdon, the son of Hillel, who came from Pirathon. Here, to "judge" means that he guided the people, settled disputes and made decisions with authority. The word "Pirathonite" means that he was from Pirathon.

This is not a speech by a character; it is the narrator of the book of Judges, who names Israel's leaders one after another. Abdon is one of the minor judges: the Bible tells us little about him. The verses that follow say that he had many sons and grandsons, that he led for eight years, and that he was buried in Pirathon. We know no more details about his leadership.

For today: God also uses people who are little known. Perhaps no one applauds your service, but God sees it. Be faithful in your place, in your family or in your work, without seeking fame.
exp.18:29:
The explanation says that those who saw the pieces of the woman's body were horrified. They said that nothing like this had been seen since Israel came up out of Egypt. Then they make an appeal: "Consider this" means think it over carefully; "take advice" means decide what to do; "speak your minds" means say what you think.

It is the narrator who records the people's reaction. The Levite sent the pieces throughout Israel to denounce the horrible crime committed in Gibeah. This account shows the moral disorder of a time when, as the book says, "there was no king in Israel." The text describes these events with grief, but it does not approve of them.

For today: we should not become accustomed to injustice or violence. When something is wrong, we should stop, think calmly, seek wise counsel, and speak up for those who suffer, especially the most vulnerable.
exp.2:17:
This verse says that Ehud, after handing over the tribute to King Eglon, sent away the people who had carried that gift. The word "present" means the gift or tribute, and "sent away" means he dismissed them to go back. The people refers to the men who had brought the payment.

The account tells that Israel was under the rule of Moab and paid tribute to Eglon. Ehud, a man whom God raised up as a deliverer, had a dagger hidden on him. By dismissing his companions, he was free to ask for a private audience with the king. The Bible presents this as part of Israel's deliverance; it does not say that every act in the account is an example to imitate.

For today: when God calls us to a difficult task, it is wise to act with wisdom and preparation, not in a rush. Before taking an important step, pray, think carefully, and try to do it with prudence and trust in God.
exp.14:1:
Here Samson's father-in-law explains why he did not let Samson see his wife. He says he thought Samson hated her, so he gave her to "su compañero," who was the friend who had attended Samson at the wedding. Then he offers the younger sister, saying she is more beautiful.

The speaker is the father of the Philistine woman. Samson had left angry after the wedding, when she revealed the riddle (ch. 14). Now he returns with a young goat as a gesture of reconciliation, and finds that she has already been given to another. The father acts on his own and treats his daughter as something that can be exchanged for another.

For today: before acting, it is wise to speak and confirm the facts. The father decided on assumption and caused a greater wound. Also, people are not interchangeable objects; they deserve respect and care.
exp.19:23:
This verse tells us that the Israelites came forward again against the tribe of Benjamin the next day, to fight once more. "Came near" means they advanced to engage in battle. "Benjamin" refers to the tribe of Benjamin, brothers of Israel.

The one telling the story is the narrator of the book of Judges. Israel is at war against one of its own tribes, because Benjamin protected men from Gibeah who had committed a terrible crime. On the first day Israel lost the battle, wept, and asked God whether they should fight again. God told them to go up, yet they still suffered another defeat. The Bible does not fully explain that outcome.

For today: sometimes we obey with good intentions and still face difficulties we do not understand. In those moments, we can do as Israel did: come to God with tears and prayer, and not trust only in our own strength.
exp.5:21:
Gideon realizes that the one who spoke to him was the angel of the Lord, and he is frightened. He says, "Alas, O Lord God!", an exclamation of fear and surprise. "Face to face" means that he saw him directly, from the front. The phrase in this verse is "face to face," so the explanation is rendered accordingly.

Gideon is an Israelite chosen to deliver his people from the Midianites. Earlier he asked for a sign, and the fire that came out of the rock confirmed to him that God was speaking. In that time it was believed that seeing God or his messenger could cost a person their life. That is why God calms him right away: "Peace be unto thee; thou shalt not die."

When God draws near, it is natural to feel fear or smallness. But He does not call us to crush us, but to give us peace and confidence. If today you feel afraid of what God asks of you, bring it to him honestly, as Gideon did, and listen for his word of calm.
exp.19:24:
This verse tells how, on the second day of battle, the men of Benjamin came out of the city of Gibeah and killed another eighteen thousand Israelites. All of them were armed soldiers who knew how to fight. The phrase that they "drew the sword" means they were trained warriors, and "destroyed down to the ground" means they struck them down dead.

The narrator is the author of the book of Judges. Israel was fighting against the tribe of Benjamin, their own brothers, over a terrible crime committed in Gibeah. The Israelites had wept and sought God's counsel, and he told them to go up. Even so, they lost. The text does not explain why, and it can be understood in several ways.

For today: obeying God does not always bring immediate or easy results. Even so, we can keep weeping, praying, and seeking him sincerely, without ceasing to trust him when we do not understand what is happening.
exp.10:34:
Jephthah sees his daughter come out to meet him, and he tears his clothes, which was a sign of deep grief. He tells her that she has left him crushed, because he made a promise to God and cannot take it back.

Jephthah, judge of Israel, speaks right after defeating the Ammonites. Before the battle he had promised God that he would offer whatever came out of his house first to meet him (Judges 11:30-31). He did not expect it to be his only daughter. Scholars debate what happened next: some believe he offered her as a sacrifice, others that he dedicated her to the service of God for life, unmarried.

For today: before we speak, let us think carefully about what we promise, especially before God. Words spoken in haste can bring pain to those we love most. Let us ask for wisdom and trust that God guides us without the need for rushed promises.
exp.17:8:
The explanation says that the five men who went out to explore returned urging their tribe to act at once. They assure them that the land is very good, and they rebuke them for staying still. The words "are ye still?" mean that they remain without moving, and "slothful" means slow to act. "To possess" means to take the land as one's own.

The five spies speak for the tribe of Dan. This tribe had not yet fully taken its territory and was looking for a place to settle. Laish seemed easy to conquer because its people lived in confidence and isolation. They say that God has given it into their hands, but note this: the story of the chapter also shows disorder, since earlier they had taken Micah's idols. For that reason the passage does not approve everything they do.

For today: do not confuse a good opportunity with God's approval. Before acting, pray, consult the Word, and ask yourself whether the way is just.
exp.11:0:
The men of the tribe of Ephraim gathered together and crossed over toward the north. They confronted Jephthah, asking why he went to fight against the Ammonites without calling them. They threatened to burn his house down with him inside it. The word "northward" in the verse is the direction the men moved as they came to confront him.

The Ephraimites speak to Jephthah in anger. They came from a strong and proud tribe, and they felt ignored when God gave the victory to someone else. Jephthah answers that he did call them, and they did not help. Some scholars see wounded pride and jealousy here, though the text itself says nothing more about their motives.

When someone else receives recognition, we can feel pushed aside. Before we make claims or pick a fight, it is wise to examine our hearts and ask whether our anger comes from pride. Rejoicing in the success of others prevents conflicts that harm many people.
exp.4:24:
Here it is told that Sisera, commander of the enemy army, asked for water, and Jael gave him milk. She also offered him "butter" in a "lordly dish," that is, a fine dish, fit for an important person. The "butter" was probably thick curdled milk or heavy cream.

Deborah speaks together with Barak in a song of victory after defeating Sisera. Jael appeared to offer hospitality and protection, but it was a trap. The verses that follow tell how she killed him. Interpreters debate how to judge her act: the song celebrates it, but the text does not hold it up as a model of conduct.

For today: this passage invites us to think about generosity and hospitality. Today we do not imitate Jael's deceit, but we can offer others fair, sincere treatment without duplicity.
exp.17:15:
This verse says that six hundred men of the tribe of Dan stood at the entrance of the gate, with their weapons of war ready. "Armed with their weapons of war" means they were equipped for fighting. The gate was the entrance to the city or the place where they were.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. The Danites were looking for a territory to settle, and five spies had already passed by the house of Micah. There they saw religious objects: an ephod, household idols, and images. While the six hundred armed men kept the young Levite busy at the gate, the spies went in and carried off everything. The account shows a time of spiritual and moral disorder.

For today: strength or cleverness does not justify doing wrong. The Danites acted as if they had a right to everything, but God does not approve of worship mixed with theft, or of shortcuts. Before you act, ask yourself whether your decision honors God.
exp.3:17:
Jael goes out to meet Sisera, the commander of the enemy army, and invites him to come into her tent. She tells him not to be afraid. He enters, and she covers him with a mantle.

Jael speaks here as the wife of Heber the Kenite. Sisera flees on foot after losing the battle against Israel, and he seeks refuge in a home he believed was friendly, since there was peace between his king and Heber's family. His trust leads him to lower his guard. The text does not explain all of Jael's reasons, but the account that follows shows that she acted in favor of Israel.

For today: kind words can be sincere or deceptive. Let us ask God for wisdom to discern, and let us take care that our words of welcome and peace are always honest.
exp.2:8:
When the people of Israel cried out to God with pleas for help, God answered by raising up a deliverer named Othniel, son of Kenaz and a close relative of Caleb. The phrase "younger brother of Caleb" can be understood as a younger brother or as a younger relative; the text allows both readings.

Context: the narrator of the book of Judges explains that Israel had forgotten God and served the Baals, false gods. Because of this, they lived for eight years under a foreign king, Cushan-rishathaim. The text shows a pattern: sin, oppression, crying out, and rescue. Othniel is the first judge.

For today: when you feel trapped by your mistakes or their consequences, return to God with sincerity. He hears the cry of anyone who turns back to Him, and He can raise up help, sometimes through ordinary people.
exp.10:11:
Jephthah sent messengers to the king of the Ammonites to ask why he was coming to fight against Israel. The question in the verse, "What hast thou to do with me?", means "What is your problem with me?" or "What is your reason?" Jephthah does not answer with a sword but with a question. Messengers are official representatives who speak on behalf of someone else.

Jephthah had just been chosen as leader of Gilead, after the elders called him to defend them. The Ammonites were already threatening them. Before fighting, Jephthah seeks to know the reason for the conflict and tries to talk it through. The king's answer, in the verses that follow, shows that he was claiming land.

Before reacting with anger or fighting, it is wise to ask and to listen. Speaking clearly about a conflict can clear up misunderstandings, and sometimes it prevents greater harm. Even when the other side does not want to listen, we will have acted with good sense and peace.
exp.2:26:
That verse tells how Ehud, after escaping, came to the hill country of Ephraim and blew a trumpet. It was a signal to call the people to war. The Israelites came down from the mountain with him, and Ehud went at their head.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel had been under the rule of King Eglon of Moab for eighteen years. Ehud had killed Eglon by cunning and escaped. Now he takes advantage of the confusion among the Moabites and gathers the people to win their freedom. He says that God has already given their enemies into their hands.

For today: God often uses people who are willing to take the first step. If He puts something good on your heart, do not wait for others to begin. Encourage others by your example, trusting that God goes before you.
exp.0:9:
This verse tells how the tribe of Judah advanced against the Canaanites who lived in Hebron, a city that was formerly called Kirjath-arba. There they defeated three men: Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai. The word "slew" here means they struck them down in battle.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Judges. After the death of Joshua, Israel was struggling to take possession of the promised land. Judah goes first, and the account draws on what Joshua 15:14 says about Caleb, who also drove these three out of Hebron. Some think these are the same events told again; others think it was a new campaign. The Bible does not make this completely clear.

For today: God often gives us victories step by step, not all at once. Trust Him and take the next step in front of you, even if the problem seems as large as a giant.
exp.8:30:
Zebul, the official in charge of the city, sent messengers to Abimelech with cunning. He warned him that Gaal, son of Ebed, and his brothers had come to Shechem and were stirring up the city against him. In this verse, the word for "privily" means done secretly or with hidden purpose. The word for "against thee" here indicates that they had turned the city against him. Some translators understand that Gaal was stirring up the people from inside the city.

Zebul had heard Gaal speak with contempt of Abimelech, and he was angry. As the authority in Shechem, he acted in secret to alert his lord. Then he proposes a plan: to attack at dawn. The account shows a time of violence, betrayal, and rivalry for power.

For today: the Bible tells this story without approving everything its characters do. It reminds us that pride, intrigue, and ambition hurt many people. Let us seek to resolve conflicts with truth, humility, and justice, trusting in God.
exp.17:30:
They set up for themselves the carved image that Micah had made, and it stayed there the whole time that the house of God was at Shiloh. The explanation says that the people of Dan set up and kept the carved image Micah had made. That image remained there for as long as the house of God, meaning the tabernacle, stood at Shiloh. "They set up" means that they put it in place and established it. A "carved image" is a carved idol.

The speaker is the narrator of Judges, who closes the story of the tribe of Dan. They took the idol and Micah's priest, and settled in Laish, which they renamed Dan. The book shows a time of religious disorder, when each person did what seemed right to them. The contrast is strong: true worship was at Shiloh, yet Dan preferred a made-up worship.

For today: we should not settle for a faith that suits only ourselves. It is worth asking whether we worship God as He has revealed Himself in His Word, or as is more comfortable for us.
exp.7:31:
This verse tells us that Gideon, son of Joash, died at an advanced age, after a long life. He was buried in the tomb of his father, in Ophrah, the town of the family of the Abiezrites.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges sums up the end of Gideon's life. He had delivered Israel from the Midianites. But just before this, his large family is mentioned, his many wives, and his son Abimelech, something that will later bring trouble. After his death, the people forgot God and worshiped Baal.

For today: a successful life does not guarantee that others will keep following God once we are gone. It is good to teach the faith steadily, at home and at church, so that it does not depend on just one person.
exp.20:5:
This verse says that the people of Israel felt grief and regret over what had happened to the tribe of Benjamin, whom they call "their brother." The word "repented" here means that they deeply mourned what had taken place. The phrase "cut off" means that the tribe was on the verge of disappearing.

The Israelites are speaking, gathered at Bethel after a terrible civil war against Benjamin, which left very few survivors. They had made a vow not to give their daughters to them as wives. Now they see that their own decision puts an entire tribe at risk. Their response, as will be seen later, was complicated and painful.

For today: when anger leads us to say or promise things without thinking, those words can hurt later. It is wise to pause, acknowledge the harm, seek reconciliation, and ask God for direction before we act.
exp.1:19:
God was greatly angered with Israel. The anger of the Lord burned hot against them, meaning that his displeasure was very strong. The reason is that the people broke faith with the covenant, that is, they violated it or disregarded it, and did not obey his voice. That covenant was the commitment God had made with Israel's forefathers.

God speaks. Israel was already living in a repeated cycle: the people turned away from God, suffered oppression, cried out, and God sent a judge who delivered them. But when the judge died, they went back to worshiping other gods. That is why God speaks with firmness. He then explains that he will no longer drive out the nations that remained, in order to test whether the people would remain faithful to him.

For today: let us not let our faith depend on good moments or on leaders who encourage us. Let us cultivate a daily obedience to God, and when we fail, let us return to him quickly and humbly.
exp.2:0:
This verse says that God left some peoples in the land of Canaan to test Israel. "Test" here means to examine, to see what is in the heart. It concerned the generation that had not experienced the wars of the conquest.

The book of Judges introduces the narrator, who tells the story of Israel after the death of Joshua. The Israelites had not finished driving out the peoples of the land. The text says that God used that situation to test them and to teach them to fight. It also shows whether they would obey the commandments of the Lord. Some peoples mentioned later are the Philistines, the Canaanites, and the Sidonians.

Today, trials are not always punishments; they can be opportunities to grow in faith and in dependence on God. When you face a difficulty, ask yourself: "Lord, what do you want to teach me here?" and seek to obey him step by step.
exp.4:29:
These women near Sisera's mother try to calm her. They assure her that her son is delayed because he is dividing up the spoils of war. The word for "young woman" in the old text is rendered here as "damsel," and the word for what is taken from a defeated enemy is "spoil." They imagine fine, embroidered cloth for Sisera and for those who are with him.

This passage is part of the song of Deborah and Barak, sung after Israel's victory. The speaker is a wise lady of the court, and Sisera's mother also convinces herself. The song shows with irony how she dreams of gains, not knowing that her son has been defeated. Some understand that the text also reflects the harshness of ancient warfare, without approving of it.

For today: beware of illusions that comfort us but are not true. Let us rather place our trust in God and seek the truth with humility.
exp.1:6:
The people of Israel served God as long as Joshua lived, and also as long as the elders who outlived him remained. Those elders had seen with their own eyes the great works that God did for Israel. Their service meant obeying God and worshiping Him alone. The elders who outlived Joshua were those who lived on after him.

The narrator of the book speaks here, and the author is not known for certain. After recounting the weeping at Bochim, he looks back and explains what Israel was like before. He prepares the reader for verse 10, where it says that a generation arose that did not know God.

For today: faith is strengthened by remembering what God has done. Tell your children and friends how God has helped you, so that others may also come to know Him.
exp.8:52:
The passage says that a woman, from the top of the tower, dropped the upper part of a millstone onto Abimelech and crushed his skull. The word "skull" here refers to the bones of the head. The millstone was the stone used at home to grind grain.

This is part of the story, not a speech by a character. Abimelech had made himself king of Shechem by killing his brothers. Later he attacked a city that had rebelled and tried to burn the tower where the people had taken refuge. The narrator presents this ending as God's justice for his violence (Judges 9:56-57). His pride shows when he asks his armor-bearer to kill him, so that people will not say that a woman killed him.

For today: violence and pride sooner or later turn against the one who practices them. God can use the person we least expect. Let us seek to be humble and not to live guarding our reputation.
exp.11:13:
This verse speaks of Abdon. It says he had forty sons and thirty grandsons, and that they rode on seventy donkeys (asses). He also judged Israel for eight years, that is, he was a leader who guided and governed the people.

The narrator of the book of Judges gives here a brief summary of a little-known judge. He tells of no battles and no miracles. Many understand that having so many sons and donkeys showed wealth and importance in that time, although the text does not explain this. We also know no further details about his rule.

God also works through ordinary people who are not famous. Perhaps no one will remember your name, but your faithfulness in your family and in your community has value. Serve God today where you are, without needing applause.
exp.6:6:
God tells Gideon that with only the three hundred men who lapped the water he will save Israel and give the Midianites into their hand. The other soldiers are to go home. The phrases "I will save you" and "deliver" are old forms of speech in the verse above; "deliver" here means to hand over the victory. The words "let all the other people go every man unto his place" mean that each one should return to his own home.

The Lord is speaking. Gideon had a large army, but God reduced it little by little so that Israel would not boast that it had won by its own strength. The texts do not fully explain why those who lapped were the ones chosen; some think they showed more alertness, but this is not certain. What is clear is that God chose a few to show his power.

For today: when you feel small or short on resources, remember that God does not depend on your strength. Listen to him, take the step he asks of you, and trust that he sustains the result.
exp.7:13:
Gideon seized a young man from the city of Succoth and questioned him. The young man wrote down for him the names of the town's leaders: the princes and the elders, seventy-seven men in all.

The narrator tells how Gideon was pursuing the kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna. Earlier, when he and his men were tired and hungry, the leaders of Succoth refused to give his men bread and mocked him. Now Gideon returns and wants to know exactly who was responsible. We do not know why a young man knew those names, but it served to identify them.

For today: when someone needs help and we have the chance to give it, let us not refuse out of fear or selfishness. God sees our decisions, and refusing support to those who serve a good cause has consequences.
exp.0:1:
The Lord answers the people's question: the tribe of Judah will be the first to go up to fight. God affirms that he has already handed the land into their hands, as a sure promise. "Shall go up" refers to going up into the highlands of Canaan. "Delivered" means giving the victory.

After Joshua died, Israel was left without its main leader. The Israelites did well to ask God before acting. God himself speaks and points to Judah. Afterward, Judah invites his brother Simeon to help him, and together they win the victory. Some scholars see here a good beginning, although the book later shows the people's failures.

For today: before making important decisions, seek God's guidance in prayer and in his Word. Then act with courage and seek the help of brothers and sisters, as Judah did with Simeon.
exp.6:10:
God tells Gideon that, if he is still afraid, he should go down to the enemy camp and listen to what they say. By this, his hands will be made strong, meaning he will regain courage and strength. The "armed men" are the soldiers carrying weapons. The "servant" is an attendant or helper. Gideon goes down with Phurah (as it is spelled today) to the edge of the camp.

The LORD speaks to Gideon at night. He had already promised him victory, but He knows Gideon's fear and does not scold him. He gives him a concrete step to strengthen his faith. The Midianites were very numerous, and Gideon had only three hundred men, so his fear was understandable.

For today: when you are afraid, do not hide it. Bring it honestly before God. He can give you signs and support to take the next step. Obey even if it is with fear, and seek the company of someone, as Gideon had with Phurah.
exp.15:9:
Delilah accuses Samson because he gave her a false answer about the secret of his strength. She says that he deceived her and told her lies. Then she asks him again to tell her how he could be tied.

Delilah, whom Samson loved, is speaking. The Philistine lords had offered her money to find out the source of his strength. She had already tried once with the fresh bowstrings, and there were spies hidden in the room. She pretends to feel hurt and trust, but in reality she seeks to hand him over to his enemies.

For today: let us take care about who and what we allow into our hearts. A relationship that presses us again and again to give in on what God has entrusted to us should alert us. Let us ask for wisdom to set boundaries in time.
exp.12:13:
The angel repeats the rules the wife of Manoah was to follow while she waited to bear a child. She could not take anything that comes from the vine: no grapes and no wine. "Strong drink" was a strong, fermented beverage, unlike the apple juice of today. She also was not to eat anything "unclean," that is, what the law of Moses declared impure. She was to observe all that had been commanded.

The angel of the LORD is speaking. Manoah had asked how to raise the promised child, who would be Samson, set apart for God from his birth as a Nazirite. These rules prepared the mother for that calling. The angel answers with firmness, and then Manoah still does not understand who is speaking to him.

For today: when God entrusts us with something, it is worth caring for the small details of obedience. We can ask ourselves what habit we should let go of in order to live with more devotion and trust in Him.
exp.2:4:
This verse says that the people of Israel lived mixed in with the nations that were already in the land. Six peoples are named: Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites.

The book of Judges tells this as narrative. God had left these nations in the land to test whether Israel would obey his commands. Instead of living apart in faithfulness, Israel stayed and lived alongside them. The next verses show what followed: they intermarried with them and ended up serving their gods.

Today we also live alongside people who think differently, and that is not wrong in itself. But we must be careful that our customs and relationships do not gradually pull us away from God. It is worth asking ourselves honestly: who influences my heart more, God or my surroundings?
exp.19:33:
It says that ten thousand chosen soldiers from all of Israel attacked Gibeah, and that the fighting became very fierce. The word "sore" means that the battle grew stronger and heavier. The Benjamites did not realize that disaster was already coming toward them. The phrase "evil was near them" speaks of their ruin being close at hand.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Israel was at war against the tribe of Benjamin, because that tribe had protected criminal men from Gibeah. Israel pretended to flee in order to draw the Benjamites out of the city, while an ambush waited. The Benjamites trusted in their earlier victories and did not see the trap.

For today: past success can make us careless. When a person feels secure because of what they have already achieved, and does not examine their path with humility, they may fail to see the danger. Let us ask God for wisdom and honestly review our decisions.
exp.0:24:
He showed them the way into the city of Bethel. Joseph's men attacked the city with the sword, meaning with violence and without pity, but they let the man and all his family go free.

The author of the book of Judges is the one telling this, describing how the tribes of Israel were taking over Canaan after Joshua's death. The spies had promised mercy in exchange for help, just as Israel had done earlier with Rahab. The Bible does not say whether that man believed in God. Afterward, he founded another city called Luz, in the land of the Hittites.

For today: keeping what we promise is part of living with integrity. Also, the mercy we give to others reminds us of the mercy God has given us.
exp.6:0:
This verse tells us that Gideon, also called Jerubbaal, got up early with all his people and camped beside the spring of Harod. The Midianite camp was to the north, on the other side of the hill of Moreh, in the valley. The phrase "pitched beside the well of Harod" refers to the same act of setting up camp.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. Israel was oppressed by Midian, and God had called Gideon to deliver it. The name Jerubbaal was given to him when he destroyed his father's altar to Baal. The verse sets the scene: two armies facing each other, and soon God will say that Israel has too many people.

For today: Gideon rose early and acted in obedience, but God would teach him that victory does not depend on our own strength. We can take our steps with diligence and, at the same time, trust that God is the one who sustains the outcome.
exp.8:15:
This verse is the start of a pointed question. Jotham tells the people of Shechem: if you really acted with sincerity and integrity in making Abimelech king, and if you dealt well with Jerubbaal (another name for Gideon) and his family, then all is well. Giving Gideon back the good he did is what it means to repay him according to what his hands had done.

Jotham, the only one of Gideon's sons who survived, speaks from Mount Gerizim after Abimelech has killed his brothers. He has just told the parable of the trees. With this "if" he shows them, ironically, that their action was unjust and treacherous. He warns that it will bring consequences.

For today: before supporting a leader or making an important decision, ask yourself whether you are acting with truth, gratitude, and justice. God looks at the heart and at the consequences of our decisions.
exp.8:39:
It says that Abimelech chased Gaal, and Gaal fled before him. Along the way many fell wounded, and the bodies reached as far as the entrance of the city gate. The word meaning "chased him" is the sense of "he pursued him." The phrase about those who fell refers to men who were killed or badly wounded in the battle.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Gaal had boasted that he could defeat Abimelech, and Zebul, the ruler of the city, provoked him to come out and fight. Gaal went out and lost. It was the result of a violent rivalry for power in Shechem, where many paid the price.

For today: proud words can leave us in trouble when the test comes. Before speaking arrogantly or looking for quarrels, it is wise to stop, be humble, and seek peace. As Proverbs 16:18 says, pride goes before a fall.
exp.10:14:
This verse begins Jephthah's reply to the king of Ammon. Jephthah says that Israel did not take away the land of Moab or the land of the children of Ammon.

The phrase "thus saith" is the same as "says the following," and the word "Jephthah" is the same name spelled in an older way.

Jephthah, judge of Israel, speaks through messengers. The Ammonite king claimed the land between the Arnon and Jabbok rivers and demanded that it be returned. Jephthah answers with the history: when Israel came out of Egypt, it respected the borders of Moab and Ammon. He tries to settle the conflict with words before fighting.

For today: before reacting in a conflict, seek the facts and speak with truth and calm. Pursuing peace through honest dialogue honors God, even when the other side does not want to listen.
exp.7:3:
This verse tells that Gideon came to the Jordan River to cross it, together with his three hundred men. They were very worn out because they had been pursuing the enemy. The word "pursuing" here refers to the chase of the fleeing Midianites.

It is the narrator of Judges who speaks. Gideon had just calmed the men of Ephraim, who were upset, with a humble answer. Now he keeps going after the kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna. Although his group was small and exhausted, he did not stop. Soon he will ask for bread in Succoth, but there he will not receive it.

For today: sometimes we keep going with our strength nearly spent. We can finish what God has placed in our hands, but it is also wise to ask for help in time and to rest in Him, without being ashamed of our weariness.
exp.20:17:
The elders of Israel explain a problem: they cannot give their daughters as wives to the surviving men of Benjamin, because all Israel made a vow and placed a curse on anyone who broke it. The word "Howbeit" simply means "but," and the phrase "cursed be he" means the one who breaks the oath is under a curse.

After the terrible war against Benjamin, nearly the whole tribe died, and the women as well. The elders want the tribe not to disappear, but they are trapped by their own hasty promise. That is why they look for a way out, which in the verses that follow turns out to be very questionable.

For today: let us think before we speak and promise. Words spoken in anger or haste can bring painful consequences. And when we fail, let us seek God with humility instead of inventing solutions that cause even more harm.
exp.20:7:
This verse tells how the Israelites asked who had not come up to gather before the LORD at Mizpah. On checking, they found that no one from Jabesh-gilead had come to the camp. "Gone up to the LORD" means having come to the assembly called before the LORD.

The speaker is the congregation of Israel, at the end of the book of Judges, a time of great disorder. After the war they had nearly wiped out the tribe of Benjamin, and now they were looking for wives for the survivors without breaking their oath. They found an excuse to attack Jabesh-gilead. The account describes what happened but does not approve of it; the book itself shows a people who did what was right in their own eyes.

For today: be careful about using religion to justify hasty decisions. Before you act, ask yourself whether you are seeking God's will or simply fixing your own mistakes in your own way.
exp.12:3:
It says that the woman of Manoah, while she waits for her son, must not drink wine or strong drink (a fermented beverage, such as apple or fruit cider), nor eat anything unclean, that is, anything that the law of Moses declared impure for God's people. "Now therefore beware" is like saying: "So be careful from now on."

The angel of the LORD speaks to this woman who could not have children. He announces that she will have a son who will be a Nazirite, set apart for God from before birth, and who will begin to deliver Israel from the Philistines. Since the boy will be consecrated, she also takes care of her own life from the time of her pregnancy. How this connects with the care of the child in the womb is understood in several ways, but the text shows that God's calling begins very early.

For today: when God entrusts us with something important, such as a family or a job, it is worth looking after our habits from the beginning, with obedience and gratitude.
exp.0:17:
This verse says that the tribe of Judah conquered three Philistine cities: Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron, along with the land around each of them. The word "coast" in the verse means the land or region surrounding each city.

The book of Judges begins by telling how each tribe tried to take the promised land after the death of Joshua. Here the narrator presents the achievements of Judah, the strongest tribe. But notice: the next verse clarifies that they could not drive out those who lived in the plains, and some scholars believe these cities were lost later, although this is debated.

Today we can learn that a victory is not permanent if we stop taking care of it. God gives us progress in life, but we must keep trusting him steadily, never taking anything for granted forever.
exp.12:5:
Here the wife of Manoah tells her husband what happened to her. A man of God appeared to her, and his appearance was terrible, that is, so awe-inspiring that it brought great respect and fear. She did not ask him where he came from or what his name was, and he did not tell her.

The wife of Manoah was from the tribe of Dan. She could not have children, and the messenger announced that she would have a son who would be a Nazirite, set apart for God. She tells this so that her husband may know what God said. This son would be Samson, at a time when the Philistines ruled over Israel.

When God speaks to us or gives us a responsibility, it is good to share it with those closest to us, such as a spouse or family. In this way we walk together, with humility and reverence.
exp.8:5:
All the men of Shechem and all the people of Beth-millo gathered together and went and made Abimelech king, beside the oak or pillar that stood in Shechem. The phrase about the plain of the pillar probably refers to a well-known place in the city, perhaps next to a tree or a standing stone.

It is the narrator of Judges who speaks. Abimelech, son of Gideon (Jerubbaal), had paid reckless men with silver from the temple of Baal-berith and had killed his seventy brothers. Only Jotham escaped. So this kingship is born out of violence, ambition, and the support of people willing to stay silent about injustice.

For today: it is not enough that something is popular or gains support for it to be good. Before we follow a leader or back a decision, let us ask how it came about and whether it honors God and respects people's lives.
exp.0:31:
The explanation says that the tribe of Asher did not drive out the Canaanites from the land that had been allotted to it. On the contrary, the Israelites stayed to live among them. The sense of the verse is that the Asherites did not dispossess the Canaanites; instead they dwelt alongside them. The land that should have been theirs was now shared with the peoples God had commanded them to drive out.

Context: The book of Judges tells, in the narrator's voice, how Israel failed to complete the conquest. God had commanded that these peoples be removed so that they would not lead Israel into idolatry. Here several tribes are listed who gave way one after another. The text notes that Asher did so even more clearly: it does not say they made the Canaanites pay tribute, but that they lived among them. This prepares the cycles of disobedience that follow in the book.

For today: When we allow something into our lives that God asked us to remove, such as a habit or a harmful influence, sooner or later it begins to take charge. Ask God for the courage to obey completely, not halfway.
exp.18:4:
He says that on the fourth day, very early in the morning, the Levite got up to return home. But his father-in-law, the young woman's father, asked him to first eat a morsel of bread to gain strength, and then to go on his way. "Damsel" is a young woman, "son-in-law" is the husband of the daughter, and "comfort thine heart" means to cheer up or regain strength.

The young woman's father is the one speaking. The Levite had come to get his wife back in order to reconcile with her, and the father-in-law received him with great hospitality. In that time, taking good care of a guest was very important. Yet the father keeps stretching out the farewell, and that will end up affecting the journey.

For today: hospitality is good, but we also need wisdom to know when a kind invitation is delaying us from what we should be doing. Be grateful for the warmth, but act with prudence.
exp.16:0:
This verse introduces a new character: a man who lived in the hill country of Ephraim, whose name was Micah. "Mount Ephraim" refers to the hill country of the tribe of Ephraim. It is a simple introduction, but it opens an important story.

The narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. This story begins a dark section of the book, where it shows how the people were turning away from God. Later, Micah confesses that he took money from his mother, and she uses it to make an image, something God's law forbade.

Today we can learn that what is religious and what is right are not always the same. We can talk about God and still do things our own way. Let us ask God that his Word guide our faith.
exp.7:12:
This verse says that Gideon, son of Joash, returned from the battle before the sun was up. In other words, he came back from the fight very early, while it was still dawn. Some modern translations understand the phrase differently: that he returned by the ascent of Heres. The Hebrew can be read in either way, so there is no complete certainty.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Gideon had just surprised a Midianite camp that was overconfident, and he had captured the two kings, Zebah and Zalmunna. Now he returns, and the account sets up his encounter with the men of Succoth, who had earlier refused to give bread to his weary people.

For today: finishing well what God has given us to do requires perseverance. Gideon did not stop when he was tired; he pressed on until he brought the matter to its close. Let us ask for strength to persevere and to carry out our responsibilities to the end.
exp.3:20:
This verse tells how Jael, the wife of Heber, took a tent peg and a hammer, approached Sisera quietly while he was sleeping from exhaustion, drove the peg through his temple into the ground, and so he died. A hammer is a heavy hand tool used to strike, and the temples are the flat areas on each side of the forehead.

It is part of the account in Judges 4. Israel was oppressed by Jabin, king of Canaan, and Sisera was his commander, who fled after being defeated. Jael offered him shelter and trust, and then killed him. The text says that God subdued Jabin that day, but it does not approve of every detail of the action. Some see courage here and others note the deception; the Bible simply narrates what happened.

For today: God can work even in violent and confusing times, and his justice does not depend on our strength. Trust in him, and seek to resolve conflicts with integrity, without deceit.
exp.5:13:
This verse says that the Lord looks at Gideon and tells him: "Go in this might you have, and you will save Israel from the Midianites." Then he asks: "Have I not sent you?" The explanation of the archaic wording has been removed, since the reader's verse uses modern forms.

Israel was suffering under the oppression of Midian. Gideon had complained, asking where the wonders of God were. Here the Lord himself answers. The text speaks of the angel of the Lord and then of the Lord, and many see in this God speaking through his messenger. God does not argue with him; he sends him. Gideon felt small, but the sending did not depend on his size, but on the presence of God.

For today: when God gives you a task that feels too big for you, do not look only at your limits. Take the step, trusting that the one who sends you goes with you.
exp.12:23:
This verse says that the woman of Manoah gave birth to a son and named him Samson. The child grew, and the Lord blessed him. The words "bare" and "called his name" are older forms: they mean "gave birth" and "gave him the name." About the meaning of "Samson," some connect it with the Hebrew word for "sun," but this is not entirely certain.

The narrator tells this after an angel announced to Manoah and his wife the birth of a son. Manoah was afraid he would die for having seen God, but his wife calmed him with good judgment: God would not have accepted their offering or given them that promise if he wanted to destroy them. Here we see the promise fulfilled.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when we feel fear or doubt. Let us trust his character, and when we raise or guide others, let us ask for his blessing on their growth.
exp.1:1:
God tells them not to make agreements or friendly dealings with the peoples who lived in Canaan, and to tear down their altars, where they worshiped other gods. The explanation's note on the old word spelling and the phrase about listening to God's voice would not apply to this English verse, so those comments are left out. The question "why have you done this?" expresses grief and rebuke, not just anger.

The one speaking is the angel of the LORD, who carries a direct message from God. He says it to Israel at Bochim, after the death of Joshua. He reminds them that God was faithful in bringing them out of Egypt and giving them the land, but they did not keep their part. Some understand this "angel" to be an ordinary messenger, and others to be a special appearance of God himself; the text does not fully settle the question.

Today, ask yourself which things God asked you to leave behind and which you have put off until later. Obeying only in part often brings bigger problems. Ask him for help to obey with a sincere heart.
exp.17:29:
The children of Dan set up a carved image, that is, an idol. Jonathan and his descendants served as their priests until the day of the captivity, an old word meaning exile or being taken away as prisoners. Some ancient texts say that Jonathan was a grandson of Moses, not of Manasseh, and scholars debate which reading is original.

The narrator of Judges tells how the tribe of Dan conquered Laish and took the idol of Micah along with his priest. It is a disordered time, when each person did whatever seemed right to them. The account shows how worship became corrupted.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we worship God as He has revealed Himself or as it suits us. A comfortable faith, made to our own measure, ends up pulling us away from Him.
exp.19:10:
This verse says that all the men of Israel gathered together against the city of Gibeah, united as one man. That is, they acted with one decision, without divisions. The explanation of the other words in the phrase is not needed here, since the verse above is what the reader sees.

After a terrible crime committed in Gibeah, a city of the tribe of Benjamin, the tribes came together and decided to act jointly. They organized the response by casting lots and gathering supplies for the journey. Then they asked Benjamin to hand over the guilty men, but Benjamin refused. The account shows unity in facing evil, although Judges is a book of very chaotic times, and not everything the people do is approved by God.

For today: unity has great strength, but it needs to be guided by justice and humility. Before we join together to act, let us ask God for wisdom, so that our unity serves good and not anger.
exp.3:19:
Here Sisera, the commander of the Canaanite army, asks Jael to stand at the entrance of the tent and, if anyone comes asking whether there is someone inside, to say that there is no one. The word "Stand" means "stay," and "tent" is the tent where the family lived.

Sisera speaks as one who was fleeing exhausted after his army was defeated by Israel. He felt safe and wanted to hide. He trusted Jael, but she used that trust to kill him, as the following verses tell. Interpreters debate how to evaluate her act; the text presents it as part of how God gave Israel the victory.

Today, this verse invites us not to place our security in human shelters that seem firm. Only in God is there a true refuge. It also reminds us to ask for wisdom to know whom we should trust.
exp.17:17:
This verse tells how the five men from the tribe of Dan entered the house of Micah and took his religious objects: a carved image, the ephod (a garment used by priests), the teraphim (household figures used in religious practices), and a molten image made of cast metal. The priest, surprised, asked them what they were doing.

The one speaking is the young priest whom Micah had hired. The Danites were looking for a territory where they could settle, and they also wanted a priest of their own. This takes place in a disordered period of Israel's history, when each person did whatever seemed right to them. The armed men waiting outside show that they were acting by force.

For today: it is not acceptable to worship God in our own way or according to what suits us. It is wise to examine whether our faith rests on the Word of God or on customs, objects, or personal interests. God deserves sincere obedience, not convenient religion.
exp.5:6:
This verse says that the people of Israel asked God for help with cries and pleas because of the Midianites. The word "cried" means calling out with force, out of pain. The verse is incomplete, because the sentence continues into the next verse.

The narrator of the book of Judges tells how Midian kept invading Israel's harvests and left them in poverty, like a plague of locusts. Here Israel was already desperate. What stands out is that God does not first respond by sending a deliverer, but by sending a prophet who reminds them how he brought them out of Egypt. In this way he shows them that their suffering was connected to having left him.

For today: when you are in trouble, cry out to God without waiting until you are perfect. And let him also speak to you, not only to take the problem away, but to heal what is twisted in your heart.
exp.1:15:
This verse says that, even while Israel was suffering because of its disobedience, God did not completely abandon them. He "raised up" judges, meaning he stood them up and set them in place. These judges were leaders who rescued the people from those who "spoiled" them, that is, who plundered them and took what belonged to them.

The book of Judges tells the story of Israel after the death of Joshua. The narrator explains that the people turned away from God and worshiped other gods, and for that reason they suffered oppression. But when they cried out, God responded with compassion. The judges were not kings; they were deliverers and leaders chosen by God for each situation.

For today: although our mistakes bring consequences, God remains merciful. If you are in a difficult situation because of your own decisions, you can return to Him sincerely, trusting that He is still willing to help you.
exp.2:12:
It says that Eglon, king of Moab, did not attack alone. He allied himself with the Ammonites and the Amalekites, went against Israel, and defeated them. Then he took "the city of palm trees," which many understand to be Jericho, although the text does not give the name. The words "went" and "struck" mean "went" and "struck down" or "overcame."

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. He explains that, after the death of Othniel, Israel again did what was evil, and God allowed Eglon to grow strong against them. It was a consequence of abandoning God. Eighteen years of oppression would follow, until they cried out and God sent Ehud.

For today: sin almost always brings consequences, and sometimes they pile up. But the account also shows that God listens when we cry out. If you have drifted away from Him, do not wait until you are oppressed: return today with sincerity.
exp.10:37:
Jephthah let his daughter go for two months, as she had asked. She went off with her friends to the mountains and wept there because she would never marry or have children. Her unlived life is what the word translated here as "virginity" refers to. Her friends are her companions.

Jephthah, a judge of Israel, had made a vow to the LORD before fighting against the Ammonites. His daughter was the first to come out to meet him. She accepts her father's vow and asks only for time to mourn with her friends. The text does not explain everything clearly: some understand that she was offered as a sacrifice, others that she was dedicated to remain unmarried in God's service. Those who study the Bible do not agree.

For today: let us think before making a promise in haste, because our words can affect others. And let us accompany with tenderness the one who grieves a loss.
exp.19:18:
It says that the Israelites rose early in the morning and camped opposite Gibeah, the city of Benjamin. The phrase about setting up camp against it means they set up their camp in order to attack. Gibeah was the place where the terrible events of the previous chapter had happened.

Here the narrator tells the story. Israel had gathered together as one people, and God told them that Judah would go first. They wanted to punish the crime committed at Gibeah, since the tribe of Benjamin refused to hand over the guilty men. It is a difficult time, when everyone did as they saw fit. Notice that, although they consulted God, the battle that follows does not turn out as they expected.

For today: rising early and seeking God is good, but it does not guarantee that everything will go easily. When you face a problem, pray, act with humility, and do not assume the outcome. Keep seeking God even in the middle of difficulties.
exp.20:21:
Here the elders of Israel tell the tribe of Benjamin what to answer if the fathers or brothers of the young women of Shiloh complain. They should ask for mercy. They argue that in the war they did not take wives for every Benjamite, and that, since the Israelites did not hand over their daughters of their own will (because of the oath they had made), they would not be guilty now.

The elders speak near the end of the book, in a chaotic time. Israel had nearly destroyed Benjamin and had sworn not to give them daughters. Now they look for a way out that keeps the oath only in appearance. The text does not approve the seizing of the women; it shows it as part of the disorder, for everyone did what seemed right in his own eyes.

For today: let us not justify one wrong with another. When we have made promises or committed faults, let us seek honest and just solutions, not shortcuts that hurt others.
exp.0:6:
Adoni-bezek, a Canaanite king, acknowledges that what happened to him was the same as what he had done to others. He says that seventy kings, with their thumbs and big toes cut off, used to gather scraps of food under his table. Then they brought him to Jerusalem, and there he died.

Adoni-bezek speaks after being captured by Judah and Simeon, while Israel was conquering Canaan. He had humiliated and left disabled the enemies he had defeated. He himself sees his punishment as a just repayment from God. The text does not say that God approved his cruelty or anyone else's; it only records his acknowledgment.

For today: our actions have consequences, and sometimes life gives them back to us. It is wise to treat others with compassion and mercy, especially when we have power over them, remembering that one day we will give an account to God.
exp.6:11:
This verse describes the enormous enemy camp. Midian, Amalek, and the peoples of the east (groups who lived east of Israel) were spread out across the valley. They are compared to locusts because of their great number, and their camels to the sand on the seashore, too many to count.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. God had offered Gideon the chance to go down by night into the enemy camp, together with his servant Phurah (called Phara in this version), so that he could listen and be encouraged. Gideon was afraid, and the text shows how great the challenge was: a few men of Israel facing a multitude.

For today: sometimes our problems seem like an endless army. God does not deny that they are great, but he invites us to come to him with our fear, and he knows how to give us courage at just the right moment.
exp.12:22:
Here the wife of Manoah answers her husband calmly. She tells him that if the Lord had wanted to kill them, he would not have accepted their burnt offering and their meat offering from their hands. Nor would he have shown them all these things or told them such things as these.

Manoah was afraid to die because they had seen the angel of the Lord. At that time it was believed that seeing God brought death. His wife reasons with faith: God had dealt with them in favor and with promises, not in anger. Afterward Samson was born, and God blessed him.

When you feel fear before something of God that you do not understand, remember how he has been good to you and what he has promised you. His past dealings can give you calm to trust him today.
exp.7:14:
Gideon arrives at Succoth and shows them Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian whom he had captured. He reminds them how they mocked him. The word "upbraid" means that they insulted him with scorn or reproach. They had asked him whether he already had those kings in his power, so that he could then give bread to his weary men.

Gideon speaks here after pursuing the Midianite armies. Earlier he had asked them for food for his exhausted people, and the leaders of Succoth refused. They did not want to take a risk in case Gideon failed. Now, with the victory won, he returns to hold them accountable. The text tells what he did, but it does not say that God approved of that punishment.

For today: when someone fights for a good cause, helping them is an act of faith and love, not of calculation. And if we have been wronged, we should seek justice without letting revenge take control of us.
exp.9:13:
The explanation says that God invites the Israelites to go and ask for help from the gods they themselves chose. The word "Go" means to go, and "cry out" means to call loudly. It is a sentence with irony: if those gods are so good, let them save you in your trouble.

The Lord speaks, and He does so after Israel had turned away from Him and served foreign gods. He reminds them that He had earlier delivered them from Egypt and from other peoples when they cried out to Him. Now He confronts them with their unfaithfulness. Then they acknowledge their sin, remove the idols, and return to serving Him. The text says that God was grieved by the suffering of His people.

For today: let us not seek God only when there are problems. Let us examine what things take His place in our hearts, such as money or success, and return to Him with sincerity, for His mercy remains open.
exp.15:1:
This verse tells that someone warned the people of Gaza that Samson was in their city. So they surrounded him and posted watchers at the city gate all night. They stayed quiet, waiting for the light of morning to kill him.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Gaza was a Philistine city, and the Philistines dominated Israel at that time. Samson, a judge of Israel, had gone there and got involved with a prostitute. The people of Gaza saw their chance to finish off their enemy. Even so, the following text shows that Samson escaped.

For today: Samson put himself in danger by neglecting his life and his holiness. God can rescue us from our mistakes, but it is wise not to play with them. Let us watch our steps and seek to live with integrity.
exp.19:0:
All of the people of Israel came out together, and the assembly gathered as one person, from Dan in the north to Beersheba in the south, and also from the land of Gilead, on the other side of the Jordan. They gathered before the Lord, that is, in the presence of God, at Mizpah. An assembly means a group of people gathered together.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Before this, a terrible crime had happened in Gibeah, a city in the tribe of Benjamin, and the people gather to decide what to do. According to the text that follows, they want to hear how that wickedness happened. Interpreters debate whether their reaction was entirely fair or whether it went too far, since the situation later becomes very violent.

For today: when there is a serious problem, let us seek unity, prayer, and truth before acting. Listening calmly and placing everything before God helps us not to react only with anger.
exp.0:5:
Adoni-bezek, king of Bezek, tried to escape from the battle, but the men of Judah chased him down and caught him. They captured him, and then they cut off the thumbs and big toes of his hands and feet, a punishment that left him badly limited in fighting or walking firmly.

This is part of the account of how Judah, one of the tribes of Israel, began to take possession of the land of Canaan after the death of Joshua. Here it is not a character who speaks; the narrator tells what happened. The next verse explains that this same king had done this to seventy kings, and he acknowledges that he received what he had done. The text reports it, but it does not say that every human punishment is a model to imitate.

For today: our actions leave a mark, and cruelty or abuse eventually catches up with us. We can choose to treat others with mercy, remembering that God treats us that way.
exp.16:8:
Here Micah asks a young man who has arrived at his house: "Whence comest thou?" The young man answers that he is a Levite from Bethlehem in Judah, and that he is wandering to find a place to live, "where I may find a place," that is, a place where he can settle.

Micah had in his house a shrine with idols, made according to his own way. This Levite was wandering aimlessly, without a fixed place to serve God. Micah sees the opportunity to hire him as his personal priest. The book of Judges repeats that in those days there was no king in Israel and each person did what seemed right in his own eyes, so the scene shows a time of spiritual disorder.

For today: when we lack direction, let us not accept just any offer merely for comfort or out of need. Let us seek God's guidance and his Word before deciding where and with whom to serve.
exp.15:17:
This verse tells that Delilah realized Samson had finally told her the whole truth. Then she sent for the leaders of the Philistines and asked them to come up "this once," because she now had the secret. They came with the money in their hands. The word "lords" refers to the rulers or chiefs of the Philistines, and "shewed me all his heart" means he had opened up completely what was most inward.

The narrator describes here the moment of betrayal. Delilah had pressed Samson day after day, and the Philistines had promised her money in exchange for discovering the source of his strength. She had called them before, but now she trusts that Samson spoke the truth.

For today: let us guard the deepest part of our hearts. We should open it with wisdom, and not give in to the constant pressure of someone who seeks their own gain. God is the safest refuge in whom to entrust everything.
exp.5:22:
God speaks to Gideon and says: "Peace be unto you; fear not, you shall not die." The word "peace" here is a greeting and also a promise of calm. "The Lord" is the name of God.

Gideon had just realized that his visitor was the angel of the Lord, and that the fire had consumed his offering. He was very frightened, because at that time it was believed that seeing God face to face could cost a person his life. The Lord himself calms him. Afterward, Gideon builds an altar and calls it "The Lord is peace," and later he receives the task of tearing down the altar of Baal.

When we feel fear before God or before what he asks of us, we can remember that he draws near to give us peace. Before asking us something difficult, he gives us assurance. We can come to him with confidence and honesty.
exp.3:5:
Deborah sends for Barak, a man from Kedesh in the tribe of Naphtali. She reminds him that God had already given him an order: to gather people on Mount Tabor and take ten thousand men from the tribes of Naphtali and Zebulun. The phrase "gather an army" is what the Hebrew-based wording expresses in this verse, and the word "sent for" simply means she had him summoned.

Deborah speaks as a prophetess and judge of Israel, the one to whom the people came to have their disputes settled. Israel was oppressed by Jabin, a Canaanite king, and she passes on to Barak a message from God. Her question is not a doubt: she reminds him of something he already knew. The text does not explain why Barak had not yet acted.

For today: when we know what God is asking of us, it is best to obey without delay. Ask yourself what concrete step you have been putting off, and take a first step today, trusting that God goes ahead of you.
exp.19:7:
The explanation says that all the people of Israel, united "as one man," stood up and promised not to return to their houses or to their homes until a decision was made about the crime committed. The word "home" here simply means the place where each family lived.

The Levite, whose concubine was mistreated and killed in Gibeah, had just told what happened before the assembly of the tribes. They answered with one voice. What follows is their plan to act against Gibeah of Benjamin. It should be noted that we hear the account from only one side, and that this book describes a time of great violence and disorder.

For today: when there is a serious injustice, unity and seriousness help, but it is wise to seek the truth and act with calm and justice, not only with anger. Let us ask God for wisdom before we react.
exp.17:19:
It says the priest was glad. Then he took the ephod (a sacred garment used in worship), the teraphim (figures used for religious purposes in the home), and the graven image, and went in the midst of the people of Dan. His joy did not come from obeying God, but from receiving a better offer.

The men of the tribe of Dan were looking for territory, and they passed by the house of Micah. They took his religious objects and persuaded the Levite to go with them, offering him a more important position. Judges shows a disordered time, in which each person did whatever seemed right to them. Here worship and the priesthood are treated as a business.

For today: examine what makes you glad when you make decisions. A greater position or more benefits do not always mean God's will. Before deciding, ask yourself whether you are drawing closer to God or only to your own convenience.
exp.15:4:
This verse tells how the rulers of the Philistines went to Delilah. They asked her to trick Samson so they could find out the secret of his great strength, and then be able to tie him up and make him suffer. In return, each of them would give her eleven hundred pieces of silver.

The ones speaking are the Philistine lords, rulers and enemies of Israel. Samson had humiliated them again and again, and they wanted to stop him. The Bible says that he loved Delilah, but it does not clearly say whether she was a Philistine or whether she loved him. That is left open to interpretation.

For today: money and pressure can push us to betray the trust of others. Let us be careful about whom we open our hearts to, and let no gain lead us to hurt someone who trusts us.
exp.5:29:
The men of the city demand that Joash hand over his son Gideon so that they can kill him. They accuse him of having torn down the altar of Baal and of having cut down the grove beside it, which here is the wooden post or tree dedicated to the goddess Asherah.

The people of the town of Ophrah speak in anger after discovering what happened during the night. God had asked Gideon to destroy that altar, which belonged to his own father. For them, attacking Baal was a serious offense that deserved death. Joash, however, challenges them: if Baal is a god, let him defend himself.

Obeying God can bring rejection, even from people close to us. But God cares for those who are faithful to Him. Ask Him for courage to leave behind whatever competes with Him, even when others do not understand.
exp.18:14:
It says that the Levite, his concubine, and his servant turned off the road to spend the night in Gibeah. When they arrived, they sat down in the square, which was the open space of the city, because no one offered them a place in their home.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He tells of the return journey of a Levite toward the region of Ephraim. Gibeah belonged to the tribe of Benjamin, that is, it was an Israelite town. Even so, no one received them. In that time hospitality was a very important duty, and this failure foreshadows the great wickedness that comes later in the story. Only an old stranger will help them.
