For today: open your eyes to those who are alone or passing through, in your church, workplace, or neighborhood. A simple gesture, such as a meal or a place to rest, can be a real act of love.
exp.2:11:
This verse says that the Israelites again did what was evil, that is, they disobeyed God. Then God gave Eglon, king of Moab, the power to rule over Israel.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. After the death of the judge Othniel, there were forty years of peace, but the people fell again into the same pattern: sin, punishment, and crying out to God. The text explains that God allowed that oppression as a consequence of their wickedness. Afterward, Moab, together with Ammon and Amalek, dominated Israel for eighteen years.

For today: let us not easily forget what God has done for us in times of peace. When everything goes well, it is easy to become careless. Let us make a habit of giving thanks, praying, and obeying every day, and if we fail, let us return to Him quickly.
exp.10:3:
This verse says that, after a while, the Ammonites (descendants of Ammon) attacked Israel. The phrase "in process of time" is an old way of saying "after some time had passed." The text does not say how much time it was.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. He tells us that Jephthah had been driven out by his brothers and was living far away, in Tob. Now a real threat strikes Israel, and the very people who rejected him are going to need him. This verse sets up that turn: the crisis leads them to seek the one they had once despised.

For today: do not write anyone off because of their past or because of how others treated them. God often uses people who were rejected. And if someone has rejected you, ask God for wisdom to respond with humility when circumstances change.
exp.17:13:
Here the five men who had earlier spied out the land of Laish speak with their brothers of the tribe of Dan. They remind them that in Micah's house there is an ephod (a sacred garment used in worship), teraphim (household objects used in religious practice), a carved image, and a molten image. They say to them: "Now therefore consider what ye have to do."

The Danite spies speak now, and they go with six hundred armed men. They were looking for territory where they could settle. The text does not state clearly what their intentions are, but what follows shows that these objects interest them, and in the end they take them away. It is a disorderly time, in which each person did what seemed right to him.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are really seeking God or only religious things that give us security. Before deciding anything, it is wise to pause and ask: does this please God, or does it only suit me?
exp.11:3:
Jephthah gathered all the men of Gilead and fought against the tribe of Ephraim, and the Gileadites defeated them. Ephraim had insulted them, calling the people of Gilead "fugitives of Ephraim," as if they were people without land or worth of their own, lost among the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh. The word "smote" here means that they struck them down in battle.

The narrator of the book tells of the moment when Ephraim, upset at not having been called to fight against Ammon, attacks Jephthah. Ephraim was a proud and powerful tribe. Its contempt wounded Gilead, and the quarrel ended in a war between Israelite brothers, a very sad thing.

For today: pride and words of disdain can ignite enormous conflicts. Before responding with anger or mockery, it is wise to listen, to speak with humility, and to seek peace, as Proverbs 15:1 teaches.
exp.14:4:
He says that Samson set fire to the torches (firebrands) and let the foxes loose in the fields of the Philistines. The fire burned the shocks (piles of cut grain), the standing corn (grain not yet harvested), the vineyards and the olive groves. It was a hard blow to their food and their livelihood.

It is the narrator who tells what Samson did. Shortly before, his father-in-law had given his wife to another man, and Samson decided that now he would bear no guilt if he harmed them. The Philistines responded by burning the woman and her father, and Samson took revenge again. The Bible shows here a cycle of violence, though it also says that God used these conflicts against the Philistines (Judges 14:4).

Today: revenge begins with a wound and almost always ends in more pain. Before responding in anger, let us ask God for wisdom to seek justice without destroying others or ourselves.
exp.18:25:
It says that at dawn the woman returned to the house where her master was and fell down in front of the door. There she lay until it was light. The word "concubine" here refers to a secondary wife, and "master" means her husband or owner. The phrase "it was light" means that it had already grown bright.

The narrator recounts one of the darkest episodes in Judges. Some men of Gibeah, in Benjamin, wanted to abuse a Levite who was a guest. Instead of protecting her, the man handed over his concubine, and she suffered violence through the night. The book repeats that there was no king in Israel and everyone did what seemed right to them. It is a condemnation of wickedness, not an approval of it.

For today: God calls us to protect the vulnerable, not to sacrifice them to save ourselves. Today we can listen, believe, and accompany those who suffer abuse, and defend their dignity.
exp.15:14:
Delilah challenges Samson, asking how he can say he loves her when he does not trust her. She reminds him that he has already deceived her three times and still has not told her the secret of his great strength. "To uncover" here means to reveal or tell.

The speaker is Delilah, the woman Samson loved. The Philistine rulers had asked her to find out the source of his strength so they could subdue him. She insists with accusations and emotional pressure, and Samson had already deceived her with false answers. In the end, tired of her persistence, he tells her that his strength is tied to his Nazirite vow, and that for this reason he had never cut his hair.

For today: true love shows itself in trust and sincerity, not in pressure or manipulation. If someone keeps pressing us again and again to give in to what we know we should not do, let us ask God for wisdom to set boundaries and to care for what He has entrusted to us.
exp.19:9:
The explanation says that Israel will organize its army and its supplies. From every hundred men they will take ten, from every thousand they will take a hundred, and from every ten thousand they will take a thousand. They will carry provisions, meaning food, for those who are going to fight against Gibeah of Benjamin. The reason is the terrible wickedness that was committed there.

The people of Israel, gathered together as one man, speak after the horrible crime against the Levite's concubine. Before they fight, they decide how to divide the work and cast lots. Note that they will first ask the tribe of Benjamin what happened, as the following verse shows.

For today: even when something is unjust and stirs our anger, it is wise to act with order, cooperation, and a search for the truth. A just cause is not defended with haste or anger, but with responsibility and wisdom.
exp.5:16:
Gideon says to the Lord: "If you truly look on me with favor, give me a sign that it is you who is speaking to me." The phrase "found grace" means being accepted and favored. A "sign" is a clear and visible proof.

Gideon speaks, a humble young man from the tribe of Manasseh. God, through his angel, has just called him to deliver Israel from the Midianites. Gideon feels small and unsure. Although God promises to be with him, he asks for confirmation. Some see here a lack of faith, while others see a sincere desire to be certain that it is God who is speaking.

For today: when you doubt what God asks of you, bring your fears to him honestly. Seek him in his Word and in prayer, and do not act on impulse alone. He patiently deals with those who want to obey him.
exp.14:14:
It says that Samson found a donkey's jawbone that was still fresh, that is, recently dead and not dried out or brittle. He took it in his hand and with it defeated a thousand men. The word for "struck" here means that he hit them or killed them.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Samson had just been handed over by his own people from Judah to the Philistines, bound with new ropes. But the Spirit of the LORD came upon him, the ropes fell off, and with no other weapon at hand, he used what he found. The text credits the strength to God, not to the jawbone.

For today: God can use what you have at hand, even when it seems small or improvised. Instead of waiting until you have better resources, offer him with faith what you have today, and trust that his power works through you.
exp.6:22:
This verse tells how, after the Midianites fled in fear, the men of Israel from the tribes of Naphtali, Asher, and all Manasseh gathered together and went out to pursue them. "Pursued" here means they went after them in order to catch up with them. Before this, only three hundred men had been with Gideon.

Context: This is the account in the book of Judges; the narrator is telling what happened, not a character speaking. God had reduced Gideon's army so that Israel would know the victory came from Him. With trumpets, torches, and shouting, the enemy camp fell into panic. Now, with the enemy in flight, other Israelites join in and take advantage of the victory.

For today: God can begin a work with a few people and then encourage others to join. If He gives you a step of faith, take that step without waiting for crowds, and when others come alongside, work together with humility and give God the credit.
exp.16:4:
The verse says that Micah had a house of gods, made an ephod, and teraphim, and consecrated one of his sons, who became his priest. So the explanation tells us that Micah kept a shrine with idols in his home. He also made an ephod (a priestly garment) and teraphim (household figures used to seek guidance). Then he set apart one of his sons to be his priest.

The narrator of Judges describes a time without a king and without a clear direction. Micah mixes the name of the LORD with images and rites of his own invention, something the law of Moses forbade. The texts that follow show that the author tells this as a sign of spiritual disorder, not as an example to follow. Furthermore, a priest had to be of the tribe of Levi, and his son was not.

We can have good intentions and still worship God in our own way. It is worth asking ourselves whether we serve Him as He has revealed in His Word, or as is more comfortable for us.
exp.2:5:
They say the Israelites married into the peoples who lived in the land: they took the daughters of those peoples as wives for their sons, and gave their own daughters to the sons of those peoples. And in the end they ended up worshiping the gods of those peoples.

The book of Judges tells the story of Israel after Joshua. The narrator (tradition says it may have been Samuel, though this is not known for certain) explains that God left those peoples in the land to test whether Israel would obey the law given through Moses. That law warned against marriages that would turn the heart away from God. This verse shows how the fall that follows began.

For today: close relationships influence us a great deal. Take care with your friendships, your courtship, and your important decisions, so that they draw your heart closer to God and do not pull it away little by little.
exp.18:0:
It says that, in a time when Israel had no king, a Levite lived as a sojourner in the farthest part of the hill country of Ephraim. This man had taken as his partner a concubine from Bethlehem of Judah. A concubine was a wife of lesser legal standing, something common in that era. "Sojourning" means he lived as a stranger, without roots of his own.

It is the beginning of a very painful story at the end of the book of Judges. The one speaking is the narrator, not a character. The phrase "when there was no king in Israel" is repeated in the book to show the moral disorder of those years, when people acted without guidance and without respect for God's law. Scholars understand that phrase in different ways, but all of them see a warning.

For today: when each person does what seems right to them, respect and care for others are lost. Ask yourself whom and what you are allowing to guide your life.
exp.18:17:
He tells the old man where he is coming from and where he is going. He says he is traveling from Bethlehem in Judah toward the high hill country of Ephraim, which is his home. He says he went to Bethlehem, but now he is going to the house of the Lord. Some scholars think the original text said "to my house." What is clear is that no one in the town has invited him to spend the night.

A Levite traveler is speaking, answering the old man who asked him who he was and where he was going. They were in the square of Gibeah, a town of Benjamin. It was normal to take in travelers, but no one had done so. That shows how cold that place was.

Today we can open the door to someone who is alone or in need, without waiting for someone else to do it first. A meal, a phone call, or a place to rest can be a real way of showing love.
exp.10:28:
This verse says that the Spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah, and he traveled through Gilead and Manasseh to gather people. Then he passed through Mizpeh of Gilead and from there advanced toward the Ammonites, ready for battle. The word "passed" in the verse means that he went across or through the land, and the name "the Lord" refers to God.

The narrator is the author of the book of Judges. Jephthah, a man from Gilead, had first tried to settle the conflict with words, but the Ammonite king would not listen to him. Then the Spirit of God empowers him to lead Israel. What follows, Jephthah's vow, is not presented as a command from God, and the Bible lets us see how painful it was.

For today: seek peace and dialogue first, and when you must act, ask for God's guidance. Do not add hasty promises that He has not asked of you.
exp.7:4:
Gideon arrives at Succoth with his three hundred men, worn out from chasing the enemy. He asks for some "loaves of bread," that is, a little food, for his people. He explains that they are pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the two kings of Midian. The word "people" here means his soldiers.

Gideon, judge of Israel, speaks. He has just defeated the Midianites with God's help, and now he continues the pursuit of their kings. The people of Succoth were Israelites, so he expected support from his own nation. They refused, perhaps out of fear of reprisal, though the text does not state this clearly.

For today: when someone is tired but keeps doing a good task, we can help them with something simple. And if we need to ask for help, let us do so with humility. A little bread shared in time can sustain others in their work.
exp.14:16:
It says that Samson, when he had finished his song of victory, threw away the jawbone he had used as a weapon. Then he gave the place a name: Ramath-lehi. In Hebrew that name can sound like "the height of the jaw," though some also understand it as "he threw away the jaw." Perhaps the name holds both meanings.

Here the narrator is speaking, telling what Samson did. The Philistines had bound him to hand him over, but he broke the ropes and defeated a thousand men. After shouting his triumphant poem, he lays down the weapon and marks the spot to remember what happened there.

For today: after a victory, it is easy to keep the jawbone and boast. Samson spoke about himself, but soon he was thirsty and cried out to God. When something goes well for you, remember that you depend on God, and thank him before you move on.
exp.5:23:
This verse tells that Gideon built an altar to God in that place and named it "Jehovah-shalom," which means "the Lord is peace." The text adds that the altar was still there "unto this day," that is, at the time the account was written, in Ophrah, a town of the Abiezrites.

The one narrating is the author of the book of Judges. Gideon had just seen the angel of the Lord and feared he would die, because it was believed that seeing God face to face meant death. God said to him: "Peace be unto thee; fear not." The altar was his grateful response to that word of peace.

For today: when God gives you calm in the middle of fear, do not let it pass. Thank Him with a concrete act, such as a prayer, a written note, or a moment of worship, to remember that He is your peace.
exp.4:13:
The verse names several tribes of Israel who answered the call to fight. From Ephraim came warriors who went out after Benjamin, together with their people. From Machir, of the tribe of Manasseh, came leaders. From Zebulun came those who handled the scribe's stylus, a rod or tool used by someone who recorded or directed the people. The phrase about Amalek is difficult, and scholars explain it in several ways.

Deborah speaks, along with Barak, in a song of victory over the Canaanites. She remembers who joined the battle and who did not, as Reuben does later on.

For today: God uses people of every kind, from warriors to scribes. Ask yourself what gift you have, and offer it gladly to serve in your church or community.
exp.8:3:
The people of Shechem gave Abimelech seventy pieces of silver, taken from the temple of Baal-berith. With that money he hired men who were idle and worthless, that is, people without a trade, without direction, and ready for anything. These men followed him.

The narrator describes how Abimelech, son of Gideon (Jerubbaal) and of a woman from Shechem, seeks to become king. He had already won over his mother's relatives and the people of Shechem. Now he uses money from the temple of a false god to form his small band. The next verse shows what for: to kill his seventy brothers.

For today: power gained with tainted money and people without convictions ends in violence. Before following a leader or an opportunity, let us ask where their support comes from and what they really want.
exp.2:2:
This verse continues the list of the peoples that God left in the land of Canaan. It mentions the five lords of the Philistines, all the Canaanites, the Sidonians (from Sidon, a Phoenician city), and the Hivites who lived in Mount Lebanon, from Mount Baal-hermon to the entrance of Hamath, a region in the north.

The book of Judges is told in the voice of a narrator, and it is not known with certainty who its author was. It explains why these peoples were left: to test Israel and to teach war to a generation that did not know the wars of Canaan. It then says that the test was whether they would obey the commandments given through Moses.

For today: the trials of life reveal whether we trust God and obey him. When you face a difficulty, ask yourself how you can respond with faithfulness.
exp.0:25:
The explanation says that the man who helped the Israelites enter Bethel went into the land of the Hittites. There he built a city and called it Luz, the same name as the city he had left. The text adds that this name was still in use when the book was written. The explanation of the old wording: "went" means the word "went," "built" is "built," and "unto this day" means until the time of the writer.

Here the narrator of Judges speaks. He tells how the tribes of Joseph took Bethel, which was formerly called Luz. That man showed them the way in exchange for mercy, and he and his family were saved. We do not know for certain where that land of the Hittites was.

For today: God cares for people even in the middle of difficult stories. We can recognize that mercy is remembered and leaves a mark. Let us ask him for help to be thankful and kind toward those who help us.
exp.18:5:
It says that the Levite and his father-in-law sat down together, ate and drank. Then the young woman's father urged the Levite to stay one more night, so that his heart would be merry. "Damsel" means young woman, and "man" refers to the Levite, her husband.

The one speaking is the father-in-law, the father of the Levite's concubine. The Levite had come to bring his wife back home. The father-in-law welcomed him warmly and treats him with great hospitality, insisting that he stay. Later, that insistence delays the journey until it grows late, and this brings serious consequences in the account.

Today we can learn to be hospitable and generous toward others. But we also need to take care that our good intentions do not pressure others or make them lose the time they need. Good hospitality also respects the decisions and plans of the other person.
exp.15:21:
It says that Samson's hair began to grow again after it had been cut. "Shaven" means shaved or cut very short, so it is a brief detail, but a very important one in the story.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. Samson had been set apart for God from birth as a Nazirite, and his long hair was a sign of that commitment. Delilah cut it while he slept, and the Philistines captured him. The text does not say the hair had magical power; it stresses that God had departed from him. By mentioning the growth of the hair, the account shows that the story is not yet over.

For today: even though we have failed and feel we have lost everything, God can give a new beginning to anyone who turns back to Him with humility.
exp.11:11:
Elon of the tribe of Zebulun died and was buried in Aijalon, within the territory of his tribe. "Was buried" means that they put him in the ground.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is recording the leaders whom God allowed in Israel. About Elon we are only told that he judged for ten years; no deeds are recounted. This Aijalon is not the same one near Jerusalem, since here it is located in Zebulun, in the north. Its exact location is uncertain.

For today: not everyone leaves a famous story, but a faithful and steady life also counts before God. Serve where you are, without worrying about applause.
exp.3:8:
Débora accepts going with Barak into battle, but she gives him an important warning. Because of the way he is acting, the credit for the victory will not be his. "Honor" here means glory or recognition, and the verb about selling means that God will hand Sisera, the enemy commander, over into the hand of a woman. Then Deborah gets up and goes with Barak to Kedesh.

Deborah, prophetess and judge of Israel, speaks here. God had commanded Barak to fight against Sisera, but Barak set a condition: he would go only if she went with him. Her reply is not a punishment but a warning. Many think the "woman" is Jael, although the text does not say so yet.

For today: when God asks something of you, obey with confidence and without conditions. And if you do what is right, do not seek applause, because God can use whomever he chooses to give the victory.
exp.6:14:
This verse tells how Gideon, after hearing a Midianite soldier's dream and what his companion said it meant, bowed down to worship God. Then he returned to the Israelite camp and gave the order to get up, because God had already handed the enemy camp over to them.

Gideon had gone down into the Midianite camp at night, along with his servant Purah, to strengthen his courage. There he heard the dream of a barley loaf that tumbled into the tents. The companion understood it as a sign that Gideon would win. The text does not explain how God used those words, but Gideon received them as confirmation from God.

Before acting, Gideon first worshipped. When God gives you encouragement or answers a prayer, take a moment to thank him. That thankfulness strengthens your confidence to take the next step with courage.
exp.10:9:
The elders of Gilead answer Jephthah with a solemn oath. They say, "The Lord be witness between us," meaning that God is witness and judge of what they agree to. They add, "if we do not so according to thy words," which in plain terms means "if we fail to keep what we have promised." It is like saying, "May God hold us accountable if we do not do it."

The leaders of Gilead speak here. Years earlier they had rejected Jephthah, but now the Ammonites were attacking them and they needed a leader to defend them. Jephthah distrusted them and asked for a clear promise: if he fought and won, they would make him their head. They seal the agreement by calling God as witness.

For today: when you make a promise, remember that God hears it. Keep your word, especially when the favor you asked for is no longer urgent, and work to make amends humbly for past offenses.
exp.19:41:
The explanation says that the men of Benjamin fled before Israel and ran toward the wilderness, but they could not escape. The army of Israel caught up with them, and those who came out of the city also attacked them. So they were trapped in the middle, with no way out. The word "battle" here refers to the fighting that overtook them, and "turned their backs" means that they turned around and ran away.

The narrator tells the end of a civil war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin. Benjamin had defended the guilty men responsible for a terrible crime in Gibeah (chapter 19). Israel set up an ambush, set the city on fire, and the smoke was the signal. When they saw it, Benjamin understood that their defeat was certain.

For today: sin that is protected or justified ends up closing in around us. It is better to recognize evil in time and correct our course, instead of hardening ourselves and defending what is wrong out of pride or misplaced loyalty.
exp.6:16:
Gideon tells his three hundred men: "Look at me and do the same as I do." When he reaches the edge of the enemy camp, they must copy each of his movements. The words "look on me" and "do likewise" are simply saying "look at me" and "do what I do."

Gideon speaks here as judge of Israel. God had already encouraged him through the dream of a Midianite soldier, and now he arranges everything for an attack at night. With so few men, the victory depended on their acting together and paying close attention to their leader, trusting that God would fight for them.

For today: sometimes God calls us to follow with careful attention and obedience, without rushing ahead or hesitating. We can ask ourselves: am I watching God and following his direction, or acting on my own? Taking small, obedient steps alongside others may be part of what God uses to accomplish his purposes.
exp.6:12:
This verse tells how Gideon went down to the enemy camp and overheard a Midianite soldier telling his companion about a dream. In the dream, a loaf of barley bread rolled into the camp, struck the tents, and knocked them down completely. The soldier's words for "struck" and "overturned" are clear in the verse itself: the bread hit the tent and turned it over until it lay flat.

God had told Gideon to go down to the camp with his servant Purah, because there he would hear something that would encourage him. Gideon was afraid, and the enemy army was enormous. The barley bread was humble and simple food, and the companion interpreted it as Gideon's sword. In this way, God used an enemy to confirm his promise.

For today: when you feel small before a large problem, remember that God can use what is humble to accomplish great things. Ask him for encouragement and trust his guidance.
exp.14:12:
The men of Judah assured Samson that they would not kill him. They would only tie him up and hand him over to the Philistines. They bound him with two new ropes and brought him up from the rock.

[Delete this sentence: it explains source-language words not in the reader's verse.]

The men of Judah speak, about three thousand of them. They lived under Philistine rule and were afraid. They chose to hand Samson over rather than face their oppressors. Samson agreed to be tied up, but asked that they not be the ones to kill him. The text does not explain why he let himself be bound. Some think he trusted that God would deliver him, although the Bible does not say this directly.

For today: sometimes fear leads us to choose the easy way out instead of the brave one. The people of Judah could have sought help from God, but they preferred to give in. Let us ask God for the courage not to give up what is right merely out of fear of trouble.
exp.7:26:
It says that Gideon took the gold the people gave him and made from it an ephod, a sacred garment similar to the one the priest used. He placed it in Ophrah, his city. The word "whoring" here means that Israel was unfaithful to God, using that object as if it were something to worship.

It is the narrator of Judges who speaks. Gideon had just defeated Midian, and the people gave him the spoils as a thank-you. We do not know for certain what Gideon meant to do with the ephod. Some think he wanted to remember the victory, others that he sought a way to consult God. Whatever his intent, it ended up becoming an idol.

For today: even good things, such as a memory, a success, or a tradition, can take the place of God. Let us ask Him to keep us from making into the center of our lives what should only help us remember Him.
exp.20:2:
Here the people of Israel cry out to God in grief. They ask why something so serious has happened: that one of the twelve tribes, Benjamin, is about to disappear. The phrase about being incomplete means that the tribe is no longer whole.

The people have gathered at Bethel, the house of God, weeping since the evening. Shortly before, in a terrible war against Benjamin, they had nearly killed the entire tribe. They had also sworn at Mizpah not to give their daughters in marriage to the men of Benjamin. Now they see that their own oath and their violence led them to this loss. Their question is sincere, even though they themselves had a part in the problem.

For today: when we suffer the consequences of hasty decisions, it is good to bring our grief to God, but also to examine with humility what our own part was, before making promises or passing judgments on impulse.
exp.11:10:
After Ibzan, this verse says, Elon became the next judge of Israel. He was from the tribe of Zebulun and led the people for ten years. The word "judged" does not refer only to giving verdicts, but to guiding, defending, and governing the people. Calling him "a Zebulonite" means that he belonged to the tribe of Zebulun.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks, giving a brief record of the minor judges. About Elon's time no battle or deed is told, only his tribe, the years of his rule, and his burial. We do not know why so little was written, and scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: God values faithful service, even when it is not famous and leaves no great stories behind. If today you carry out your work, your family, or your church with steadiness, your faithfulness does not go unnoticed by God.
exp.19:16:
This verse says that the men of Israel were counted, not including the tribe of Benjamin. There were four hundred thousand men who knew how to fight with the sword, that is, who were trained to use it. All of them were men of war, meaning soldiers prepared for battle.

The one counting is the narrator of the book, who describes how Israel organized itself to fight against Benjamin. This happens after a terrible crime in Gibeah, and the Benjamites refused to hand over the guilty men. Both sides prepare for a war between brothers, in a disordered time in which, according to the book, everyone did whatever seemed right in their own eyes.

For today: before facing a conflict, let us ask whether we truly seek justice and reconciliation, or only to win. Numbers and strength are not enough, and it is wise to seek God with humility and in time.
exp.14:19:
This verse says that Samson judged Israel for twenty years, while the Philistines dominated the region. "Judged" here does not mean only pronouncing sentences, but also guiding and defending the people.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Judges, who summarizes Samson's life. Earlier, Samson had defeated many Philistines and, exhausted and thirsty, cried out to God, who gave him water. This verse closes that part of his story. Samson was a man with great flaws, but God kept working through him. Some scholars think the twenty years came before his final fall; the text gives no further detail.

For today: when you feel weak, cry out to God with sincerity. He can sustain you and use your life, even with your weaknesses.
exp.4:11:
Here the command is repeated with force: "Awake, awake". Deborah is called to rise up and sing a song of praise. Barak is told to arise and to lead away with him the enemies who were taken. The word "utter" in the verse means to speak out or to sing aloud. "Captivity" refers to the prisoners of war.

This verse is part of the song of Deborah and Barak, sung after Israel defeated the army of Sisera. The one speaking is the song itself, which addresses Deborah and Barak as in a poetic call. Some think Deborah urges herself to sing; others think it is the people who invite her. The text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: when God gives you a victory, do not stay silent or still. Stir your heart to thank him, and then rise up to keep obeying with courage.
exp.17:5:
Here the priest of Micah tells the five men from the tribe of Dan: "Go in peace; the way you are going is before the Lord's eyes." That is, he assures them that God approves their journey. "Before the Lord" means that God sees it and directs it.

The Danites were looking for a place to settle. They stopped at the house of Micah, where this young Levite served as a paid priest, with an idol and an ephod. They asked him to seek God's answer. He gave them a reassuring reply, but the text does not say that God spoke. This happens in a time of religious disorder, so his answer may be more convenient than faithful.

Today, not every religious voice that encourages us speaks on God's behalf. Before deciding, let us compare what we hear with the Bible and seek wise counsel.
exp.8:11:
It says that the trees, after the olive tree and the fig tree refused, approach the vine and ask it to be their king.

Now the explanation has to be reworked, since the quoted old-spelling and wording notes do not appear in the verse your reader sees. The sentence about the old form and the sentence giving the meaning of the quoted phrase are removed.

It is part of a fable that Jotham, son of Gideon, tells the men of Shechem. They had made Abimelech king, a man who had killed his brothers to take power. Jotham uses the trees to show that good, fruitful people did not seek to rule, and that in the end someone harmful reigned, represented by the bramble, a thorny plant.

For today: let us value those who serve with humility and good fruit, and be wary of anyone who seeks power at any cost. Before choosing a leader, let us look at their character, not only their ambition.
exp.8:37:
Zebul throws back at Gaal his own proud words. Gaal had said, "Who is Abimelech, that we should serve him?" Now Zebul tells him that the people he looked down on, "is not this the people that thou hast despised?", is the very one coming to attack. So he challenges him: "go out, I pray now, and fight with them."

Zebul is the ruler of the city of Shechem and serves Abimelech. Meanwhile he pretends to be on Gaal's side. Earlier he told Gaal that what they were seeing were only shadows of the mountains, in order to buy time. When Abimelech is already close, Zebul stops pretending and turns Gaal's own words against him. The text does not say that Zebul was sincere with Gaal, and the account shows everyone acting with violence and deceit.

For today: let us be careful about what we say when we are full of pride, because sooner or later our words can come back to us. It is better to speak with humility and not to promise what we cannot fulfill.
exp.13:13:
Samson poses a riddle to the guests at his wedding. He says that out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness. He is referring to the honey he found in the body of the lion he had killed. The guests could not solve it in three days.

Samson speaks during the seven-day wedding feast with a Philistine woman. The guests were thirty young men, and he made a wager with them over clothing. Only Samson knew the story of the lion and the honey, so the riddle was nearly impossible to solve without help. Afterward they pressured his wife with threats.

For today: clever words and games with wagers can end in pressure and conflict. Before making a bet or sharing a secret, think about who will be affected. Care for your relationships with wisdom and sincerity.
exp.8:35:
Gaal sees people coming down from the highest points of the mountains and tells Zebul about it. Zebul answers him that it is only the shadow of the mountains, which looks to him like people.

Gaal is the one who had risen up against Abimelech and was leading the men of Shechem. Zebul, the governor of the city, also speaks; he was secretly on Abimelech's side. Zebul wants Gaal not to take the danger seriously and to stay confident, while Abimelech draws near. Afterward Zebul confronts him for his proud words.

For today: let us not downplay clear warnings, nor trust someone who reassures us while hiding their own interests. Let us be humble, look at reality carefully, and seek sincere counsel, above all from God, before it is too late.
exp.6:7:
It says Gideon took the people's provisions and their trumpets, or "horns," which were rams' horns used to give signals. Then he sent home all the other men of Israel, each to his own tent, and kept only the three hundred. Meanwhile, the camp of Midian lay below him, in the valley.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. God had already reduced Gideon's army, first from 32,000 to 10,000 and then to 300, so that Israel would not think it had been saved by its own strength. The Midianites were very numerous and were oppressing Israel. Interpreters explain in different ways why those who lapped the water were chosen, but the clear point is that God made the decision.

For today: when you feel small or short on resources, remember that God can work through you. Obey step by step, and trust that the outcome will depend on Him.
exp.6:20:
This verse says that Gideon's three hundred men did not advance or fight. They stayed still, each one in his place, surrounding the enemy camp. Meanwhile, the whole army of Midian was thrown into confusion (the word "host" here refers to the army, and "ran, and cried, and fled" describes their panic and disorder) and they ran off shouting and fleeing.

The account tells what happened at night, when Gideon and his men surrounded the Midianites with trumpets, pitchers, and torches. God had reduced Israel's army so that it would be clear the victory came from Him. The text says that the enemies turned their swords against one another, so the confusion was not only human fear.

For today: sometimes God asks us for faithfulness in the place He has given us, not for us to be the ones in the spotlight. Stand firm in your place, obey what He shows you, and trust that He can act beyond your strength.
exp.9:9:
The people of Israel, oppressed and suffering, cried out to God for help. They acknowledged their guilt: they had abandoned their God to serve the Baals, which were the false gods of the neighboring peoples, tied to rain and harvest. "Cried unto the Lord" means they called out to the Lord. "Lord" is the name of God.

The narrator of the book tells this after eighteen years of oppression by the Ammonites and the Philistines. Israel repeated a cycle: they turned away from God, suffered, cried out, and received help. Here the sin is confessed, but God's response in the following verse shows that He wanted to see a real change and not only words.

For today: when you feel your life is falling apart, come to God with sincerity. Acknowledge what you have put in His place and ask Him for help to truly change, not only to get out of the problem.
exp.8:41:
This verse tells us that on the next day the people of Shechem went out to work in the field, and someone told Abimelech. The phrase "they told Abimelech" means that they informed him or brought him the news. The verse does not say who did it or why.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Gaal had already been driven out of Shechem by Zebul, and Abimelech was waiting in Arumah. When Abimelech learned that the people had gone out of the city, he prepared a surprise attack. So the people were left exposed outside the walls, and the account shows how violence and rebellion led to more death.

For today: what seems like an ordinary day may be shaped by decisions made earlier. It is wise to seek peace, to avoid conflicts that grow out of pride, and to remember that our actions have consequences that reach other people.
exp.8:10:
The explanation says that the fig tree does not want to give up its sweetness or its good fruit to go and rule over the other trees. She prefers to keep giving what she knows how to give.

It is part of a fable that Jotham, son of Gideon, tells to the people of Shechem. The trees look for a king: first the olive, then the fig tree and the vine refuse the position. Jotham speaks because Abimelech, his brother, made himself king by killing almost all his brothers. The fable criticizes that desire for power.

For today: value the fruit that God has given you to serve, even when no one applauds you. Serving with humility and kindness is worth more than seeking a position only to stand out.
exp.8:2:
This verse tells that Abimelech's uncles went to speak to the people of Shechem and repeated what he had asked them to say. The men of Shechem let themselves be persuaded and sided with Abimelech, because they thought: "He is one of ours, he is our relative." The phrase about their hearts means that their hearts turned toward him.

Abimelech was the son of Gideon (Jerubbaal) and of a woman from Shechem. He wanted to be king, and he used family ties to win the city's support. What follows shows that his plan was unjust: he paid violent men and killed almost all of his brothers.

For today: let us not follow someone only because he is "one of ours," whether by family, friendship or group. Before supporting a person, let us look at his character, his intentions and his fruits, and ask God for wisdom to choose well.
exp.5:34:
This verse tells how Gideon sent messengers throughout the territory of the tribe of Manasseh, and the people there gathered to follow him. He also sent messengers to the tribes of Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they came up to meet them.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges. The Midianites, the Amalekites, and other peoples from the east had camped in the valley of Jezreel to attack Israel. God had put his Spirit upon Gideon, and he began to gather his people. Shortly afterward, Gideon would ask God for a sign with the fleece of wool.

For today: when God calls you to a difficult task, you do not have to carry it alone. Ask for help, bring other believers together, and walk with them, trusting that God is the one who gives the strength.
exp.5:5:
This verse says that Israel was left very poor and weak because of the Midianites, who were taking their crops and their animals. Then the people cried out, that is, they asked for help loudly, to the LORD. The word "impoverished" in the verse means they were left without resources, and "greatly" means very much.

It is part of the book of Judges. The narrator tells that Israel had turned away from God, and for that reason spent seven years under the oppression of Midian. The Midianites came like a plague of locusts, with so many camels that they could not be counted. After their cry, God sent a prophet to remind them that He had brought them out of Egypt.

For today: when you feel weak or without resources, do not wait until you hit bottom to pray. Speak to God honestly, and let Him also remind you of His faithfulness in the past.
exp.0:22:
The explanation says that the tribe of Joseph (made up of Ephraim and Manasseh) sent scouts to watch the city of Bethel. This city was formerly called Luz. "Scouts" here are men who observe in order to learn how to attack or enter.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges. Israel is taking possession of the land after the death of Joshua. The text has just said that the LORD was with them, so it presents this plan as an action carried out with God's help. Bethel held a special value in the history of Israel, and the account recalls its older name, Luz.

For today: trusting God does not remove the responsibility to think and prepare. Before an important decision, we can pray, seek counsel, and gather good information, believing that God accompanies us in that process.
exp.18:11:
Here the Levite, who travels with his concubine and his servant, rejects the suggestion to spend the night in Jebus. He says they will not stay in a city of foreigners, that is, a city that is not of the people of Israel. He prefers to keep going to Gibeah.

The Levite, who is the owner of the group, speaks to his servant, who suggested resting in Jebus because it was already late. Jebus was then a Jebusite city, which would later become Jerusalem. The Levite seeks safety among his own people. But the story shows something bitter: in Gibeah, an Israelite city, a great wickedness will take place. This climate of corruption in Israel is summed up in Judges with the statement that everyone did what seemed right in their own eyes.

For today: let us not blindly trust that a place or group is safe just because it carries the label "ours." Let us ask God for wisdom and examine real fruits with humility.
exp.9:1:
Judges 10:2 says that Tola led Israel for twenty-three years. Then he died and was buried in Shamir, the town where he lived.

"Judged" means that he guided the people, settled disputes, and protected them, not merely that he handed down verdicts. The word "buried" in the verse is the same as "was buried" in the verse text itself.

The narrator of the book of Judges is the one speaking. Tola comes right after the violent rule of Abimelech, which had left much suffering. God raised up Tola to bring Israel deliverance, that is, to give the nation stability. The text does not recount battles or great deeds of his; it gives only brief facts. After him comes Jair, and then the people return to idolatry.

For today: not all service to God is showy. Tola was faithful quietly, and his life helped others live in peace. We can value and practice steady service, even when almost no one notices it.
exp.12:24:
This verse says that the Spirit of God began to act in Samson when he was already a young man, in a place called "the camp of Dan," between the towns of Zorah and Eshtaol. The word "stir" here translates a Hebrew word that can also mean to push or to drive; that is why other versions read "move him" or "stir him."

The one telling this is the narrator of the book of Judges. Earlier, an angel had announced Samson's birth to his parents, and Manoah's wife trusted that God had a purpose. Now the boy grew up, God blessed him, and He began to prepare him to deliver Israel from the Philistines. Zorah and Eshtaol were in the territory of the tribe of Dan.

For today: God cares for and prepares His children from an early age, even before we see results. Trust that He is at work in your life and in the lives of your children, and ask Him to guide you by His Spirit.
exp.13:10:
When the people of the place saw Samson, they chose thirty young men to accompany him during the wedding feast.

Samson was in Timnath, at his wedding banquet, following the custom of young men in those days. The text does not say why they surrounded him with thirty men. It may have been a gesture of courtesy, or it may have been distrust toward a foreigner. Some older translations suggest they were afraid of him, but this is not certain. These thirty men will be the ones who hear Samson's riddle.

For today: companions matter. Before entering a gathering or celebration, it is wise to ask ourselves who surrounds us and what influence they will have on us. Let us ask God for wisdom to choose our friendships well and to act with prudence.
exp.3:13:
It says that Deborah encouraged Barak to rise up and attack, because God had already given the enemy into his hands. The phrase "Up" in the verse means to get moving, so the explanation's wording is covered by the verse itself. "Is not the Lord gone out before thee?" means that God was going ahead of them, opening the way.

Barak went down from Mount Tabor with ten thousand men.

Deborah was a prophetess and judge of Israel. Sisera, commander of the Canaanite army, had nine hundred chariots of iron, a force that terrified Israel. Barak had hesitated before, and Deborah reminded him that the victory came from God, not from weapons. God acted, as the following verses show.

For today: when you know that God is calling you to do something, do not wait until you feel fearless. Take the step with confidence, remembering that God goes before you, even when the challenge seems enormous.
exp.19:5:
Here the Levite tells the tribes of Israel what he did: he took the body of his concubine, cut it into pieces, and sent them throughout the territory of Israel. A concubine was a wife of secondary rank. The words "cut her" and "sent her" in the verse mean what the explanation here renders as "cut" and "sent." A "crime" refers to a serious wrong.

The Levite speaks before the assembly of Israel. He seeks justice for what happened in Gibeah, where violent men abused his concubine and she died. His account is not entirely complete, since it leaves out that he himself handed her over to them. The Bible records this brutal act; it does not approve of it.

Today, when we learn of an injustice, we should seek the complete truth and act with justice and compassion, without being carried away by anger or by partial accounts. God calls us to defend the vulnerable.
exp.0:3:
The explanation says that the tribe of Judah went out to fight, and that God gave them victory over the Canaanites and the Perizzites, peoples who lived in the land. In Bezek they struck down ten thousand men.

After the death of Joshua, the people of Israel asked God who should fight first against the Canaanites. God chose Judah and promised to give them the land. Judah invited his brother Simeon to help him, and together they went into battle. The book of Judges tells how Israel took possession of the promised land little by little.

For today: God often guides us when we ask him, and he also invites us to work as a team. Before facing a challenge, pray and seek the support of trusted brothers and sisters.
exp.7:17:
Gideon asks Zebah and Zalmunna, the two kings of Midian whom he had captured, what kind of men they were whom they killed at Tabor. They answer that the men were like him, with a noble appearance, "each one resembled the children of a king."

Gideon has been pursuing the Midianites. He had already punished Succoth and Penuel because they had not helped him. With his question, he discovers that those men who were killed were his own brothers. The Bible does not tell us here how that killing happened. That is why his next answer sounds like grief and personal revenge.

For today: when pain or anger takes control of us, it is easy for justice to become mixed with revenge. Before we act, it is wise to stop, pray, and ask God to guide our hearts. And remember that He calls us to trust in His justice.
exp.4:25:
This verse describes how Jael took a tent peg and a workman's hammer, and with them struck Sisera on the head until she pierced his temples. The peg was the stake that held the tent in place.

It is part of the Song of Deborah and Barak, a victory song after the battle against the Canaanite army. Sisera, their commander, had fled and arrived at Jael's tent. She welcomed him with hospitality, and then killed him while he slept (Judges 4). The song celebrates this act as a deliverance for Israel. The Bible tells the story, but it does not explain whether everything Jael did is an example to follow.

Today we can learn that God can use unexpected people to deliver his people. Let us ask him for courage to act with justice and wisdom, without resorting to violence.
exp.10:36:
She asks her father for a favor before fulfilling the vow: two months to go up and down the mountains with her friends and mourn that she would never marry or have children.

The speaker is Jephthah's daughter. He had made a vow to God before fighting against the Ammonites, and she was the first to come out to meet him. She accepts her father's word. Scholars debate whether she was offered as a sacrifice or dedicated for life to service at the sanctuary, and the text does not fully settle the question.

For today: promises made carelessly can cause great pain. Think carefully before you promise, and comfort with tenderness anyone who suffers a loss, as her friends did.
exp.19:40:
This verse describes the moment when the battle turns. The men of Israel, who had pretended to flee, turned around to attack. The men of Benjamin were filled with fear, because they understood that disaster had already come upon them.

It is part of the account in the book of Judges, which tells of the war between the tribes of Israel and Benjamin. This happened after a terrible crime in Gibeah, and the Benjamites protected the guilty. Israel set an ambush and sent up a great smoke from the city as a signal. When Benjamin saw the smoke, they realized they were surrounded. The narrator does not speak in a personal voice but simply reports the events.

For today: confidence in oneself can be deceiving. The Benjamites believed they were winning, but they did not see the danger behind them. It is wise to examine our decisions with humility, to turn back to what is right in time, and not to defend wrong out of pride or misplaced loyalty.
exp.4:28:
This verse says that the wisest and most sensible women of the court would answer the mother of Sisera when she wondered why her son was taking so long to return. But she herself ended up answering her own question, repeating what she wanted to believe.

This happens within the song of Deborah and Barak, which celebrates Israel's victory. Sisera's mother waits for her son at the window and imagines that the delay is because he is dividing the plunder. She does not know that Sisera is already dead. The text contrasts her false sense of security with reality.

Today it reminds us that we can comfort ourselves with answers that merely repeat our own desires. It is wise to seek the truth with humility, and to place our trust in God, not in comfortable assumptions.
exp.13:1:
Samson returns from Timnah and tells his parents that he has seen a young Philistine woman. He respectfully asks them to get her for him as his wife. Philistines were a neighboring people who dominated Israel.

The one speaking is Samson, an Israelite set apart for God from his birth. In those times parents often arranged marriages. His parents object, because God had asked Israel not to intermarry with neighboring peoples. The text says that God used this situation against the Philistines, but it does not say that he approved of Samson's choice. Some see it as an example of God working in spite of human mistakes.

For today: before making an important decision, do not be guided only by what attracts you. Seek God's voice and listen to the counsel of wise people who love you.
exp.13:0:
He says that Samson went down to Timnah, a town near his own land, and there he saw a young Philistine woman. The word "went down" is used because Timnah lay at a lower elevation. "Saw" here points to the fact that she caught his attention, and "of the daughters of the Philistines" means that she was a woman of that people.

It is the narrator who tells this. The Philistines dominated Israel at that time, and God had forbidden marrying neighboring peoples who would turn them away from Him. Samson's parents are worried, but he is guided by what he sees. The book of Judges also says, in verse 4, that God would use this against the Philistines; interpreters explain it in different ways.

For today: do not make important decisions only because something attracts you. Listen to the advice of wise people, and ask God whether that decision fits with His will.
exp.15:24:
The explanation says that the Philistines, already very merry from the feast, asked that Samson be brought out of the prison to entertain them. The verse's "make us sport" is rendered here in plain terms: they wanted him brought out to amuse them, and they treated him as a thing to be mocked. They stood him up between the pillars of the house.

The speakers are the Philistine rulers and people, gathered to worship their god Dagon. They believed their god had given them victory over Samson. He was blind and a prisoner, for earlier he had failed in his calling. They did not know that God would still work in him, and that this mockery was setting the stage for the final moment.

For today: when someone mocks us, or it seems that all is lost, let us not forget that God can work even in our weakness. And let us not celebrate with pride, because the victory we boast of may be fleeting.
exp.11:4:
The explanation says that the men of Gilead, the group of Jephthah, took the crossing points of the Jordan River to cut off the escape of the Ephraimites. The fords are shallow places where a person could cross on foot. When a fugitive asked to pass, they asked him whether he was an Ephraimite, that is, from the tribe of Ephraim. If he answered that he was not, came the test that follows in verse 6.

The narrator recounts a civil war between tribes of Israel. Ephraim complained that Jephthah had not called them to fight against Ammon. Jephthah replied that he had already asked for their help and they did not come. Then there was battle, and the Gileadites won. The text only relates what happened; it does not say that God approved of so much violence.

For today: wounded pride and harsh words can grow until they cause enormous harm. Let us seek to resolve conflicts with humility and dialogue, and not divide anyone by their accent, origin or group.
exp.3:7:
Barak tells Deborah that he will go into battle only if she goes with him. If she does not accompany him, he will stay behind.

Deborah was a prophetess and a judge of Israel. She had passed on to Barak a clear command from God, with the promise of victory over Sisera. Barak does not reject the command, but he sets a condition. Some see here a lack of trust; others see that he valued the presence of God's prophetess. The text does not say exactly what he was thinking. Deborah agrees, but she warns him that the honor will not be his.

For today: When God has already spoken to us and promised his help, let us trust in him without demanding further guarantees. Even so, it is wise to seek the company of people of faith who encourage us to obey.
exp.6:1:
God tells Gideon that Israel's army is too large. If they won with so many soldiers, the Israelites would become proud and say, "Our own strength saved us." The phrase "my own hand hath saved me" means "I did it all myself." Words like "hath" are old forms of speech.

The Lord, the God of Israel, is speaking. The Midianites were oppressing the people, and Gideon had gathered troops to fight. God wants it to be clear that the victory comes from Him, not from the number of soldiers. So He begins to reduce the army, first with those who were afraid, and then with a test at the water.

For today: when God helps us get through difficulties, let us give Him the credit. Recognizing His help keeps us humble and teaches us to trust Him, not only our own resources or abilities.
exp.7:1:
Gideon asks the men of Ephraim what he has done in comparison with what they have done. He uses an image from the field: the gleaning is what is left in the vineyard after the harvest, and the vintage is the grape harvest. He says that the little Ephraim gathered is worth more than the whole harvest of Abiezer, which was Gideon's clan.

The men of Ephraim were upset because Gideon did not call them at the beginning to fight against Midian. Gideon, who is the one speaking, answers with humility. Then he reminds them that God put the Midianite leaders Oreb and Zeeb into their hands. With those words, their anger was calmed.

For today: a humble answer can put out an argument. Before defending yourself, acknowledge the good that others have done. Valuing others helps to protect peace and keeps unity.
exp.9:4:
Judges 10:5 says that Jair, the judge of Israel, died and was buried in a place called Camon. It is a simple ending for a man who governed for twenty-two years.

The book of Judges is a narrative, so there is no one speaking in it; the narrator is telling the story of Israel. This verse closes the brief summary of Jair. Right after, the text shows that, with the judge gone, the people returned to idolatry. As for where Camon was, it is thought to have been in Gilead, east of the Jordan, but this is not known for certain.

For today: good leaders are not enough; each person needs their own faithfulness to God. We should not depend only on others for our faith. Let us cultivate a personal relationship with Him today, so that our faith remains firm even when the people around us change.
exp.4:2:
Deborah calls on the kings and the princes to listen closely. Where the verse says "Hear, O ye kings," the wording here is rewritten simply as "listen," and "give ear" is rewritten as "pay attention." She declares that she will sing and offer praise with songs to the Lord, the God of Israel. The song is not centered on her, but on God.

Deborah speaks together with Barak, after a victory over the Canaanites. This song celebrates what God did for Israel and also that the people offered themselves willingly. The "kings" and "princes" may be rulers of other nations or leaders in general; interpreters do not fully agree. What is clear is that the praise is proclaimed in public.

Today we can thank God openly, without shame, for what he has done in our lives. A simple testimony, a song, or a shared prayer can encourage others and place the glory where it belongs: in the Lord.
exp.5:9:
He reminds them who he is: "I am the Lord your God." He tells them not to fear or worship the gods of the Amorites, a people who lived in Canaan before Israel. The explanation's two glosses on old wording are dropped, since the verse above already uses the words "said unto you" and "but," and the reproach is clear: God spoke to them, but they did not obey his voice.

A prophet speaks here, whose name is not mentioned, sent by God. Israel was suffering oppression from Midian because they had followed other gods. Before sending Gideon as their deliverer, God shows them that their suffering is not because he has abandoned them, but because they had turned away from him.

For today: God reminds us of his faithfulness so that we return to trusting him. Today you can ask yourself: what is it that frightens me, or that has taken God's place in my life? Hand it over to him in prayer, and obey the one thing he has already shown you.
exp.13:3:
This verse explains that Samson's parents did not know that all of this came from the LORD. The phrase "sought an occasion" means that God was looking for an opportunity or a reason to confront the Philistines. The verse also reminds us that at that time the Philistines had dominion over Israel.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Samson has just asked to marry a Philistine woman, and his parents opposed it, because the Philistines were not part of God's people. The text does not approve Samson's decision; it shows that God can use even confusing situations to advance his purposes. Some scholars understand it this way, while others place more emphasis on Samson's responsibility.

For today: even when we do not understand everything that is happening, God continues to work. Even so, do not use this as an excuse to decide badly; seek his guidance and trust that he can bring something good out of it.
exp.10:10:
Then the explanation says that Jephthah went back with the elders of Gilead, and the people made him "head and prince" over them, that is, leader and ruler. Next, Jephthah set out all his words before the Lord in Mizpeh, that is, he repeated his agreement and his cause in the presence of God, as one who lays the matter before Him.

The narrator tells us that Gilead was threatened by the Ammonites. The elders had rejected Jephthah earlier, but now they sought him because they needed him. He asked that his leadership be real, and they swore to keep it. Mizpeh was a place where the people gathered. The text does not say in detail what Jephthah prayed or said there.

For today: before taking on an important responsibility or resolving a conflict, bring it before God with sincerity. Present your commitments and your plans in prayer, and ask Him for guidance to act with humility and truth.
exp.10:1:
This verse tells us that Gilead, Jephthah's father, also had a wife who was his lawful wife, and she bore him other sons. When those sons grew up, they drove Jephthah out of the house and told him he would receive no inheritance because he was the son of a strange woman. Here the wording is quoted as "the son of a strange woman," which is the phrase in the verse itself, so it needs no further explanation.

The speakers are Jephthah's half-brothers. According to the law and custom of the time, the inheritance belonged to the sons of the main wife. That is why they rejected him, and that rejection led him to flee to the land of Tob, where he gathered around himself men without direction.

For today: our origin or the rejection we suffer does not define our worth or our future. God can use the person others set aside. And we can look with respect on those whom people leave out.
exp.15:7:
This verse tells how the Philistine rulers brought Delilah seven fresh green willow branches, that is, flexible and moist twigs that had not yet dried out. With them she tied up Samson, just as he had told her to do.

Delilah asked Samson to reveal the secret of his strength. The Philistine leaders wanted to defeat him, and she was working with them. Samson answered with a deception: he said that fresh green branches would weaken him. There were spies hidden in the room, but he snapped the branches easily. The Bible does not explain in detail why he kept playing this game with her.

For today: toying with temptation and with people who do not look out for you is dangerous, even when you believe you have everything under control. Seek wise boundaries and surround yourself with people who help you stay faithful to God.
exp.0:26:
This verse tells us that the tribe of Manasseh did not manage to drive out the inhabitants of several Canaanite cities: Beth-shean, Taanach, Dor, Ibleam, and Megiddo, along with their villages (the smaller towns around them). The phrase "drove out" in the verse means the tribe failed to expel those people. The Canaanites were determined to remain in that land.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Judges, who reviews how each tribe only partly carried out the task of taking the promised land. Earlier, God had commanded Israel not to live alongside those peoples. The book shows that this incomplete obedience prepared the spiritual problems that would come later, when Israel mixed with their customs.

For today: when we leave halfway what God asks us to change, the things we tolerate tend to grow. Ask God for honesty to recognize which habit or attitude you have allowed to live in your heart, and for courage to face it with his help.
exp.0:15:
The explanation says that the descendants of the Kenites, the family of Moses' father-in-law, went up from the city of palm trees together with the tribe of Judah. They went to the wilderness of Judah, in the southern area near Arad, and settled there among the people. The word "south" in this passage means the southern direction. Many understand the city of palm trees to be Jericho, though some see it differently.

Context: it is the narrator of the book who speaks. Judges 1 describes how each tribe took its territory after the death of Joshua. The Kenites were not Israelites by birth, but they joined the people of God and shared their journey. Kenite is named as the father-in-law of Moses; the Bible refers to him in several ways, and nothing more precise can be said.

For today: God opens a place for those who want to walk with his people. We can welcome with warmth those who come to our church or community from outside, and help them feel at home.
exp.14:5:
The Philistines ask who caused the burning of their crops, and they are told: it was Samson, the son-in-law of the man from Timnah, because this man took his wife and gave her to his companion (the friend who had accompanied him at the wedding). The phrase "were told" means the answer was given to them. Then the Philistines burn the woman and her father.

The Philistines speak in anger over the loss of their fields. Earlier they had threatened to burn that woman and her family (Judges 14:15). Now, instead of punishing Samson, they carry out that threat against them. The Bible shows here a chain of revenge, without presenting it as an example to follow.

For today: revenge almost always grows and harms people who are not at the center of the conflict too. When someone wrongs us, we can stop, pray, and seek justice without repaying evil with evil. As Romans 12:19 says, let us leave room for God.
exp.17:23:
Micah answers with grief and anger: the Danites carried off the idols he himself had made, along with the priest he kept in his house. He says he has nothing left. Then he protests: how dare they ask him "what is wrong with you," as if they did not understand his loss? The word "together" means "along with," and "for what purpose" means "with what reason?"

Micah speaks to the men of Dan, who passed by his house during their search for territory. He followed them with his neighbors, but seeing that they were stronger, he went back home. His gods could not defend themselves or defend him; his religion depended on objects and a hired priest. The text shows the spiritual confusion of that time.

Today, the question is: what do I trust so much that, if it were taken from me, I would feel I had nothing left? Only God cannot be taken away. We should place our security in Him, and not in things we build ourselves.
exp.7:15:
Gedeón took the elders of the city of Succoth, along with thorns and briers from the wilderness, and with them he punished the men of the city. The word "briers" refers to plants with very sharp thorns. "Punished" can also be understood as "taught a lesson" or "made them pay for it." Some scholars think he struck them with these plants, though the text gives no further details.

Gideon was pursuing the Midianite kings Zebah and Zalmunna. When he asked the men of Succoth for bread for his exhausted soldiers, the city's leaders mocked him and refused to help. Now, after capturing the kings, Gideon returns and carries out the warning he had given them. His reaction mixes a sense of justice with personal anger, and the Bible here simply tells what happened without fully approving of it.

Today we can learn to help those who are worn out from serving others. Refusing support when we are able to give it has consequences. And as we seek justice, we must be careful that revenge does not take control of us.
exp.20:6:
What it says: The Israelites ask how they can get wives for the surviving men of Benjamin. The problem is that they had made a solemn oath before the Lord: not to give them their daughters in marriage. The word "á" is "to", and "han quedado" means "those who survived."

Context: The leaders of Israel are speaking, gathered at Mizpah. After a civil war, nearly the whole tribe of Benjamin had died, and now they feel grief because a tribe could disappear. Their own hasty vows have left them trapped. The book shows a time of great disorder, and it does not approve of everything the people do.

For today: Think before you promise or swear something in the heat of the moment, because words carry weight. And if you have already made a mistake, seek repentance and God's wisdom, not solutions that cause more harm.
exp.12:1:
This verse introduces a man named Manoah, who lived in Zorah and belonged to the tribe of Dan. His wife was barren, meaning she could not have children, and had never borne a child, that is, had never given birth.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Judges. Israel had once again turned away from God and was under Philistine rule for forty years. In the midst of that dark situation, the account begins with an ordinary family and a deep need. Later God will act through them, and from them Samson will be born.

For today: when your situation seems closed or without a way out, remember that God can begin something important in ordinary places and with ordinary people. Keep trusting Him and obeying Him, even when you cannot yet see the whole path.
exp.7:5:
The leaders of Succoth answer Gideon with mockery. They ask whether he already has Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian, in his hand, as if they should give bread to his army. "Princes" means the chiefs or rulers of the city. "Army" refers to Gideon's company of men.

Gideon and his three hundred men were exhausted, pursuing the enemy kings across the Jordan. They asked only for some food. The leaders of Succoth did not want to help, perhaps out of fear of reprisals from Midian if Gideon failed, though the text does not explain this. Their answer shows contempt and a lack of solidarity with those who were fighting for Israel.

Today we can learn not to deny help to someone who works with sacrifice for the good of others. Sometimes fear or calculation holds us back, but a simple, timely help is also obedience to God.
exp.4:4:
The explanation says the mountains "melted", that is, they trembled or came apart before God's presence. It mentions Sinai, the mountain where God revealed himself to Israel. The phrase "from before the Lord" in the verse reflects this same sense of God's presence. The language is poetic: it shows that even the firmest parts of creation tremble before the Lord.

The speaker is Deborah, together with Barak, in a song of victory over the Canaanites. She remembers how God showed his power and majesty in the past. Some think it also alludes to rain or a storm that helped in the battle, but the text does not make this clear. With this she means that the same God of Sinai is the one who gave victory to his people.

For today: when you face something that seems immense and impossible, remember that God is greater than any mountain. Trust in him and praise him with gratitude.
exp.2:16:
This verse tells us that Ehud brought the tribute to Eglon, king of Moab. It also tells us that Eglon was a very fat man. The word "present" here means the payment or gift that Israel had to give the king as a subject people.

The narrator of the book of Judges speaks here. Israel was oppressed by Moab because of its disobedience, and it cried out to God. He raised up Ehud as a deliverer. Ehud carried the tribute, but he also carried a hidden dagger. The detail about Eglon's great size sets up what happens next in the story.

For today: God can use people the world would overlook, such as a left-handed or limited man, to carry out his plan. When you feel you do not have what you need, cry out to God with confidence, and be willing to obey him with what you have.
exp.10:0:
This verse introduces Jephthah, a man from the region of Gilead. It describes him as a mighty man of valour, that is, a strong and capable warrior. It also says that he was the son of an harlot, a term for a prostitute, and that his father was named Gilead. Here "Gilead" may refer to the father or to his family line; the text does not fully clarify this.

The narrator of the book of Judges speaks here. Israel was going through a difficult time, and God was raising up unexpected leaders. The verses that follow tell how his half-brothers drove him out of the house because he was the son of another woman. So Jephthah's story begins with him as one who was rejected, before he is called to lead.

For today: our origins or the rejection we suffer do not define our worth before God. He can use people who are wounded or looked down upon. If someone made you feel less, remember that your story does not end there, and that God is still at work in you.
exp.11:5:
Here the account tells how the men of Gilead kept watch over the crossings of the Jordan River. Each fugitive from Ephraim was asked to say "Shibboleth." If he said "Sibboleth," they recognized him by the way he spoke and put him to death. To "slay" someone is to kill them, and the word used for the crossing places is the shallow spots where people could wade across a river. The figure of forty-two thousand Ephraimites who died is the number the text gives.

The writer of the book describes a civil war between tribes of Israel. Ephraim had taken offense at Jephthah and insulted him, and the fighting broke out. We are in the time of the judges, when the people lived in disorder. The account does not approve of the violence; it shows it as the fruit of that chaos.

For today: wounded pride and insults can grow until they cause enormous harm. Before responding harshly, let us seek to speak calmly and to be reconciled quickly. Jesus calls the peacemakers blessed.
exp.3:0:
This verse says that the people of Israel again did what God considered evil, after Ehud had died. The word "again" shows they had returned to their old ways, and "in the sight of the Lord" means what displeased God.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Ehud had been a judge who rescued Israel from their oppressors, and while he lived there was peace. The book shows a cycle that repeats: the people turn away from God, suffer the consequences, cry out for help, and God sends them a deliverer. Who wrote Judges is not known with certainty.

For today: it is not enough to have lived a good season of faith. If our steadfastness depends on a person or a period, we may fall when that is gone. It is wise to put down roots of our own in God and to keep seeking him every day.
exp.0:23:
The spies of the house of Joseph were keeping watch over Bethel. They saw a man come out of the city, and they asked him to show them the way in. In return, they promised him mercy, that is, kind treatment and the protection of his life. The word the source uses for "they said" is not a word the verse above uses, so that comment is removed.

The ones speaking are the spies of Ephraim and Manasseh, the descendants of Joseph. After the death of Joshua, each tribe was fighting to take the land that had fallen to it. Bethel, formerly called Luz, was in their territory. The text says that the LORD was with them. The man helped and was spared, along with his family.

For today: the mercy we promise must be carried out. They kept their word, and that invites us to be people who can be trusted in what we say, even with those who are not of our own.
exp.3:6:
God himself says he will bring Sisera, the commander of King Jabin's army, to the river Kishon. Sisera will come with his chariots and all his soldiers. There God promises to hand him over into Barak's hands.
