The speaker is Deborah, a prophetess and judge of Israel. She passes on to Barak what God had already commanded him: to gather ten thousand men on Mount Tabor. Israel was oppressed by Jabin, and his iron chariots caused great fear. Deborah reminds Barak that the victory would come from God, not from Israel's own strength.

For today: when you face something that seems bigger than you, obey the step that God shows you, even if you cannot see the whole path. He can go before you and fulfill what he promised, so trust him and take that step in faith.
exp.3:10:
This verse tells us that a man named Heber, from the family of the Kenites, had separated himself from his people and pitched his tent near a place called Kedesh. "Father-in-law" is the father of one's wife; Hobab appears here as Moses' father-in-law. "Separated" means that he had moved away from the group.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. While Barak and Deborah gather Israel's army, the account introduces Heber, who seems like an isolated detail. But it sets up what comes next, since his wife Jael will play a key role in the story. Scholars are not certain why Heber separated himself from his people.

For today: God can use people and details that seem small or unimportant. Trust that your life, even in its ordinary parts, can be part of what He is doing, and be faithful where you are.
exp.10:21:
This verse says that Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites. That land stretched from the Arnon river in the south to the Jabbok river in the north, and from the wilderness in the east to the Jordan river in the west. The word "coasts" in the verse means the territory or borders, and "possessed" means taking something as one's own.

The speaker is Jephthah, a judge of Israel. He sends a message to the king of the Ammonites, who claimed those lands. Jephthah explains that Israel did not start the war: they asked peacefully for passage, Sihon refused, and attacked. Jephthah insists that God gave them that victory, so the Ammonite claim had no basis.

For today: when you face a conflict, try to act with honesty and remember what God has already done for you. Recognizing his work in your own story gives you firmness to defend what is right without unnecessary violence and without pride.
exp.7:7:
He went up from there to Penuel and made the same request to them. The men of Penuel answered him just as the men of Succoth had answered him, meaning they also refused to help him.

Gideon was pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian, with three hundred men who were tired and hungry. These cities belonged to his own people, but they did not want to risk supporting him, out of fear of the Midianites' revenge if Gideon failed. Their refusal was selfish and disloyal. The following verses show that Gideon responded with threats.

For today: when God works through someone, let us not be among those who stand by and watch out of fear or comfort. Let us support those who serve with generosity and faith, even when the result is not yet visible.
exp.8:31:
It says that Abimelech should get up at night, together with the people who are with him, and hide his men in the field. "Lie in wait" means to prepare a surprise attack, hiding in order to fall upon the enemy. "Now therefore" means "so, right away."

The one speaking is Zebul, the officer in charge of the city of Shechem. He is speaking to Abimelech, who ruled there. Gaal had stirred up the men of Shechem against Abimelech, and Zebul, angry, warned him in secret. The text says he did it "craftily," that is, with cunning, so that Gaal would not notice.

For today: this passage shows a story of violence and deceit, and the Bible tells it without approving it. It invites us to distrust cunning and anger as ways of resolving conflicts, and to seek peace and truth.
exp.19:2:
The tribe of Benjamin heard that the other Israelites had gathered at Mizpah. Then the Israelites asked that they be told how this evil had come about, meaning this terrible crime.

The speakers are the Israelites who have gathered, and the question is addressed to all of them, so that they may hear the case. The Levite, whose concubine was mistreated and died in Gibeah, will be the one to tell what happened. Notice that Benjamin only heard about the gathering; the text does not say they attended it. Before acting, the people want to hear the testimony.

For today: before judging or reacting to an injustice, let us take time to hear the facts calmly and truthfully. Seeking justice calls for listening carefully, without being carried away by rumors or by anger.
exp.5:0:
The explanation says that the people of Israel again did what God considered evil. Because of this, God allowed the Midianites to rule over them for seven years. The phrase "delivered them into the hand of" means that he let them fall under the power of another people.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Israel lived in the promised land, but again and again it turned away from God and followed other religious customs. The book shows a cycle: the people turn away, suffer the consequences, cry out to God, and He sends them a deliverer. The verses that follow describe how the Midianites ruined their harvests and how the people lived hidden in caves.

For today: our decisions have consequences, and turning away from God leaves us vulnerable. But this passage also invites us to return to Him, for in Judges God always hears the cry of those who repent.
exp.20:4:
The explanation says that the Israelites asked who among all the tribes of Israel had not come to the assembly before the Lord. They had made a solemn oath: whoever did not go up to Mizpah before the Lord would be put to death. The word "went up" is used because they were going toward a higher place. The "assembly" is the gathering of the people.

The Israelites are speaking after the terrible war against Benjamin because of a horrible crime in Gibeah. Now they grieve because one tribe has nearly disappeared. They look for who was absent from the gathering, because the oath has left them trapped. This leads to the plan to seek out Jabesh-gilead. The book shows a time of great confusion, when everyone did whatever seemed right to them.

For today: let us think before promising something lightly. Hasty oaths can cause pain and leave us in dead ends. Before speaking with firmness, let us ask God for wisdom, and when we fail, let us seek to make things right with humility and not with more mistakes.
exp.0:11:
Caleb makes a public promise: whoever attacks the city of Kirjath-sepher and captures it will receive his daughter Achsah as his wife. "Smiteth" means "attacks" or "defeats," and "Achsah" is the name we write as Achsah today. Kirjath-sepher was the former name of Debir.

Caleb, a faithful man of the tribe of Judah, speaks here, and he was already elderly. Judah was taking possession of its territory, and Caleb offers a reward to encourage someone to conquer Debir. According to the following verse, Othniel, a nephew or close relative of Caleb, took the city. Marriages were then arranged between families, and this promise was a way of honoring courage.

For today: Caleb trusted that God would give the victory and sought out people willing to act. Ask yourself what difficult task God is inviting you to undertake, and take a concrete step in faith, without waiting for others to do it for you.
exp.15:12:
Delilah accuses Samson that until now he has been lying to her, and she asks him to finally tell her how he could be tied up. This time he answers that if she weaves the seven locks of his head into the cloth, he would lose his strength. He is speaking of the seven locks of his hair being woven into the cloth on a loom.

Delilah speaks because the Philistine rulers had asked her to discover the secret of Samson's strength. She had already tried twice to tie him up, and both attempts failed. Samson plays with her, coming closer and closer to the truth, without realizing the danger. This is the third attempt.

For today: playing with what can harm us often slowly lowers our guard. If something or someone keeps seeking our downfall, it is not wise to flirt with the risk. It is better to keep our distance and ask God for wisdom.
exp.6:5:
This verse tells how only three hundred men were left. They took the water in their hand and brought it to their mouth. All the others knelt down to drink straight from the water.

God speaks to Gideon before the battle against Midian. Israel had a large army, and God wanted to reduce it so that no one would think the victory came from their own strength. It is not known for certain why this way of drinking made a difference; some think it showed greater alertness, but the text does not say so.

For today: God does not depend on our abundance, but on our willingness to trust Him. When you feel small or short on resources, remember that God can work with the little you have.
exp.15:30:
After Samson died in the Philistine temple, his brothers and all his father's family went down to get him. They took the body and buried it between Zorah and Eshtaol, in the tomb of his father Manoah. The text also says that Samson governed Israel for twenty years. Here the word "governed" means leading and delivering the people, not only passing judgments.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. He closes the story of Samson, who was an imperfect deliverer, full of flaws, yet used by God against the Philistines. His family was able to recover the body and give him a proper burial, something important in that culture. Some understand the twenty years as a single period, and others see some uncertainty about how they fit with 15:20.

For today: God can work even through people with serious flaws. We must not trust in our own strength, but we can return to God with humility and serve him to the end.
exp.15:29:
Samson says, "Let me die with the Philistines." Then he pushes with all his strength against the pillars, and the house falls on the lords and all the people. In his death he kills more enemies than in all his life. "Leaning" means resting his weight on the pillars and pushing hard.

Samson speaks, blind and a prisoner, in the temple of Dagon, where the Philistines had mocked him. Earlier he had prayed to God, asking for strength one last time. His life was full of mistakes, but God heard him. Some see here a personal revenge, and others a final act of self-giving for his people. The text shows both.

For today: even if we have failed often, we can return to God with humility and ask for his help. He can use even our last steps for something good.
exp.7:23:
Gideon asks the Israelites for a favor: that each one give him the gold earrings he took from the spoils of war. "Earrings" here means the same thing as the earrings or pendants we wear today. The text explains that the defeated enemies wore gold earrings because they were Ishmaelites, a name used here for those desert peoples.

Gideon had just refused to be king and had said that only the LORD would rule over them. But now he asks for gold. Later, with that gold, he makes an ephod, and the people end up worshiping it as something sacred (Judges 8:27). The Bible does not state clearly what his intention was; many think he wanted a reminder of the victory, but it ended up becoming a trap.

For today: a good work can be damaged by a poorly considered decision. Let us ask God for wisdom so that our good desires do not become a stumbling block for others.
exp.7:2:
Gideon tells the men of Ephraim that God gave them the greater victory: they captured Oreb and Zeeb, the leaders of Midian. Then he asks, "What was I able to do in comparison of you?" With those words, their anger was calmed.

Gideon speaks to the tribe of Ephraim, which was upset because he did not call them at the beginning of the battle. They felt ignored and complained harshly. Gideon does not argue or defend himself; he acknowledges what they did and honors it. Ephraim probably also cared about its pride, although the text does not say this clearly.

For today: a humble and kind answer can calm an argument. When someone feels hurt or ignored, instead of fighting, we can recognize the good they have done and give them their place. As Proverbs 15:1 says, a soft answer turns away wrath.
exp.8:48:
This verse tells that all the people with Abimelech each cut a branch, followed him, and piled them against the stronghold of Shechem. Then they set it on fire, and about a thousand men and women who were inside the tower died.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Abimelech had made himself king by killing his brothers, and the people of Shechem had supported him, but later they rebelled against him. Judges presents this outcome as the consequence of that betrayal and violence (Judges 9:56-57). The text recounts what happened and does not approve of the cruelty.

For today: the evil that is sown often comes back. For that reason it is wise to seek power and agreements through justice, not through violence or deceit.
exp.10:20:
It says that God handed Sihon and his army over into the hands of Israel, and that the Israelites defeated them. So Israel took possession of all the land of the Amorites who lived there.

The speaker is Jephthah, a judge of Israel. He sends a message to the king of Ammon, who was claiming that land. Jephthah reminds him that Israel asked for passage peacefully, Sihon distrusted them and attacked, and that is why there was war. He tells the story to show that Israel did not seize that territory unjustly. Some scholars debate details of that land dispute, but Jephthah's argument is clear.

For today: before fighting for something, seek dialogue and the truth. And when you receive something good, recognize that it comes from God and not from your own strength.
exp.12:8:
God listened to Manoah's prayer and sent the angel again. What stands out is that the angel did not appear to Manoah this time, but once more to his wife, who was alone in the field.

The phrase "came again" means that he came a second time. The old spelling of "to" as "unto" is simply an older English form.

Manoah and his wife had no children. The angel had already told her that she would have a son who would be a Nazirite, that is, set apart for God. Manoah, worried, asked for help in knowing how to raise him. God answered, though not in the way he had expected. Some believe the woman had a special sensitivity for receiving the message, but the text does not explain this.

Today we can pray with confidence when we need direction. God listens, even when his answer comes in a way different from what we imagined. Let us learn to be attentive and to value those whom God uses to guide us.
exp.12:19:
This verse tells how, as the flame of the sacrifice rose from the altar toward heaven, the angel of the Lord also went up in the flame, and Manoah and his wife saw it. They fell with their faces to the ground. The phrase "in the sight of" means "before" or "in front of," and "bowing down" means lowering oneself to the ground as a sign of respect and worship.

Manoah and his wife were expecting a child, who would be Samson. The angel had given them instructions, and Manoah wanted to offer a sacrifice. When he asked the angel's name, the angel answered that it was secret, a name beyond understanding. Seeing him rise in the flame, they understood that he was a messenger of God. Then Manoah became afraid, because it was believed that seeing God was dangerous.

For today: when God reveals himself to us in unexpected ways, the best response is humility and worship. We can draw near to him with reverence and gratitude, trusting that his plans are greater than our own.
exp.10:32:
He defeated the Ammonites with a very great slaughter. The defeat stretched from Aroer to near Minnith, about twenty cities, and reached as far as the fields of the vineyards (probably a place called Abel-keramim). The Ammonites were brought low before Israel.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jephthah, a judge of Israel, had made a vow to God before the battle. God gave him the victory, but the verse that follows shows the painful cost of that vow. Scholars discuss how to understand what happened to his daughter, and it is good to recognize that difference.

For today: God may give us victories, but we should speak with Him carefully and humbly. Let us not make hasty promises that God has not asked for. We can trust His help without trying to buy it with impulsive vows.
exp.7:18:
Gideon explains why he is going to kill the two Midianite kings. He says that the men they killed at Tabor were his brothers, the sons of his own mother. He swears, "As the Lord liveth," which is a way of saying, "As surely as God lives." If the kings had spared them alive, he would not kill them.

Gideon, judge of Israel, speaks after pursuing and capturing Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian. His earlier answer confirms that the victims were men of high rank. Gideon acts as an avenger of his family, following the custom of his time. The account does not say that God commanded him here, and some readers see in this more personal revenge than justice.

For today: grief for our own people is real, but revenge can cloud judgment. When we are wounded, it is wise to bring our pain to God and seek justice with humility, without letting resentment rule us.
exp.7:8:
Gideon tells the people of Penuel that when he comes back in peace, that is, victorious and safe, he will tear down their tower. The word "come back" is a word that appears in the verse you are reading, so the phrase is simply rendered as "When I come again in peace," and the meaning is that he is returning from battle. "Break down" means to pull down or destroy, as the verse says.

Gideon is pursuing Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian. He is tired, and he asked the men of Penuel for bread for his soldiers, but they refused, just as the men of Succoth did. They probably feared reprisals if the Midianites remained alive. The tower was surely their place of defense and their pride. Gideon answers with a harsh threat. The text tells us what he said, and later he carries it out.

For today: helping someone who works for a good cause is an act of courage and generosity. Refusing out of fear or comfort can bring consequences. Let us ask God for the courage to support others when they need it most.
exp.20:3:
It says that at dawn the people of Israel built an altar in that place and presented two kinds of offerings: burnt offerings, which were burned whole in honor of God, and peace offerings, which expressed fellowship and thankfulness, and from which a portion was shared. The words "built" and "early in the morning" are the ones that matter here; "built" means constructed, and "early" means very early in the morning.

The narrator recounts what happened after the war between Israel and the tribe of Benjamin. The Israelites wept before God because one tribe was almost gone. They had made a severe oath and now regretted it. The text does not say that God commanded this, so we do not know whether their way of acting was the right one. We see a people who seek God, but with hasty decisions.

Today we can learn that seeking God with grief and repentance is good, but it is wise to think before making promises or decisions of great weight. It is better to pray first and ask for wisdom.
exp.15:11:
Delilah took new ropes, the ones Samson had told her about, and tied him with them. Then she shouted that the Philistines were coming against him. Some men were waiting in hiding in a room, that is, in an inner chamber. Samson snapped the ropes from his arms as easily as if they were a thread.

The Philistine leaders had asked Delilah to find out the secret of Samson's strength. She keeps pressing him again and again. Samson gives her false answers, yet he keeps playing with her and stays close to danger. This is the third time she tests him, and she still does not know the true secret.

For today: playing with temptation is dangerous, even if so far we have come through unharmed. Samson escaped three times, but each time he came closer to the truth that would destroy him. It is wise to flee quickly from whatever drags us along, rather than seeing how far we can go.
exp.19:11:
This verse says that the tribes of Israel sent messengers to the whole tribe of Benjamin to ask what terrible evil had been committed among them. The word "men" in the verse refers to the men who were sent, and "wickedness" refers to a dreadful crime.

The tribes of Israel are speaking together here, after the horrible crime in Gibeah, where the concubine of a Levite was abused and killed. Before going to war, they seek an explanation and give Benjamin the chance to hand over the guilty. But Benjamin refused to listen and defended its own, which led to a war between brothers.

For today: when there is a serious injustice, the right response is to confront it with the truth and not cover it up, even if the guilty person belongs to our own group or family. Defending the guilty out of loyalty alone ends up harming everyone.
exp.2:9:
The explanation says that the Spirit of the Lord came upon Othniel, and because of that he was able to lead Israel as judge and go out to battle. God gave him victory over Cushan-rishathaim, the enemy king. "Judged" here means that he governed and defended the people. "Came upon" is what the phrase means when it says the Spirit came over him, and "his hand prevailed" means that he won. The text calls the region "Syria," which it earlier calls Mesopotamia.

The narrator of the book explains a cycle: Israel turns away from God, suffers oppression, cries out, and God sends a deliverer. Othniel is the first judge. After his victory there was peace for forty years, until the people again turned to disobedience.

For today: Othniel's victory did not come only from his own strength, but from God. When you face something bigger than yourself, pray and ask for His help. And when He gives you peace, do not forget Him.
exp.6:17:
Gideon gives an order to his three hundred men. He will blow the horn (a ram's horn, like a shofar) together with the hundred who are with him. Then the other groups must blow theirs, surrounding the entire enemy camp, and shout: "For the Lord and Gideon!" The word "camp" refers to the Midianite encampment, and the phrase "are with me" is the same as "are with me" in the verse you are reading, so no further explanation is needed.

Gideon speaks as a leader before the night attack against Midian. God had already reduced the army to three hundred so that it would be clear that the victory came from Him. That is why the plan uses no swords, but horns, jars, and torches. Gideon asks that everyone imitate him and follow his signal.

For today: God often works when we obey in faith, even when the plan seems weak or strange. Unity also matters: each person has a place and fulfills it, trusting that the victory belongs to God.
exp.14:7:
He attacked the Philistines with terrible force and killed a great many of them. The phrase about the "hip and thigh" is an old way of speaking, and it is not known for certain what it means; it probably describes a brutal and complete blow. He went down and lived in a cave in the rock of Etam, in the territory of Judah.

The one telling the story is the narrator of the book of Judges. The Philistines had burned Samson's wife and her father, and Samson answered with personal revenge. God used Samson against Philistine domination, although his motives were very human and mixed.

For today: revenge rarely ends a conflict; it almost always makes it grow, as what follows shows. When faced with an offense, first seek calm, prayer and wise counsel, and let God do justice.
exp.17:24:
The men of Dan tell Micah to stop shouting at them. They warn him that some men with a violent, angry temper might attack him, and that he would lose his life and the lives of his household.

The tribe of Dan speaks here. They are looking for land, and they have already taken Micah's idols and his priest. Micah protests, but they openly threaten him. He withdraws when he sees that they are stronger. The account shows a time of disorder, without law or justice, where force and manipulated religion are mixed together. The Bible only recounts this; it does not approve of it.

Today we can remember that having power does not make something right. Before we use our strength, our voice, or our influence, let us ask ourselves whether we are honoring God and treating others with justice.
exp.8:20:
Jotham ran away and fled, and went to live in a place called Beer. He stayed there, far from his family, because he was afraid of his brother Abimelech. Nobody knows for certain where Beer was; we only know it was a remote place.

Jotham was the youngest son of Gideon (Jerubbaal). Abimelech, his half-brother, had killed the other sons of Gideon in order to become king in Shechem. Jotham escaped, climbed Mount Gerizim, told a parable to the people of Shechem, and warned them with a curse. Afterward he fled, since Abimelech would have killed him too.

For today: sometimes it is wise to step away from danger and leave justice in God's hands. Jotham did not take revenge on his own; he trusted that God would see what had been done, and the account shows that this is what happened.
exp.8:7:
The trees wanted to have a king, so they first went to the olive tree and asked it to reign over them. The verb "choose" means pick out, and "over them" means over themselves. It is a fable: the trees stand for people, and the olive was a very valuable tree because of its oil.

The speaker is Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon, who survived when Abimelech killed his brothers. From Mount Gerizim, Jotham tells this story to the people of Shechem, who had just made Abimelech king. Through the fable he shows them, with irony, what they had done wrong. Many understand that he is criticizing an unjust choice filled with violence.

For today: before following a leader or accepting a position of power, it is wise to ask ourselves whether that person or that path is worthy and whether it honors God. Not everyone who wants to rule serves well.
exp.15:18:
She made him fall asleep with his head on her lap. Then she called for a man, who cut off the seven braids of his hair. The "locks" are long strands or braids. "Shaving" the head means cutting the hair very close. So she began to overpower him, because his strength had left him.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Samson was a Nazirite, that is, set apart for God from before his birth, and his long hair was the sign of that vow. After much pressure, Samson revealed his secret to Delilah, and she betrayed him for money from the Philistines. His strength was not in the hair as something magical, but in the presence of God, who withdrew because of Samson's disobedience.

For today: let us guard what God has entrusted to us and not play with temptation. Small compromises can lead us far from God without our noticing.
exp.20:0:
This verse says that the men of Israel had made a solemn vow at Mizpah. They promised that none of them would give his daughter in marriage to a man of the tribe of Benjamin.

The writer explains what had happened before. The other tribes had fought against Benjamin because of a terrible crime in Gibeah (chapters 19 and 20). Benjamin had nearly been wiped out. Now the people weep, because their own vow threatens to erase one tribe of Israel.

Today this teaches us to think before we make strong promises, especially when we are angry. Words spoken in haste can bring painful consequences. Before promising something, it is wise to pray and ask God for wisdom.
exp.2:28:
This verse tells that the Israelites defeated about ten thousand Moabite soldiers, strong men trained for war, and that not one of them managed to escape. "They killed" means they struck them down in battle. "About ten thousand" is an approximate number.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. He has just described how Ehud, a judge whom God raised up, called Israel to fight against Moab, which had oppressed them. Israel seized the fords of the Jordan, that is, the crossing points of the river, and so cut off the enemy's retreat. The text presents this victory as the work of God, who gave the enemies into their hands. It is an account of warfare from that period, not a guide for resolving conflicts today.

For today: when you face something that weighs on you, such as a habit, a fear, or an injustice, trust that God can give you freedom. But act with courage and wisdom, like Israel, which followed its leader and closed off the enemy's escape routes.
exp.6:15:
This verse tells that Gideon divided his three hundred men into three groups. He gave each man a trumpet (a horn, usually made from an animal's horn) and an empty clay jar with a burning torch inside it.

The one acting here is the narrator, who describes Gideon. He had just secretly overheard the dream of a Midianite soldier, which foretold their defeat. This encouraged him, and he worshiped God. Now he prepares a simple plan: at first they will not use swords, but sound and light, to confuse the enemy. The jar hid the fire until the moment they broke it.

For today: God can use small and fragile things, like a jar, when we obey Him with trust. Before taking a difficult step, stop to worship and remember that God goes before you.
exp.6:13:
This verse tells how a Midianite soldier explains his dream of the barley loaf to his companion. He says that the loaf is nothing other than the sword of Gideon, and that God has already given the Midianites and their whole camp into Gideon's hand. Being given into his hand means God has granted him the victory. A man of Israel simply means an Israelite man.

Gideon had gone down at night into the enemy camp, afraid, because God had directed him to. There he heard one soldier tell his dream and another interpret it. The barley loaf was humble food, just like Gideon and his small army of three hundred. God used an enemy to encourage Gideon, and Gideon responded by worshiping.

For today: when you feel small or afraid before a great problem, remember that God can encourage you in unexpected ways. Respond as Gideon did: give thanks, trust, and take the next step.
exp.9:2:
After Tola, God allowed another leader to arise in Israel, named Jair. He was a Gileadite, that is, from the region of Gilead, east of the Jordan River. Judging here does not mean only settling disputes, but also governing and guiding the people. He did this for twenty-two years. The phrase "arose" means that he appeared as a leader. "After him" means "following him" in time.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Judges, who is recounting the periods of leadership in Israel. Jair appears between two judges who led during times of great instability. The text gives no details of his deeds; it only says there was peace and order under his guidance, and that his family had standing. Soon after, the people would turn away from God again.

Even though the Bible says little about someone, their steady faithfulness counts for a great deal. God uses people who serve with constancy, without fame or great accomplishments. Today you can serve with that same spirit in your home, your work, or your church.
exp.8:18:
This verse says: "If you have acted today with truth and uprightness toward Jerubbaal and his household, then enjoy Abimelech, and let him enjoy you." It is a sentence with irony. "Jerubbaal" is another name for Gideon. "Uprightness" means honesty and righteousness. "Enjoy" means to be glad or to make good use of something.

Jotham, the youngest son of Gideon, who escaped the massacre, is the speaker. From the top of Mount Gerizim he shouts to the people of Shechem after telling them a parable. They had killed seventy sons of Gideon and had made Abimelech king. Jotham tells them that if they truly acted justly, they should enjoy their decision; if not, punishment will come.

For today: before supporting a leader or making a decision, let us ask whether it is just and honest, not only convenient. God sees the intentions of the heart.
exp.10:5:
The elders of Gilead ask Jephthah to come back and be their "captain," that is, their military leader, to fight against the Ammonites. The name "Ammon" is written today as "Amon," and "let us fight" means they would battle together against them.

The leaders of Gilead are speaking. Israel was under threat of war. Earlier they had rejected Jephthah and driven him out of his family, and he was living far away, in the land of Tob. Now, in their trouble, they seek him out because they need his courage and experience. Jephthah will point this out to them right away.

For today: when we are called to ask forgiveness or seek help from someone we have hurt, let us do it with humility and sincerity, and not merely out of convenience. And if someone wronged us and later comes looking for us, let us ask God for wisdom to respond with truth and grace.
exp.4:30:
This verse closes the song of Deborah and Barak with a prayer: that all of God's enemies would perish, and that those who love him would shine like the sun when it rises in full strength. The text then says that the land had peace for forty years.

Deborah and Barak speak after the victory over Sisera and the Canaanite army. Earlier, the song showed Sisera's mother and her ladies waiting for a plunder that never arrived. With that contrast, the song ends by asking that God's justice be fulfilled and that his people flourish. The forty years can be understood as an exact number or as a long period of peace.

For today: loving God is not only a feeling, but a life that is visible, like the light of a sunrise. Today you can ask him to give you strength to live with faithfulness and hope.
exp.1:8:
This verse tells where Joshua was buried: in his own inherited land, in a place called Timnath-serah, in the hill country of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash. "Border" here means territory or boundary, and "inheritance" is the land that fell to him as his share. Joshua is known to have received that town (Joshua 19:49-50), although today not everyone agrees on its exact location.

Context: the narrator of the book of Judges, whose author is not known for certain, summarizes what happened after Joshua's death. First he shows that the people remained faithful as long as those who had seen the works of God were alive. Then he announces that the next generation did not know the LORD and turned away. In this way he prepares the account of the cycles of sin and rescue that follow.

For today: faith is not inherited on its own. If we have known God's work in our lives, let us tell our children, grandchildren, and friends about it, and personally teach them to know him.
exp.19:45:
This verse sums up how many soldiers of the tribe of Benjamin died in the battle that day: twenty-five thousand men who were armed with swords. The phrase about "drawing the sword" means they were trained warriors. The total adds up the eighteen thousand, the five thousand, and the two thousand from the verses before, although that exact sum does not quite match (it gives twenty-five thousand), and some scholars explain that these are approximate numbers.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges speaks. He tells of the war between the tribes of Israel and Benjamin, after the terrible crime committed in Gibeah and Benjamin's refusal to hand over the guilty men. It is a time of great disorder, and the book ends by saying that everyone did what seemed right to them.

For today: when wrong is not confronted in time and with humility, pride and stubbornness can destroy whole families and communities. Let us seek to correct the error soon.
exp.18:22:
The master of the house goes out to speak with the violent men surrounding his home. He asks them not to commit this wickedness, because the traveler is his guest. "Sons of Belial" means wicked people with no respect for God. "Know," in the previous verse, here refers to sexual abuse. "Wickedness" means a very serious and unjust act.

The one speaking is an old man who had taken in a Levite and his concubine in Gibeah. In those times, protecting a guest was a sacred duty. Yet the account shows a corrupted society: shortly afterward he offers his daughter and the concubine, something terrible. The Bible records this as a sign of Israel's moral decline, without approving it.

For today: defending the vulnerable is good, but we must never do so by sacrificing other innocent people. Let us ask God for courage and wisdom to protect people with justice and compassion.
exp.10:31:
This verse tells how Jephthah advanced against the Ammonites to fight them, and how God gave them into his hands. "Give into his hand" means to give him the victory.

Here the narrator of the book of Judges is speaking. Jephthah was a leader whom Israel sought out in the middle of oppression. Before the battle he made a rash vow, promising to offer to God whatever came out of his house first. The text says the victory came from the Lord, and it does not present the vow as something God had asked for. Scholars discuss how the fulfillment of that vow should be understood.

For today: God can work even when our words are clumsy. Let us learn to speak with him sincerely, but without haste or impulsive promises. Let us trust his help without trying to bargain for it.
exp.0:2:
It says that Judah invited his brother Simeon to join him in fighting against the Canaanites. "Lot" refers to the land that each tribe received by drawing lots. Judah proposes: "Help me take my portion, and I will help you with yours." Simeon agreed and went with him.

After the death of Joshua, Israel asked God who should go up first to fight, and God pointed to Judah. Judah is the one speaking. Instead of going alone, he looks for Simeon, whose land lay inside the territory of Judah (Joshua 19:1). It was a partnership of mutual help between sister tribes.

For today: even when God gives us a task, we do not have to do it alone. We can ask other believers for help and offer our own help too, generously and without selfishness.
exp.19:42:
This verse describes how the army of Israel surrounded the men of Benjamin, chased them without giving them rest, and trampled them down, that is, they utterly defeated them. The pursuit went from a place called Menuhah to the front of Gibeah, on the eastern side. "Chased" means to pursue with determination, and "trampled" means to crush underfoot.

It is part of the account of the war between the tribes of Israel and Benjamin. No one speaks here; the narrator reports the events. Benjamin had defended the men of Gibeah, who were guilty of a terrible crime against a Levite's concubine. The text shows a time of great moral disorder, and the book repeats that there was no king in Israel. Some details of the place, such as Menuhah, are not entirely certain.

For today: when we do not correct wrong in time, and out of pride we defend it, the consequences can grow and harm many people. Let us ask God for humility to acknowledge our faults early.
exp.10:38:
After the two months had passed, Jephthah's daughter returned to her father, and he carried out the vow he had made. "She knew no man" means that she never had relations with a man and never married. The text does not clearly say what Jephthah did: some understand that he offered her as a sacrifice, and others that he dedicated her to serving God her whole life, without marriage.

Jephthah, a judge of Israel, had promised God that he would offer whatever came out of his house first if he won the battle. His daughter came out. She accepted her father's vow, but asked for two months to weep with her friends because she would have no marriage or children. The account says that Israel remembered her every year.

Before promising anything, think carefully about what you say. Hasty words can wound those we love most. Ask God for wisdom, and remember with respect those who suffer because of other people's decisions.
exp.4:12:
The explanation says that God made the few survivors of the people of Israel rule over the nobles and the powerful. The words that the verse renders as "have dominion over" mean to rule or have authority over. The "nobles" are the great and powerful men, and "the mighty" are the enemy warriors. The speaker says it was the LORD who gave them this victory.

This verse is part of the song of Deborah and Barak, sung after the victory over the army of Sisera, which had many iron chariots. Deborah, a prophetess and judge, sings that Israel, though it had become small and weakened, won thanks to God. Some understand "he made me have dominion" to refer to Deborah and others to the whole people; the text allows both readings.

For today: when you feel small or without strength in the face of a large problem, remember that victory does not depend on your size but on God's help. Trust in Him and thank Him when He helps you.
exp.6:9:
God offers Gideon a gentle way out: if he still feels fear about attacking, he may first go down to the enemy camp, accompanied by Purah, his servant or attendant. The word "go down" means to go down, and the camp refers to the Midianite encampment, which was in the valley.

God is the one speaking, and He addresses Gideon at night. Gideon had just reduced his army to three hundred men, and even so God had promised him the victory. God knows Gideon's fear and does not scold him. He suggests that Gideon listen to what the enemies are saying so that his courage may be strengthened. The verses that follow show that Gideon did go down.

For today: when you feel fear before a great challenge, do not hide it. Bring it honestly before God, and take the next step, even if it is small and taken with someone you trust. He knows how to strengthen those who come to Him with humility.
exp.9:15:
This verse tells how the Israelites put away the foreign gods they had been worshiping and returned to serving the Lord. It also says that "his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel," meaning that God was saddened or moved with compassion as he saw the suffering of his people. Here "misery" means suffering or hardship.

The narrator of the book of Judges describes this moment. Israel had fallen into idolatry and was suffering oppression from the Ammonites. God had told them to cry out to the gods they had chosen, and the people answered by acknowledging their sin. Their actions showed that their repentance was sincere. Some interpreters understand that God was moved by their distress; others see a human expression used to describe his compassion.

For today: true repentance is not only saying "I was wrong," but also removing whatever has taken the place of God. Ask yourself what you have been giving first place, and hand it over to him with confidence in his compassion.
exp.1:17:
It says that every time God raised up a judge for his people, he himself was with that judge and rescued the Israelites from their enemies for as long as the judge lived. God "repented," that is, he had compassion and changed his course, when he heard the groaning of the people who were suffering oppression.

The one telling the story is the author of the Book of Judges, who summarizes a pattern that repeats. Israel abandoned God, suffered at the hands of its neighbors, cried out, and God sent a deliverer. The following verses show that when the judge died, the people returned to their evil ways.

For today: God hears the cry of those who suffer and has compassion, even when our own mistakes have caused the problem. But his help should lead us to a lasting change, not just temporary relief. We can pray with confidence and, once we have been delivered, remain faithful to God.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that the people of Israel abandoned the Lord, the God of their ancestors, who had rescued them from Egypt. Instead of following him, they went after the gods of the neighboring peoples and worshiped them. This made God angry.

The book of Judges is told by an author who is not named in the text. It explains why Israel faced so many troubles. The generation that had seen God's works had already died, and the new one did not know what he had done. This began a cycle of forgetting, punishment, and rescue.

For today: let us not assume that faith passes on by itself from parents to children. It is wise to tell at home what God has done, to read his Word together, and to thank him often, so that his work is not forgotten.
exp.19:22:
The explanation says that the Israelites went up to Bethel (the place where the ark was, according to the context of the chapter) and wept before God until evening, and asked him whether they should go back to fight against Benjamin, whom they call "my brother." God answered them: "Go up against him." The word "again" in the question means "once more," and "asked counsel" means that they sought direction from God.

The narrator tells of the war between the tribes of Israel and Benjamin. Benjamin protected the guilty men of a terrible crime in Gibeah, and the other tribes went to punish them. They had already lost twenty-two thousand men on the first day. That is why they weep and ask again. Although God tells them to go up, the following text shows that they will suffer another defeat, and the Bible does not fully explain why. Some think that God was also correcting them.

For today: when something goes wrong for us, it is good to weep and seek God sincerely. But we must also be willing to listen and examine our own hearts, not only ask him to accompany us in what we have already decided.
exp.9:5:
This verse says that Israel again did what was evil in the sight of God. They served the Baals and Ashtaroth, and also the gods of Syria, Sidon, Moab, Ammon, and the Philistines. The sentence explaining the word "turned" has been removed, and "Baals" is simply the name of the gods in the verse above: Baal, a god of fertility and rain, in its many forms. At the end it says they forsook the Lord and did not serve Him.

Context: the narrator of the book of Judges tells the story of Israel after the death of the judge Jair. It is a pattern that repeats: the people turn away from God, suffer the consequences, and then cry out for help. Here the idolatry is wider than before, since they adopt the gods of seven neighboring peoples. The following verse shows that God allowed them to be oppressed for eighteen years.

For today: it is not easy to serve God with a divided heart. Today we can ask ourselves what things have taken the place of God in our lives, and return to Him with sincerity.
exp.9:10:
God answers Israel's cry with a question that reminds them of their own history. He asks whether they were not oppressed before by Egypt, the Amorites, the Ammonites, and the Philistines. The next verse continues the question, where God reminds them that he always delivered them.

The Lord speaks. Israel had just confessed its sin: it had left God to serve the Baals, false gods. But God does not respond right away with relief. First he shows them that he had already rescued them many times, and that they kept turning away from him again. His answer aims to make them see how serious their unfaithfulness is.

For today: asking for help only when trouble arrives is not enough. God wants a heart that is faithful to him every day. Remembering how many times he has helped us invites us to return to him sincerely, not merely out of need.
exp.15:27:
Samson prays to God with urgency. He asks God to remember him and to give him strength "only this once" so that he can take revenge on the Philistines for taking out his eyes. The phrase meaning "strengthen me" is the verse's own wording, so there is no separate word to explain here.

Samson speaks while he is already blind and a prisoner. The Philistines have brought him into their temple to mock him while they celebrate their god Dagon. Earlier he had failed badly, and yet here he calls out to the Lord again. His prayer mixes faith with a desire for personal revenge. The text does not say that everything about his attitude was exemplary, but it shows that God heard him.

For today: even if you have failed and feel weak or humbled, you can return to God with sincerity. Ask Him for strength, but also ask Him to purify your motives, so that you do not act out of resentment alone.
exp.11:1:
Jephthah answers the men of Ephraim that he and his people were at great strife with the Ammonites. He says he called them to ask for help, but they did not deliver him out of the enemy's hands. "Strife" here means a fierce struggle or conflict, and "delivered" means rescued or set free.

Here Jephthah, the judge of Gilead, is speaking to the men of Ephraim, who are threatening to burn down his house because they were not invited to the war. He replies that he did call them. The book of Judges does not record that call earlier, so we do not know the details. What we do see is that Ephraim demands honor, while Jephthah insists they did not help when help was needed.

For today: before making demands or reacting in anger, it is wise to ask what really happened and to speak truthfully and calmly. Many quarrels grow out of wounded pride and misunderstanding, and a calm answer can prevent greater harm.
exp.10:16:
The verse tells how Israel asked the king of Edom for permission to pass through his land, and he refused. Israel did the same with the king of Moab, and he did not agree either. So the people stayed at Kadesh.

The word "messengers" refers to people who speak on behalf of someone else.

Here Jephthah, a judge of Israel, speaks. He is sending a message to the king of the Ammonites, who was claiming land. Jephthah reviews the history to show that Israel acted with respect: it asked for passage peacefully and did not take land from Edom or Moab. With this, he argues that the Ammonite claim has no basis.

For today: when there is a conflict, look first for dialogue and peace, and respect the limits of others. Even when you are told no, you can accept it with patience, without responding with violence or resentment.
exp.20:19:
This verse tells how the leaders of Israel gave an order to the men of Benjamin: "Go and lie in wait in the vineyards." "Lie in wait" means to hide and prepare in order to surprise someone. It was the beginning of a plan so that they could get wives.

The elders of Israel are speaking. After a civil war, the tribe of Benjamin was nearly wiped out, and the other tribes had sworn not to give them their daughters. To keep the oath without letting Benjamin disappear, they came up with this way out: to seize women during the festival at Shiloh. The book shows a time of great disorder, and it does not present this plan as an example to follow.

For today: when we make mistakes, we should not fix them with another deception or injustice. Let us seek honest solutions, with humility, that respect both people and God.
exp.13:18:
Samson, in a rage, went down to Ashkelon and killed thirty men, took their clothes and gave them to those who had explained the riddle. Then, burning with anger, he went back to his father's house.

Samson had told a riddle during his wedding feast with a Philistine woman and had made a bet with the guests. She wept and pressed him for seven days until he explained it to her, and she told it to her people. Samson felt betrayed and mocked. In the previous verse he accused the men of using his wife to get the answer, with an image many read as an insult, though the text gives no more detail.

For today: constant pressure can wear down trust. Let us keep secrets and promises, and not manipulate others with tears or insistence. Let us seek wisdom and honesty in our relationships.

sum.1: An angel of God rebuked Israel at Bochim for not obeying, and the people wept. After Joshua died, the new generation forgot God and served Baal, so they suffered oppression. God raised up judges to rescue them, but the people returned to their wickedness, and God left those nations in place to test them.
sum.16: Micah, a man from Ephraim, returns to his mother the silver he had stolen from her, and she uses some of it to make an image and place it in his house. He sets up his own place of worship and hires a Levite as his priest, believing that this way God will bless him. The text shows the disorder of a people where "everyone did what seemed right in their own eyes."
sum.11: The men of Ephraim were angry with Jephthah because he had not called them to fight against the Ammonites, and they threatened him. Jephthah replied that he had called them, but they did not come to help. Then the Gileadites defeated them, and forty-two thousand Ephraimites were killed. After that, Ibzan, Elon, and Abdon judged Israel.
sum.18: A Levite went to bring back his concubine, who had left him, and on the way home he spent the night in Gibeah of Benjamin. There some wicked men abused her until she died, and he cut her body into pieces and sent them throughout Israel. The chapter shows how dark wickedness had become when "there was no king in Israel."
sum.20: The people of Israel grieved because the tribe of Benjamin had nearly disappeared. Since they had sworn not to give their daughters to the Benjaminites in marriage, they looked for a way out. They attacked Jabesh-gilead and took four hundred young women. Then they allowed the Benjaminites to seize women at Shiloh. The chapter ends by showing the chaos of a people without a king, where everyone did whatever seemed right to them.
sum.4: Deborah and Barak sing to praise Jehovah for the victory over Sisera. They commend the tribes that volunteered to fight and rebuke those that stayed behind. They celebrate Jael, who killed Sisera, and the song ends by asking that those who love God be like the sun, and the land rested for forty years.
sum.5: Israel did what was evil, and God allowed the Midianites to oppress them for seven years, until they cried out to Him. Then God called Gideon, a humble and fearful man, and promised to be with him, and Gideon tore down the altar of Baal. Afterward he asked for a sign with the fleece of wool, and God answered him with patience.
sum.3: Israel again did what was evil, and God allowed Jabin, king of Canaan, to oppress them for twenty years; then they cried out to God. The prophetess Deborah encouraged Barak to fight, and God gave the victory over Sisera and his iron chariots. Sisera fled and died at the hands of Jael, showing that God delivers his people when they cry out to him.
sum.15: Samson falls in love with Delilah, and the Philistines pay her to find out the secret of his strength. After deceiving her three times, he gives in to her persistent pleading and reveals that he is a Nazirite; they cut his hair, capture him, and blind him. In the end, he calls out to God and, by pulling down the temple, dies together with many Philistines.
sum.17: The tribe of Dan was looking for land and sent out five scouts, who found the city of Laish quiet and peaceful. Then six hundred armed men set out, took the idols and the Levite priest from Micah's house, attacked Laish, burned it down, and renamed it Dan. It shows how, without faithful guidance from God, the people mixed violence with false worship.
sum.6: God reduced Gideon's army from thousands of men to only three hundred, so that Israel would know that the victory came from Him and not from their own strength. At night, with trumpets, clay jars, and torches, the three hundred surprised the enemy, who fled in confusion. Afterward, Israel pursued them, and they captured Oreb and Zeeb.
sum.2: God left some nations in Canaan to test whether Israel would obey him. But the people mixed with them and worshiped their gods. Because of this, Israel was oppressed. Each time they cried out to God, he sent deliverers such as Othniel, Ehud, and Shamgar, and the land had rest.
sum.0: After the death of Joshua, Israel asks the Lord who should go up first to fight against the Canaanites. Judah, together with Simeon, goes up, and they win important victories. The Lord is with them. However, several tribes do not drive out the inhabitants of the land completely, and they live alongside them, which shows an incomplete obedience.
sum.14: Samson went to visit his wife, but her father had already given her to another man. Samson took revenge by setting fire to the Philistine fields. The Philistines killed the woman and her father, and Samson attacked them violently in response. The men of Judah bound him and handed him over. God gave him strength, and he killed a thousand men with the jawbone of a donkey. Then God gave him water when he was thirsty.
sum.10: Rejected by his brothers, Jephthah is called by the elders of Gilead to lead the war against the Ammonites. With the Spirit of the LORD he wins the victory, but before the battle he makes a rash vow, and when he returns, the first to come out to meet him is his only daughter. The text tells of her grief and that she accepted the vow, and it does not clearly explain what happened to her.
sum.9: After Abimelech, Tola and Jair led Israel as judges. But the people went back to worshiping idols, and God allowed the Philistines and the Ammonites to oppress them. When they were in great distress, Israel admitted their sin, got rid of the false gods, and went back to serving God, who was moved by their suffering. Meanwhile, the leaders of Gilead were looking for someone to lead them in battle.
sum.19: All of Israel gathers at Mizpah to punish the crime committed at Gibeah, but the tribe of Benjamin refuses to hand over the guilty men and goes to war. Israel loses two battles, weeps, fasts, and asks God for guidance, and in the third battle it wins through an ambush. The chapter shows the grief of a divided nation and the violence that spirals out of control.
sum.13: Samson wants to marry a Philistine woman, and although his parents object, God uses the situation to act against the Philistines who were ruling over Israel. At the wedding, Samson poses a riddle about the lion and the honey, but his wife betrays him, and he ends up angry, striking down thirty men in Ashkelon.
sum.12: Israel again did what was evil, and the LORD left them under the Philistines for forty years. Then the angel of the LORD announced to the barren wife of Manoah that she would have a son who was a Nazirite, and that he would begin to deliver Israel. Manoah and his wife offered a sacrifice to the LORD, and Samson was born, and God blessed him.
sum.8: Abimelech, the son of Gideon, killed his seventy brothers with the help of the people of Shechem and made himself king. Only Jotham, the youngest, escaped, and he warned the people of Shechem with a parable. After three years, violence and betrayal broke out between Abimelech and Shechem, and both ended up destroyed. The chapter shows that God holds people accountable for the evil they have done.
sum.7: Gideon calmed the men of Ephraim, pursued the kings of Midian, punished Succoth and Penuel for refusing him help, and killed Zebah and Zalmunna. He refused to be king, saying that the LORD is the Lord, but he made an ephod that the people worshiped. When he died, Israel forgot God.
